note: THE CONTENT DOCUMENT — the course. This is the slot the course goes in: one document, loaded through src/lib/contentLoader.js and checked by src/lib/contentSchema.js, so adding the course is a data change here rather than a code change anywhere. The general-knowledge set that used to sit here came out for the beta (`git log -- src/content/test-content.json` is where it lives if it is ever wanted back); from 2026-09-21 it held the owner's own material; on 2026-10-03 all three chapters came out at his word and the replacement batches went in the same day, under chapter ids that had never existed. The `content.test` switch in src/lib/flags.js is on for everyone so every visitor loads it. Module NAMES are here and in src/data.js, and the two must agree: data.js is what the Flight Deck draws before this document arrives. Module CODES (M1–M4) never change — progress and saves are keyed to them.
contentModel: modules[] -> chapters[] -> lessons[] and one quiz per chapter. A chapter may also carry cards[] — its study-card set, same shape as a quiz question; without it the card set is the quiz's questions. A module may carry downloads[] — {id, title, file, pages}, a file under public/ offered as a plain download, never opened in the reader. notes, threads, replies, people and presence are the lesson surface's own rows. See contentSchema.js for the exact shape and the validator that enforces it.

questions.question: What is the leading edge of a rotor blade
options: The outer end of the blade opposite the root
The edge opposite the one that cuts into the wind
The edge that cuts into the wind when the rotor is turning
questions.explain: The leading edge cuts into the wind.

questions.question: How is the relative wind directed in relation to the flight path of the blade
options: Always perpendicular to the path
Always along the same flight path
Always opposite to the flight path
questions.explain: The relative wind is always opposite to the blade's flight path.

questions.question: What is the axis of rotation
options: The plane formed by the average tip path
The line about which the rotor blades turn
The line from the leading edge to the trailing edge
questions.explain: The rotor blades turn around the axis of rotation.

questions.question: Why is the helicopter often referred to as a rotary-wing aircraft
options: Its primary airfoil is the tail rotor
Its primary airfoil is the main rotor
Its fuselage acts as a rotating wing
questions.explain: Because its main lifting surface is a rotating rotor, the helicopter is called rotary-wing.

questions.question: Which force produced by the main rotor blades holds the helicopter up against gravity?
options: Lift
Thrust
Drag
questions.explain: Of the two forces the airfoil produces, lift is the one the manual gives as counteracting gravity.

questions.question: A rotor blade is moving forward and downward through the air. In which direction does its relative wind act?
options: Forward and upward
Backward and downward
Backward and upward
questions.explain: The relative wind is always exactly opposite to the flight path of the blade, so forward and downward movement gives a backward and upward relative wind.

questions.question: Why does the relative wind on a rotor blade change when a hovering helicopter begins to move horizontally
options: Movement of the helicopter through the air is one of the factors that affect it
The horizontal movement of the helicopter changes the chord line of the rotor blade
The horizontal movement of the helicopter changes the span of the rotor blade
questions.explain: Horizontal movement of the helicopter is one of the factors that affect the relative wind.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes pitch angle from angle of attack?
options: Pitch angle is referenced to the plane of rotation, angle of attack to the relative wind
Pitch angle is referenced to the relative wind, angle of attack to the plane of rotation
Pitch angle is referenced to the axis of rotation, angle of attack to the span line
questions.explain: Both use the chord, but pitch angle uses the plane of rotation and angle of attack uses the relative wind.

questions.question: Why do the same factors that affect the relative wind also affect the angle of attack
options: Because the angle of attack depends upon the blade span
Because the angle of attack depends upon the relative wind
Because the relative wind depends upon the pitch angle
questions.explain: Angle of attack is measured to the relative wind, so what changes one changes the other.

questions.question: What is lift
options: The force that is produced by the airfoil
The force that is produced by gravity
The force produced by torque reaction
questions.explain: Lift is the airfoil's force.

questions.question: Why must gyroscopic precession be considered on the tail rotor as well as on the main rotor
options: Because the tail rotor blades have feathering hinges
Because the tail rotor turns opposite to the fuselage
Because the effect applies to every rotating body
questions.explain: Gyroscopic precession applies to all rotating bodies, so it applies to the tail rotor as well as the main rotor.

questions.question: An external force tries to turn a spinning wheel about its input axis. Around which axis does the movement actually take place?
options: Only around the input axis
Only around the spin axis
Around the output axis
questions.explain: Because of precession the movement occurs around the output axis.

questions.question: Why must the steering input to the rotor be applied 90° before the point where the tilt is wanted
options: Because the swash plate is mounted 90° to the rotor
Because the output occurs 90° later in the direction of rotation
Because the output occurs 90° earlier in the direction of rotation
questions.explain: Precession shifts the result 90° in the direction of rotation, so the input must lead by 90°.

questions.question: Why must the torque of the main rotor be counteracted before flight is possible
options: Because the fuselage would otherwise turn in the direction opposite to the rotor blades
Because the rotor blades would otherwise turn in the direction opposite to the fuselage
Because the main rotor would otherwise produce thrust instead of lift
questions.explain: Torque makes the fuselage rotate opposite to the blades, so it must be counteracted before flight.

questions.question: A helicopter's main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above and the tail rotor is not yet producing thrust. Which way does the fuselage tend to turn?
options: Clockwise
Not at all
Counterclockwise
questions.explain: The fuselage reaction is opposite to a counterclockwise rotor, so clockwise.

questions.question: What does lift counteract on a helicopter
options: Thrust
Weight
Torque
questions.explain: Lift counteracts weight.

questions.question: What does a helicopter gain from being able to tilt its rotor plane slightly in any direction
options: Thrust can act in all directions, giving directional control
Torque can act in all directions, giving heading control
Lift can act in all directions, giving collective control
questions.explain: Tilting the rotor plane lets the thrust act in any direction, which is how directional control is obtained.

questions.question: A helicopter's main rotor is driven by the engine. Which consequence follows for the fuselage
options: Its downwash cannot escape from under the fuselage
Its torque reaction on the fuselage has to be counteracted
Its rotor cannot be tilted out of the horizontal plane
questions.explain: An engine driven rotor makes the fuselage tend to rotate the opposite way, and this torque has to be counteracted.

questions.question: How is a helicopter able to fly sideways
options: The blade pitch is increased on one side, so the lift acts sideways
The tail rotor thrust is increased, so the fuselage is pushed sideways
The rotor plane is tilted sideways, so the thrust acts sideways
questions.explain: Thrust acts perpendicular to the rotor plane, so tilting the plane sideways points the thrust sideways.

questions.question: How do the cyclic control and the collective control differ in the way they change the pitch angle of the main rotor blades
options: The cyclic changes it during each revolution, the collective changes all blades together
The collective changes it during each revolution, the cyclic changes all blades together
Both change it during each revolution, but only the cyclic changes all blades together
questions.explain: Cyclic pitch varies around the disc each revolution while collective pitch moves all blades by the same amount.

questions.question: Which hinge allows the pitch change commanded from the cockpit, and which allows the blade to move under aerodynamic forces
options: The feathering hinge for the pitch change, the flapping hinge for the movement
The flapping hinge for the pitch change, the feathering hinge for the movement
The lead-lag hinge for the pitch change, the flapping hinge for the movement
questions.explain: Feathering hinges take the commanded pitch change, flapping hinges let the blade move under the air loads.

questions.question: A pilot pushes the left pedal forward during a hover and holds the new heading. What else now needs attention?
options: The rotor RPM, because the tail rotor pitch has changed
The lateral drift, because the tail rotor thrust has changed
The pitch angle, because the collective lever has changed
questions.explain: Tail rotor thrust is what produces the translating tendency, so changing it changes the drift the pilot must hold off.

questions.question: A pilot pushes the cyclic stick forward to fly forward. Which chain of events takes place at the swash plate and the blades?
options: The swash plate tilts, the control rods move and the blade pitch varies through the revolution
The swash plate turns, the bell cranks move and the blade pitch is held through the revolution
The swash plate is lifted, the control rods move and the blade pitch rises on every blade at once
questions.explain: A cyclic input tilts the swash plate, which moves the control rods and varies blade pitch through each revolution.

questions.question: What acts on the stationary part of the swash plate, and what does the rotating part act on
options: Control rods from the blades act on it; it drives the cockpit controls through bell cranks
The rotor head acts on it through a bearing; it drives the bell cranks through control rods
Control rods and bell cranks from the cockpit act on it; it drives the blades through control rods
questions.explain: The cockpit acts on the stationary part and the rotating part is connected onward to the blades.

questions.question: Why are the two parts of the swash plate held parallel but joined through a bearing
options: So the cockpit input can be passed to blades that are turning with the rotor
So the rotor plane can be tilted without moving the control rods above it
So the cockpit input can be passed to blades that are fixed to the rotor mast
questions.explain: The bearing lets the upper part turn with the rotor while the parallel lower part stays still, passing the input across.

questions.question: During a ground check the whole swash plate is seen to rise without tilting, and every blade takes a larger pitch angle. What will the helicopter do if this is done in flight?
options: It flies forward, because the rotor plane is tilted forward
It climbs, because all blades gain pitch together
It yaws left, because the tail rotor pitch is increased
questions.explain: Lifting the swash plate is a collective pitch increase, which makes more lift and a climb.

questions.question: Which cockpit control changes a blade pitch angle without acting through the main rotor swash plate
options: The collective lever, which changes the main rotor blade pitch
The cyclic stick, which changes the main rotor blade pitch
The pedals, which change the tail rotor blade pitch
questions.explain: The swash plate serves the main rotor blades, while the pedals act on the tail rotor blades.

questions.question: A technician watches the swash plate while a helper moves one cockpit control, and the whole swash plate moves up without tilting. Which control is being moved?
options: The tail pedals
The cyclic stick
The collective lever
questions.explain: Lifting the swash plate is collective; tilting would be cyclic.

questions.question: A helicopter hovers on the spot in a steady strong wind. Why can its blades not all produce the same lift?
options: The wind adds to the speed of one half of the disc and subtracts from the other
The wind raises the pitch angle on one half of the disc and lowers it on the other
The wind increases the rotational speed of the whole rotor disc
questions.explain: Wind is a relative wind just like forward speed, so it adds on the advancing side and subtracts on the retreating side.

questions.question: In forward flight the retreating blade flaps down. Combining the flapping and centre-of-mass facts, how does this blade move in the plane of rotation?
options: It decelerates and moves backward (lags)
It keeps its position in the plane
It accelerates and moves forward (leads)
questions.explain: The retreating blade flaps down, its CG moves outward, so it decelerates and lags.

questions.question: On which blade does flapping increase the angle of attack, and why must it do so
options: The retreating blade, because it is the one producing too much lift
The retreating blade, because it is the one producing too little lift
The advancing blade, because it is the one producing too little lift
questions.explain: The retreating blade is short of lift, and flapping down raises its angle of attack and so its lift.

questions.question: A rotor head is built with no flapping hinges at all. How can dissymmetry of lift still be balanced on this rotor?
options: The feathering hinges let the blades change pitch instead
The lead-lag hinges let the blades move up and down instead
The blades themselves flex and absorb the forces acting on them
questions.explain: Where there is no flapping hinge, the blades must instead have properties that allow them to absorb the forces.

questions.question: A pilot in forward flight moves the cyclic stick to the right. Which blade movement is produced in addition to the pitch change?
options: A feathering movement, because the rotor plane tilts
A lead-lag movement, because the rotor RPM changes
A lead-lag movement, because the rotor plane tilts
questions.explain: A cyclic input tilts the rotor plane and the tilt generates a lead-lag movement.

questions.question: Which turning force does a counterclockwise turning main rotor generate on the fuselage
options: A nose-down pitching force
A counterclockwise turning force
A clockwise turning force
questions.explain: The fuselage force is opposite, so clockwise.

questions.question: A helicopter is in a steady hover. Which two jobs is the thrust of the tail rotor doing at the same time?
options: Maintaining heading control and tilting the main rotor disk slightly
Compensating the main rotor torque and maintaining heading control
Compensating the main rotor torque and preventing the lateral drift
questions.explain: In the hover the tail rotor thrust both compensates the main rotor torque and maintains heading control; the drift it causes is held off with the main rotor disk instead.

questions.question: Which cockpit control does the pilot use to hold off the drift caused by translating tendency
options: The pedals, which tilt the tail rotor thrust line
The cyclic stick, which tilts the main rotor disk
The collective lever, which lifts the main rotor disk
questions.explain: Tilting the rotor disk is a cyclic input, so the cyclic stick is the control that holds off the drift.

questions.question: How does tilting the main rotor disk stop the lateral drift of a helicopter in the hover
options: The lift then acts partly against the torque direction
The thrust then acts partly in the opposite sideways direction
The thrust then acts partly against the rotor mast axis
questions.explain: Thrust acts perpendicular to the rotor plane, so tilting the disk the other way points some thrust against the drift.

questions.question: During hover, tail rotor thrust makes the helicopter drift to the right. How must the main rotor disk be tilted to prevent this?
options: Slightly to the left
Slightly to the right
Slightly forward
questions.explain: The disk is tilted opposite to the drift, so to the left for a right drift.

questions.question: A helicopter hovering just above the ground climbs slowly until it is just under one rotor diameter up. What has happened to ground effect?
options: It is lost once the skids leave the ground
It is stronger and still present
It is weaker but still present
questions.explain: Ground effect reaches to one rotor diameter and weakens with height, so it is still there but reduced.

questions.question: An engine fails in cruise. In which order does the pilot use energy during the autorotation?
options: Rotor kinetic energy cushions the descent, then altitude drives the rotor at touchdown
Altitude drives the rotor in the descent, then rotor kinetic energy cushions touchdown
Engine power drives the rotor in the descent, then altitude cushions touchdown
questions.explain: Phase 1 converts altitude into rotor energy; phase 2 uses the rotor energy for touchdown.

cards.question: What is an airfoil by definition
options: Any surface which generates a useful dynamic reaction of the air
Only a wing surface which generates lift in forward flight
Any surface which generates a useful static pressure of the air
cards.explain: An airfoil is any surface that gives a useful dynamic reaction from the air it moves through.

cards.question: Which two forces does an airfoil produce as the useful reaction for flying and manoeuvring
options: Thrust and weight
Lift and drag
Lift and thrust
cards.explain: The text names lift and thrust as the two forces needed for flying and manoeuvring.

cards.question: What is the leading edge of a rotor blade
options: The edge that cuts into the wind when the rotor is turning
The edge opposite the one that cuts into the wind
The outer end of the blade opposite the root
cards.explain: The leading edge cuts into the wind.

cards.question: What is the advancing blade
options: The backward moving blade
The forward moving blade
The blade at the tail boom
cards.explain: The blade moving forward is the advancing blade.

cards.question: What is the relative wind
options: The direction of the airflow with respect to the ground
The direction of the airflow with respect to the rotor blade
The speed of the natural wind at the landing site
cards.explain: Relative wind is airflow direction relative to the blade.

cards.question: How is the relative wind directed in relation to the flight path of the blade
options: Always along the same flight path
Always opposite to the flight path
Always perpendicular to the path
cards.explain: The relative wind is always opposite to the blade's flight path.

cards.question: What is the axis of rotation
options: The line from the leading edge to the trailing edge
The plane formed by the average tip path
The line about which the rotor blades turn
cards.explain: The rotor blades turn around the axis of rotation.

cards.question: Which cockpit input changes the pitch angle of all main rotor blades
options: The tail rotor pedals
The collective pitch control
The cyclic pitch stick
cards.explain: The collective pitch control changes the pitch angle.

cards.question: Why does a technician have to study the basic principles of helicopter flight
options: To obtain the flight crew licence required for ground running of the rotor
To understand the maintenance and troubleshooting practices on the systems
To calculate the lift and thrust produced by the main rotor blades
cards.explain: Understanding the maintenance and troubleshooting practices carried out on the various systems is the reason a technician needs a thorough knowledge of the principles.

cards.question: Which surfaces act as the airfoils on a fixed-wing aircraft and on a helicopter
options: Primarily the wings on the fixed-wing aircraft, the main rotor on the helicopter
Primarily the fuselage on the fixed-wing aircraft, the tail rotor on the helicopter
Primarily the propellers on the fixed-wing aircraft, the fuselage on the helicopter
cards.explain: The wings are the primary airfoil of a fixed-wing aircraft and the main rotor is the primary airfoil of the helicopter.

cards.question: Why is the helicopter often referred to as a rotary-wing aircraft
options: Its fuselage acts as a rotating wing
Its primary airfoil is the main rotor
Its primary airfoil is the tail rotor
cards.explain: Because its main lifting surface is a rotating rotor, the helicopter is called rotary-wing.

cards.question: Which force produced by the main rotor blades holds the helicopter up against gravity?
options: Drag
Lift
Thrust
cards.explain: Of the two forces the airfoil produces, lift is the one the manual gives as counteracting gravity.

cards.question: A rotor blade is moving forward and downward through the air. In which direction does its relative wind act?
options: Backward and downward
Forward and upward
Backward and upward
cards.explain: The relative wind is always exactly opposite to the flight path of the blade, so forward and downward movement gives a backward and upward relative wind.

cards.question: Why does the relative wind on a rotor blade change when a hovering helicopter begins to move horizontally
options: Movement of the helicopter through the air is one of the factors that affect it
The horizontal movement of the helicopter changes the span of the rotor blade
The horizontal movement of the helicopter changes the chord line of the rotor blade
cards.explain: Horizontal movement of the helicopter is one of the factors that affect the relative wind.

cards.question: A helicopter stands with its rotor stopped while a strong natural wind passes across the blades. Which statement about the relative wind is correct?
options: The relative wind is created only by blade flapping
There is no relative wind because the rotor is stopped
The wind blowing over the blade creates the relative wind
cards.explain: Even with the rotor stopped, wind over the blade is airflow relative to the blade.

cards.question: How can one cockpit control change both the pitch angle and the angle of attack of a rotor blade
options: It tilts the plane of rotation, moving the relative wind against the chord
It rotates the blade around the hub axis, moving the chord against each reference
It lifts the whole blade, moving the axis of rotation against the chord
cards.explain: Both angles are measured from the chord, so rotating the blade about the hub axis changes both.

cards.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes pitch angle from angle of attack?
options: Pitch angle is referenced to the relative wind, angle of attack to the plane of rotation
Pitch angle is referenced to the plane of rotation, angle of attack to the relative wind
Pitch angle is referenced to the axis of rotation, angle of attack to the span line
cards.explain: Both use the chord, but pitch angle uses the plane of rotation and angle of attack uses the relative wind.

cards.question: Why do the same factors that affect the relative wind also affect the angle of attack
options: Because the angle of attack depends upon the relative wind
Because the angle of attack depends upon the blade span
Because the relative wind depends upon the pitch angle
cards.explain: Angle of attack is measured to the relative wind, so what changes one changes the other.

cards.question: Two reference dimensions of a rotor blade are quoted, one measured along the blade centreline and one across the blade section. Which pair is correct?
options: Span along the centreline, chord across the section
Span along the centreline, root across the section
Chord along the centreline, span across the section
cards.explain: Span runs root to tip along the centreline, and the chord runs leading edge to trailing edge across the section.

cards.question: A helicopter is in forward flight and one blade is on the advancing side. In which direction does the relative wind on that blade act?
options: Backward and upward, across the blade movement
Horizontally forward, with the blade movement
Horizontally backward, opposite to the blade movement
cards.explain: The advancing blade moves forward, and the relative wind is always opposite to the blade's flight path.

cards.question: What creates the relative wind on a helicopter hovering in completely still air
options: The turning of the rotor blades
The forward speed of the helicopter
The wind speed and the wind direction
cards.explain: With no wind and no forward speed, only the turning of the blades is left to produce the relative wind.

cards.question: A blade is set so that its chord lies exactly along the average tip path of the blades. What is its pitch angle?
options: Forty-five degrees, because the chord lies between the two references
Ninety degrees, because the chord and the axis of rotation coincide
Zero, because the chord and the plane of rotation coincide
cards.explain: The pitch angle is measured between the chord and the plane of rotation, so a chord lying in that plane gives zero.

cards.question: The relative wind on a blade lies in the same direction as the plane of rotation and the pilot then increases the pitch angle. What happens to the angle of attack?
options: It increases and becomes larger than the pitch angle
It stays constant while the pitch angle increases
It increases and stays equal to the pitch angle
cards.explain: With the relative wind in the plane of rotation the two angles are equal, and the angle of attack follows the pitch angle up.

cards.question: Why can the angle of attack of a blade change while the collective pitch control is held still
options: An outside influence has changed the plane of rotation
An outside influence has changed the relative wind
An outside influence has changed the chord of the blade
cards.explain: Angle of attack is measured from the relative wind, so it changes when outside influences move the relative wind.

cards.question: On a turning blade the relative wind does not lie in the direction of the plane of rotation. What follows for the pitch angle and the angle of attack?
options: They cannot be equal to each other
They must change at the same rate
They must be equal to each other
cards.explain: The two angles are equal only when the relative wind has the same direction as the plane of rotation, so with the relative wind elsewhere they cannot be equal.

cards.question: What is lift
options: The force that is produced by the airfoil
The force that is produced by gravity
The force produced by torque reaction
cards.explain: Lift is the airfoil's force.

cards.question: How is gyroscopic precession defined
options: The turning of the fuselage opposite to the rotor
The change of the rotational axis as a result of an external force
The change of the rotor RPM as a result of an external force
cards.explain: Precession is a change of the rotational axis caused by an external force.

cards.question: Why must gyroscopic precession be considered on the tail rotor as well as on the main rotor
options: Because the tail rotor blades have feathering hinges
Because the tail rotor turns opposite to the fuselage
Because the effect applies to every rotating body
cards.explain: Gyroscopic precession applies to all rotating bodies, so it applies to the tail rotor as well as the main rotor.

cards.question: An external force tries to turn a spinning wheel about its input axis. Around which axis does the movement actually take place?
options: Only around the spin axis
Around the output axis
Only around the input axis
cards.explain: Because of precession the movement occurs around the output axis.

cards.question: Why must the steering input to the rotor be applied 90° before the point where the tilt is wanted
options: Because the swash plate is mounted 90° to the rotor
Because the output occurs 90° later in the direction of rotation
Because the output occurs 90° earlier in the direction of rotation
cards.explain: Precession shifts the result 90° in the direction of rotation, so the input must lead by 90°.

cards.question: A downward force is applied on the right side of a counterclockwise turning rotor. Where does the output appear?
options: Right in front
Right at the rear
On the left side
cards.explain: 90° later in counterclockwise rotation from the right side is the front.

cards.question: What happens to the direction in which lift acts on a blade when the relative wind changes direction
options: It stays fixed, remaining perpendicular to the plane of rotation
It changes with it, staying parallel to the relative wind
It changes with it, staying perpendicular to the relative wind
cards.explain: Lift is defined as perpendicular to the relative wind, so its direction follows the relative wind.

cards.question: What must happen to the plane of rotation when an external force tilts the axis of rotation
options: It tilts the opposite way, staying parallel to the axis
It stays level, while the axis tilts away from it
It tilts with the axis, staying perpendicular to it
cards.explain: The plane of rotation is always perpendicular to the axis of rotation, so it tilts with the axis.

cards.question: A helicopter rotor turns counterclockwise. The tip-path plane must tilt backward for rearward flight. Following the precession rule, where must the downward force be put in?
options: Right at the rear
On the left side
On the right side
cards.explain: The output is wanted at the rear; 90° earlier in counterclockwise rotation is the left side.

cards.question: Which law explains torque reaction on a helicopter fuselage
options: Newton's Second Law
Newton's Third Law
Newton's law of inertia
cards.explain: Torque reaction is action and reaction, Newton's Third Law.

cards.question: Why must the torque of the main rotor be counteracted before flight is possible
options: Because the fuselage would otherwise turn in the direction opposite to the rotor blades
Because the main rotor would otherwise produce thrust instead of lift
Because the rotor blades would otherwise turn in the direction opposite to the fuselage
cards.explain: Torque makes the fuselage rotate opposite to the blades, so it must be counteracted before flight.

cards.question: A helicopter's main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above and the tail rotor is not yet producing thrust. Which way does the fuselage tend to turn?
options: Clockwise
Not at all
Counterclockwise
cards.explain: The fuselage reaction is opposite to a counterclockwise rotor, so clockwise.

cards.question: A pilot raises the collective lever and the turning force on the fuselage rises. Why must the tail rotor thrust then change too?
options: Because it is what balances the lift of the main rotor
Because it is what compensates the torque on the airframe
Because it is what balances the drag of the main rotor
cards.explain: The tail rotor is what compensates the torque, so a change in torque has to be matched by a change in its thrust.

cards.question: What do a gyrocopter in normal flight and a helicopter after an engine failure have in common
options: The rotor is driven by the airflow in autorotation
The rotor is driven by the engine through the drive shafts
The rotor is held at a fixed pitch angle by the collective
cards.explain: Both have an unpowered rotor kept turning by the airflow, which is autorotation.

cards.question: The lift-producing rotor of a gyroplane stays connected to the engine in flight. What follows from that?
options: The rotor has to be tilted slightly aft
The rotor can no longer stall in flight
The rotor torque has to be compensated
cards.explain: An engine-driven rotor produces a torque reaction on the airframe, so it must be compensated.

cards.question: A convertiplane has accelerated to the airspeed at which its rotor turns freely in autorotation. What is then providing lift and what is providing thrust?
options: The wings give the lift, the rotor gives the thrust
The rotor gives the lift, the propellers or turbines give the thrust
The wings give the lift, the propellers or turbines give the thrust
cards.explain: Once the rotor autorotates it makes no lift, so the wings carry the aircraft and the propellers or turbines push it.

cards.question: How does the rotor of a convertiplane in cruise differ from the rotor of a type 3 transformation helicopter in cruise
options: Both rotors turn in autorotation and carry part of the aircraft weight
The convertiplane rotor turns in autorotation, the type 3 rotor is shut down and stowed
The type 3 rotor turns in autorotation, the convertiplane rotor is shut down and stowed
cards.explain: The convertiplane rotor keeps turning in autorotation while the type 3 rotor is deactivated and stowed.

cards.question: What does lift counteract on a helicopter
options: Thrust
Torque
Weight
cards.explain: Lift counteracts weight.

cards.question: How do helicopters change direction, unlike other aircraft
options: By deflecting control surfaces on the fuselage
By changing the RPM of the main rotor
By changing the angle of the rotor blade plane
cards.explain: Helicopters tilt the rotor blade plane instead of deflecting surfaces.

cards.question: A pilot moves the cyclic stick in the direction of the nose. What does the rotor plane do
options: It tilts backward
It moves upward
It tilts forward
cards.explain: Forward cyclic tilts the rotor plane forward.

cards.question: What does the helicopter do when the pilot moves the collective lever upwards
options: It turns left
It descends
It climbs
cards.explain: More pitch gives more lift and the helicopter climbs.

cards.question: What does a helicopter gain from being able to tilt its rotor plane slightly in any direction
options: Torque can act in all directions, giving heading control
Thrust can act in all directions, giving directional control
Lift can act in all directions, giving collective control
cards.explain: Tilting the rotor plane lets the thrust act in any direction, which is how directional control is obtained.

cards.question: Why does a helicopter need no pull or push propellers
options: Because the rotors generate both lift and thrust
Because the rotors are driven by the airflow
Because the tail rotor generates the thrust
cards.explain: The rotor provides both lift and thrust.

cards.question: During an autorotation after an engine failure, which statement about control is correct?
options: Only the pedals remain effective and the touchdown point cannot be chosen
The helicopter is fully controllable and the pilot can choose the touchdown point
The helicopter is not controllable and lands wherever the descent takes it
cards.explain: During an autorotative landing the helicopter stays fully controllable and the pilot determines the location for touchdown.

cards.question: Why does moving the collective lever also alter the torque effect on the fuselage
options: Because the movement of the lever also changes the engine power
Because the movement of the lever also tilts the rotor plane
Because the movement of the lever also changes the tail rotor pitch
cards.explain: The collective lever changes engine power as well as blade pitch, and with it the torque.

cards.question: A pilot wants to yaw the helicopter around the rotor mast axis. How do the pedals bring this about?
options: They change the pitch angle of the main rotor blades and so vary its thrust
They change the pitch angle of the tail rotor blades and so vary its thrust
They tilt the tail rotor plane and so vary the direction of its thrust
cards.explain: Pedal movement changes tail rotor blade pitch, which varies tail rotor thrust and yaws the aircraft.

cards.question: A helicopter's main rotor is driven by the engine. Which consequence follows for the fuselage
options: Its torque reaction on the fuselage has to be counteracted
Its rotor cannot be tilted out of the horizontal plane
Its downwash cannot escape from under the fuselage
cards.explain: An engine driven rotor makes the fuselage tend to rotate the opposite way, and this torque has to be counteracted.

cards.question: How is a helicopter able to fly sideways
options: The blade pitch is increased on one side, so the lift acts sideways
The rotor plane is tilted sideways, so the thrust acts sideways
The tail rotor thrust is increased, so the fuselage is pushed sideways
cards.explain: Thrust acts perpendicular to the rotor plane, so tilting the plane sideways points the thrust sideways.

cards.question: How do the cyclic control and the collective control differ in the way they change the pitch angle of the main rotor blades
options: The cyclic changes it during each revolution, the collective changes all blades together
The collective changes it during each revolution, the cyclic changes all blades together
Both change it during each revolution, but only the cyclic changes all blades together
cards.explain: Cyclic pitch varies around the disc each revolution while collective pitch moves all blades by the same amount.

cards.question: In terms of the law of acceleration, why must the rotor plane be tilted when changing from a hover into forward flight
options: A force is needed in the direction of flight, and thrust acts perpendicular to the rotor plane
A force is needed in the direction of flight, and thrust acts parallel to the rotor plane
A torque is needed in the direction of flight, and thrust acts perpendicular to the rotor mast
cards.explain: Accelerating forward needs a forward force, and the only way to point the thrust forward is to tilt the rotor plane.

cards.question: In straight-ahead flight the blade has minimum incidence in front and maximum incidence at the rear. What is the result for the rotor plane?
options: It tilts backward, giving lift and rearward thrust
It tilts forward, giving lift and forward thrust
It stays level, giving lift but no thrust
cards.explain: More lift at the rear and less at the front tilts the plane forward, producing lift and forward thrust.

cards.question: Why does raising the collective lever make the rotor produce more lift
options: The plane of rotation of every blade rises, and with it the relative wind
The pitch angle of every blade rises, and with it the angle of attack
The rotational speed of every blade rises, and with it the chord
cards.explain: More pitch means more angle of attack on every blade, so the rotor makes more lift.

cards.question: Which hinge allows the pitch change commanded from the cockpit, and which allows the blade to move under aerodynamic forces
options: The flapping hinge for the pitch change, the feathering hinge for the movement
The lead-lag hinge for the pitch change, the flapping hinge for the movement
The feathering hinge for the pitch change, the flapping hinge for the movement
cards.explain: Feathering hinges take the commanded pitch change, flapping hinges let the blade move under the air loads.

cards.question: A pilot raises the collective lever to climb and the torque effect on the fuselage changes. Which control must the pilot then use to vary the thrust that compensates it?
options: The collective lever
The cyclic pitch stick
The tail rotor pedals
cards.explain: Torque is compensated by the tail rotor, whose thrust the pilot varies with the pedals.

cards.question: Why does varying the tail rotor thrust make the helicopter turn around the rotor mast axis
options: The thrust no longer exactly balances the torque reaction on the fuselage
The thrust tilts the main rotor disk away from the rotor mast axis
The thrust no longer exactly balances the lift produced by the main rotor
cards.explain: The tail rotor thrust is what holds the torque reaction in balance, so changing it lets the fuselage turn.

cards.question: A pilot pushes the left pedal forward during a hover and holds the new heading. What else now needs attention?
options: The lateral drift, because the tail rotor thrust has changed
The pitch angle, because the collective lever has changed
The rotor RPM, because the tail rotor pitch has changed
cards.explain: Tail rotor thrust is what produces the translating tendency, so changing it changes the drift the pilot must hold off.

cards.question: A pilot pushes the cyclic stick forward to fly forward. Which chain of events takes place at the swash plate and the blades?
options: The swash plate turns, the bell cranks move and the blade pitch is held through the revolution
The swash plate is lifted, the control rods move and the blade pitch rises on every blade at once
The swash plate tilts, the control rods move and the blade pitch varies through the revolution
cards.explain: A cyclic input tilts the swash plate, which moves the control rods and varies blade pitch through each revolution.

cards.question: What is dissymmetry of lift
options: The difference in lift between advancing and retreating blade
The difference in lift between main and tail rotor
The difference in lift in and out of ground effect
cards.explain: The lift difference between advancing and retreating blade is dissymmetry of lift.

cards.question: Where does the blade's centre of gravity move when the blade flaps downwards
options: Closer to the blade tip
Closer to the rotational axis
Closer to the leading edge
cards.explain: Downward flapping moves the CG outward toward the tip.

cards.question: What acts on the stationary part of the swash plate, and what does the rotating part act on
options: Control rods and bell cranks from the cockpit act on it; it drives the blades through control rods
The rotor head acts on it through a bearing; it drives the bell cranks through control rods
Control rods from the blades act on it; it drives the cockpit controls through bell cranks
cards.explain: The cockpit acts on the stationary part and the rotating part is connected onward to the blades.

cards.question: Why does the swash plate have to act as an interface
options: It transfers engine power between the main gearbox and the rotating rotor mast
It transfers control signals between the stationary input system and the rotating rotor
It transfers torque between the main rotor and the tail rotor drive system
cards.explain: Cockpit inputs are stationary but the blades rotate, so the swash plate links the two.

cards.question: A helicopter is hovering with no wind at all. Why is there no dissymmetry of lift in this condition?
options: There is no airstream from speed of flight, so both blades have the same parameters
There is no pitch angle on either blade, so both blades have the same parameters
There is no rotational speed at the blade tips, so both blades have the same parameters
cards.explain: Without the airstream caused by the speed of flight there is nothing to add to one blade and subtract from the other.

cards.question: Why does the advancing blade produce more lift in forward flight
options: The opposing airstream is subtracted from its rotational speed
Its pitch angle is increased by the collective
The opposing airstream is added to its rotational speed
cards.explain: The airstream adds to its speed, giving more lift.

cards.question: Why does an upward flapping rotor blade accelerate while the rotor RPM stays constant
options: Its centre of gravity moves closer to the blade tip
Its centre of gravity moves closer to the rotational axis
Its centre of gravity moves closer to the trailing edge
cards.explain: A mass moved towards the centre of rotation tries to speed the rotation up, so the up-flapping blade accelerates.

cards.question: A mass point on a rotating disk is moved towards the centre of rotation. What does it do to the rotational speed?
options: It has no effect on the rotational speed
It tries to accelerate the rotational speed
It tries to decelerate the rotational speed
cards.explain: Moving inward, it keeps its higher speed and so accelerates the rotation.

cards.question: Why does the advancing blade flap up
options: It experiences decreased relative wind and generates less lift
It experiences increased relative wind and generates more lift
Its centre of gravity moves closer to the blade tip
cards.explain: More relative wind means more lift, so it flaps up.

cards.question: How far does blade flapping go towards restoring rotor balance
options: It helps to balance the rotor but is not enough alone
It increases the dissymmetry of lift instead
It restores the balance of the rotor completely
cards.explain: Flapping helps but does not fully restore balance.

cards.question: Why must a rotor blade be able to move and occupy a new position
options: Because the swash plate rotates with the rotor
Because aerodynamic forces act on the rotor blade
Because the torque reaction turns the fuselage
cards.explain: Aerodynamic forces require the blade to move.

cards.question: Why are the two parts of the swash plate held parallel but joined through a bearing
options: So the rotor plane can be tilted without moving the control rods above it
So the cockpit input can be passed to blades that are turning with the rotor
So the cockpit input can be passed to blades that are fixed to the rotor mast
cards.explain: The bearing lets the upper part turn with the rotor while the parallel lower part stays still, passing the input across.

cards.question: During a ground check the whole swash plate is seen to rise without tilting, and every blade takes a larger pitch angle. What will the helicopter do if this is done in flight?
options: It flies forward, because the rotor plane is tilted forward
It climbs, because all blades gain pitch together
It yaws left, because the tail rotor pitch is increased
cards.explain: Lifting the swash plate is a collective pitch increase, which makes more lift and a climb.

cards.question: Which cockpit control changes a blade pitch angle without acting through the main rotor swash plate
options: The collective lever, which changes the main rotor blade pitch
The cyclic stick, which changes the main rotor blade pitch
The pedals, which change the tail rotor blade pitch
cards.explain: The swash plate serves the main rotor blades, while the pedals act on the tail rotor blades.

cards.question: A technician watches the swash plate while a helper moves one cockpit control, and the whole swash plate moves up without tilting. Which control is being moved?
options: The cyclic stick
The tail pedals
The collective lever
cards.explain: Lifting the swash plate is collective; tilting would be cyclic.

cards.question: During a control check the swash plate tilts but its mean height does not change. Which pitch change is being made?
options: Collective pitch change
Cyclic pitch change
Tail rotor pitch change
cards.explain: Tilting the swash plate produces cyclic pitch change.

cards.question: Where on the rotor disc does the highest airspeed occur when a helicopter flies forward
options: At the root of the advancing blade
At the tip of the retreating blade
At the tip of the advancing blade
cards.explain: Speed rises towards the tip and the opposing airstream adds on the advancing side, so the advancing tip is fastest.

cards.question: A helicopter hovers on the spot in a steady strong wind. Why can its blades not all produce the same lift?
options: The wind adds to the speed of one half of the disc and subtracts from the other
The wind raises the pitch angle on one half of the disc and lowers it on the other
The wind increases the rotational speed of the whole rotor disc
cards.explain: Wind is a relative wind just like forward speed, so it adds on the advancing side and subtracts on the retreating side.

cards.question: A blade flaps up and therefore accelerates and moves forward in the plane of rotation. Which hinge has to allow this?
options: The lead-lag hinge
The feathering hinge
The flapping hinge
cards.explain: Movement forward and backward in the plane of rotation is taken by the lead-lag hinge.

cards.question: In forward flight the retreating blade flaps down. Combining the flapping and centre-of-mass facts, how does this blade move in the plane of rotation?
options: It accelerates and moves forward (leads)
It keeps its position in the plane
It decelerates and moves backward (lags)
cards.explain: The retreating blade flaps down, its CG moves outward, so it decelerates and lags.

cards.question: Why is blade flapping a self-correcting effect
options: The blade with more lift flaps down, which reduces its angle of attack and its lift
The blade with more lift flaps up, which reduces its pitch angle and its lift
The blade with more lift flaps up, which reduces its angle of attack and its lift
cards.explain: The extra lift causes the up-flap, and the up-flap takes the angle of attack and the lift back down again.

cards.question: On which blade does flapping increase the angle of attack, and why must it do so
options: The retreating blade, because it is the one producing too much lift
The retreating blade, because it is the one producing too little lift
The advancing blade, because it is the one producing too little lift
cards.explain: The retreating blade is short of lift, and flapping down raises its angle of attack and so its lift.

cards.question: Why does upward flapping reduce the angle of attack of the advancing blade?
options: Moving up reduces the blade pitch angle
Moving up adds an upward relative wind component
Moving up adds a downward relative wind component
cards.explain: Relative wind is opposite to blade motion, so an upward-moving blade meets air from above, reducing the angle of attack.

cards.question: A rotor head is built with no flapping hinges at all. How can dissymmetry of lift still be balanced on this rotor?
options: The blades themselves flex and absorb the forces acting on them
The feathering hinges let the blades change pitch instead
The lead-lag hinges let the blades move up and down instead
cards.explain: Where there is no flapping hinge, the blades must instead have properties that allow them to absorb the forces.

cards.question: A helicopter is in steady forward flight and the pilot makes no control input at all. Is there still lead-lag movement, and why?
options: Yes, because dissymmetry of lift keeps the blades flapping
Yes, because the collective lever holds the blades at a fixed pitch
No, because lead-lag only follows a cyclic control input
cards.explain: Dissymmetry of lift makes the blades flap in forward flight even with no input, and flapping always makes lead-lag.

cards.question: A pilot in forward flight moves the cyclic stick to the right. Which blade movement is produced in addition to the pitch change?
options: A lead-lag movement, because the rotor RPM changes
A lead-lag movement, because the rotor plane tilts
A feathering movement, because the rotor plane tilts
cards.explain: A cyclic input tilts the rotor plane and the tilt generates a lead-lag movement.

cards.question: Which turning force does a counterclockwise turning main rotor generate on the fuselage
options: A clockwise turning force
A nose-down pitching force
A counterclockwise turning force
cards.explain: The fuselage force is opposite, so clockwise.

cards.question: During powered flight, how is the rotor drag overcome
options: With rotor inertia
With upward airflow
With engine power
cards.explain: In powered flight, engine power overcomes rotor drag.

cards.question: In which two failure cases must some other force sustain the rotor RPM
options: Engine failure or broken drive shafts
Tail rotor failure or broken pedals
Swash plate failure or broken control rods
cards.explain: Engine failure or broken drive shafts require another force.

cards.question: A helicopter is in a steady hover. Which two jobs is the thrust of the tail rotor doing at the same time?
options: Compensating the main rotor torque and preventing the lateral drift
Maintaining heading control and tilting the main rotor disk slightly
Compensating the main rotor torque and maintaining heading control
cards.explain: In the hover the tail rotor thrust both compensates the main rotor torque and maintains heading control; the drift it causes is held off with the main rotor disk instead.

cards.question: A helicopter in hover drifts sideways although torque is compensated. What causes this drift?
options: The thrust of the tail rotor
Dissymmetry of lift
Gyroscopic precession
cards.explain: The tail rotor's sideways thrust causes translating tendency.

cards.question: Why does ground effect become more pronounced the nearer the ground is approached
options: Because it is caused by the surface reducing the rotational speed of the blades
Because it is caused by the surface increasing the pitch angle of the blades
Because it is caused by the surface interfering with the rotor airflow pattern
cards.explain: The effect comes from the surface interfering with the rotor airflow, so it grows as the surface gets closer.

cards.question: Why must a helicopter in autorotation descend
options: Because the collective pitch is lowered to its minimum stop during autorotation
Because the airflow up through the rotor in the descent supplies the energy
Because the engine power is needed to overcome the drag of the rotor blades
cards.explain: The upward airflow that keeps the rotor turning only exists while the helicopter is descending.

cards.question: Which cockpit control does the pilot use to hold off the drift caused by translating tendency
options: The collective lever, which lifts the main rotor disk
The pedals, which tilt the tail rotor thrust line
The cyclic stick, which tilts the main rotor disk
cards.explain: Tilting the rotor disk is a cyclic input, so the cyclic stick is the control that holds off the drift.

cards.question: How does tilting the main rotor disk stop the lateral drift of a helicopter in the hover
options: The thrust then acts partly against the rotor mast axis
The lift then acts partly against the torque direction
The thrust then acts partly in the opposite sideways direction
cards.explain: Thrust acts perpendicular to the rotor plane, so tilting the disk the other way points some thrust against the drift.

cards.question: During hover, tail rotor thrust makes the helicopter drift to the right. How must the main rotor disk be tilted to prevent this?
options: Slightly to the right
Slightly forward
Slightly to the left
cards.explain: The disk is tilted opposite to the drift, so to the left for a right drift.

cards.question: Why does the reduced downward airflow in ground effect increase the angle of attack of the blades
options: The pitch angle changes, and the angle of attack is measured from it
The relative wind direction changes, and the angle of attack is measured from it
The plane of rotation changes, and the angle of attack is measured from it
cards.explain: A slower downward airflow changes the relative wind, and the angle of attack is taken from the relative wind.

cards.question: A helicopter settles into a hover close to the ground and the pilot wants to stay there. Which lever does he move and what happens to the power needed?
options: He lowers the collective, and more power is needed
He raises the collective, and more power is needed
He lowers the collective, and less power is needed
cards.explain: Reducing blade pitch is done with the collective, and hovering in ground effect needs less power.

cards.question: A helicopter hovering just above the ground climbs slowly until it is just under one rotor diameter up. What has happened to ground effect?
options: It is stronger and still present
It is lost once the skids leave the ground
It is weaker but still present
cards.explain: Ground effect reaches to one rotor diameter and weakens with height, so it is still there but reduced.

cards.question: In ground effect the lift vector of the blades becomes more vertical. Why does that reduce the power the pilot needs?
options: More of the rotor force acts straight against the weight
More of the rotor force acts straight along the blade span
More of the rotor force acts straight against the drag
cards.explain: Lift is what overcomes weight, so a more vertical lift vector puts more of the rotor force where it is needed.

cards.question: Once the engine has failed, what does the collective pitch lever control
options: The engine power that keeps the rotor turning in the descent
The tail rotor thrust that keeps the heading in the descent
The force that keeps the rotor turning in the descent
cards.explain: With no engine the collective no longer sets engine power; it controls the force that sustains rotor RPM.

cards.question: An engine fails in cruise and the pilot chooses a field to land in. What makes that choice possible?
options: The rotor keeps turning at an RPM that provides aircraft control
The rotor keeps turning at an RPM that provides enough lift to hover
The engine keeps turning at an RPM that provides hydraulic power
cards.explain: Autorotation keeps the rotor at a controlling RPM, so the helicopter stays fully controllable and the pilot picks the spot.

cards.question: An engine fails in cruise. In which order does the pilot use energy during the autorotation?
options: Altitude drives the rotor in the descent, then rotor kinetic energy cushions touchdown
Rotor kinetic energy cushions the descent, then altitude drives the rotor at touchdown
Engine power drives the rotor in the descent, then altitude cushions touchdown
cards.explain: Phase 1 converts altitude into rotor energy; phase 2 uses the rotor energy for touchdown.

questions.question: Which other name is given to closed loop control
options: actuation
regulation
correction
questions.explain: Closed loop control is also called regulation, because the control value is permanently monitored and compared with the reference value.

questions.question: Which quantity is denoted by Xw in the terms used for closed loop control
options: control value
reference value
error
questions.explain: Xw is the symbol given for the error in a closed loop system.

questions.question: For a P - Regulator, to what is the change in the output value always proportional
options: the change in the input value
the magnitude of the input value
the rate of change of the input value
questions.explain: A proportional regulator ties the change of its output directly to the change of its input.

questions.question: For an I - Regulator, to what is the rate of change of the output value proportional
options: the change in its output value
its input value
the rate of change of its input value
questions.explain: In an integral regulator it is how fast the output moves that follows the input.

questions.question: What do flight parameters describe
options: the state of the aircraft fixed coordinate system
the state of the autopilot regulators
the state of motion of an aircraft
questions.explain: A flight parameter is a physical quantity that describes how the aircraft is moving.

questions.question: Under which condition does a P - Regulator generate a controller output value
options: when an error value exists at its input
when the input value is changing at a constant rate
when the error value at its input is zero
questions.explain: No error at the input means no output from a proportional regulator.

questions.question: The input of a D - Regulator changes at a constant rate. What does the output value do?
options: It remains steady at one level
It falls back towards zero
It increases linearly without limit
questions.explain: The differential regulator reacts to rate of change, so a steady rate gives a steady output.

questions.question: What are the three degrees of translatory freedom
options: the rotations about the X, Y and Z axes
the linear movements along the roll and pitch axes
the linear movements along the X, Y and Z axes
questions.explain: Translatory freedom is straight line movement along each of the three axes.

questions.question: Which other legs are taken in by the leg category that ends at the active runway
options: all the legs of the departure route
all the legs of a missed approach
all the legs of the arrival route
questions.explain: The approach category also takes in the missed approach legs.

questions.question: Flying leg by leg, what must the pilot take into consideration when he selects the heading for each leg?
options: The initial approach fix
The flight path angle
The wind correction angle
questions.explain: Heading for a leg must allow for the wind correction angle.

questions.question: Besides separately, how may each regulator offered by the autoflight system be used
options: in combination with the auto-throttle / auto-thrust system
in combination with the flight management computer system
in combination with the measurement unit of the control loop
questions.explain: A regulator can work alone or together with the thrust system.

questions.question: What are the reference values supplied by the flight management system at the managed automatic level based on
options: the air traffic control clearances passed during the flight
a stored flight plan and any modifications made to it in flight
a stored flight plan which cannot be modified once in flight
questions.explain: The FMS works to the stored plan including whatever the pilot has changed in flight.

questions.question: What is the objective of the managed automatic level of guidance
options: To support the pilot flying with attitude commands
To relieve the crew of manual control tasks
To let the crew leave the FMS profile at short notice
questions.explain: Relieving the crew of the manual control tasks is the objective given, which leaves them time to monitor the overall situation.

questions.question: At the basic manual level, what does the pilot flying have to do?
options: Maintain altitude, heading and airspeed by selecting modes and reference values
Maintain altitude, heading and airspeed by manipulating the controls and thrust
Maintain pitch and roll attitude by following the flight director commands
questions.explain: With no autoflight support the pilot holds the values himself on the controls and the thrust levers.

questions.question: What do the flight condition regulators on their own make up
options: the outer control loop of an autopilot
the mode control panel of an autopilot
the simplest form of an autopilot
questions.explain: An attitude stabilising regulator on its own is the simplest autopilot there is.

questions.question: The pilot pushes firmly on the control column while the autopilot is engaged. What happens to the auto- trim function?
options: It is deactivated until the force is removed
It is switched over to its high trim speed
It is transferred to the elevator actuator
questions.explain: Force on the control column deactivates auto-trim for as long as it is applied.

questions.question: Every engage interlock condition is satisfied as the pilot selects the autopilot on. What follows?
options: The servo clutches close and the autopilot takes over attitude control
The servo clutches open and the pilot keeps manual control
The trim clutches close and the pilot keeps stabilizer control
questions.explain: Meeting all conditions closes the servo clutches and hands attitude control to the autopilot.

questions.question: What happens to the AP engage switch when an interlock condition becomes invalid
options: It is held at its last selected mode
It is latched in the ON position
It is reset to the OFF position
questions.explain: Loss of a condition resets the engage switch to OFF.

questions.question: What supplies the force acting along the aircraft X-axis
options: Rudder deflection
Spoiler drag
Engine thrust
questions.explain: Thrust acts along the X-axis.

questions.question: What job does the stabilizer do among the primary control surfaces
options: It trims out a roll-moment generated by aileron deflection
It trims out a yaw-moment generated by rudder deflection
It trims out a pitch-moment generated by elevator deflection
questions.explain: The stabilizer trims out the pitch moment the elevator has produced.

questions.question: A flight director mode is already active when the pilot engages the autopilot. How does the autopilot behave?
options: It takes the mode over and runs in the matching upper mode at once
It holds the mode armed until the basic mode is cancelled
It drops the mode and reverts to pitch attitude hold at once
questions.explain: An active FD mode is adopted by the autopilot, so no basic mode appears.

questions.question: The pitch channel is said to behave like a PI-regulator. How is that behaviour produced?
options: The error goes direct to the elevator actuator and also to the gain schedule
The error goes direct to the elevator actuator and also to the auto-trim
The error goes direct to the stabilizer actuator and also to the auto-trim
questions.explain: Splitting the error between the elevator actuator and auto-trim gives proportional plus integral action.

questions.question: The autopilot is disengaged after a long cruise during which auto-trim has been working. Why is there no abrupt pitch attitude change?
options: The elevator is already held by the torque limiter
The elevator is already resting in its neutral position
The stabilizer is already resting in its neutral position
questions.explain: With the standing moment carried by the stabilizer and the elevator at neutral, nothing springs back at disengagement.

questions.question: The Mach number rises in the cruise. Which way does the Mach trim drive the stabilizer and what does that counter?
options: Leading edge up, countering the pitch down effect
Leading edge down, countering the pitch down effect
Leading edge down, countering the pitch up effect
questions.explain: Stabilizer leading edge down opposes the nose-down tuck under tendency.

questions.question: An aircraft has a high longitudinal static stability. Why must the onset of auto-trim action be deferred?
options: Large elevator displacements are needed to counter short term disturbances
Large stabilizer displacements are needed to counter long term disturbances
Small elevator displacements are needed to counter short term disturbances
questions.explain: High stability makes the surfaces less effective, so ordinary gust corrections already use large deflections and trimming must wait.

questions.question: The aircraft is to hold the same rate of turn while flying faster through the air. What must happen to the bank angle?
options: It has to be decreased
It has to be increased
It has to be held unchanged
questions.explain: Rate of turn at higher TAS needs more bank, which the outer loop gain schedule provides.

questions.question: The autopilot has just been engaged and no upper mode has been selected. Which attitudes do its two channels control straight away?
options: The pitch channel the pitch attitude, the roll channel the roll attitude or heading
The pitch channel the flight path, the roll channel the roll attitude or heading
The pitch channel the pitch attitude, the roll channel the heading only
questions.explain: Each channel takes its basic mode at once, pitch attitude in pitch and roll attitude or heading in roll.

questions.question: A pilot holds a steady force on the control wheel in CWS. What do the inner loops make of it, and what does the aircraft do?
options: A fixed roll rate, which changes the heading but not the attitude
A proportional roll rate, which changes the attitude and the heading
A proportional roll angle, which changes the turn rate and the track
questions.explain: The force becomes a proportional roll rate, and a lasting roll rate changes the attitude and so the heading.

questions.question: A pilot applies force to the column and to the wheel at the same time in CWS. What two commands does the computer form from the sensor voltages?
options: A vertical speed or a turn rate command
A pitch rate or a roll attitude command
A pitch attitude or a roll rate command
questions.explain: The computer makes a pitch attitude command or a roll rate command out of the sensor voltage.

questions.question: The pilot reaches the speed he wanted and lets go of the control column after a supervisory override input. What does the pitch channel do at that moment?
options: It waits for the trim integrator to run out before any mode is reactivated
It sees the sensor signal fall to zero and reverts to the previous pitch attitude
It sees the sensor signal fall to zero and reactivates pitch attitude hold at once
questions.explain: Zero sensor signal is the trigger that immediately brings pitch attitude hold back.

questions.question: A meal is being served in the cabin and the pilot winds the outer knob below the heading window to its lower setting. What is he achieving?
options: A smaller maximum roll angle, which improves passenger comfort
A smaller maximum heading change, which improves passenger comfort
A slower heading capture rate, which improves passenger comfort
questions.explain: Reducing the maximum roll angle is what that knob does, and comfort is the stated reason for using it.

questions.question: The reference value reaching the inner loop no longer matches the actual value fed back to it. What does the inner loop do?
options: It commands a change in heading reference
It commands a change in rudder deflection
It commands a change in roll attitude
questions.explain: A difference between reference and actual roll angle makes the inner loop command a roll attitude change.

questions.question: An altitude or vertical speed controller is left to correct a turn on its own, with no lift compensation fitted. What is the consequence?
options: It reacts too early and causes a lasting offset from the reference value
It reacts correctly but leaves a permanent slip angle in the turn
It reacts too late and causes large errors or even unstable pitch control
questions.explain: Altitude and vertical speed change slowly, so the controller is late and large errors or instability follow.

questions.question: Leaving aside the thrust of the engines, how is the flight path of an aircraft changed in principle
options: By acting on the rotary degrees of freedom, that is by changing attitude
By acting on the thrust setting, that is by changing engine rating
By acting on the aerodynamic configuration, that is by changing flap setting
questions.explain: The aircraft is moved about its path by changing its attitude.

questions.question: The autopilot pitch channel lowers the nose while it is controlling speed. What energy change takes place and what does the speed do?
options: Potential energy becomes kinetic energy and the speed increases
Potential energy becomes kinetic energy and the speed decreases
Kinetic energy becomes potential energy and the speed decreases
questions.explain: Pitching down converts height into speed, so the aircraft accelerates.

questions.question: A level change climb is being flown. What decides the amount of pitch change and the climb rate that result?
options: Only the surplus of thrust from the rating set by the thrust system
Only the altitude error between present and preselected flight level
Only the pitch attitude limit applied by the autopilot pitch channel
questions.explain: Both depend only on the surplus of thrust left after the thrust system has set its rating.

questions.question: When should a crew with only IAS hold available select it during a climb or a descent?
options: Once the new flight level has been selected
Once the new reference speed has been reached
Before the thrust system reaches its climb limit
questions.explain: Because it only freezes the current value, it is selected after the wanted speed has been reached.

questions.question: The crew look at the speed window on the mode control panel and see dashes. What does that tell them?
options: The speed target has been lost and the autothrottle has disengaged
The speed target is being supplied by the flight management system
The speed target is outside the limits of the flight envelope
questions.explain: Dashes in the window mean the target is managed by the FMS rather than selected by hand.

questions.question: A crew wants to work to a Mach reference well below the normal transition height. What can they do and where?
options: Press the crossover pushbutton beside the altitude select display
Re-enter the target as a Mach number in the flight management system
Press the crossover pushbutton beside the speed and Mach display
questions.explain: The crossover pushbutton beside the speed and Mach display allows a change over at any altitude.

questions.question: A descent at a lower reference speed is commanded. In what order does the pitch controller act?
options: It reduces the speed error to zero first and then pitches down
It reduces the speed error and pitches down at the same time
It pitches down first and then reduces the speed error to zero
questions.explain: The speed error is taken out first, and only then does the aircraft pitch down.

cards.question: Which other name is given to closed loop control
options: actuation
correction
regulation
cards.explain: Closed loop control is also called regulation, because the control value is permanently monitored and compared with the reference value.

cards.question: Which quantity is denoted by Xw in the terms used for closed loop control
options: control value
reference value
error
cards.explain: Xw is the symbol given for the error in a closed loop system.

cards.question: Besides permanent monitoring of the control value, which feature is typical of closed loop control
options: its chain like sequence of effects through the actuator
its feedback to and comparison with the reference value
its conversion by the controller into an input value
cards.explain: Closed loop control is defined by feeding the control value back and comparing it with the reference value.

cards.question: Which feature is characteristic of open loop control
options: the comparison made at the controller input
the chain like sequence of effects
the permanent monitoring of the output
cards.explain: In open loop control the effects run in a chain from input to output with no return path.

cards.question: In a closed loop system the control value and the reference value are found to differ. What happens to that difference?
options: It is passed to the measurement unit and stored until the next comparison
It is converted in the actuator into an output which acts on the controller
It is converted in the controller into an output which acts on the actuator
cards.explain: The error goes to the controller, whose output drives the actuator.

cards.question: In a closed loop system, which quantity of the controlled system does the actuator modify
options: the disturbance acting on it
its output, the control value
its input, the reference value
cards.explain: The actuator acts on the controlled system so that the control value changes.

cards.question: In an open loop arrangement, on what does the controller output act?
options: On the system to be controlled, which in turn acts on an actuator
On a measurement unit, which in turn acts on the reference value
On an actuator, which in turn acts on the system to be controlled
cards.explain: The order runs controller, then actuator, then controlled system.

cards.question: An open loop system holds its output value constant while a disturbance acts; the reference value is varied until which condition is reached
options: the disturbance is measured and fed back to the controller input for comparison
the controller output and the reference value become equal to each other
the effect of the controller output and that of the disturbance equalize each other
cards.explain: With no feedback the only way to hold the output is to trim the reference until the two effects cancel.

cards.question: A controlled system is acted on by disturbances whose effect cannot be predicted. Why is open loop control the wrong choice here?
options: It needs a measurement unit that unpredictable disturbances overload
It feeds the disturbance back and so amplifies the error further
It can only correct for what was allowed for in advance
cards.explain: Without feedback the correction must be worked out beforehand, which an unpredictable disturbance makes impossible.

cards.question: A gust disturbs an aircraft that is being regulated. How is that disturbance dealt with?
options: It is fed back to the controller input and so more or less equalized
It is removed by the actuator before it reaches the controlled system
It is predicted by the controller and allowed for before it arrives
cards.explain: Feedback carries the disturbance back to the controller input, where it is largely cancelled.

cards.question: For a P - Regulator, to what is the change in the output value always proportional
options: the rate of change of the input value
the change in the input value
the magnitude of the input value
cards.explain: A proportional regulator ties the change of its output directly to the change of its input.

cards.question: For an I - Regulator, to what is the rate of change of the output value proportional
options: the change in its output value
its input value
the rate of change of its input value
cards.explain: In an integral regulator it is how fast the output moves that follows the input.

cards.question: How are the six degrees of freedom of an aircraft in the air divided
options: four rotary and two translatory degrees of freedom
three rotary and three translatory degrees of freedom
two rotary and four translatory degrees of freedom
cards.explain: The six split evenly into three rotary and three translatory.

cards.question: Which axes do the three degrees of rotary freedom turn about
options: roll, pitch and yaw axes
longitudinal, lateral and flight path axes
roll, pitch and heading axes
cards.explain: Rotation takes place about the X or roll, Y or pitch and Z or yaw axes.

cards.question: What do flight parameters describe
options: the state of the aircraft fixed coordinate system
the state of motion of an aircraft
the state of the autopilot regulators
cards.explain: A flight parameter is a physical quantity that describes how the aircraft is moving.

cards.question: Which motions are described by flight condition parameters
options: translatory motions
rotary motions
oscillatory motions
cards.explain: Flight condition parameters belong to the rotary degrees of freedom.

cards.question: Into which two parts is the flight path of a transport category airplane separated
options: an inner and an outer profile
a horizontal and a vertical profile
a rotary and a translatory profile
cards.explain: The path is split into a horizontal profile and a vertical profile.

cards.question: Which autopilot channel is used to follow a vertical profile
options: longitudinal or pitch channel
directional or yaw channel
lateral or roll channel
cards.explain: The vertical profile is flown by the longitudinal, that is the pitch, channel.

cards.question: A control loop contains one energy storage device. What does this produce?
options: An output value that follows the input value without any delay
An oscillation of the output value after a change of the input
A delay in the development of the output value over time
cards.explain: One storage device gives P1 behaviour, which is a lag in the output.

cards.question: A control loop contains two energy storage devices. What is the consequence?
options: Energy is held fast, so the output value is merely delayed
Energy is dissipated, so the output value follows without delay
