options: By deflecting the rudder in coordination with the ailerons
By deflecting the elevator in coordination with the ailerons
By deflecting the spoilers in coordination with the rudder
cards.explain: Rudder deflection coordinated with the aileron deflection takes the slip out.

cards.question: A meal is being served in the cabin and the pilot winds the outer knob below the heading window to its lower setting. What is he achieving?
options: A smaller maximum roll angle, which improves passenger comfort
A smaller maximum heading change, which improves passenger comfort
A slower heading capture rate, which improves passenger comfort
cards.explain: Reducing the maximum roll angle is what that knob does, and comfort is the stated reason for using it.

cards.question: What is the heading error turned into before it leaves the outer control loop
options: A roll rate reference value fed to the inner loop
A roll angle reference value fed to the inner loop
An aileron position demand fed to the servo
cards.explain: The outer loop converts heading error into a roll angle reference for the inner loop.

cards.question: The reference value reaching the inner loop no longer matches the actual value fed back to it. What does the inner loop do?
options: It commands a change in heading reference
It commands a change in rudder deflection
It commands a change in roll attitude
cards.explain: A difference between reference and actual roll angle makes the inner loop command a roll attitude change.

cards.question: The autopilot banks the aircraft into a turn and must not let it descend. Why does the elevator have to be deflected as well?
options: Total lift must fall so its horizontal part still curves the path
Total lift must rise so its vertical part still balances the weight
Total drag must rise so the airspeed stays at the reference value
cards.explain: Banking tilts the lift, so total lift must be increased to keep the vertical part equal to the weight.

cards.question: An altitude or vertical speed controller is left to correct a turn on its own, with no lift compensation fitted. What is the consequence?
options: It reacts too early and causes a lasting offset from the reference value
It reacts too late and causes large errors or even unstable pitch control
It reacts correctly but leaves a permanent slip angle in the turn
cards.explain: Altitude and vertical speed change slowly, so the controller is late and large errors or instability follow.

cards.question: A turn is entered and the bank angle goes on increasing. How does the input the pitch channel receives from the lateral channel change?
options: It increases aileron deflection in proportion to the existing pitch angle
It increases elevator deflection in proportion to the existing turn rate
It increases elevator deflection in proportion to the existing roll angle
cards.explain: Lift compensation adds elevator in proportion to the bank angle to raise the vertical lift component.

cards.question: The autopilot increases lift to hold altitude in a turn. Why must the thrust system then be brought in as well?
options: Because the extra lift brings extra weight, which would lower the ceiling
Because the extra bank brings extra slip, which would raise the fuel flow
Because the extra lift brings extra drag, which would lower the airspeed
cards.explain: More lift means more drag and a loss of speed, so a roll to thrust coupling adds thrust to hold the speed.

cards.question: The autoflight system lets the altitude wander slightly instead of correcting it at once. What does the airline gain from that?
options: Fewer thrust changes, so less fuel is burnt and comfort improves
Fewer altitude errors, so less drag is created and comfort improves
Fewer mode changes, so less wear occurs and comfort improves
cards.explain: Trading energy cuts the number of thrust changes, which saves fuel and makes the ride smoother.

cards.question: From which two sources does the airspeed or Mach reference number come
options: Dialled by the pilot at the mode control panel or supplied by the ADC
Dialled by the pilot at the mode control panel or supplied by the FMS
Computed by the autopilot from the flight plan or supplied by the FMS
cards.explain: It is either dialled by hand on the mode control panel or passed over by the FMS.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the LVL/CH mode
options: To transfer speed control automatically to the auto-thrust system
To transfer the aircraft automatically to a higher or lower flight level
To transfer the aircraft automatically onto a selected vertical speed
cards.explain: The mode exists to take the aircraft automatically from one flight level to another.

cards.question: Which computer normally calculates the thrust limits for each flight phase
options: The flight control computer
The flight warning computer
The FADEC computer
cards.explain: The FADEC computer works out the thrust limits for each flight phase.

cards.question: In which memory is the reference value stored
options: The speed and Mach memory
The altitude capture memory
The attitude command memory
cards.explain: It is held in the speed and Mach memory.

cards.question: What is the source of the control value used for airspeed or Mach number control
options: The air data computer
The inertial reference system
The flight management system
cards.explain: Calibrated airspeed or Mach comes from the air data computer.

cards.question: What part does the pilot himself play when he is flying the aircraft along its flight path by hand
options: He makes up a feedback path for the attitude command memory
He makes up an outer loop for the translatory degrees of freedom
He makes up an inner loop for the three rotational degrees of freedom
cards.explain: A hand-flying pilot is himself the outer loop for the translatory degrees of freedom.

cards.question: How did the term autopilot become established
options: From the automatic trim function of relieving the loads at the control column
From the automatic stability function of damping the aircraft about its axes
From the automatic pilot function of guiding the aircraft along its flight path
cards.explain: The name comes from the system doing the pilot's job of guiding the aircraft along the flight path.

cards.question: A flight path controller is doing its job on a normal sector. Which upper autopilot modes do its tasks correspond to?
options: Takeoff, climb, descend, flare and automatic braking
Climb, cruise, hold, go around and automatic taxi
Climb, enroute, descend, approach and automatic landing
cards.explain: Those five are the upper modes listed.

cards.question: What does a flight management system relieve the pilot of
options: Most manual control tasks, which it trims automatically
Most monitoring tasks, which it displays automatically
Most routine tasks, which it sequences automatically
cards.explain: The FMS takes over most routine tasks and sequences the events itself.

cards.question: An FMS is sequencing a flight path segment by segment. What does it do automatically at each one?
options: Choosing navigation aids and tuning their frequencies for each path segment
Choosing engine ratings and setting their thrust limits for each path segment
Choosing autopilot channels and testing their servos for each path segment
cards.explain: Selecting the right navigation aids and tuning them is the example given.

cards.question: Which quantities does a flight management system calculate for lowest fuel consumption
options: Optimal thrust limits, bleed air settings and flap schedules
Optimal bank angles, turn radii and track changes
Optimal climb and sink rates, cruise altitudes and airspeeds
cards.explain: Those are the optimal values the FMS works out for the lowest fuel burn.

cards.question: How does the autopilot pitch channel control airspeed or Mach number
options: By altering the thrust rating through the power lever position
By altering the drag through the speed brake panel setting
By altering the flight path angle through the aircraft's attitude
cards.explain: The pitch channel changes the flight path angle by changing pitch attitude with the elevator.

cards.question: How widely is the airspeed or Mach reference value applied once it is set
options: It is always applied to both speed control systems
It is always applied to the system holding priority only
It is always applied to the auto-thrust system only
cards.explain: The one reference value goes to both of the speed controlling systems.

cards.question: Under which condition does the autoflight system maintain the reference airspeed or Mach number during a level change
options: As long as no autopilot or auto-thrust channel has failed
As long as no thrust or flight envelope limits are exceeded
As long as no altitude or vertical speed limits are exceeded
cards.explain: The reference speed is held while thrust limits and envelope limits are respected.

cards.question: What does thrust alone have to overcome during an unaccelerated horizontal flight
options: Drag
Inertia
Weight
cards.explain: In level unaccelerated flight the thrust only has to balance the drag.

cards.question: Which system takes charge of airspeed or Mach number the moment a level change is triggered
options: The autopilot, which holds it by adjusting the flight path angle
The autopilot, which holds it by adjusting the thrust rating
The auto-thrust, which holds it by adjusting the thrust rating
cards.explain: At level change the autopilot always takes the speed and holds it with flight path angle.

cards.question: The crew select a higher flight level and trigger a level change. What thrust does the auto-thrust system set?
options: The maximum thrust for the present flight phase
The flight idle thrust for the present flight phase
The cruise thrust for the present flight phase
cards.explain: For a climb the system sets the maximum thrust applicable to the flight phase.

cards.question: What does the auto-thrust system do for a level change in the descending direction
options: It sets the flight idle rating
It disengages until capture
It sets the maximum continuous rating
cards.explain: A descent needs a lack of thrust, so flight idle is set.

cards.question: What do the thrust limits depend on
options: Actual gross weight and the amount of bleed air tapped from an engine
Actual air data and the amount of fuel remaining in the tanks
Actual air data and the amount of bleed air tapped from an engine
cards.explain: They depend on the air data of the moment and on how much bleed air is being taken.

cards.question: Why is the capture point needed
options: To give a smooth transition from a climb or descent to level flight
To give an accurate indication of the time left to the target level
To give a smooth transition from thrust mode to speed mode
cards.explain: It exists so that the levelling off at the selected flight level is smooth.

cards.question: The aircraft is in the capture phase and the altitude error is shrinking. How is the vertical speed brought down?
options: By decreasing the thrust rating in proportion to the decreasing altitude error
By decreasing the flight path angle in proportion to the decreasing speed error
By decreasing the flight path angle in proportion to the decreasing altitude error
cards.explain: The flight path angle is reduced in step with the shrinking altitude error.

cards.question: What happens to speed control when altitude acquisition becomes active
options: The pitch channel hands it to the thrust system, which goes to speed mode
The thrust system hands it to the pitch channel, which goes to speed mode
The pitch channel keeps it and the thrust system goes to thrust mode
cards.explain: The pitch channel is now needed for the capture, so speed passes to the thrust system in speed mode.

cards.question: Which is the only system performing speed control in IAS hold or Mach hold
options: The autothrottle system
The flight management system
The autopilot pitch channel
cards.explain: In this mode the autothrottle alone does the speed control.

cards.question: An autopilot offers only IAS hold and Mach hold. What is the limitation of that control mode?
options: It does not allow a change over between speed and Mach
It does not allow bracketing of a pre-selected reference speed
It does not allow the autothrottle to reach its thrust limit
cards.explain: There is no bracketing of a pre-selected reference speed in this mode.

cards.question: Which two names are used for the reference value according to where it comes from
options: Selected speed target or computed speed target
Preset speed target or managed speed target
Selected speed target or managed speed target
cards.explain: The two printed names are selected speed target and managed speed target.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs to the level at which speed control passes from airspeed to Mach number. What is that altitude called?
options: The optimum or cruise altitude
The capture or transition altitude
The crossover or changeover altitude
cards.explain: That altitude is called the cross or changeover altitude.

cards.question: How does the autoflight system stop an entered speed target from exceeding the flight envelope
options: By warning the crew and leaving the entered value in force
By rejecting the entered value and reverting to the last valid one
By voting between the entered value and the computed limits
cards.explain: The system votes between the entered value and the limits so the envelope is not exceeded.

cards.question: At which pressure altitude is the automatic change over performed during a climb or a descent
options: Approximately 18 000 feet
Approximately 36 000 feet
Approximately 26 000 feet
cards.explain: The printed altitude is approximately 26 000 feet.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs through the changeover altitude and the reference changes over by itself. Which system has done it?
options: The auto-throttle and auto-thrust system
The air data and inertial reference system
The autopilot and flight director system
cards.explain: The AP/FD system carries out the automatic change over.

cards.question: How is the airspeed and Mach control loop built up
options: An outer loop is added to the roll attitude controller
An outer loop is added to the pitch attitude controller
An inner loop is added to the altitude hold controller
cards.explain: The pitch attitude controller gains an outer loop to make the speed controller.

cards.question: Which autoflight mode sets up the airspeed and Mach outer control loop when it is selected
options: Heading select
Altitude hold
Level change
cards.explain: Selecting level change is what makes the mode logic build the outer loop.

cards.question: The speed controller is running in level change. Where is the speed error formed, and from what?
options: At S2, by comparing reference speed with actual speed
At S2, by comparing reference attitude with actual speed
At S1, by comparing reference attitude with actual attitude
cards.explain: S2 is the summing point where reference and actual speed are compared.

cards.question: What are the two jobs of the pitch attitude limiter
options: It curtails extreme commands and sets the gain schedule of the inner loop
It curtails extreme commands and sets the timing and direction of the change
It curtails the speed error and sets the timing and direction of the change
cards.explain: It both limits extreme attitude commands and governs when and which way the pitch change happens.

cards.question: Gusts push an aircraft away from its altitude and its track. Why can the inner control loops not put that right on their own?
options: The inner loops cannot compensate disturbances acting on the attitude
The inner loops cannot compensate disturbances acting on the flight path
The inner loops cannot drive the control surfaces without a servo
cards.explain: Inner loops stabilize attitude only, so outer loops are added for flight path disturbances.

cards.question: Leaving aside the thrust of the engines, how is the flight path of an aircraft changed in principle
options: By acting on the rotary degrees of freedom, that is by changing attitude
By acting on the thrust setting, that is by changing engine rating
By acting on the aerodynamic configuration, that is by changing flap setting
cards.explain: The aircraft is moved about its path by changing its attitude.

cards.question: Why does the autopilot have to treat interception and stabilization as two separate jobs?
options: The path is in segments, and each must be caught without overshoot or offset
The path is continuous, but the sensors update at two different rates
The path is in segments, and each one has to be flown at a different airspeed
cards.explain: Because the path is built of segments, each one has to be intercepted cleanly and then held.

cards.question: What must be in place before an FMS can guide an aircraft laterally and vertically from departure to destination?
options: A flight plan of waypoints and the relevant modes selected for the autoflight system
A flight plan of waypoints and the relevant frequencies tuned at the radio panel
A route clearance entered and the relevant altitudes set at the mode control panel
cards.explain: Both a waypoint flight plan and the FMS modes selected for the autoflight system are required.

cards.question: Both the pitch channel and the thrust system can hold the speed. Which of them gets the job, and why can they not share it?
options: The autopilot, because the flight management system cannot supply two targets
The autopilot, because the two systems cannot both control speed at once
The auto-thrust, because the two systems cannot both control speed at once
cards.explain: Only one may control speed, and the priority is given to the autopilot.

cards.question: The autopilot pitch channel lowers the nose while it is controlling speed. What energy change takes place and what does the speed do?
options: Potential energy becomes kinetic energy and the speed decreases
Kinetic energy becomes potential energy and the speed decreases
Potential energy becomes kinetic energy and the speed increases
cards.explain: Pitching down converts height into speed, so the aircraft accelerates.

cards.question: The pilot selects altitude hold, so the pitch channel is now given another job. Who controls the speed and how?
options: The auto-thrust system, by thrust control to a reference speed
The flight management system, by thrust control to a reference speed
The auto-thrust system, by drag control to a reference speed
cards.explain: With the pitch channel busy, speed passes to the auto-thrust, which holds it with thrust.

cards.question: The autopilot pitch channel is taken off speed control and put onto altitude hold. What does that decide for the thrust system?
options: Its engagement, which the pitch channel determines
Its mode of operation, which the pitch channel determines
Its thrust limit, which the pitch channel then determines
cards.explain: In current systems what the pitch channel is doing sets the mode the thrust system runs in.

cards.question: The autopilot is controlling speed in level flight and the thrust is then increased. What does the autopilot do with the aircraft?
options: It increases the flight path angle and the aircraft begins to accelerate
It increases the flight path angle and the aircraft begins to climb
It decreases the flight path angle and the aircraft begins to climb
cards.explain: The autopilot holds speed by raising the flight path angle, so the surplus thrust becomes a climb.

cards.question: A level change climb is being flown. What decides the amount of pitch change and the climb rate that result?
options: Only the pitch attitude limit applied by the autopilot pitch channel
Only the surplus of thrust from the rating set by the thrust system
Only the altitude error between present and preselected flight level
cards.explain: Both depend only on the surplus of thrust left after the thrust system has set its rating.

cards.question: How does the thrust system decide whether to apply its thrust limit or flight idle at the start of a level change?
options: It evaluates the size of the altitude error, taken as preselected minus actual
It evaluates the sign of the speed error, taken as reference minus actual
It evaluates the sign of the altitude error, taken as preselected minus actual
cards.explain: The sign of the altitude error tells the system whether the aircraft must go up or down.

cards.question: An aircraft is climbing fast towards the selected level. How does its high vertical speed affect the point at which the capture starts?
options: The capture point is unaffected, being a fixed distance from the level
The capture point is placed closer to the level, in proportion to it
The capture point is placed further from the level, in proportion to it
cards.explain: The capture point is a vertical distance from the selected level set in proportion to the vertical speed of the moment.

cards.question: The aircraft reaches the capture point during a level change climb. Which mode changes take place?
options: Level change is rearmed and altitude acquisition is turned off
Level change is turned off and altitude acquisition is activated
Level change is turned off and altitude hold is activated
cards.explain: At the capture point level change drops out and altitude acquisition takes over.

cards.question: Why can the altitude acquisition law not simply be left running until the selected level is reached?
options: Its transition follows a ramp function, which would overshoot the level
Its transition follows an e-function, which would take an infinite time
Its gain is scheduled with airspeed, which would change during the capture
cards.explain: The capture is exponential, so in theory it never quite arrives and must be terminated.

cards.question: When should a crew with only IAS hold available select it during a climb or a descent?
options: Once the new flight level has been selected
Once the new reference speed has been reached
Before the thrust system reaches its climb limit
cards.explain: Because it only freezes the current value, it is selected after the wanted speed has been reached.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs through the changeover altitude with a speed target that was dialled in by hand. What becomes of the number in the window?
options: It is replaced by dashes until the pilot enters a Mach number
It is converted to the equivalent true airspeed and displayed there
It is converted to the equivalent Mach number and displayed there
cards.explain: At the transition the value is converted to the equivalent Mach number, and a value entered at the panel is shown there.

cards.question: The crew look at the speed window on the mode control panel and see dashes. What does that tell them?
options: The speed target is outside the limits of the flight envelope
The speed target has been lost and the autothrottle has disengaged
The speed target is being supplied by the flight management system
cards.explain: Dashes in the window mean the target is managed by the FMS rather than selected by hand.

cards.question: A Mach target is being flown at a high flight level. What does the reference speed marker on the primary flight display show?
options: A calibrated airspeed, because the tape is in CAS at any altitude
A Mach number, because the tape follows the active reference
An indicated airspeed, because the tape is in IAS at any altitude
cards.explain: The tape reads calibrated airspeed only, so a marker on it is a CAS value whatever the altitude or active reference.

cards.question: The actual speed differs from the stored reference when a speed mode is armed. Why is the stored value synchronized first, and how?
options: To avoid a hard over, by storing the envelope limit at mode activation
To avoid a hard over, by storing the actual value at mode activation
To avoid an envelope exceedance, by storing the actual value at mode activation
cards.explain: Synchronizing to the actual speed at activation stops the controller making a violent correction.

cards.question: The flaps and the landing gear are extended. Which of the two configuration speed limits does VMAX take?
options: The lower of VFE and VLE
The higher of VFE and VLE
The lower of VMO and MMO
cards.explain: For an extended flap, slat and gear configuration the printed rule takes whichever of VFE and VLE is the lower.

cards.question: A crew wants to work to a Mach reference well below the normal transition height. What can they do and where?
options: Re-enter the target as a Mach number in the flight management system
Press the crossover pushbutton beside the altitude select display
Press the crossover pushbutton beside the speed and Mach display
cards.explain: The crossover pushbutton beside the speed and Mach display allows a change over at any altitude.

cards.question: Which parameter is held constant above the automatic change over level and which below
options: Indicated airspeed above and Mach number below
Mach number above and indicated airspeed below
True airspeed above and indicated airspeed below
cards.explain: Above the change over the Mach number is held and below it the indicated airspeed is held.

cards.question: What does the PI behaviour of the outer loop prevent, and how
options: A standing speed error, by limiting the pitch attitude being commanded
A standing speed error, by integrating it into the attitude reference
An unstable speed loop, by integrating it into the thrust demand
cards.explain: Integrating the lasting error corrects the attitude reference until the error is removed.

cards.question: A descent at a lower reference speed is commanded. In what order does the pitch controller act?
options: It reduces the speed error and pitches down at the same time
It reduces the speed error to zero first and then pitches down
It pitches down first and then reduces the speed error to zero
cards.explain: The speed error is taken out first, and only then does the aircraft pitch down.

cards.question: What is the result of changing pitch attitude whenever a speed error appears at a given thrust
options: The aircraft adopts a thrust rating that restores the reference speed
The aircraft adopts a flight path angle that restores the reference speed
The aircraft adopts a vertical speed that restores the reference altitude
cards.explain: Changing attitude puts the aircraft on the flight path angle that holds the reference speed for the thrust set.

questions.question: Which quantity does the vertical speed mode bracket and maintain
options: A climb or descend rate
A pitch attitude value
A flight path bank angle
questions.explain: The mode brackets and holds a vertical speed, which is the same thing as a climb or descend rate.

questions.question: An autopilot is holding a rate of climb in vertical speed mode. Which unit supplies the controlled value used by the outer loop?
options: The flight management system
The air data computer
The inertial reference system
questions.explain: Vertical speed is an air data parameter and comes from the air data computer.

questions.question: With what is the commanded rate of climb compared to give the output error of the outer loop in the rate of climb mode
options: The actual vertical speed measured by the air data computer
The target flight level set on the autoflight control panel
The pitch attitude measured by the inertial reference system
questions.explain: An error is reference minus actual, and the actual rate is the air data computer measurement.

questions.question: What does the mode annunciation read while the level off mode is in use
options: LVL CHG
ALT
V/S = 0
questions.explain: The level off condition is annunciated as a commanded vertical speed of zero.

questions.question: What is true of the provisions protecting against violation of airspeed and Mach limits
options: They are identical in every modern autoflight system
They apply only to the vertical speed mode
They differ a lot between aircraft types
questions.explain: The provisions vary so much from one type to another that no single description covers them all.

questions.question: Into which altitude does the altitude acquisition mode transfer an aircraft at the end of a climb or descent
options: A pilot selected vertical speed or flight path angle
A pilot selected QNH-altitude or pressure altitude
A pilot selected capture altitude or transition level
questions.explain: The target is an altitude the pilot has set, read either against QNH or as a pressure altitude.

questions.question: At what point is the outer control loop closed in the altitude acquisition mode
options: When the tolerance band is reached
When an altitude is pre-selected
When the capture condition is met
questions.explain: Arming only starts the detector, and the loop is not closed until the capture condition is met.

questions.question: With which system does the profile or vertical navigation mode connect the autoflight system
options: The flight management system
The inertial reference system
The air data computer
questions.explain: Vertical navigation is flown on data the flight management system supplies, so the two are coupled.

questions.question: Over what span of a flight do the sequential segments of profile or vertical navigation guidance run
options: From the capture point to the transition altitude
From after take off to the instrument approach
From the top of climb to the top of descent
questions.explain: The sequential segments are stated as running from just after take off through to the approach.

questions.question: In which mode does the autothrust system work while the altitude hold mode is active
options: Thrust mode
Idle mode
Speed mode
questions.explain: With the pitch channel holding height, the autothrust takes the speed and works to a speed target.

questions.question: Below what size of airspeed disturbance is the soft altitude deviation permitted
options: 10 Kts
5 Kts
4 Kts
questions.explain: The allowance applies only to disturbances below four knots.

questions.question: Why does the roll controller change over to the On-Course Phase once the preselected radial is almost reached
options: To hand the lateral guidance over to the heading hold controller
To increase the rate at which the heading error is reduced
To improve its behaviour with respect to cross wind disturbances
questions.explain: Cross wind disturbance behaviour is what the change of phase improves.

questions.question: Which heading error does the roll controller have to leave standing while an aircraft tracks a radial in a steady crosswind
options: The one equivalent to the VOR course deviation angle
The one equivalent to the wind correction angle
The one equivalent to the preselected course
questions.explain: The crab angle must be kept, so the heading error equal to the wind correction angle is left alone.

questions.question: A waypoint has to be passed at a given altitude with a given airspeed maintained during a climb. What does the flight management computer calculate?
options: An optimum thrust for the required flight path angle
An optimum vertical speed for the required altitude
An optimum flight path angle for the required thrust
questions.explain: The constraint fixes the path to be flown, so what the computer works out is the thrust that path needs.

questions.question: The radial deviation rate rises above eight millivolts per second. What does the roll controller do?
options: It transits to heading control and maintains the present heading
It transits to capture control and re-intercepts the radial
It transits to heading control and reverses the pre-selected course
questions.explain: A fast moving deviation signals the cone of confusion, so the controller freezes the heading and flies on.

questions.question: A washout has been added to the navigation loop and the aircraft is tracking a radial in a steady crosswind — what is the relationship between the aircraft heading and the PSC?
options: The heading is aligned with the PSC and the track is offset
The heading differs from the PSC by the measured VOR deviation angle
The heading differs from the PSC by the wind correction angle
questions.explain: With the washout fitted the radial is tracked, so the crab is carried as a heading difference from the PSC.

questions.question: The VOR deviation signal has been switched off and the heading error signal connected to S3 during the Over Station Phase — how does the controller then behave?
options: The heading loop is off and it acts as a navigation controller only
The navigation loop is off and it acts as a heading controller only
The navigation loop is off and it acts as a roll rate controller only
questions.explain: With the deviation signal gone and the washout bypassed, only the heading loop remains in use.

questions.question: Why does the back beam mode count as a Non-Precision Approach
options: Because no vertical guidance is available in this mode
Because no lateral guidance is available in this mode
Because the deviation signal polarity is inverted in this mode
questions.explain: Only lateral guidance exists on the back beam, so the approach is non-precision.

questions.question: The localizer mode has been selected on its own on the autoflight control panel as an independent lateral mode — which phase is left out?
options: The Localizer-Track Phase
The Approach-Track Phase
The Capture Phase
questions.explain: Selecting LOC as an independent lateral mode omits the Approach-Track Phase.

questions.question: Two aircraft intercept the same localizer from very different distances to the transmitter antenna — what does the adaptive capture threshold guarantee?
options: The same intercept angle onto the beam for both
The best possible beginning of the transition onto the beam for both
The same bank angle throughout the transition onto the beam for both
questions.explain: The threshold is written to be independent of range, so the turn-on point is right in either case.

questions.question: Why does a further 180° have to be subtracted from the heading error built on the preselected front course
options: Because the actual heading error has to be taken from the back course
Because the actual heading error has to be taken from the front course
Because the deviation bar polarity has already been reversed
questions.explain: The usable heading error is referenced to the back course, so another 180° comes off.

questions.question: Which common mode is available for the flight director only
options: ILS APPROACH/LAND
GO AROUND
TAKE OFF
questions.explain: The take off mode is listed as a flight director function only.

questions.question: An aircraft is below the JAR-AWO height with the Land mode engaged — what are the only two ways of deactivating it?
options: Turning off the autopilot or turning off the auto-thrust
Selecting Go Around or selecting another vertical mode
Selecting Go Around or turning off the autopilot
questions.explain: Only a Go Around selection or switching the autopilot off removes the mode below that height.

questions.question: The Approach/Land mode is engaged at 200 ft AGL and the crew decides to discontinue the approach — which mode can still take over?
options: The altitude hold mode
The heading select mode
The Go Around mode
questions.explain: Go Around can supersede Approach/Land at any height, unlike other upper modes.

questions.question: An automatic landing is being flown and the glide path has just been left — what is held until the flare phase begins?
options: The momentary glide slope angle
The momentary sink rate
The momentary pitch attitude
questions.explain: The sink rate at that moment is frozen until the flare starts.

questions.question: Beam convergence has been left uncompensated on an ILS approach — how does the glide path controller behave at long range and close in?
options: Sluggish far out and prone to oscillation near the runway
Sluggish far out and unable to hold the beam near the runway
Prone to oscillation far out and sluggish near the runway
questions.explain: Low gain far out makes it sluggish, and rising gain close in makes it oscillate.

questions.question: An aircraft intercepts the glide path from above — what does the pitch controller command at synchronization?
options: A pitch-up, so the aircraft levels off above the glide path
A pitch-over, so the aircraft flares onto the glide path
A pitch-up, so the aircraft flares onto the glide path
questions.explain: All signs invert from above, giving a pitch-up and a flare onto the beam.

questions.question: From where does the preselected course reach the yaw channel as its reference value
options: From the flight management computer
From the autoflight control panel
From the inertial reference system
questions.explain: The crew sets the preselected course on the autoflight control panel and that is the yaw reference.

questions.question: Which signal guides the aircraft along the runway centre line after touch-down
options: The radio altitude signal
The localizer deviation signal
The glide path deviation signal
questions.explain: Roll out steering uses the localizer deviation.

questions.question: The landing controller adds a height bias to the measured radio altitude close to the ground — what does this achieve at the wheels?
options: A thrust increase is still commanded once the aircraft is on the ground
A sink rate is still commanded once the aircraft is on the ground
A pitch up is still commanded once the aircraft is on the ground
questions.explain: Because the controller thinks it is higher than it is, it keeps commanding a descent and so forces a positive touch down.

questions.question: The flare controller stops rounding the path off at its upper limit — what would happen beyond that limit?
options: The aircraft would risk a long float before touch down
The aircraft would risk a nose gear strike at touch down
The aircraft would risk a tail strike at touch down
questions.explain: Too much nose up at touchdown would put the tail on the runway.

questions.question: The auto-trim is switched off at the same time as the derotation — what would otherwise drive the trim?
options: A constant pitch error caused by the elevator's negative moment
A constant pitch rate caused by the elevator's negative moment
A constant pitch error caused by the stabilizer's positive moment
questions.explain: The elevator holds a steady nose down moment after derotation, and the standing pitch error that leaves would wake the trim system up.

questions.question: Why is the aircraft headed into the wind during a cross wind approach
options: To prevent a displacement from the localizer beam
To prevent a bank angle on the localizer beam
To prevent a lateral load on the landing gear
questions.explain: Crabbing into the wind stops the aircraft being blown off the beam, so it drifts along it instead.

questions.question: The aircraft is rolling out fast with the nose gear still off the ground — how is the direction held?
options: By rudder deflections and nose wheel steering
By rudder deflections only
By nose wheel steering only
questions.explain: With the nose off the ground only the rudder is available, and at that speed it still bites.

questions.question: The aircraft is being steered along the centre line after landing — which two signals does the yaw controller process?
options: The heading error and the localizer deviation
The crab angle and the localizer deviation
The heading error and the glide path deviation
questions.explain: Both a heading error and a lateral displacement have to be removed, so both signals are used.

questions.question: Which name is given to the transition phase from an approach to a stabilized climb
options: An align manoeuvre
A go around manoeuvre
A roll out manoeuvre
questions.explain: That transition is exactly what is called a go around.

questions.question: A go around is selected on the approach — which three parts of the autoflight system come in together?
options: The pitch channel, the roll channel and the auto-thrust system
The roll channel, the yaw channel and the auto-thrust system
The pitch channel, the yaw channel and the auto-thrust system
questions.explain: Go around is a common mode and brings pitch, roll and the thrust system in together.

questions.question: The aircraft touches down while a go around is being flown — what happens to the mode?
options: It changes into the rollout mode
It is terminated at once
It stays active
questions.explain: The mode survives a touch down, which is what makes a touch and go possible.

questions.question: The go around controller rotates the aircraft to a fixed positive pitch attitude — what follows from that?
options: Lift increases and the momentary sink rate decreases
Lift increases and the momentary airspeed increases
Drag increases and the momentary sink rate decreases
questions.explain: More attitude means more lift, and more lift arrests the descent.

questions.question: Which angle appears when the airspeed reference is changed while the thrust is held constant
options: A correction angle that changes the present flight path angle
An error angle that changes the present angle of attack
A demand angle that changes the present pitch attitude
questions.explain: The speed error is worked off by a correction angle that tilts the flight path so the aircraft accelerates or decelerates.

cards.question: Which quantity does the vertical speed mode bracket and maintain
options: A climb or descend rate
A pitch attitude value
A flight path bank angle
cards.explain: The mode brackets and holds a vertical speed, which is the same thing as a climb or descend rate.

cards.question: Which system safeguards airspeed control automatically while the vertical speed mode is bracketing a rate
options: The autothrust system
The flight management system
The inertial reference system
cards.explain: The autothrottle/autothrust system is what keeps the airspeed safe while pitch holds the rate.

cards.question: How many control loops make up the cascade used for closed loop control of vertical speed
options: One
Two
Three
cards.explain: The cascade for vertical speed has two loops.

cards.question: An autopilot is holding a rate of climb in vertical speed mode. Which unit supplies the controlled value used by the outer loop?
options: The flight management system
The inertial reference system
The air data computer
cards.explain: Vertical speed is an air data parameter and comes from the air data computer.

cards.question: Which kind of controller is the vertical speed controller
options: A D-controller
A PI-controller
A P-controller
cards.explain: The vertical speed controller is a PI-controller.

cards.question: What decides how many ways there are of selecting the vertical speed mode on a given aircraft
options: The transition altitude in force
The vertical speed value stored
The type of autopilot installed
cards.explain: How many ways there are depends on which autopilot is fitted to the aircraft.

cards.question: Where the vertical speed mode is a basic mode, which condition alone maintains the momentary rate of climb
options: The autopilot is disengaged
The autopilot is engaged
A target flight level is dialled up
cards.explain: As a basic mode it needs no separate selection, so engaging the autopilot alone holds the rate the aircraft already has.

cards.question: The autopilot is holding a vertical speed as a basic mode and the crew want a different rate. How is a new reference value introduced?
options: By pressing the vertical speed button on the control panel
By rotating the vertical speed knob on the control panel
By disengaging and re-engaging the autopilot at the new rate
cards.explain: With the mode already running, turning the knob is what changes the reference value, and it may be done at any time.

cards.question: How is the vertical speed mode brought in where it is an upper mode rather than a basic one
options: It is maintained automatically by engaging the autopilot alone
It is selected explicitly at the control panel
It is armed by the air data computer at take off
cards.explain: An upper mode is not automatic, so the crew must select it deliberately on the panel.

cards.question: When may the reference rate be dialled up in the selection sequence for the vertical speed mode as an upper mode
options: Only before mode activation
Only once the target level is reached
Either before or after mode activation
cards.explain: The reference value may be set on either side of mode activation.

cards.question: At what point is the outer control loop closed during vertical speed control
options: When the mode is selected
When the capture point is reached
When the target level is reached
cards.explain: Selecting the mode is what closes the outer loop for vertical speed control.

cards.question: From where does the outer loop of the rate of climb mode obtain its reference value
options: The flight management computer
The vertical speed memory
The altitude memory
cards.explain: The stored reference for this mode is held in, and supplied from, the vertical speed memory.

cards.question: With what is the commanded rate of climb compared to give the output error of the outer loop in the rate of climb mode
options: The pitch attitude measured by the inertial reference system
The target flight level set on the autoflight control panel
The actual vertical speed measured by the air data computer
cards.explain: An error is reference minus actual, and the actual rate is the air data computer measurement.

cards.question: What does the vertical speed controller determine and pass on to the inner loop
options: A vertical speed reference value
A pitch attitude reference value
An elevator deflection angle
cards.explain: The outer loop controller sets an attitude reference which the inner loop then follows.

cards.question: An upper pitch mode is switched off in flight on an aircraft whose basic pitch mode holds the momentary rate of climb. Which mode does the autopilot then adopt?
options: Altitude acquisition mode
Altitude hold mode
Vertical speed mode
cards.explain: Where vertical speed is the basic mode, switching off any upper vertical mode leaves the autopilot in vertical speed.

cards.question: The vertical speed mode is an upper mode on the aircraft. Which action comes first in the sequence of events to be observed?
options: Pressing the vertical speed button
Selecting the target flight level
Arming the altitude acquisition mode
cards.explain: The printed sequence begins with selection of the wanted target flight level, before the mode is activated.

cards.question: What is synchronisation of the vertical speed reference value intended to prevent
options: Controller activity at the moment of mode activation
A reference value being changed after mode activation
A loss of the air data computer rate signal in flight
cards.explain: A stored value unlike the actual rate would make the controller act the instant the mode came in, and synchronisation removes that step.

cards.question: In the vertical speed mode the pitch attitude is altered. Why does the actual rate of climb then change?
options: Because the trim integrator alters the stabiliser setting
Because the air data computer re-corrects its altitude output
Because the flight path angle changes at constant airspeed
cards.explain: With speed held, a change of attitude becomes a change of flight path angle and therefore of rate of climb or descent.

cards.question: To what value is the vertical speed reference set when the level off mode is selected
options: The momentary vertical speed
The last value held in memory
A rate of zero
cards.explain: Levelling off means commanding no rate at all, so the reference becomes zero.

cards.question: What does the mode annunciation read while the level off mode is in use
options: LVL CHG
V/S = 0
ALT
cards.explain: The level off condition is annunciated as a commanded vertical speed of zero.

cards.question: An altitude has just been pre-selected at the autoflight control panel. What does the autoflight system annunciate?
options: ALT active
ALT ACQ armed
ALT ACQ active
cards.explain: Pre-selection arms the mode, so the armed annunciation appears first.

cards.question: The level off mode has just been selected during a climb. What does the vertical speed controller do?
options: It reduces the actual rate to zero and holds zero
It reduces the actual rate by half and then holds it
It holds the altitude reached when the mode was selected
cards.explain: The same controller drives the rate down to nothing and then keeps it there.

cards.question: What is true of the provisions protecting against violation of airspeed and Mach limits
options: They differ a lot between aircraft types
They apply only to the vertical speed mode
They are identical in every modern autoflight system
cards.explain: The provisions vary so much from one type to another that no single description covers them all.

cards.question: While a commanded climb rate is being held, over what does the task of the pitch channel take precedence
options: Track controlled by the roll channel
Speed controlled by the autothrust system
Altitude controlled by the altitude memory
cards.explain: The pitch channel holds the rate first, which is exactly why the speed can drift to a limit.

cards.question: Into which altitude does the altitude acquisition mode transfer an aircraft at the end of a climb or descent
options: A pilot selected capture altitude or transition level
A pilot selected vertical speed or flight path angle
A pilot selected QNH-altitude or pressure altitude
cards.explain: The target is an altitude the pilot has set, read either against QNH or as a pressure altitude.

cards.question: When is the capture detector of the altitude acquisition mode activated
options: When an altitude is pre-selected on the panel
When the aircraft reaches the capture point
When the altitude hold mode becomes active
cards.explain: Dialling the altitude is enough to start the detector running, long before any capture.

cards.question: Together with the actual rate of climb, what else enters the continuous calculation of the capture point
options: The barometric correction applied by the air data computer
The momentary airspeed error against the speed limit
The momentary vertical distance to the selected altitude
cards.explain: The two quantities entering the calculation are the rate of closure and the height still to go.

cards.question: In which case is the altitude representing the capture point baro-corrected
options: When it is at or below the transition altitude
When it is anywhere above the transition altitude
When it is at or above the selected flight level
cards.explain: Below the transition altitude altitudes are flown on QNH, so the baro correction is applied.

cards.question: The aircraft reaches the calculated capture point in a descent. What does the mode logic do?
options: It makes the altitude acquisition mode active
It arms the altitude acquisition mode
It makes the altitude hold mode active instead
cards.explain: Reaching the point is the capture condition, so the mode goes from armed to active.

cards.question: At what point is the outer control loop closed in the altitude acquisition mode
options: When the capture condition is met
When an altitude is pre-selected
When the tolerance band is reached
cards.explain: Arming only starts the detector, and the loop is not closed until the capture condition is met.

cards.question: To what does the vertical speed reference value correspond in the altitude acquisition outer loop
options: The altitude error
The measured vertical speed
The selected altitude
cards.explain: Height still to go is converted directly into a commanded rate, which is why the rate falls as the gap closes.

cards.question: With what is the pre-selected altitude compared in S3 to form the altitude error
options: The aircraft's actual altitude
The baro-corrected capture altitude
The aircraft's actual vertical speed
cards.explain: An altitude error can only be the difference between the target altitude and the one being flown.

cards.question: An altitude acquisition is running and the altitude error has become the reference for the outer loop. With what is that reference compared in S2?
options: The actual vertical speed
The pre-selected altitude
The pitch reference value
cards.explain: The reference built from the height still to go is set against the rate the aircraft actually has, and the difference is the vertical speed error the controller works on.

cards.question: A pilot selects the level off mode. Why does this mode need no control loop of its own?
options: The autothrust system is used with a reference of zero
The altitude controller is used with a reference of zero
The vertical speed controller is used with a reference of zero
cards.explain: Level off changes nothing but the reference value: the same vertical speed controller works, now to a reference of zero.

cards.question: An aircraft climbing in vertical speed mode with a very high commanded rate reaches its lower speed limit. What happens to the pitch channel?
options: It reduces the commanded vertical speed to zero and levels off
It switches over from vertical speed to airspeed/Mach control
It hands pitch control over to the autothrust system
cards.explain: Envelope protection takes the rate target away from the pitch channel and gives it the speed target instead.

cards.question: The pitch channel has just reverted to speed control during a climb. What does the autothrust system do at the same moment?
options: It remains in speed mode and raises the commanded airspeed
It changes from thrust mode to speed mode and holds the commanded airspeed
It changes from speed mode to thrust mode and sets a thrust limit
cards.explain: The two channels swap jobs, so the autothrust gives up speed and goes to a fixed thrust rating.

cards.question: After a reversion, to which mode does the combination of pitch speed control and autothrust thrust control correspond
options: Altitude acquisition mode
Level change mode
Altitude hold mode
cards.explain: Pitch flying the speed with a fixed thrust rating is what defines level change.

cards.question: After a reversion during a climb, by which pitch movement is the commanded reference speed reached again?
options: Pitch hold
Pitch up
Pitch down
cards.explain: The aircraft was slow, so lowering the nose trades height for the speed it needs.

cards.question: A descent is flown with a very high negative vertical speed command and the aircraft approaches its upper speed limit. What does the autoflight system do?
options: It transfers airspeed control to the pitch channel integrator
It reduces the commanded vertical speed until the limit clears
It reverts from vertical speed control to airspeed control
cards.explain: The same envelope protection works at the top of the range as at the bottom, so vertical speed gives way to speed.

cards.question: To what does the thrust rating taken up after a reversion in the descent correspond
options: The minimum thrust previously set in vertical speed mode
The maximum thrust previously set in vertical speed mode
The thrust required for the commanded vertical speed
cards.explain: The rating taken up on reversion in a descent is the minimum thrust the autothrust had set in vertical speed mode, while trying not to exceed the upper speed limit.

cards.question: An excessive vertical speed causes an automatic reversion to level change. What is retained and what is modified?
options: The flight path is retained and the speed target is modified
The speed target is retained and the flight path is modified
A new speed target is set and the flight path is retained
cards.explain: Envelope protection keeps the speed and lets the profile change, which is the whole point of the reversion.

cards.question: An aircraft is levelling off in altitude acquisition mode above the transition level. Which reference is the selected target expressed against?
options: A radio height above ground
A pressure altitude
A QNH corrected altitude
cards.explain: Above the transition level flight levels are flown on standard setting, so the target is a pressure altitude.

cards.question: The capture point is calculated from the vertical speed instead of being set at a fixed distance. Why is it done this way?
options: So the altitude is reached without oscillating about it afterwards
So the capture point can always be baro-corrected by the air data computer
So the autothrust system can hold a constant airspeed during the capture
cards.explain: A high rate needs an earlier start, and scaling the point with rate is what stops the aircraft overshooting and hunting.

cards.question: Two aircraft level off at the same altitude but close on it at different vertical speeds. Which one starts its capture further out?
options: The one with the higher airspeed
The one with the higher vertical speed
The one with the lower vertical speed
cards.explain: Capture distance grows with vertical speed, so the faster approach needs the earlier start.

cards.question: As an aircraft in altitude acquisition gets closer and closer to the pre-selected altitude, what happens to its rate?
options: It is held constant until the tolerance band
It becomes steadily less
It becomes steadily greater
cards.explain: The rate is held in proportion to the distance left, so as the distance shrinks the rate shrinks with it.

cards.question: In what time does the e-function representing the acquisition transition theoretically reach the final altitude
options: The time to the capture point
An infinite time
The time to the tolerance band
cards.explain: An exponential approach never quite arrives, which is exactly why a tolerance band has to be defined.

cards.question: The aircraft has just entered the tolerance band at the end of an altitude acquisition. Which mode becomes active and what is annunciated?
options: Vertical speed, annunciated V/S = 0
Altitude acquisition, annunciated ALT ACQ
Altitude hold, annunciated ALT
cards.explain: Acquisition hands over to hold at the edge of the band and the annunciation changes with it.

cards.question: On what condition does the comparator of the capture detector declare the altitude acquisition active
options: Distance to go equals the calculated capture distance
Distance to go exceeds the calculated capture distance
Distance to go equals the width of the tolerance band
cards.explain: Capture happens where the remaining distance has shrunk to the distance the detector has calculated.

cards.question: An aircraft is climbing in level change to a pre-selected flight level. Which mode is armed at that point?
options: Altitude acquisition
Altitude hold mode
Speed and Mach control
cards.explain: The acquisition is waiting for its capture condition, so it sits armed while the climb mode is active.

cards.question: During an altitude acquisition the autothrust holds a constant airspeed in speed mode. What is the effect of a pitch attitude change?
options: The flight path angle changes, which modifies vertical speed
The altitude error changes, which in turn modifies pitch attitude
The airspeed changes, which in turn modifies vertical speed
cards.explain: With speed pinned by the autothrust, attitude translates straight into flight path angle and so into rate.

cards.question: The flight management system is guiding the aircraft in the vertical navigation mode. In which phases of a flight can it do this?
options: Climb, cruise and descend
Take off, climb and cruise
Cruise, descend and landing
cards.explain: The three named phases are climb, cruise and descend.

cards.question: At what deviation from the FM-altitude is profile or VNAV altitude hold entered automatically
options: 20 ft
50 ft
100 ft
cards.explain: The altitude band for this transit is fifty feet.

cards.question: What does the ALT mode of the pitch channel maintain
options: A pre-selected pitch attitude or trim setting
A pre-selected rate or flight path angle
A pre-selected altitude or flight level
cards.explain: The mode is named for what it holds, which is the altitude or flight level already selected.

cards.question: What deviation from the pre-selected altitude do modern control laws permit
options: 50 ft
100 ft
40 ft
cards.explain: The printed allowance in the soft altitude mode is a hundred feet either side.

cards.question: With which system does the profile or vertical navigation mode connect the autoflight system
options: The inertial reference system
The flight management system
The air data computer
cards.explain: Vertical navigation is flown on data the flight management system supplies, so the two are coupled.

cards.question: Over what span of a flight do the sequential segments of profile or vertical navigation guidance run
options: From the capture point to the transition altitude
From after take off to the instrument approach
From the top of climb to the top of descent
cards.explain: The sequential segments are stated as running from just after take off through to the approach.

cards.question: How does the pilot give clearance for a flight level change demanded by the flight management system
options: By selecting an appropriate altitude on the control panel
By entering the new flight level into the flight management system
By pressing the profile button at the autoflight control panel
cards.explain: The altitude selector on the panel is the place where the crew confirm the clearance to the system.

cards.question: An aircraft in profile mode approaches the FM-altitude within fifty feet. What happens?
options: The system automatically transits to altitude hold
The system automatically reverts to vertical speed
The system automatically arms altitude acquisition
cards.explain: Fifty feet of deviation is the printed trigger for the automatic change into hold.

cards.question: In which mode does the autothrust system work while the altitude hold mode is active
options: Speed mode
Thrust mode
Idle mode
cards.explain: With the pitch channel holding height, the autothrust takes the speed and works to a speed target.

cards.question: The altitude hold button is pressed while the aircraft is climbing. Which altitude does the system then maintain?
options: The altitude momentarily reached
The pre-selected altitude on the panel
The altitude at which the climb began
cards.explain: A manual selection freezes whatever altitude the aircraft has at that instant.

cards.question: The crew has not pressed the altitude hold button. Under what condition does the altitude hold mode still come in automatically?
options: On passing the transition altitude during a climb or descent
On approaching a pre-selected altitude with acquisition armed
On approaching a pre-selected altitude with acquisition active
cards.explain: The acquisition must already be running, not merely armed, for the hold to follow automatically.

cards.question: Why is the soft altitude mode not explicitly annunciated
options: It is subordinate to the altitude hold mode
It is a function of the altitude memory alone
It is an armed mode only and never an active one
cards.explain: It works underneath altitude hold rather than beside it, so it gets no annunciation of its own.

cards.question: Below what size of airspeed disturbance is the soft altitude deviation permitted
options: 10 Kts
5 Kts
4 Kts
cards.explain: The allowance applies only to disturbances below four knots.

cards.question: The flight management system requests a climb. Why must the autoflight system have a pilot input before it starts that climb?
options: To prevent altitude changes being made without ATC-clearance
To prevent the autothrust system reverting to thrust mode
To prevent the flight management system losing its reference
cards.explain: The pilot input stands in for the clearance, so the aircraft never changes level on its own.

cards.question: Where must both the panel selection and the FM-altitude lie before a climb to an FM-altitude is cleared
options: Below the momentary altitude of the aircraft
Exactly at the momentary altitude of the aircraft
Above the momentary altitude of the aircraft
cards.explain: Both targets have to lie above the aircraft before a climb can be cleared.

cards.question: How must the FM-altitude stand against the panel selection for a climb to be cleared
options: Exactly equal to it
Equal to or above it
Equal to or below it
cards.explain: In a climb the panel selection is the ceiling the crew have cleared, so the flight management target may not sit above it.

cards.question: Where must both the panel selection and the FM-altitude lie before a descent to an FM-altitude is cleared
options: Exactly at the momentary altitude of the aircraft
Below the momentary altitude of the aircraft
Above the momentary altitude of the aircraft
cards.explain: Both targets have to lie below the aircraft before a descent can be cleared.

cards.question: A descent to an FM-altitude is to be cleared. How must the FM-altitude stand against the panel selection?
options: Exactly equal to it
Equal to or below it
Equal to or above it
cards.explain: In a descent the panel selection is the floor the crew have cleared, so the flight management target may not sit below it.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs in profile mode with the panel selection above the level the flight management system is aiming for. Where does it level off?
options: At the selected flight level
At the FMS target level
Midway between the two levels
cards.explain: In a climb the aircraft stops at whichever of the two lies lower, which here is the flight management target.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs in profile mode with the panel altitude below the FMS target level. Where does it level off?
options: It continues the climb unrestricted
At the flight management target level
At the selected flight level
cards.explain: The crew input acts as the cleared ceiling, so the aircraft stops there.

cards.question: An aircraft descends in profile mode with the panel altitude above the FMS target level. Where does it level off?
options: At the selected flight level
At the flight management target level
At the transition level
cards.explain: In a descent the aircraft stops at whichever of the two lies higher, which here is the crew input.

cards.question: The altitude hold button is pressed during a descent. Why does the aircraft then have to acquire that altitude again?
options: Because it undershoots that altitude while still descending
Because the autothrust reverts to thrust mode and sets flight idle
Because the altitude memory is only synchronised once the button is released
cards.explain: The altitude is frozen while the aircraft is still going down, so it undershoots and then has to acquire that altitude again.

cards.question: In which condition is manual activation of the altitude hold mode mainly used
options: When the aircraft is approaching a pre-selected altitude
When the aircraft is in the capture phase
When the aircraft is already in level flight
cards.explain: If there is no rate to arrest there is nothing to overshoot, so the manual selection is clean.

cards.question: The soft altitude mode lets the aircraft wander within its band. What is traded for what?
options: Potential energy as airspeed against kinetic energy as altitude
Kinetic energy as thrust against potential energy as airspeed
Potential energy as altitude against kinetic energy as airspeed
cards.explain: Height is the potential energy and speed the kinetic energy, and the band lets one be swapped for the other.

cards.question: What is the immediate benefit of the energy trade allowed in the soft altitude mode
options: Fewer corrections of the altitude reference in memory
Fewer transient oscillations about the altitude
Fewer changes of engine thrust for airspeed control
cards.explain: Letting the altitude move absorbs the speed disturbance so the engines do not have to.

cards.question: Which two results does the smoother thrust control of the soft altitude mode bring?
options: Reduced fuel consumption and increased passenger comfort
Reduced engine wear and increased thrust response rate
Reduced altitude deviation and increased airspeed stability
cards.explain: The two stated results of the smoother thrust are less fuel burned and a smoother ride.

cards.question: The altitude hold mode is not yet active. What is the altitude memory doing?
options: It is holding the last altitude at which the mode was active
It is updated permanently with the pre-selected altitude from the panel
It is updated permanently with the current air data altitude
cards.explain: Continuous updating keeps the stored reference equal to the actual altitude so there is no step at engagement.

cards.question: After the flight path angle has changed in altitude hold, what is the order of the remaining effects
options: Vertical speed changes and then altitude changes
Thrust changes and then altitude changes
Altitude changes and then vertical speed changes
cards.explain: Rate comes before height, because altitude only moves once a rate exists.

cards.question: The altitude hold loop is compared with the altitude acquisition cascade. Why does altitude hold need no intermediate rate command?
options: Because its reference value is not stored in any memory at all
Because its vertical speed is supplied by the autothrust system
Because its own controller sets the attitude reference directly
cards.explain: Holding needs no rate step because the altitude controller produces the attitude reference itself.

cards.question: What relation do the several operating modes covered by the generic vertical navigation term bear to one another
options: They have separate annunciations
They have identical meaning
They have opposing control laws
cards.explain: The listed names are different labels for the same thing.

cards.question: A crew uses the term vertical navigation. Which mode name has the same meaning?
options: Altitude acquisition
Level off
Profile
cards.explain: Profile is one of the names printed for the same mode as vertical navigation; altitude acquisition and level off are separate pitch modes.

cards.question: Which phase follows the arm phase of the horizontal navigation mode
options: The over station phase
The active phase
The on course phase
cards.explain: This mode runs as an arm phase followed by an active phase; on course and over station phases belong to the VOR mode.

cards.question: Above which radio height can the autopilot and flight director be coupled with the flight management system
options: 50 ft
100 ft
30 ft
cards.explain: The printed minimum radio height for coupling is thirty feet.

cards.question: How is a VOR radial described
options: A variable line of position
A fixed line of position
A fixed line of equal altitude
cards.explain: The radial is a line of position fixed in space relative to the station.

cards.question: How many sub-modes does the VOR controller have to distinguish
options: Two
Four
Three
cards.explain: Capture, on course and over station make three.

cards.question: The VOR mode has just been selected but the angular deviation limit has not yet been passed. What does the flight mode annunciator show?
options: VOR capture phase
VOR mode active
VOR mode armed
cards.explain: Until the limit is passed the mode is only waiting, so it reads armed.

cards.question: Which pair of values does the roll controller use as the criterion for transiting to the On-Course Phase
options: VOR deviation 15° and heading error 5°
VOR deviation 5° and heading error 15°
VOR deviation 2° and heading error 10°
cards.explain: The printed criterion is a VOR deviation of 5° or less together with a heading error of 15° or less.

cards.question: A steady heading error is sitting at the input of the washout — roughly which time constant governs how quickly it decays?
options: 10 sec
100 sec
200 sec
cards.explain: The washout time constant is approximately 100 sec.

cards.question: Which criterion is used to recognise the cone of confusion
options: A deviation signal change of more than 5 mV/sec or more than 0,8°/sec
A deviation signal change of more than 8 mV/sec or more than 0,2°/sec
A deviation signal change of more than 8 mV/sec or more than 0,5°/sec
cards.explain: Those are the two printed rates that define the cone of confusion.

cards.question: Which four sub-modes does managed level-change comprise
options: Climb, altitude hold, altitude constraint, descent
Climb, altitude acquisition, level off and descent
Climb, cruise, instrument approach and descent
cards.explain: Climb, altitude hold, altitude constraint and descent are the four sub-modes of managed level-change.

cards.question: Which two systems are coupled with the flight management system in all the vertical navigation modes
options: The autopilot/director and the autothrust system
The air data computer and the inertial reference system
The roll channel of the autopilot and the yaw damper
cards.explain: Both the guidance and the thrust systems have to be tied to the flight management system for automatic vertical guidance.

cards.question: In the vertical navigation modes, which channel performs the vertical guidance?
options: The pitch channel
The autothrust channel
The roll channel
cards.explain: Vertical guidance is a pitch task and thrust control is left to the autothrust.

cards.question: Which unit determines the speed and Mach reference values in the vertical navigation modes
options: The flight management system
The autothrust control system
The central air data computer
cards.explain: The targets come from the flight management system, which is what makes the guidance managed.

cards.question: Where the autothrust system is working in thrust mode, what decides the source of the thrust ratings it uses?
options: The type of aircraft
The selected altitude
The momentary vertical speed
cards.explain: The source of the ratings varies from one aircraft type to another.

cards.question: From the drift between the wanted on-track point and what else does the pilot work out a wind correction angle
options: The actual position
The desired track angle
The selected course
cards.explain: Drift is measured between where the aircraft should be and where it actually is.

cards.question: The capture phase of the navigation mode has just been entered. What is annunciated?
options: NAV active
NAV armed
Heading select active
cards.explain: Entering the capture phase makes the mode active, and the annunciation says so.

cards.question: Which unit directs the autoflight system to intercept and follow the track once the navigation mode is active
options: The flight management system
The capture detector
The inertial navigation system
cards.explain: The flight management system holds the flight plan, so it is what directs the interception.

cards.question: With the help of which autopilot channel does the VOR mode intercept and follow a radial
options: The roll channel
The pitch channel
The yaw channel
cards.explain: A radial is a lateral path, so the roll channel flies it.

cards.question: Besides selecting an appropriate receiver frequency, what else is required before the VOR mode can be activated?
options: The intercept angle must be determined by selecting a track
The radial must be determined by selecting a course
The radial must be determined by selecting a heading
cards.explain: The radial is told to the system as a course set on the pre-selected course knob.

cards.question: In which order do the three VOR sub-modes follow the flight phase sequence
options: Capture, on course and over station
Capture, over station and on course
Arm, capture and over station
cards.explain: The aircraft joins the radial, tracks it, and only then passes the station.

cards.question: The VOR mode has just entered its capture phase. What is that phase intended to achieve?
options: Guidance of the aircraft through the area where the deviation is useless
Guidance of the aircraft along the radial with cross wind correction
Transfer from an intercept heading onto the radial without oscillations
cards.explain: Capture is the joining manoeuvre, and it must settle the aircraft on the radial cleanly.

cards.question: Besides guiding the aircraft on the radial from or to the station, what does the on course phase do
options: It corrects any cross wind disturbances
It corrects any deviation rate above the threshold
It corrects the pre-selected course for station passage
cards.explain: Tracking a radial means holding it against the wind, which is what this phase does.

cards.question: At approximately what angular deviation is the transfer to the pre-selected course said to start
options: 5 degrees
2 degrees
10 degrees
cards.explain: The capture starts early, at about two degrees of angular deviation.

cards.question: Which unit is activated first on selection of the VOR mode to measure angular deviation from the pre- selected course
options: The lateral beam sensor
The capture detector
The course comparator
cards.explain: The lateral beam sensor is the device that watches the angular deviation while the mode is armed.

cards.question: What becomes the controlled value of the third loop that augments heading control during the capture phase
options: The pre-selected course value
The actual aircraft heading
The actual VOR-radial
cards.explain: The outermost loop added at capture controls the radial the aircraft is actually on.

cards.question: With what is the pre-selected course compared to obtain the deviation used by the outermost VOR loop
options: The actual roll attitude from the gyros
The actual heading from the compass system
The actual radial at the aircraft's position
cards.explain: Deviation is the difference between the course wanted and the radial the aircraft is actually on.

cards.question: Why does the roll controller change over to the On-Course Phase once the preselected radial is almost reached
options: To hand the lateral guidance over to the heading hold controller
To increase the rate at which the heading error is reduced
To improve its behaviour with respect to cross wind disturbances
cards.explain: Cross wind disturbance behaviour is what the change of phase improves.

cards.question: An aircraft tracking a VOR radial meets a permanent cross wind component — what does comparing the VOR deviation with the heading error in S3 then produce?
options: A permanent oscillation about the radial
A permanent loss of the VOR deviation signal
A permanent Stand-Off from the radial
cards.explain: A standing cross wind leaves a residual difference in S3, and that residual is the permanent Stand-Off.

cards.question: Which heading error does the roll controller have to leave standing while an aircraft tracks a radial in a steady crosswind
options: The one equivalent to the preselected course
The one equivalent to the wind correction angle
The one equivalent to the VOR course deviation angle
cards.explain: The crab angle must be kept, so the heading error equal to the wind correction angle is left alone.

cards.question: An aircraft is established on a pre-selected radial in a steady crosswind — how does it travel along that radial?
options: Wings level, with the heading error equal to the wind correction angle
In small banked corrections, with the heading error slowly decaying
Wings level, with the heading error equal to the VOR deviation angle rate
cards.explain: Once the washout has settled the crab is held and no roll command remains, so the aircraft drifts wings level.

cards.question: An aircraft is passing the cone of confusion overhead a VOR — for how long after leaving that area does the deviation signal stay switched off?
