options: A further 100 seconds
A further 20 seconds
A further 10 seconds
cards.explain: The printed period is the cone of confusion plus a further 20 seconds.

cards.question: What determines the operating mode of the autothrust system in the vertical navigation modes
options: The roll channel
The air data computer
The pitch channel
cards.explain: The pitch channel takes the lead and the autothrust mode follows from what pitch is doing.

cards.question: A waypoint has to be passed at a given altitude with a given airspeed maintained during a climb. What does the flight management computer calculate?
options: An optimum flight path angle for the required thrust
An optimum vertical speed for the required altitude
An optimum thrust for the required flight path angle
cards.explain: The constraint fixes the path to be flown, so what the computer works out is the thrust that path needs.

cards.question: By selecting what does the flight management system determine the control loops for the different flight phases
options: Appropriate thrust ratings for the autothrust system
Appropriate pitch channel modes of the autopilot
Appropriate reference altitudes for the altitude memory
cards.explain: The flight management system works by picking pitch channel modes, and those modes define the loops.

cards.question: A fixed inertial flight path is being flown in heading select mode. Why must the heading reference be corrected from time to time?
options: Because the required value depends on the prevailing wind
Because the compass system drifts away from magnetic north
Because the roll channel loses its attitude reference in a turn
cards.explain: A heading only produces the wanted track for one particular wind, so it has to be reset as the wind changes.

cards.question: Besides an inertial system or a flight management system with position sensors, what third source makes automatic lateral guidance possible
options: A compass system with a heading hold function
An air data computer with altitude correction
A radio navigation system with track capability
cards.explain: The third option listed is a radio aid that defines a track, such as a radial or a localizer.

cards.question: An active flight plan was entered into the flight management system during cockpit preparation. How will the autopilot couple to it?
options: Manually only, after take off
Only once the capture phase begins
Automatically, without crew action
cards.explain: An active flight plan already loaded before departure gives automatic coupling.

cards.question: The navigation mode is active. Apart from pressing its button again, how is it terminated?
options: Automatically, as soon as another vertical mode is selected
Automatically, as soon as another lateral mode is selected
Automatically, as soon as the cross-track distance grows again
cards.explain: Two lateral modes cannot run together, so selecting another one ends this one.

cards.question: The navigation mode is active and a heading change is needed. How is that change actually brought about?
options: By track error values fed to the roll channel inner loop
By roll attitude reference values fed to the roll inner loop
By heading reference values fed to the roll channel outer loop
cards.explain: The aircraft is turned by banking it, so the command reaching the inner loop is a roll attitude.

cards.question: An aircraft tracking a radial passes overhead the VOR station. Why does the VOR mode need a separate over station phase?
options: Because the deviation signal is useless in the cone of confusion
Because the receiver frequency must be re-tuned as the station is passed
Because the pre-selected course must be reversed as the station is passed
cards.explain: With no usable deviation overhead, the controller cannot keep steering on it and needs another rule.

cards.question: The radial deviation rate rises above eight millivolts per second. What does the roll controller do?
options: It transits to heading control and maintains the present heading
It transits to capture control and re-intercepts the radial
It transits to heading control and reverses the pre-selected course
cards.explain: A fast moving deviation signals the cone of confusion, so the controller freezes the heading and flies on.

cards.question: An aircraft is closing on the pre-selected course. Why must the transfer onto it start early rather than at the course itself?
options: So the lateral beam sensor has time to measure the deviation
So the flight mode annunciator can indicate the mode armed
So the bracketing is soft and free of oscillations
cards.explain: Turning early gives room for a gentle turn that settles on the course instead of swinging through it.

cards.question: The aircraft passes the angular deviation limit on its way to the radial. What does the lateral beam sensor do?
options: It switches the roll controller into heading control
It switches the roll controller into the on course phase
It switches the roll controller into the capture phase
cards.explain: The sensor passing its limit is the capture trigger, and it works through the operating mode logic.

cards.question: A signal used by the VOR mode becomes invalid in flight. What actually happens, given the permanent monitoring of signal validity?
options: The VOR mode goes back to capture
The VOR mode holds its last command
The VOR mode is terminated
cards.explain: Monitoring drops the mode rather than letting it fly on a missing signal.

cards.question: A washout has been added to the navigation loop and the aircraft is tracking a radial in a steady crosswind — what is the relationship between the aircraft heading and the PSC?
options: The heading differs from the PSC by the measured VOR deviation angle
The heading differs from the PSC by the wind correction angle
The heading is aligned with the PSC and the track is offset
cards.explain: With the washout fitted the radial is tracked, so the crab is carried as a heading difference from the PSC.

cards.question: How does the washout let the VOR deviation prevail over the heading error in the long run
options: Only changes of VOR deviation are still compared with the heading error
Both signals are compared but the heading error is given a lower gain
Only changes of heading error are still compared with the VOR deviation
cards.explain: The washout passes only the changing part of the heading error, so the steady deviation signal dominates.

cards.question: The VOR deviation signal has been switched off and the heading error signal connected to S3 during the Over Station Phase — how does the controller then behave?
options: The heading loop is off and it acts as a navigation controller only
The navigation loop is off and it acts as a roll rate controller only
The navigation loop is off and it acts as a heading controller only
cards.explain: With the deviation signal gone and the washout bypassed, only the heading loop remains in use.

cards.question: Which kind of approach does the localizer mode support when it is used as an independent auto flight mode
options: A Precision Approach
A Non-Precision Approach
A fully automatic landing
cards.explain: Used on its own the localizer mode gives lateral guidance only, which is a Non-Precision Approach.

cards.question: Which flight mode annunciation belongs to the localizer Capture Phase
options: LOC (TRACK)
LOC (ARM)
LOC (ACTIVE)
cards.explain: The Capture Phase is annunciated as LOC (ARM).

cards.question: Which other name is given to the back beam of a localizer
options: The back radial
The reciprocal localizer
The back course
cards.explain: Back course is the alternative name for the back beam.

cards.question: Which two forms of guidance can the back beam mode provide
options: Autopilot guidance or radar vectoring
Flight director guidance or auto-thrust guidance
Flight director guidance or autopilot guidance
cards.explain: The mode works for either the flight director or the autopilot.

cards.question: A back beam approach is being set up on the HSI — by how much must the deviation scale and the deviation bar be rotated?
cards.explain: The printed rotation for a correct back beam indication is 180°.

cards.question: How many radials does a VOR provide compared with the number of beams a localizer transmitter generates
options: 36 radials against one beam
360 radials against one beam
180 radials against one beam
cards.explain: A VOR provides 360 radials, whereas the localizer transmitter provides a single beam.

cards.question: A crew selects Approach/Land on the autoflight control panel — what happens to the localizer mode?
options: It must still be armed separately by its own key
It is activated automatically as a submode
It is inhibited until the glide path is captured
cards.explain: As a submode of Approach/Land it comes up with that selection and needs no separate key.

cards.question: The lateral annunciation changes from armed to active — which phase has just begun?
options: The Capture Phase
The Loc-Track Phase
The Approach-Track Phase
cards.explain: That annunciation change marks the beginning of the Loc-Track Phase.

cards.question: What are angular deviations converted into during the Approach-Track Phase, and why
options: Into roll rate commands, to counteract the funnel effect
Into lateral distances, to counteract the beam convergence effect
Into lateral distances, to counteract the funnel effect
cards.explain: They become lateral distances, which is what counteracts the funnel effect.

cards.question: From which two quantities does the Capture Detector calculate the Capture Point
options: The heading error and the LOC deviation rate
The heading error and the LOC deviation angle
The roll attitude and the LOC deviation rate
cards.explain: Heading error and rate of change of localizer deviation are the two printed inputs.

cards.question: Why is the capture threshold of the localizer mode called adaptive
options: Because the capture point is reset each time the deviation changes sign
Because the capture point location depends particularly on the deviation rate
Because the capture point location depends particularly on the radio altitude
cards.explain: The threshold moves with the closure rate, which is why it is called adaptive.

cards.question: Which property of the aircraft are the Approach-Track control laws written to exploit
options: Its weather cock stability
Its spiral stability
Its longitudinal stability
cards.explain: Weather cock stability is the printed property relied on near the ground.

cards.question: Why does the back beam mode count as a Non-Precision Approach
options: Because no vertical guidance is available in this mode
Because no lateral guidance is available in this mode
Because the deviation signal polarity is inverted in this mode
cards.explain: Only lateral guidance exists on the back beam, so the approach is non-precision.

cards.question: A crew is setting up for a localizer back beam approach — which course must be set as the pre- selected course?
options: The back course
The runway heading plus 90°
The front course
cards.explain: The front course, not the back course, is what the system expects at the PSC.

cards.question: The deviation bar on the HSI has to read correctly during a back beam approach — how is the required 180° rotation obtained?
options: By inverting the heading signal from the compass system
By setting the back course as the pre-selected course
By setting the front course as the pre-selected course
cards.explain: Selecting the front course at the PSC rotates the scale and bar by 180°.

cards.question: What happens to the polarity of the localizer deviation signal on the back beam
options: It is inverted and the inversion has to be undone in the navigation loop
It is inverted and the inversion is left in place for the navigation loop
It is unchanged and the heading error is inverted instead
cards.explain: The mirror image situation inverts the signal, and the controller has to reverse that inversion.

cards.question: Which inverter reverses the localizer deviation signal for a back beam approach
options: Inverter 2
Inverter 1
The rate taker
cards.explain: The deviation signal is reversed by Inverter 2, while Inverter 1 works on the heading error.

cards.question: Which two signals are added to form the roll attitude reference value in the heading loop
options: The heading error and the localizer deviation
The heading error and the roll attitude error
The localizer deviation and the roll rate
cards.explain: The reference roll attitude comes from the sum of heading error and localizer deviation formed in S2.

cards.question: The localizer mode has been selected on its own on the autoflight control panel as an independent lateral mode — which phase is left out?
options: The Approach-Track Phase
The Localizer-Track Phase
The Capture Phase
cards.explain: Selecting LOC as an independent lateral mode omits the Approach-Track Phase.

cards.question: Two aircraft intercept the same localizer from very different distances to the transmitter antenna — what does the adaptive capture threshold guarantee?
options: The best possible beginning of the transition onto the beam for both
The same bank angle throughout the transition onto the beam for both
The same intercept angle onto the beam for both
cards.explain: The threshold is written to be independent of range, so the turn-on point is right in either case.

cards.question: The localizer deviation signal has just fallen to 60 mV during an intercept — what is now fed into the outer control loop?
options: The PSC error, through a wash out
The PSC error, directly without a wash out
The localizer deviation rate, through a wash out
cards.explain: Reaching that beam value starts the Loc-Track Phase, in which the PSC error enters through the wash out.

cards.question: The aircraft is in the Approach-Track Phase and a gust pushes the heading off — under what condition will the roll controller still act?
options: If the gust changes the sink rate or displaces it from the beam
If the gust changes the bank angle or displaces it from the beam
If the gust changes the bank angle or the heading error exceeds 0,5°
cards.explain: Only upsets that move the bank angle or move the aircraft off the beam are corrected.

cards.question: Why does a further 180° have to be subtracted from the heading error built on the preselected front course
options: Because the actual heading error has to be taken from the back course
Because the actual heading error has to be taken from the front course
Because the deviation bar polarity has already been reversed
cards.explain: The usable heading error is referenced to the back course, so another 180° comes off.

cards.question: What is the inversion applied to the heading error of a back beam approach equivalent to
options: Subtraction of 180° from the localizer deviation obtained at S1
Subtraction of 180° from the heading error obtained at S1
Addition of 180° to the heading error obtained at S2
cards.explain: Inverter 1 reverses the sign, which amounts to taking 180° off the S1 heading error.

cards.question: The pilot is flying the back beam manually on the flight director and keeps the roll bar centred — what is the result?
options: There is no heading error and the back beam is tracked
There is no localizer deviation and the roll bar stays centred
There is no roll attitude error and the back beam is tracked
cards.explain: Centring the bar removes the roll attitude error, which is what the flight director displays.

cards.question: How does the sequence of effects of the flight director differ from that of the autopilot on a back beam approach
options: The pilot is directly involved as part of the inner control loop
The inner control loop is replaced by the roll attitude limitation
The pilot is directly involved as part of the navigation loop
cards.explain: With the flight director the pilot closes the inner loop himself.

cards.question: Which common mode is available for the flight director only
options: TAKE OFF
ILS APPROACH/LAND
GO AROUND
cards.explain: The take off mode is listed as a flight director function only.

cards.question: Below which height above ground can the Approach/Land or Go Around mode no longer be deactivated by pressing its button again
options: 400 ft
cards.explain: Four hundred feet above ground is the height given for this lock-out.

cards.question: Below which height above ground can the Approach or Land mode be left in only two ways
options: 500 ft
cards.explain: Five hundred feet is the height given with the JAR-AWO reference for this restriction.

cards.question: Which vertical flight mode annunciation appears once the prerequisites for the glide path mode are met
options: G/S - CAPTURE
G/P - ARM
G/P - ACTIVE
cards.explain: The armed condition is annunciated as G/P - ARM.

cards.question: Within which angular range is the glide path signal usable
cards.explain: The printed usable range of the glide path signal is plus or minus 0,5 degrees.

cards.question: Below which height AGL does beam convergence make direct glide path control by zeroing the angular deviation unworkable
options: 500 ft
cards.explain: Below fifteen hundred feet AGL the angular deviation can no longer be used directly, because of beam convergence.

cards.question: Which unit monitors the angular glide path deviation signal as soon as Approach/Land is selected
options: The over station sensor
The vertical beam sensor
The capture point detector
cards.explain: The vertical beam sensor watches the glide path deviation from the moment the mode is selected.

cards.question: Below which angular deviation does the vertical beam sensor trigger the glide path capture phase
cards.explain: Capture is triggered when the angular deviation falls below 0,2 degrees.

cards.question: An aircraft is at 300 ft AGL with the Approach/Land mode engaged and the crew presses the Approach button again — what happens?
options: The mode disengages immediately
The mode stays in operation
The mode reverts to the localizer submode
cards.explain: Below 400 ft the button press no longer deactivates the mode.

cards.question: What does a precision approach require on board the aircraft or on the ground
options: A localizer transmitter showing deviation from the runway centre line
A glide path indicator showing deviation from the intended glide path
A marker beacon showing the distance to the runway threshold
cards.explain: A precision approach is defined by a glide path indicator that permanently shows deviation from the intended glide path.

cards.question: What do all non-precision approaches have in common
options: They lack any lateral guidance
They lack any distance information
They lack any vertical guidance
cards.explain: The absence of vertical guidance is what makes an approach non-precision.

cards.question: The pilot decides to discontinue an approach — according to what must the missed approach be flown?
options: The procedures published in instrument approach charts or ATC guidance
The procedures published in the aircraft flight manual or ATC guidance
The procedures stored in the flight management system or the approach plate
cards.explain: Charted missed approach procedures or ATC guidance are the two printed sources.

cards.question: How are the terms Approach mode and Land mode related
options: The approach mode is armed and the land mode is active
They are equivalent names for the same mode
The land mode is a sub-mode of the approach mode
cards.explain: The two names stand for one and the same mode.

cards.question: An automatic approach is being flown with the Approach mode engaged — which span of flight phases does it control?
options: From glide path intercept, via flare, until the end of the missed approach
From localizer intercept, via flare, until the take off mode is selected
From localizer intercept, via glide path intercept, until roll out
cards.explain: The mode runs from localizer intercept through glide path intercept to roll out.

cards.question: An aircraft is below the JAR-AWO height with the Land mode engaged — what are the only two ways of deactivating it?
options: Selecting Go Around or selecting another vertical mode
Selecting Go Around or turning off the autopilot
Turning off the autopilot or turning off the auto-thrust
cards.explain: Only a Go Around selection or switching the autopilot off removes the mode below that height.

cards.question: Which two settings are a prerequisite before the glide path mode can work
options: The back course of the active runway and the runway heading at the PSC
The ILS frequency of the active runway and the decision height at the PSC
The ILS frequency of the active runway and the runway heading at the PSC
cards.explain: Both the ILS frequency and the runway heading at the PSC knob have to be set first.

cards.question: The aircraft is in altitude hold on the localizer and passes an angular deviation of approximately -0,2° — what happens?
options: Altitude hold switches off and a descent starts
Altitude hold is retained until the beam centre is reached
Altitude hold switches off and the flare law is armed
cards.explain: At about -0,2° the altitude hold drops out and the aircraft begins descending onto the beam.

cards.question: What does an angular deviation of approximately -0,2° correspond to on the glide path deviation indicator
options: Roughly one dot below
Roughly half a dot above
Roughly half a dot below
cards.explain: An angular deviation of about -0,2° corresponds roughly to half a dot below on the glide path deviation indicator.

cards.question: An aircraft on an automatic approach descends through approximately 70 ft AGL — why is glide path control terminated at the latest here?
options: The glide path signal is outside its usable angular range
The radio altimeter becomes unreliable through ground reflections now
The glide path signal becomes unreliable through ground reflection
cards.explain: Ground reflection spoils the glide path signal, so control is dropped by about 70 ft.

cards.question: An aircraft holds a constant vertical distance from the glide path as it closes on the transmitter — what happens to the angular deviation?
options: It stays constant
It decreases permanently
It increases permanently
cards.explain: The same vertical offset subtends a larger angle as the range closes.

cards.question: Which name is given to the permanently increasing loop amplification of a closing glide path
options: Beam convergence
Beam sensitivity
Funnel effect
cards.explain: The effect of the permanently rising loop amplification is called beam convergence.

cards.question: Which two quantities does the first estimation method use to estimate the vertical glide path deviation
options: Angular deviation and ground speed
Angular deviation and radio height
Radio height and ground speed
cards.explain: The first method combines the angular deviation with radio height.

cards.question: Which quantity is fed back to form the inner loop of the glide slope mode
options: The pitch attitude
The radio height
The vertical speed
cards.explain: Sink rate feedback closes the inner loop.

cards.question: Why will an aircraft hold a constant sink rate during a steady descent without controller action
options: Because of the pitch trim integrator
Because of its inherent stability
Because of its weather cock stability
cards.explain: Inherent stability is the printed reason for the steady sink rate.

cards.question: The Approach/Land mode is engaged at 200 ft AGL and the crew decides to discontinue the approach — which mode can still take over?
options: The heading select mode
The Go Around mode
The altitude hold mode
cards.explain: Go Around can supersede Approach/Land at any height, unlike other upper modes.

cards.question: An automatic landing is being flown and the glide path has just been left — what is held until the flare phase begins?
options: The momentary pitch attitude
The momentary sink rate
The momentary glide slope angle
cards.explain: The sink rate at that moment is frozen until the flare starts.

cards.question: An autopilot is certified for category II approaches only — what must happen at 100 ft radio height?
options: It must be disengaged and the flare flown by the flight director
It must be switched to the flare sub-mode for the landing
It must be disengaged and the landing flown manually
cards.explain: A category II only autopilot comes out at 100 ft and the pilot flares and lands.

cards.question: Beam convergence has been left uncompensated on an ILS approach — how does the glide path controller behave at long range and close in?
options: Sluggish far out and unable to hold the beam near the runway
Prone to oscillation far out and sluggish near the runway
Sluggish far out and prone to oscillation near the runway
cards.explain: Low gain far out makes it sluggish, and rising gain close in makes it oscillate.

cards.question: Why do estimation methods have to be used to compensate the apparent increase in amplification
options: The vertical deviation from the G/P beam is generally not available
The angular deviation from the G/P is generally not available
The slant range to the G/P-transmitter is generally not available
cards.explain: Without a true slant range the deviation cannot be computed exactly, so it is estimated.

cards.question: The second estimation method is in use and the aircraft passes the outer marker — what is started there, and what has to be known?
options: A time proportional estimation, with the height of the aircraft over the marker
A radio height proportional estimation, with the distance from OM to the threshold
A time proportional estimation, with the distance from OM to the transmitter
cards.explain: Passing the marker starts a time based estimate that relies on the known OM to transmitter distance.

cards.question: A glide slope deviation appears while an aircraft is in a steady descent — which loops detect it and act on it?
options: The pitch outer loop detects it and the pitch inner loop changes the sink rate
The pitch outer loop detects it and the auto-thrust system changes the sink rate
The pitch inner loop detects it and the pitch outer loop changes the sink rate
cards.explain: The outer loop sees the beam error and the inner loop carries out the sink rate change.

cards.question: The glide path is being intercepted from below and the angular deviation is decreasing — how does the pitch controller react after synchronization?
options: With an increasing pitch-up
With an increasing pitch-over
With a constant pitch attitude until the beam centre
cards.explain: Synchronization reverses what the raw sign would command, so the aircraft pitches over onto the beam.

cards.question: An aircraft intercepts the glide path from above — what does the pitch controller command at synchronization?
options: A pitch-up, so the aircraft levels off above the glide path
A pitch-over, so the aircraft flares onto the glide path
A pitch-up, so the aircraft flares onto the glide path
cards.explain: All signs invert from above, giving a pitch-up and a flare onto the beam.

cards.question: Below which height AGL does the auto-throttle or auto-thrust system reduce the thrust to idle
options: 15 ft
50 ft
120 ft
cards.explain: The printed height for thrust reduction to idle is 15 ft AGL.

cards.question: From which vertical speed to which vertical speed does the flare reduce the descent shortly before touchdown
options: From approx. -600 to -750 ft/min down to approx. -120 ft/min
From approx. -400 to -600 ft/min down to approx. -120 ft/min
From approx. -600 to -750 ft/min down to approx. -250 ft/min
cards.explain: Those are the printed glide path and touchdown sink rates.

cards.question: The landing controller is compensating for the ground effect — how much is added to the actual radio altitude?
options: Approximately 15 ft
Approximately 20 ft
Approximately 50 ft
cards.explain: About 20 ft of bias is added to the measured radio height.

cards.question: Which movement does the pitch rollout submode command directly after touch down on the main gear
options: A controlled decrease of the bank angle
A controlled increase of the pitch attitude
A controlled decrease of the pitch attitude
cards.explain: The submode lowers the nose by reducing the pitch attitude in a controlled way.

cards.question: Which annunciation does the flight mode annunciator display once the nose gear is being lowered onto the runway
options: LAND
FLARE-ACTIVE
ROLLOUT
cards.explain: ROLLOUT is shown once the pitch rollout submode runs.

cards.question: Which name is given to the angle between the aircraft heading and its track on a crosswind approach
options: Drift angle or lateral slip angle
Crab angle or wind correction angle
Course angle or bearing angle
cards.explain: That angle is the crab angle, also called the wind correction angle.

cards.question: An automatic landing is flown in a crosswind — below which radio height is the alignment carried out?
options: Below 15 ft
Below 30 ft
Below 50 ft
cards.explain: Alignment is carried out below 30 ft of radio height.

cards.question: From where does the preselected course reach the yaw channel as its reference value
options: From the flight management computer
From the inertial reference system
From the autoflight control panel
cards.explain: The crew sets the preselected course on the autoflight control panel and that is the yaw reference.

cards.question: A wind correction angle has been carried down the approach — what does yaw attitude or heading control do during the auto land?
options: It aligns the ground track with the runway centre line
It aligns the longitudinal axis with the runway direction
It holds the wind correction angle until the nose gear is down
cards.explain: The crab is taken out by yawing the aircraft onto the runway direction.

cards.question: Which signal guides the aircraft along the runway centre line after touch-down
options: The glide path deviation signal
The radio altitude signal
The localizer deviation signal
cards.explain: Roll out steering uses the localizer deviation.

cards.question: Why does a zero sink rate have to be avoided during the flare
options: To assure a positive touchdown
To avoid a tail strike
To shorten the touch down zone
cards.explain: Some sink rate must remain so that the aircraft actually touches down.

cards.question: The flare window is being computed during an automatic landing — which two momentary quantities determine it?
options: Vertical speed and pitch attitude
Radio height and ground speed
Vertical speed and ground speed
cards.explain: The flare window is computed from the momentary vertical speed and ground speed.

cards.question: During the flare, which pair of quantities does the controller use to calculate the path to be flown down to the touch down
options: The momentary radio altitude and the derived crab angle
The momentary pitch attitude and the derived ground speed
The momentary landing gear height and the derived sink rate
cards.explain: The landing path is built from the gear height over the runway together with the derived sink rate.

cards.question: Which change to the calculated landing path would the ground effect produce if it were left uncompensated
options: A steepening of the path
A shortening of the path
A flattening out of the path
cards.explain: Extra lift in ground effect reduces the sink rate, so the path would flatten out.

cards.question: Which change behind the wing produces the ground effect as the aircraft approaches the ground
options: The angle of sweep decreases
The angle of down wash increases
The angle of down wash decreases
cards.explain: Near the ground the down wash angle falls off, which raises the effective angle of incidence.

cards.question: Which moment follows from the increased arm to the centre of gravity together with the increased lift at the horizontal stabilizer
options: A pitch up moment
A pitch down moment
A yawing moment
cards.explain: More tail lift on a longer arm pushes the nose down.

cards.question: Which two modes must already be active as the precondition for a flare activation
options: Glideslope as the vertical and localizer as the lateral mode
Altitude hold as the vertical and heading select as the lateral mode
Localizer as the vertical and glideslope as the lateral mode
cards.explain: The flare only arms out of a coupled approach with the glideslope active vertically and the localizer active laterally.

cards.question: The main gear has just touched down at the end of an automatic landing — which capability is lost at that moment?
options: An automatic go around manoeuvre
An automatic rudder alignment
An automatic deceleration process
cards.explain: Once the main gear is down the automatic go around can no longer be flown.

cards.question: Which part of the autoflight system switches itself off automatically at the touch down of the main gear
options: The autopilot roll channel
The auto-throttle
The autopilot yaw channel
cards.explain: The autothrottle switches itself off at touchdown while the yaw channel carries on through the roll out.

cards.question: Which signal is produced when the actual vertical speed is subtracted from the commanded vertical speed
options: The error signal for the pitch inner loop
The reference signal for the pitch outer loop
The feedback signal for the trim integrator
cards.explain: That subtraction is what generates the error fed to the pitch inner loop.

cards.question: The flare detector starts the flare 50 ft above the ground at the earliest. Which quantity modifies that value?
options: The derived vertical speed
The H1 height bias
The ground speed
cards.explain: The earliest flare point is the 50 ft main gear height modified by the H1 height bias that forces a positive touch down.

cards.question: The flare detector rounds the flight path off continuously — which limit does it observe?
options: The upper pitch attitude limit
The upper sink rate limit
The upper bank angle limit
cards.explain: The rounding off is bounded by the upper pitch attitude limit.

cards.question: The remaining lift has to be killed after the touch down — which two actions do that?
options: Derotation and ground spoiler extension
Auto brake application and ground spoiler extension
Derotation and reverse thrust selection
cards.explain: Lowering the nose and putting the ground spoilers out are the two actions named.

cards.question: Why does the aircraft heading have to be brought onto the runway heading shortly before touch down
options: The landing gear is aligned with the longitudinal axis
The nose wheel steering is available right after touch down
The rudder loses its effectiveness right after touch down
cards.explain: The wheels point where the fuselage points, so any crab left on would take the aircraft off the runway.

cards.question: The decrab is being flown on an automatic landing — which reference is the heading aligned with?
options: The localizer deviation
The present track
The preselected course
cards.explain: The align phase flies the heading onto the preselected course.

cards.question: The preselected course is the reference for the align phase — what must the pilot check before the alignment?
options: That it agrees with the localizer frequency
That it agrees with the present heading
That it agrees with the runway heading
cards.explain: The align phase is only as good as the preselected course, so it must match the runway heading.

cards.question: Which channel and which surface does the align phase require
options: A yaw channel acting on the rudder
A yaw channel acting on the nose wheel
A roll channel acting on the ailerons
cards.explain: The decrab is flown by the yaw channel through the rudder.

cards.question: Which axis receives a coordinated input during the alignment, depending on the type of aircraft
options: The pitch axis
The vertical axis
The roll axis
cards.explain: Some aircraft add a coordinated roll input, the low wing method, with the decrab.

cards.question: The flight director is on when the yaw align phase begins — what changes on the display?
options: The pitch bar is replaced by a yaw bar
The roll bar is simply removed from view
The roll bar is replaced by a yaw bar
cards.explain: The roll bar gives way to a yaw bar as the align phase starts.

cards.question: A crosswind automatic landing is flown — what does the flight mode annunciator show as the yaw align phase begins?
options: Nothing at all is annunciated for it
ROLLOUT appears as the lateral mode
ALIGN appears as the lateral mode
cards.explain: The align phase gets no annunciation at all.

cards.question: The align controller needs the present heading — where does it come from?
options: A magnetic heading system or a radio altimeter
A localizer receiver or an inertial reference system
A magnetic heading system or an inertial reference system
cards.explain: Present heading comes either from the compass system or from the inertial system.

cards.question: An aircraft is landing with a tailwind, which has increased its sink rate — what does this do to the flare window?
options: It leaves the flare height unchanged but steepens the flare
It decreases the height at which the flare begins
It increases the height at which the flare begins
cards.explain: A faster descent raises the flare height so that there is more time to arrest the sink rate.

cards.question: What does the simplicity of the flare controller have to be traded off against
options: A relatively narrow touch down zone and a large variation in sink rate
A relatively wide touch down zone and a large variation in sink rate
A relatively wide touch down zone and a large variation in pitch attitude
cards.explain: The price of the simple law is a wide touchdown zone and a spread of touchdown sink rates.

cards.question: An aircraft is set down so softly that the weight on wheels signal is late — what does that cost on the landing roll?
options: The ground spoilers extend early
The braking action is delayed
The reverse thrust is inhibited
cards.explain: A late weight on wheels signal or a late wheel spin up both hold up the braking.

cards.question: Which property of the tyres impedes the directional control by the landing gear after a greaser landing
options: They can accept only a limited rolling velocity
They can accept only a limited lateral force
They can accept only a limited vertical load
cards.explain: The tyres can take only a limited lateral force, so the landing gear cannot steer the aircraft.

cards.question: The landing controller adds a height bias to the measured radio altitude close to the ground — what does this achieve at the wheels?
options: A pitch up is still commanded once the aircraft is on the ground
A sink rate is still commanded once the aircraft is on the ground
A thrust increase is still commanded once the aircraft is on the ground
cards.explain: Because the controller thinks it is higher than it is, it keeps commanding a descent and so forces a positive touch down.

cards.question: An aircraft enters ground effect in the last feet of the flare — which set of changes follows?
options: More lift, less induced drag and the centre of lift further aft
Less lift, less induced drag and the centre of lift further aft
More lift, more induced drag and the centre of lift further forward
cards.explain: Ground effect gives more lift, less induced drag and moves the centre of lift rearwards.

cards.question: A heavy aircraft carries a second set of antennas at the nose landing gear — what is switched over once the gear is extended?
options: The localizer receivers go to the nose gear antennas
The radio altimeters go to the nose gear antennas
The glide path receivers go to the nose gear antennas
cards.explain: Gear extension switches the glide path receivers over to the antennas on the nose gear.

cards.question: Which result is achieved by feeding the glide path receivers from the nose gear antennas on a heavy aircraft
options: It gets the same flare window as a smaller aircraft
It gets the same approach speed as a smaller aircraft
It gets a lower flare window than a smaller aircraft
cards.explain: Measuring from the nose gear lifts the aircraft virtually on the beam so the flare window matches a small aircraft's.

cards.question: The flare controller stops rounding the path off at its upper limit — what would happen beyond that limit?
options: The aircraft would risk a long float before touch down
The aircraft would risk a tail strike at touch down
The aircraft would risk a nose gear strike at touch down
cards.explain: Too much nose up at touchdown would put the tail on the runway.

cards.question: Why does a vertical acceleration signal damp the activity of the flare controller
options: It lets the radio altitude be filtered smoothly
It lets disturbances be recognised early
It lets the sink rate be measured accurately
cards.explain: Seeing a disturbance early means the controller does not have to react violently later.

cards.question: Why does the remaining component of lift have to be decreased after the touch down
options: To increase rudder authority and yaw damping
To increase runway adhesion and brake efficiency
To increase tyre life and brake cooling
cards.explain: Killing the lift puts weight on the wheels so they grip and the brakes work.

cards.question: The auto-trim is switched off at the same time as the derotation — what would otherwise drive the trim?
options: A constant pitch error caused by the stabilizer's positive moment
A constant pitch error caused by the elevator's negative moment
A constant pitch rate caused by the elevator's negative moment
cards.explain: The elevator holds a steady nose down moment after derotation, and the standing pitch error that leaves would wake the trim system up.

cards.question: Why is the aircraft headed into the wind during a cross wind approach
options: To prevent a bank angle on the localizer beam
To prevent a displacement from the localizer beam
To prevent a lateral load on the landing gear
cards.explain: Crabbing into the wind stops the aircraft being blown off the beam, so it drifts along it instead.

cards.question: Why is the alignment left until shortly before the touch down
options: It minimizes the lateral drift
It minimizes the rudder deflection
It minimizes the crosswind component
cards.explain: Once the crab is taken out the aircraft starts drifting sideways, so the manoeuvre is kept short.

cards.question: Which comparison produces the control error used by the align controller
options: The present heading against the present track
The localizer deviation against the runway heading
The present heading against the runway heading
cards.explain: The align loop subtracts the measured heading from the runway heading set as preselected course.

cards.question: An aircraft on an automatic approach is in landing configuration and passing 200 ft radio height — what is the state of the align phase?
options: Neither armed nor active
Armed but not yet active
Active and holding the runway heading
cards.explain: The landing configuration arms the phase, but it only goes active below 30 ft, so at 200 ft it is still armed.

cards.question: An automatic landing is being flown onto the runway — which event starts the roll-out phase?
options: The compression of the nose gear
The extension of the ground spoilers
The touch down of the main gear
cards.explain: Roll out begins the moment the main gear is on the runway.

cards.question: The aircraft is decelerating on the runway under the yaw channel — which event ends the roll-out phase?
options: The lowering of the nose gear
The disengagement of the autopilot
The aircraft coming to a stop
cards.explain: Roll out runs until the crew disengages the autopilot.

cards.question: Which means takes over the directional control increasingly after the derotation
options: The nose wheel steering
The rudder deflection
The differential braking
cards.explain: Once the nose wheel is down it progressively takes over the steering.

cards.question: Why can the localizer deviation signal be used for the yaw control during the roll-out
options: The localizer is aligned with the aircraft track
The localizer is aligned with the runway centre line
The localizer is aligned with the preselected course
cards.explain: Because the beam lies along the centre line, a beam deviation is a centre line deviation.

cards.question: The aircraft is rolling out fast with the nose gear still off the ground — how is the direction held?
options: By rudder deflections only
By rudder deflections and nose wheel steering
By nose wheel steering only
cards.explain: With the nose off the ground only the rudder is available, and at that speed it still bites.

cards.question: The aircraft is being steered along the centre line after landing — which two signals does the yaw controller process?
options: The crab angle and the localizer deviation
The heading error and the localizer deviation
The heading error and the glide path deviation
cards.explain: Both a heading error and a lateral displacement have to be removed, so both signals are used.

cards.question: All three gears are on the runway during the roll-out — what else does the yaw channel now control?
options: The rudder trim actuator
The main wheel brakes
The nose wheel steering
cards.explain: Once the nose gear is down the same yaw channel steers it as well as the rudder.

cards.question: Which name is given to the transition phase from an approach to a stabilized climb
options: A roll out manoeuvre
A go around manoeuvre
An align manoeuvre
cards.explain: That transition is exactly what is called a go around.

cards.question: Which channel takes over the vertical guidance once the go around manoeuvre has started
options: The yaw channel
The roll channel
The pitch channel
cards.explain: Vertical guidance in a go around belongs to the pitch channel.

cards.question: Which form of control does the first go around concept activate at the start of the manoeuvre
options: Vertical speed control to a fixed climb value
Pitch attitude control to a fixed positive value
Airspeed control to a fixed reference value
cards.explain: The first concept rotates to and then holds a fixed nose up attitude.

cards.question: A go around is selected on the approach — which three parts of the autoflight system come in together?
options: The roll channel, the yaw channel and the auto-thrust system
The pitch channel, the roll channel and the auto-thrust system
The pitch channel, the yaw channel and the auto-thrust system
cards.explain: Go around is a common mode and brings pitch, roll and the thrust system in together.

cards.question: The crew changes the slat and flap setting during a go around — what happens to the airspeed reference values?
options: They are adapted automatically
They are frozen at the previous value
They have to be reselected by hand
cards.explain: The references follow the configuration without any crew action.

cards.question: A go around is being flown — what is the minimum climb rate that has to be observed?
options: 600 ft/min
120 ft/min
1200 ft/min
cards.explain: The minimum climb rate for the go around is 120 ft/min.

cards.question: Which minimum flight path angle has to be observed during a go around
cards.explain: Half a degree is the minimum flight path angle.

cards.question: Why does the airworthiness standard demand a minimum climb rate and a minimum flight path angle
options: To achieve obstacle clearance
To achieve a stabilized airspeed
To achieve a positive rate of climb
cards.explain: The minima exist so the aircraft will clear what is ahead of it.

cards.question: Which condition must be satisfied before the go around mode may be terminated
options: A minimum airspeed above the reference has to be passed
A minimum height above the ground has to be passed
A minimum time in thrust mode has to elapse
cards.explain: The mode is locked in until a minimum height above the ground has been exceeded.

cards.question: Which thrust does the auto-throttle command when the go around mode becomes active
options: The maximum continuous thrust available in the climb
The maximum thrust available for five minutes
The reduced climb thrust available after flap retraction
cards.explain: Go around thrust is the five minute maximum rating.

cards.question: Which track does the roll channel maintain during the go around
options: The track of the runway centre line extended
The track selected on the autoflight control panel
The track it was following at the start of the manoeuvre
cards.explain: The roll channel simply holds whatever track was being flown when the go around began.

cards.question: Which penalty follows the inversion of a sink rate into a climb rate during the go around
options: The thrust is reduced
The airspeed is reduced
The pitch attitude is reduced
cards.explain: Turning a descent into a climb is paid for in speed.

cards.question: Between which climb rates does the transition from attitude guidance to speed guidance take place
options: 1200 ft/min and 1800 ft/min
120 ft/min and 600 ft/min
600 ft/min and 1200 ft/min
cards.explain: The changeover is spread continuously over 600 to 1200 ft/min of climb.

cards.question: Which flight condition makes the climb rate drop drastically during a go around
options: A thrust reduction or a bank
A flap or a gear retraction
Wind shear or a downdraft
cards.explain: Wind shear or a downdraft is the case given for a sudden loss of climb rate.

cards.question: Which principle is the speed reference control law built on
options: Total pressure management
Total thrust management
Total energy management
cards.explain: The alternative concept works from the total energy of the aircraft.

cards.question: Which two modes is the speed reference control law used for
options: The flight director take-off mode and the go around mode
The flight director land mode and the go around mode
The flight director take-off mode and the flare mode
cards.explain: The same law serves the take-off director and the go around.

cards.question: Which quantity is the potential flight path angle directly proportional to
options: The pitch attitude on the actual flight path
The acceleration on the actual flight path
The thrust setting on the actual flight path
cards.explain: It is the acceleration along the path that the potential angle follows.

cards.question: Which property of the aircraft does the potential flight path angle reflect
options: Its total energy
Its kinetic energy only
Its potential energy only
cards.explain: The potential angle is a measure of the whole energy state, not one part of it.

cards.question: Which quantity is the correction angle proportional to
options: The speed error
The angle of attack
The flight path error
cards.explain: The correction angle is sized by the speed error.

cards.question: Which signal is formed at the last summing point and used as the reference for the pitch attitude controller
options: The sum of the flight path error and the correction angle
The difference of the actual and potential flight path angles
The sum of the pitch attitude and the angle of attack
cards.explain: S3 adds the correction angle onto the flight path error and the sum is the demand given to the pitch controller.

cards.question: A large thrust increase at the start of a go around produces a strong nose up moment — which limits must the go around controller watch?
options: The flap or landing gear speed limits
The pitch attitude or angle of attack limits
The bank angle or sideslip limits
cards.explain: The required thrust increase causes a large positive pitch moment, so the pitch attitude and angle of attack limits have to be observed.

cards.question: An aircraft has an auto-thrust system and the crew wants a go around — what do they do with the power levers?
options: Pull them back to the idle detent
Push them to the TOGA detent
Press the TOGA switch on them
cards.explain: On an auto-thrust aircraft the levers are pushed into the TOGA detent.

cards.question: Why is the go around trigger tied to uncompressed gears with slats and flaps extended
options: It prevents triggering during other flight phases
It prevents triggering below the minimum height
It prevents triggering with the autopilot engaged
cards.explain: The configuration test makes sure the mode can only come up where it belongs, on an approach.

cards.question: The aircraft touches down while a go around is being flown — what happens to the mode?
options: It changes into the rollout mode
It stays active
It is terminated at once
cards.explain: The mode survives a touch down, which is what makes a touch and go possible.

cards.question: The crew decides to level off and fly a radar heading after a go around — how is the mode taken out?
options: By selecting other upper modes for pitch and roll together
By disengaging the autopilot and flying by hand
By selecting other upper modes for pitch and roll independently
cards.explain: Picking a new upper mode ends the go around, and the vertical and lateral sides can be ended separately.

cards.question: The go around controller rotates the aircraft to a fixed positive pitch attitude — what follows from that?
options: Lift increases and the momentary sink rate decreases
Lift increases and the momentary airspeed increases
Drag increases and the momentary sink rate decreases
cards.explain: More attitude means more lift, and more lift arrests the descent.

cards.question: Which control replaces pitch attitude hold a short while after the start of the go around
options: Thrust control of the auto-throttle system
Airspeed control of the pitch channel
Vertical speed control of the pitch channel
cards.explain: Because the attitude hold is eating the speed, the pitch channel goes over to controlling airspeed.

cards.question: Airspeed control is running in a go around and the climb rate falls below 1200 ft/min — what does the vertical guidance do?
options: It reverts to vertical speed control
It stays on airspeed control
It reverts to pitch attitude control
cards.explain: Losing climb performance sends the channel back to holding attitude so lift is restored.

cards.question: Why does the aircraft keep climbing once the pitch controller holds a constant airspeed
options: The surplus of go around thrust gives a positive flight path angle
The surplus of go around thrust gives a positive pitch attitude
The surplus of lift gives a positive flight path angle
cards.explain: With the speed pegged, the spare thrust has nowhere to go but into climb angle.

cards.question: An aircraft is flying on a path whose angle equals its potential flight path angle — what are its errors?
options: Airspeed error zero and flight path error zero
Airspeed error at a maximum and flight path error at a maximum
Airspeed error zero and flight path error not zero
cards.explain: Flying at the potential angle means the energy is exactly balanced, so both errors vanish.

cards.question: Which angle appears when the airspeed reference is changed while the thrust is held constant
options: An error angle that changes the present angle of attack
A demand angle that changes the present pitch attitude
A correction angle that changes the present flight path angle
cards.explain: The speed error is worked off by a correction angle that tilts the flight path so the aircraft accelerates or decelerates.

cards.question: Go around is selected on an approach — which speed is captured in the memory as the speed target?
options: The actual airspeed at that moment
The minimum selectable speed
The approach reference speed
cards.explain: Selecting go around closes the switch that freezes the actual airspeed into the memory as the target.

questions.question: Which two tasks does the flight director accomplish
options: Commands for manual control and automatic trim of the pitch axis
Monitoring of autopilot activities and selection of the thrust rating
Commands for manual control and monitoring of autopilot activities
questions.explain: The flight director has exactly two tasks: it gives commands for manual control, and it allows monitoring of the autopilot.

questions.question: During which phases is a yaw bar displayed and the roll bar removed
options: Flare below 50 ft radio height, climb and take-off
Align below 30 ft radio height, rollout and approach
Flare below 30 ft radio height, rollout and take-off
questions.explain: Those are the three phases printed for yaw bar display.

questions.question: Why are the flight director indicators overlaid on the artificial horizon
options: They display attitude commands affecting the rotary degrees of freedom
They display speed commands affecting the linear degrees of freedom
They display track commands affecting the lateral degrees of freedom
questions.explain: Because the commands concern the rotary degrees of freedom they belong on the artificial horizon.

questions.question: For which system is the take off mode exclusively reserved
options: The flight director
The autopilot
The auto-throttle
questions.explain: The take off mode belongs to the flight director alone.

questions.question: Why are supplemental display systems fitted for low visibility take offs
options: They allow the roll bar to be shown below 30 ft radio height
They replace the artificial horizon during the take off run
They avoid a change between head-up and head-down views
questions.explain: They let the pilot see the guidance while still looking at the runway lighting.

questions.question: The aircraft passes 30 ft radio height with no FMS flight plan active. Which lateral guidance does the roll bar give?
options: It maintains the heading entered on the control panel
It maintains the runway centre line
It maintains the runway track
questions.explain: Above 30 ft the roll bar holds the runway track until another lateral mode is chosen.

questions.question: To which autopilot mode is the flight director take off yaw control mode equivalent
options: The autoland flare mode
The autoland align mode
The autoland roll-out mode
questions.explain: It is the same control arrangement as the autoland roll-out mode.

questions.question: What does the auto-thrust system do in place of moving the throttles
options: It controls the thrust over a data bus
It controls the throttle cables over the FADEC
It controls the thrust over the servo clutch
questions.explain: Thrust is commanded over a data bus rather than by moving the levers.

questions.question: What supported the development of the auto-thrust system
options: The derating of the turbine inlet temperature limits
The introduction of the para visual display systems
The electronic control of modern turbofan engines
questions.explain: FADEC engine control made the auto-thrust system possible, and the functions are often built into it.

questions.question: Which rule governs the control of airspeed by an autoflight system
options: Both systems control it together at any moment
Only one system can control it exclusively at any moment
The system with the smaller error controls it at any moment
questions.explain: Airspeed is controlled by one system at a time, never two.

questions.question: Conditions allow a reduced thrust take off. Why is that reduction recommended?
options: It shortens the take off run and lowers the noise footprint
It prolongs engine life and lowers the failure probability
It raises the thrust rating left available for the climb phase
questions.explain: Reduced thrust extends engine life and cuts the chance of a failure.

questions.question: How is go around thrust defined
options: The max continuous rating corrected for the higher altitude
The max climb rating corrected for the lower air density
The max take off rating corrected for the higher airspeed
questions.explain: It is the max take off rating adjusted for the greater airspeed in a go around.

questions.question: In an auto-thrust system which device turns lever position into the signal sent to the engine control unit
options: A rate gyro at the throttle quadrant
An angle transducer at the levers
A torque limiter in the servo drive
questions.explain: An angle transducer turns lever position into the TLA signal sent to the ECU.

questions.question: Two functions both work out ratings in thrust mode — what separates one from the other?
options: One works only in flight, the other works only on the ground
One uses the flight phase, the other the lever position
One uses the air data, the other uses the bleed demand
questions.explain: Rating calculation is keyed to the flight phase and power management to lever position.

questions.question: An integrating element is used in the speed and Mach mode in order to obtain which result
options: Less hysteresis in the linkage
A speed error of zero at the end
Faster throttle travel at large speed errors
questions.explain: Only an I-controller drives the remaining error to zero.

questions.question: The all weather approval holds good for which runways
options: Only those listed in the operator's own route manual
Only those fitted with a roll out guidance system
Those approved by the authority for that category
questions.explain: Approval follows the authority's own runway classification for the category.

questions.question: The yaw damper becomes unserviceable during the cruise — what must then be done with the aircraft?
options: It has to climb to a higher altitude
It has to slow to the minimum airspeed
It has to descend to a lower altitude
questions.explain: Lower down the natural aerodynamic damping is strong enough.

questions.question: The aircraft accelerates in the cruise — what happens to the yaw rate signal passed on to the actuator?
options: It is cut back as the speed rises
It is built up as the speed rises
It is held at its take-off value
questions.explain: Inverse proportionality means the signal is reduced as speed increases.

questions.question: The crew needs to know the capability of their automatic landing system — where do they read it?
options: As an approach category on the flight annunciator
As a decision height index on the radio altimeter
As an amber light on the ILS deviation alert
questions.explain: Capability shows up as the available approach category on the flight mode annunciator.

questions.question: An approach is planned to a decision height of 150 ft with a reported visual range of 400 m — which category applies?
options: CAT III a
CAT II
CAT I
questions.explain: A decision height between 200 ft and 100 ft with at least 300 m visual range is CAT II.

questions.question: A failure appears in the redundant part of the autoland system above the alert height — what follows?
options: The approach is broken off and a go around flown
The failure is ignored and the approach continued
The approach reverts to the next higher category
questions.explain: Above the alert height such a failure forces a go around.

questions.question: In which band must a failure happen for a reversion to another approach category to be considered
options: At or below the alert height
Above 1000 ft above the ground
Below 1000 ft above the ground
questions.explain: The general rule puts the reversion decision above 1000 ft AGL.

questions.question: The objective of CAT II autoflight operation is to hold which level of safety
options: One set by the aircraft manufacturer alone
One equivalent to manual flight operation
One above that of manual flight operation
questions.explain: The aim is equivalence with manual operation, under worse weather.

questions.question: What is the crew able to judge at a CAT III A decision height
options: Whether touch down will fall in the touch down zone
Whether the autoland has dropped to fail-passive
Whether the roll out can be supervised visually throughout
questions.explain: At CAT III A the crew can still see whether the aircraft will land in the zone.

questions.question: One of several parallel channels drops out and the output signal is unaffected — which redundancy is in use?
options: Monitored redundancy
Active redundancy
Passive redundancy
questions.explain: Only active redundancy keeps the output going with no switch over.

questions.question: The decision height planned is below 50 ft — what standard must the automatic landing system then meet?
options: Fail-operational
Fail-passive
Fail-safe
questions.explain: Below 50 ft only a fail-operational landing or hybrid system will do.

questions.question: An autopilot that detects its own failure and disengages itself is operated on its own. Which behaviour does the system then show?
options: fail passive behaviour
fail operational behaviour
fail safe behaviour
questions.explain: A single system able to detect and remove its own failure gives fail passive behaviour in single operation.

questions.question: A manufacturer limits the authority of its autopilot servos, but the aircraft has no manual control path strong enough to overrule the autopilot. Why is that not acceptable?
options: because the servos would then not reach their full travel range
because the pilot could then not over-power the autopilot
because the autopilot could then not recognize its own hard over
questions.explain: Authority limitation relies on the pilot being able to apply strong inputs and over-power the autopilot manually.

questions.question: A fail passive system must be able to disengage itself. How does it recognize that it has a failure?
options: by comparing the two autopilot computers with each other
by monitoring the hydraulic pressure at the actuator
by comparing the surface position with the commanded position
questions.explain: Recognition rests on the electrical comparison of actual surface position with commanded actuator position.

questions.question: In which respect does a dual channel fail passive autopilot differ from two parallel fail safe autopilots
options: it drives one actuator only and needs no mechanical voting
it drives three actuators and needs a mid-value voter
it drives two actuators and needs a torque limiter
questions.explain: Parallel fail safe autopilots need mechanical voting against force conflicts, while the dual channel autopilot drives a single actuator and does not.

questions.question: One of two parallel fail passive autopilots detects its own failure during an automatic landing. What happens next?
options: it disengages itself and the other one keeps control
both of them disengage and the pilot takes over
the faulty one is voted out by the mechanical voter
questions.explain: The failed autopilot takes itself out and the remaining one continues to control the aircraft.

questions.question: Which behaviour does the autopilot system of a hybrid built from two fail safe autopilots show
options: fail safe, augmented by an auto-thrust system
fail operational, augmented by a flight director
fail passive, augmented by a flight director
questions.explain: Two fail safe autopilots make the autopilot system fail passive, and the flight director augments it.

questions.question: The autoland warning comes on during an automatic approach. Which reaction is the normal one?
options: the disengagement of one autopilot
a continuation of the approach to CAT I minima
the initiation of a go around
questions.explain: A go around is the normal response to the autoland warning.

questions.question: A single failure below the alert height degrades the failure mode, yet the capability stays as it was. Why is it kept?
options: because the ground equipment can no longer be monitored
because the autoflight system still performs its duty
because the autopilot can no longer be disengaged
questions.explain: The capability stays because the system is still doing its job after the single failure.

questions.question: What does the collective pitch lever control
options: the velocity vector
the tail rotor thrust
the main rotor lift
questions.explain: The collective pitch lever is the lift control.

questions.question: On which helicopters is a twist grip throttle found
options: on those powered by a piston engine
on those powered by a turbine engine
on those with a counter clockwise rotor
questions.explain: The twist grip throttle belongs to piston engined helicopters.

questions.question: Which servos tilt the rotor plane around the longitudinal axis
options: the LH and RH servos
the front and LH servos
the front and yaw servos
questions.explain: The LH and RH servos work the longitudinal X-X' axis.

questions.question: The cyclic stick is moved to the left-hand side. Which servo stays unenergized and which movement results?
options: the front servo, and the helicopter moves nose down
the front servo, and the helicopter moves left sideward
the LH servo, and the helicopter moves left sideward
questions.explain: A sideward input leaves the front servo unenergized and moves the helicopter sideward to the left.

questions.question: The pedal position is changed in flight. Which quantity at the tail rotor changes as a result of the blade pitch change?
options: the thrust of the tail rotor
the speed of the tail rotor
the torque of the main rotor
questions.explain: Changing tail rotor blade pitch changes the tail rotor thrust.

questions.question: What follows from the helicopter having no positive stability
options: its rotor speed has to be controlled permanently by the pilot
its attitude has to be controlled permanently by the pilot
its trim actuators have to run permanently in flight
questions.explain: Without inherent stability the pilot has to control the attitude all the time.

cards.question: Which two tasks does the flight director accomplish
options: Commands for manual control and automatic trim of the pitch axis
Monitoring of autopilot activities and selection of the thrust rating
Commands for manual control and monitoring of autopilot activities
cards.explain: The flight director has exactly two tasks: it gives commands for manual control, and it allows monitoring of the autopilot.

cards.question: During which phases is a yaw bar displayed and the roll bar removed
options: Flare below 30 ft radio height, rollout and take-off
Align below 30 ft radio height, rollout and approach
Flare below 50 ft radio height, climb and take-off
cards.explain: Those are the three phases printed for yaw bar display.

cards.question: Which bars display the attitude reference commands in an ADI or PFD
options: A pitch bar, a roll bar and eventually a yaw bar
A pitch bar, a track bar and eventually a roll bar
A roll bar, a speed bar and eventually a yaw bar
cards.explain: Pitch and roll bars, and possibly a yaw bar, carry the attitude reference commands.

cards.question: Which three speeds do the pilots determine during flight preparation for the take off phase
options: V1, V2 and VLS
VR, V2 and VMAX
V1, VR and V2
cards.explain: The three take off speeds named are V1, VR and V2.

cards.question: At which height above the runway does the take off safety speed have to be obtained with one engine inoperative
options: 50 ft
30 ft
35 ft
cards.explain: V2 is defined at 35 ft above the runway surface.

cards.question: Why are the flight director indicators overlaid on the artificial horizon
options: They display speed commands affecting the linear degrees of freedom
They display attitude commands affecting the rotary degrees of freedom
They display track commands affecting the lateral degrees of freedom
cards.explain: Because the commands concern the rotary degrees of freedom they belong on the artificial horizon.

cards.question: An aircraft with a crossbar flight director is following its defined flight path. Where do the two bars lie?
options: They lie apart at an equal distance above the horizon line
They intersect at the middle mark of the own aircraft symbol
They rest at the upper edge of the own aircraft symbol
cards.explain: On path the roll bar crosses the pitch bar at the middle mark of the aircraft symbol.

cards.question: Which rotations does the yaw bar command
options: Rotations around the vertical axis only
Rotations around the longitudinal axis only
Rotations around the lateral axis only
cards.explain: The yaw bar is restricted to rotations about the vertical axis.

cards.question: The yaw bar in the ADI deflects during the take off run. Which control inputs does the pilot make?
options: Aileron or roll spoiler inputs
Elevator or stabiliser trim inputs
Rudder or nose wheel steering inputs
cards.explain: Yaw bar commands are flown with rudder or nose wheel steering.

cards.question: Below 50 ft radio altitude on an autoland the flare, align and rollout modes are selected automatically. What part does the flight director then play?
options: It serves only for monitoring the autopilot
It serves only for commanding manual control inputs
It is removed from the display until roll out has ended
cards.explain: In the autoland modes the flight director is a monitoring display only.

cards.question: The autopilot is engaged and a lateral mode is chosen on the control panel. What happens to the flight director?
options: The flight director reverts to its take off mode
The selected mode also holds for the flight director
The flight director bars are biased out of view
cards.explain: A mode selected with the autopilot engaged applies to the flight director as well.

cards.question: During a flight path mode the aircraft adopts the commanded attitude. What do the command bars do?
options: They stay deflected until the mode is deselected
They move to a steady offset from the centre
They return immediately to their centre position
cards.explain: The bars show attitude error only, so they centre as soon as the error is gone.

cards.question: The pitch bar deflects upward. Which input does it call for?
options: Push elevator, pitch down
Pull elevator, pitch up
Right aileron, turn right
cards.explain: An upward pitch bar asks for elevator back pressure to pitch up.

cards.question: Which input does a deflection of the roll bar to the right signify
options: Right aileron, turn right
Left aileron, turn left
Right rudder, yaw right
cards.explain: A roll bar to the right asks for right aileron and a turn to the right.

cards.question: The yaw bar deflects to the left. Which input does that command?
options: Right rudder pedal, yaw right
Left rudder pedal, yaw left
Left aileron wheel, turn left
cards.explain: A yaw bar to the left asks for left rudder pedal to yaw left.

cards.question: The roll bar in the ADI deflects. Which autopilot signal does that deflection correspond to?
options: The attitude error computed in the roll outer control loop
The signal fed to the roll actuator in the inner roll loop
The signal fed to the roll actuator in the outer heading loop
cards.explain: The bar is driven by the same signal the autopilot would send to its roll actuator in the inner loop.

cards.question: Which action removes a roll attitude error that the flight director indicates
options: A reset made in the outer heading loop
A servo input made by the roll actuator
A control input made by the pilot himself
cards.explain: The flight director only displays the command; the correction comes from the pilot's own input.

cards.question: Why must an aircraft be able to hold different steady pitch attitudes?
options: Because they depend on runway heading, visibility and flap setting
Because they depend on thrust rating, bleed air load and temperature
Because they depend on airspeed, centre of gravity and gross weight
cards.explain: Airspeed, CG position and gross weight each change the steady attitude required.

cards.question: Why are distances and airspeeds laid down in the airworthiness standards
options: To guarantee a sufficient safety margin in all flight phases
To allow a take off at the lowest possible runway visibility
To keep the engine ratings within their derated temperature limits
cards.explain: They exist to give a sufficient safety margin in every flight phase.

cards.question: Why does an aircraft with a tricycle gear have to be rotated at VR
options: It accelerates on its nose gear and has to unload that gear
It accelerates at a low angle of attack and needs more lift
It accelerates at a high angle of attack and needs less drag
cards.explain: The ground run is at a low angle of attack, so rotation is needed to make enough lift.

cards.question: A flight director shows a roll attitude error and the pilot moves the wheel to follow it. Which part of the loop structure has the pilot just closed?
options: The attitude limiter path
The outer heading loop
The inner control loop
cards.explain: In flight director operation the pilot himself closes the inner loop that the autopilot servo would otherwise close.

cards.question: Why does integration have to be avoided when a vertical mode drives the flight director pitch bar
options: The outer loop error is already proportional to attitude
The behaviour of the pilot cannot be predicted
The pitch bar signal is inverted before it is displayed
cards.explain: A pilot may react late or not at all, so an integrator cannot be used.

cards.question: What would a delayed pilot reaction do to the integrator in the outer loop
options: Drive it towards zero and centre the pitch bar
Drive it towards saturation and wind up the pitch bar
Hold it at a constant value and freeze the pitch bar
cards.explain: The integrator saturates, the bar winds up and the command becomes useless.

cards.question: Why can the outer loop error not be used directly as the pitch attitude reference for the inner loop
options: A zero error would then demand a pitch attitude of 20 degrees
A zero error would then demand a constant pitch rate
A zero error would then demand a pitch attitude of 0 degrees
cards.explain: With the outer loop error as reference, zero error would force the attitude to zero as well.

cards.question: The outer loop error is zero and the aircraft is held at a pitch attitude inside the suppression range. Where does the flight director pitch bar sit?
options: Deflected fully up
In its neutral position
Deflected fully down
cards.explain: With no outer loop error and the attitude still inside the suppression range, the feedback of actual pitch attitude is suppressed, so the bar rests in its neutral position.

cards.question: The aircraft pitches up beyond the suppression range. What is added to the pitch bar deflection?
options: A command proportional only to the outer loop error
A fixed command until the attitude re-enters the range
An opposing command proportional to the exceeding angle
cards.explain: Outside the range an opposing command sized by the exceeding angle is added to the bar.

cards.question: The pilot makes no input in answer to a short-term pitch bar deflection. What happens to the bar?
options: It stays deflected until the mode is reselected
It returns to its initial position again
It increases its deflection steadily
cards.explain: The washout lets the deflection decay back to the initial position.

cards.question: The pilot follows a short-term pitch bar deflection caused by a gust inside the suppression range. What keeps that deflection from winding up?
options: The washout in the pitch rate feedback path
The attitude limiter at the pitch bar output
The integrator in the outer control loop
cards.explain: The washout makes the pitch rate feedback decay, so no lasting build-up occurs.

cards.question: An engine fails while the aircraft is accelerating and is still below V1. What must be done?
options: The aircraft has to be rotated at once
The take off has to be discontinued
The take off has to be continued
cards.explain: Before V1 an engine failure obliges the crew to stop the take off.
