cards.question: An aircraft is in a V2 climb after an engine failure and below the acceleration altitude. What is the state of the gear and the flaps?
options: Gear retracted, take off flaps already retracted
Gear extended, take off flaps already retracted
Gear retracted, take off flaps still extended
cards.explain: The gear comes up but the take off flaps stay out until the acceleration altitude.

cards.question: For which system is the take off mode exclusively reserved
options: The flight director
The autopilot
The auto-throttle
cards.explain: The take off mode belongs to the flight director alone.

cards.question: The take off mode has just been selected on the ground. Which flight director channels are activated?
options: The pitch channel and the roll channel
The roll channel and the yaw channel
The pitch channel and the yaw channel
cards.explain: Selection of the take off mode brings up the pitch and yaw channels.

cards.question: At which typical airspeed is the rotation attitude indicated on the pitch bar during the acceleration
options: Typically 80 kts
Typically 60 kts
Typically 100 kts
cards.explain: The printed typical value is 60 kts.

cards.question: From which parameters is the potential flight path angle calculated
options: Longitudinal and vertical acceleration and angle of attack
Vertical acceleration, airspeed and angle of attack
Longitudinal acceleration, pitch rate and radio altitude
cards.explain: Those three parameters are the printed inputs to the potential flight path angle.

cards.question: How is the actual flight path angle obtained
options: From the difference between pitch attitude and the threshold angle
From the difference between pitch attitude and angle of attack
From the sum of the pitch attitude and the angle of attack
cards.explain: It is the pitch attitude angle less the angle of attack.

cards.question: In which mode does an armed auto-throttle system stay throughout the take off phase
options: Mach mode
Thrust mode
Speed mode
cards.explain: Through the whole take off the armed system remains in thrust mode.

cards.question: A take off is to be made at a visibility between 125 m and 75 m. Which indication gives the pilot his lateral guidance?
options: A roll bar controlled by the runway heading signal
A pitch bar controlled by the radio altitude signal
A yaw bar controlled by the localizer deviation signal
cards.explain: In that visibility band the yaw bar driven by localizer deviation provides the lateral guidance.

cards.question: Why are supplemental display systems fitted for low visibility take offs
options: They replace the artificial horizon during the take off run
They avoid a change between head-up and head-down views
They allow the roll bar to be shown below 30 ft radio height
cards.explain: They let the pilot see the guidance while still looking at the runway lighting.

cards.question: How is the flight director switched into take off mode
options: Pressing a TOGA switch or pushing the levers into the TOGA detent
Arming the auto-thrust and selecting the departure runway by hand
Pressing a NAV switch or pushing the levers into the idle detent
cards.explain: Either the TOGA switch or the TOGA detent selects the mode.

cards.question: The aircraft passes 30 ft radio height with no FMS flight plan active. Which lateral guidance does the roll bar give?
options: It maintains the runway centre line
It maintains the heading entered on the control panel
It maintains the runway track
cards.explain: Above 30 ft the roll bar holds the runway track until another lateral mode is chosen.

cards.question: When is the pitch attitude to be adopted at VR shown on the pitch bar
options: As soon as the gear struts extend, or at 35 ft above the runway
As soon as the take off mode is selected, or at a certain airspeed
As soon as the thrust levers reach the TOGA detent, or at lift off
cards.explain: Two implementations exist: at mode selection, or on passing a certain airspeed.

cards.question: Which airspeed does the flight director command for the initial climb at a normal take off
options: An actual airspeed 10 to 20 kts above V2
An actual airspeed equal to V2
An actual airspeed 10 to 20 kts above VR
cards.explain: On all engines the initial climb is flown 10 to 20 kts above V2.

cards.question: A take off run is in progress. Which reference does the pilot use to find the point of rotation?
options: Airspeed only
Radio height only
Pitch bar position only
cards.explain: The rotation point is set by airspeed alone, read from the ASI.

cards.question: Which two inputs does the flight director need for yaw bar control up to 30 ft radio height
options: Runway heading and localizer deviation
Runway heading and radio altitude
Localizer deviation and ground speed
cards.explain: Yaw bar control needs the runway heading and the localizer deviation.

cards.question: Why does pitch attitude replace angle of attack in the calculation of the potential flight path angle during the take off phase
options: Because the inertial system is not yet fully aligned
Because the angle of attack vanes are not yet heated
Because of the air flow conditions at that time
cards.explain: The air flow conditions at take off make the angle of attack unusable, so pitch attitude is taken.

cards.question: To which autopilot mode is the flight director take off yaw control mode equivalent
options: The autoland roll-out mode
The autoland align mode
The autoland flare mode
cards.explain: It is the same control arrangement as the autoland roll-out mode.

cards.question: Which input tells the yaw controller the direction in which the aircraft should be pointing?
options: The localizer deviation signal
The supplied runway heading
The radio height signal
cards.explain: Alignment with the runway comes from the supplied runway heading.

cards.question: Which input lets the yaw controller recognise a departure from the runway centre line?
options: The nose wheel steering position
The localizer deviation signal
The supplied runway heading
cards.explain: Deviations from the centre line are seen in the localizer deviation signal.

cards.question: The aircraft climbs through a radio altitude of 30 ft after lift off. What changes in the flight director?
options: The yaw channel is deactivated and the roll channel activated
The roll channel is deactivated and the yaw channel activated
The pitch channel is deactivated and the roll channel activated
cards.explain: At 30 ft the yaw channel drops out and the roll channel comes in at the same moment.

cards.question: Which guidance does the yaw bar give from brake release up to a radio height of 30 ft
options: A return to the runway centre line at any deviation
A return to the runway track after a lateral mode change
A turn onto the standard instrument departure
cards.explain: Up to 30 ft the yaw bar works the aircraft back onto the runway centre line.

cards.question: An FMS flight plan is active as the aircraft climbs through 30 ft radio height. What does the lateral command follow?
options: The runway centre line until 1500 ft
The localizer of the departure runway
The standard instrument departure
cards.explain: With an active flight plan the lateral command follows the SID instead of the runway track.

cards.question: An engine fails after V1. Which pitch attitude does the flight director command?
options: One that reaches the safety speed plus 15 kts and then holds it
One that reaches the safety speed at 35 ft and then holds it
One that holds the rotation attitude until the acceleration altitude
cards.explain: After an engine failure the commanded attitude reaches V2 at 35 ft and keeps it through the first and second segment climb.

cards.question: The pitch bar already shows a rotation attitude while the aircraft is still accelerating below VR. What must the pilot do?
options: Disregard that pitch bar command
Rotate the aircraft into the pitch bar
Reduce thrust until the rotation speed is reached
cards.explain: The flight director cannot find the rotation point, so a command before VR is ignored.

cards.question: The take off runway has been selected at flight preparation. How does the yaw channel obtain its two inputs?
options: From the IRS, which supplies the track and the drift angle
From the FMS, which tunes the ILS and supplies the heading
From the ADC, which supplies the heading and the deviation
cards.explain: The FMS tunes the ILS for the localizer deviation and reads the runway heading from its database.

cards.question: Heading mode is selected for lateral guidance after the yaw bar has been removed. Which heading is followed?
options: The heading at its activation or one entered on the panel
The heading of the standard instrument departure leg
The runway heading supplied by the navigation database
cards.explain: Heading mode follows either the heading at activation or the heading set on the control panel.

cards.question: During take off the potential flight path angle drops below the threshold while the speed is already above V2. What does the autoflight system do?
options: It raises the speed target by a further 15 kts
It reduces the speed target to the safety speed
It tries to maintain the speed held at engine failure
cards.explain: Above V2 the system holds the speed the aircraft had at the failure instead of reducing the target.

cards.question: The potential flight path angle falls below the threshold while the aircraft is still below the safety speed. What becomes the speed target?
options: VLS
VR
V2
cards.explain: The target is automatically reduced to V2.

cards.question: Which difference remains between the flight director take off yaw control mode and the equivalent autopilot mode
options: The localizer deviation signal is not made use of
The pilot is actively involved in the loop
The rudder is driven directly by the yaw servo
cards.explain: The one difference is that the pilot sits in the loop.

cards.question: The pilot flies the yaw bar commands accurately during the take off run. What happens to the localizer deviation and the heading error?
options: Both are frozen at their present values
Both are replaced by a roll demand
Both of them are progressively minimized
cards.explain: Following the bar drives both the lateral deviation and the heading error towards zero.

cards.question: Which computer function determines the thrust ratings
options: The envelope protection function of the flight control computers
The thrust limit function of the flight management computers
The power management function of the engine computers
cards.explain: Ratings come from the power management function in the EEC or ECU.

cards.question: In which two areas can an auto-throttle or auto-thrust system relieve the pilot
options: Thrust control or pitch trim control
Thrust control or airspeed control
Airspeed control or lateral guidance
cards.explain: The two areas of relief are thrust control and airspeed control.

cards.question: Which two modes of operation does an auto-throttle or auto-thrust system provide
options: Thrust mode and alpha floor mode
Speed or Mach mode and retard mode
Thrust mode and speed or Mach mode
cards.explain: The system offers a thrust mode and a speed or Mach mode.

cards.question: For how long is the maximum take off thrust rating basically available
options: 15 minutes
5 minutes
2 minutes
cards.explain: The printed basic limit is 5 minutes.

cards.question: Which rating is the highest thrust available without a time limit
options: Maximum climb thrust
Maximum take off thrust
Maximum continuous thrust
cards.explain: MCT is the highest thrust with no time limit attached.

cards.question: The auto-throttle system works in thrust mode provided the autopilot vertical mode is of which kind
options: A speed or Mach mode
An altitude hold mode
A vertical speed mode
cards.explain: Thrust mode is entered only while the pitch channel is holding speed or Mach.

cards.question: The rearward throttle movement to the idle position during cruise-descent and flare carries which name
options: Retard bias
Rate feedback
Torque limiter
cards.explain: The drive back to idle in those two phases is called the retard bias.

cards.question: In an auto-thrust system the required rating mode is brought in by which action
options: The flight management system commanding the levers
A servo motor driving the thrust levers forward
The pilot setting the thrust levers by hand
cards.explain: The pilot picks the rating mode by hand on the levers.

cards.question: In speed or Mach mode the auto-throttle system holds which quantity
options: A pre-selected airspeed or Mach number
A pre-selected rating for the flight phase
A pre-selected Mach trim setting
cards.explain: The mode holds the speed or Mach value selected by the pilot or by the FMS.

cards.question: What does the auto-thrust system do in place of moving the throttles
options: It controls the thrust over the servo clutch
It controls the thrust over a data bus
It controls the throttle cables over the FADEC
cards.explain: Thrust is commanded over a data bus rather than by moving the levers.

cards.question: An aircraft has an auto-thrust system fitted. How can its throttles be moved?
options: Only manually
Manually or by the servomotor
Only automatically
cards.explain: With auto-thrust the levers move by hand only.

cards.question: What does the position of the throttles determine on an aircraft with an auto-thrust system
options: The reference speed used by the speed mode of the system
The thrust rating and so the limits for that flight phase
The thrust demand sent straight to the fuel control unit
cards.explain: Lever position picks the rating, which sets the thrust limits for the phase.

cards.question: What supported the development of the auto-thrust system
options: The derating of the turbine inlet temperature limits
The electronic control of modern turbofan engines
The introduction of the para visual display systems
cards.explain: FADEC engine control made the auto-thrust system possible, and the functions are often built into it.

cards.question: Which demands was the auto-thrust system introduced to meet
options: Higher thrust ratings and a shorter take off run
Lower fuel burn and a wider speed envelope
Lower complexity and a better man/machine interface
cards.explain: It answered the demand for less complexity and a better man/machine interface.

cards.question: Which settings can be made in thrust mode
options: Reference speed or Mach number
Thrust ratings or thrust idle
Thrust ratings or alpha floor
cards.explain: Thrust mode sets either a rating, that is a thrust limit, or thrust idle.

cards.question: What is obtained when thrust idle is set
options: The lowest rating allowed for that flight phase
Only residual thrust from an idling engine
A thrust that just balances the aerodynamic drag
cards.explain: Thrust idle leaves only the residual thrust of the idling engine.

cards.question: The system is working in speed or Mach mode. Where does its reference speed come from?
options: The autoflight control panel or the EEC
The autoflight control panel or the FMS
The air data computer or the FMS
cards.explain: The reference is either set on the control panel or supplied by the FMS.

cards.question: From which low speed value do the protective functions keep the aircraft away
options: VLS
VR
V1
cards.explain: VLS is the low speed limit the system protects.

cards.question: With respect to what does the overspeed protection work
options: Airspeed and the thrust rating set for that flight phase
Angle of attack and the pitch attitude during the approach
Altitude and the slat/flap or landing gear configuration
cards.explain: Overspeed protection takes account of altitude and the slat/flap or gear configuration.

cards.question: In which mode does the auto-thrust system observe the thrust ratings as a protective function
options: The speed or Mach mode
The idle thrust mode
The take off thrust mode
cards.explain: This protective function belongs to the SPD/Mach mode: the thrust ratings go on being observed while the system is controlling speed.

cards.question: Which rule governs the control of airspeed by an autoflight system
options: Only one system can control it exclusively at any moment
Both systems control it together at any moment
The system with the smaller error controls it at any moment
cards.explain: Airspeed is controlled by one system at a time, never two.

cards.question: Which system holds priority for airspeed control
options: The flight management system computer
The autopilot or flight director pitch channel
The auto-throttle or auto-thrust system
cards.explain: Priority lies with the pitch channel of the autopilot or flight director.

cards.question: Why is the maximum power available from a turbofan engine reduced in service
options: To keep the thrust within the capacity of the data bus
To reach acceptable life cycles for highly stressed parts
To allow the thrust to be measured directly in flight
cards.explain: Continuous maximum thermodynamic power would wear the engine out quickly.

cards.question: Which parameter limits the thermodynamic power of a turbofan engine
options: The maximum engine pressure ratio
The maximum low pressure rotor speed
The maximum turbine inlet temperature
cards.explain: Turbine inlet temperature sets the thermodynamic ceiling, and is then derated.

cards.question: The auto-throttle is working in thrust mode. Why are N1 or EPR used as the reference values?
options: Thrust is a force and varies with the bleed air load in flight
Thrust is a force and cannot be measured directly in flight
Thrust is a force and is limited by the turbine inlet temperature
cards.explain: Thrust itself cannot be measured in flight, so derived parameters stand in for it.

cards.question: Which period do most authorities apart from the FAA accept for engine failure performance calculations
options: 10 minutes of maximum take off thrust
15 minutes of maximum continuous thrust
5 minutes of maximum take off thrust
cards.explain: Those authorities allow 10 minutes of max take off thrust for that calculation.

cards.question: Conditions allow a reduced thrust take off. Why is that reduction recommended?
options: It prolongs engine life and lowers the failure probability
It shortens the take off run and lowers the noise footprint
It raises the thrust rating left available for the climb phase
cards.explain: Reduced thrust extends engine life and cuts the chance of a failure.

cards.question: How is go around thrust defined
options: The max take off rating corrected for the higher airspeed
The max continuous rating corrected for the higher altitude
The max climb rating corrected for the lower air density
cards.explain: It is the max take off rating adjusted for the greater airspeed in a go around.

cards.question: Idle thrust has to be set with care on every engine type, so what must it still guarantee?
options: Bleed air delivery at the regulated cabin pressure
Spool-up to go-around power in the regulated time
Minimum fuel flow throughout the whole descent
cards.explain: Idle may not be so low that the engine cannot spool up to go-around thrust in the required time.

cards.question: Apart from other factors, idle thrust depends on which characteristic of the engine fitted
options: Its acceleration characteristic
Its bleed extraction characteristic
Its compression characteristic
cards.explain: How fast the engine accelerates decides how low idle may be set.

cards.question: The permanent rating calculation takes account of which two inputs
options: Thrust lever angle and fuel flow
Air data and bleed air demand
Radio height and flap position
cards.explain: Those are the two inputs named for the rating calculation.

cards.question: The crew has made no manual selection of the phase used for the rating — what else can supply it?
options: The flight management system
The autothrottle computer unit
The engine control computer
cards.explain: The flight phase comes either from the pilot or from the FMS.

cards.question: Level change is engaged and the aircraft is descending — what thrust does the auto-throttle set?
options: The take-off rating
The climb rating
Idle
cards.explain: In a level change descent the auto-throttle sets idle thrust.

cards.question: Thrust mode is engaged on the auto-throttle — what type of control does the system itself apply?
options: Open loop control
Cascaded loop control
Closed loop control
cards.explain: In thrust mode the auto-throttle itself works open loop.

cards.question: Thrust mode has just been selected — what does the determined thrust rating then serve as?
options: The reference for N2 closed loop control by the autothrottle computer
The reference for fuel flow control by the hydromechanical unit
The reference for N1 closed loop control by the engine computer
cards.explain: The rating becomes the N1 reference that the engine computer then closes the loop on.

cards.question: The power management function works out the rating for which quantity
options: Each engine bleed demand
Each defined flight phase
Each throttle position
cards.explain: Power management maps throttle position to a rating, phase by phase is the other function.

cards.question: In an auto-thrust system which device turns lever position into the signal sent to the engine control unit
options: An angle transducer at the levers
A torque limiter in the servo drive
A rate gyro at the throttle quadrant
cards.explain: An angle transducer turns lever position into the TLA signal sent to the ECU.

cards.question: A technician finds no throttle servo motor on an auto-thrust aircraft — how is that to be judged?
options: As a defect, since the servo must drive the levers to the rating
As a defect, since without it the retard bias cannot operate
As normal, since the levers of such a system are not driven automatically
cards.explain: An auto-thrust system has no lever servo at all, so none is missing.

cards.question: The speed and Mach control structure is built on how many control loops
options: A single loop
Three parallel loops
Two cascaded loops
cards.explain: Speed and Mach control uses one single loop.

cards.question: The time response of the speed and Mach controller is fixed by which two factors
options: Air data computer lag and thrust lever angle range
Thrust change dynamics and aircraft aerodynamics
Servo rate feedback and clutch torque limiter setting
cards.explain: Those are the two things named as setting the controller response.

cards.question: The engine control input lever position is fed back to the servo — which effect is this meant to cut down?
options: Overshoot from the longitudinal acceleration
Hysteresis from the mechanical components
Drift from the air data computer
cards.explain: The position feedback is there to reduce mechanical hysteresis.

cards.question: Which components of the earlier auto-throttle installation become superfluous with auto-thrust
options: Thrust rating computers, data buses and engine computers
Throttle levers, thrust limit displays and mode panels
Servomotors, clutch mechanisms, cables and TOGA switches
cards.explain: Those mechanical items and the TOGA switches drop out with auto-thrust.

cards.question: Why does the relief given by an auto-thrust system only materialise when the pitch axis is also under autopilot control?
options: Thrust changes trim the aircraft out and automatic trim is needed
The autopilot has to hold the attitude while the levers are moving
The pitch channel supplies the reference speed to the thrust computer
cards.explain: Every thrust change puts the aircraft out of trim, and the automatic trim comes from the autopilot pitch channel.

cards.question: During an approach the angle of attack becomes extreme. Which protection acts and with which thrust?
options: Alpha floor protection, with go around thrust
Low speed protection, with climb thrust
Overspeed protection, with idle thrust
cards.explain: Alpha floor protection answers an extreme angle of attack by applying go around thrust.

cards.question: The pitch channel is given the task of holding a certain altitude. Which system then controls the airspeed?
options: The auto-throttle or auto-thrust system
The flight management system computer
The pitch channel, which keeps its priority
cards.explain: The pitch channel delegates speed control once it is busy with another task.

cards.question: The pitch channel is the system controlling the airspeed. In which mode is the auto-throttle then working?
options: Speed mode, setting the reference airspeed
Thrust mode, setting a rating or idle thrust
Mach mode, setting the cruise Mach number
cards.explain: When the pitch channel has the speed, the thrust system sits in thrust mode on a rating or idle.

cards.question: An aircraft takes off at a low mass from a long runway at a low air temperature. Which rating is recommended?
options: Maximum take off thrust
Maximum continuous thrust
Flexible take off thrust
cards.explain: Those conditions are exactly the case for the reduced, flexible take off rating.

cards.question: A go around is flown at go around thrust. For how long may that thrust be held?
options: For the same period as maximum take off thrust
For as long as the approach has to be repeated
Until climb thrust is set at the acceleration altitude
cards.explain: Go around thrust carries the same time limit as maximum take off thrust.

cards.question: The maximum take off thrust period has elapsed but maximum thrust is still needed. Which rating is used?
options: Maximum continuous thrust
Maximum climb thrust
Flexible take off thrust
cards.explain: That abnormal case is one of the two uses printed for maximum continuous thrust.

cards.question: The servo drive is running the throttles forward in thrust mode — when does the movement stop?
options: The engine reaches the commanded N1 at its control unit
The power management value equals the rating reference
The thrust lever angle transducer reaches its forward stop
cards.explain: The servo runs until the fed back power management value cancels the rating reference in the summing point.

cards.question: The aircraft climbs in thrust mode while pressure and temperature change — why do the throttles stay put?
options: Both functions work from the same input data
The retard bias holds the levers against the idle stop
The servo drive is declutched above the transition altitude
cards.explain: Both values move together, so their difference stays zero and no servo signal is produced.

cards.question: Two functions both work out ratings in thrust mode — what separates one from the other?
options: One works only in flight, the other works only on the ground
One uses the flight phase, the other the lever position
One uses the air data, the other uses the bleed demand
cards.explain: Rating calculation is keyed to the flight phase and power management to lever position.

cards.question: An integrating element is used in the speed and Mach mode in order to obtain which result
options: Faster throttle travel at large speed errors
Less hysteresis in the linkage
A speed error of zero at the end
cards.explain: Only an I-controller drives the remaining error to zero.

cards.question: No hysteresis limit applies and the speed error grows — what happens to the rate of throttle movement?
options: It falls as the limiter takes over
It stays fixed until the error has gone
It rises in proportion to the error
cards.explain: Rate feedback makes throttle speed directly proportional to the error.

cards.question: Adding the engine control input position feedback to the servo makes which further item necessary
options: A torque limiter behind the servo clutch
An electronic integrator ahead of the servo
A rate gyro ahead of the band pass filter unit
cards.explain: The feedback destroys the servo's own integrating action, so an electronic integrator must replace it.

cards.question: The compromise between precise speed control and smooth thrust is reached by feeding back which signal
options: Actual throttle lever position
Longitudinal acceleration
Actual pitch attitude angle
cards.explain: Longitudinal acceleration feedback is the means of reconciling the two demands.

cards.question: A higher reference has been commanded and the aircraft is still accelerating with the error already gone — what stops an overshoot?
options: The retard bias driving the throttles to idle
The limiter holding the error at ten knots
The acceleration bias on the speed error
cards.explain: The acceleration bias pulls the throttles back before the speed is reached.

cards.question: A head-on gust raises the indicated speed while the aircraft itself is slowing — what keeps the throttles still?
options: The integrator inside the speed controller
The acceleration bias on the airspeed error
The hysteresis of the throttle control cables
cards.explain: The acceleration bias cancels the false speed rise so the levers do not move.

cards.question: A gust suddenly raises the airspeed and no acceleration feedback is fitted — what would the throttles do?
options: No movement of the throttles
A cut back of the throttles
An advance of the throttles
cards.explain: The loop would read the gust as excess speed and close the throttles.

cards.question: On a jet aircraft the swept wing reduces which stability, compared with the lateral stability
options: The directional static stability margin
The vertical dynamic stability
The longitudinal dynamic stability
cards.explain: The swept wing costs longitudinal dynamic stability relative to the lateral.

cards.question: The oscillation caused by longitudinal dynamic instability takes place about which axes
options: The yaw and pitch axes
The yaw and roll axes
The pitch and roll axes
cards.explain: The motion is a combined yaw and roll oscillation.

cards.question: The angular velocity about the yaw axis is sensed by which device
options: A pitot probe
An accelerometer
A rate gyro
cards.explain: Yaw rate is picked up by a rate gyro.

cards.question: The band pass filter in the yaw damper suppresses which unwanted signals
options: Structural oscillations sensed by the rate gyro
Speed adaption signals from the air data computer
Rudder pedal movements made by the pilot
cards.explain: Airframe structural modes sensed by the gyro are filtered out.

cards.question: An all weather operation approval may be restricted in which two ways
options: In scope and in time
In crew and in aircraft
In altitude and in speed
cards.explain: Scope and time are the two named restrictions.

cards.question: Insufficient longitudinal dynamic stability spoils which two things
options: Range of the aircraft and the life of the engines
Controllability of the aircraft and passenger comfort
Accuracy of the ILS and of the automatic landing system
cards.explain: Both handling and passenger comfort suffer.

cards.question: A jet is rolling and slipping sideways in a repeating four second cycle — what is this motion called?
options: Spiral dive
Phugoid
Dutch roll
cards.explain: The combined roll and sideslip oscillation is named Dutch roll.

cards.question: A damper is fitted to stop the roll and slip motion of a swept wing jet — which surface does it move?
options: The ailerons
The spoilers
The rudder
cards.explain: The yaw damper works through the rudder.

cards.question: A yaw damper is required during which part of the flight
options: The enroute phase
The take-off roll
The flare
cards.explain: It is the cruise, at altitude, where the damper is needed.

cards.question: The yaw rate signal is adapted to airspeed in which manner
options: Directly proportional to the airspeed
Independently of the airspeed
Inversely proportional to airspeed
cards.explain: The adaptation is inversely proportional to speed.

cards.question: A constant yaw rate signal reaching the band pass filter is treated in which way
options: It is passed unchanged
It is damped out
It is amplified
cards.explain: A steady yaw rate is damped by the filter rather than fed through.

cards.question: The yaw damper actuator output is combined with which other demand at the mechanical summing point
options: The rudder pedal input
The band pass filter output
The speed adaption signal
cards.explain: Damper demand and pedal demand are summed before the rudder actuator.

cards.question: The yaw damper is making continuous rudder corrections in the cruise — what do the rudder pedals do?
options: They move in step with the rudder
They are locked until the damper drops out
Nothing, they stay where they are
cards.explain: In series mode a damper input does not move the pedals.

cards.question: An operator intends to fly in all weather conditions — which flight rules must its approval take in?
options: Visual flight rules
Special visual flight rules
Instrument flight rules
cards.explain: The approval must cover IFR flight before all weather operation can follow.

cards.question: An operator gains an all weather approval in its air operators certificate — what does that approval cover?
options: Each individual aircraft registration
The aircraft type or series of types
Each individual flight crew member
cards.explain: The approval is granted against a type or series of types.

cards.question: The all weather approval holds good for which runways
options: Those approved by the authority for that category
Only those listed in the operator's own route manual
Only those fitted with a roll out guidance system
cards.explain: Approval follows the authority's own runway classification for the category.

cards.question: Directional guidance for take-off in low visibility is covered by which subpart of the all weather operations requirements
options: Subpart 2
Subpart 4
Subpart 1
cards.explain: Subpart 4 deals with low visibility take-off guidance.

cards.question: Dutch roll grows into a problem at high altitude for which reason
options: The lift of the swept wing rises with altitude
The rudder travel available falls off with altitude
The damping aerodynamic forces fall with altitude
cards.explain: Thin air means weaker aerodynamic damping, so the oscillation is no longer suppressed naturally.

cards.question: The yaw damper becomes unserviceable during the cruise — what must then be done with the aircraft?
options: It has to slow to the minimum airspeed
It has to descend to a lower altitude
It has to climb to a higher altitude
cards.explain: Lower down the natural aerodynamic damping is strong enough.

cards.question: The aircraft accelerates in the cruise — what happens to the yaw rate signal passed on to the actuator?
options: It is held at its take-off value
It is built up as the speed rises
It is cut back as the speed rises
cards.explain: Inverse proportionality means the signal is reduced as speed increases.

cards.question: The pilot presses a rudder pedal while the yaw damper is working — how do the two demands reach the rudder?
options: The damper demand overrides any pedal demand made
The pedal demand switches the damper out of use
They are added or subtracted at a summing point
cards.explain: Both demands are summed, so neither cancels the other.

cards.question: ILS precision approaches are subdivided into which categories
options: CAT I to CAT III
CAT I to CAT VIII
CAT A to CAT C
cards.explain: The subdivision runs from CAT I to CAT III.

cards.question: A low visibility take-off is any take-off made below which runway visual range
options: 550 metres
300 metres
400 metres
cards.explain: Below 400 m RVR the departure counts as a low visibility take-off.

cards.question: The decision height is measured above which reference
options: The touch down zone
The mean sea level datum
The runway threshold
cards.explain: Decision height is referenced to the runway threshold.

cards.question: The alert height is defined by which party
options: The airport operator
The aircraft manufacturer
The national aviation authority
cards.explain: It is the manufacturer who sets the alert height.

cards.question: A system failure during an approach can be met by which three courses of action
options: Continue, revert or go around
Continue, descend or go straight in
Revert, divert or go straight in
cards.explain: Those three are the courses of action named.

cards.question: A CAT III b approach is being planned — what decision height condition applies?
options: Below 50 ft or no decision height
No decision height and no visibility limit
Below 100 ft but not below 50 ft
cards.explain: CAT III b covers decision heights under 50 ft and the no decision height case.

cards.question: An airport has no runway visual range measuring equipment — which value may be converted instead?
options: The meteorological visibility
The cloud base height measured
The decision height selected
cards.explain: Met visibility can be converted where no RVR equipment exists.

cards.question: The aircraft reaches the decision height without the required visual reference — what must the crew do?
options: Revert to a lower category
Continue down to the alert height
Initiate a missed approach
cards.explain: Without the visual reference at decision height a missed approach is compulsory.

cards.question: The alert height is quoted in an aircraft's approach data — which approaches does it belong to?
options: CAT I approaches flown with the autopilot engaged
CAT III approaches with a fail-operational autoland
CAT II approaches with a fail-passive autoland fitted
cards.explain: The term belongs to fail-operational CAT III approaches.

cards.question: On what does the value chosen for the alert height depend
options: The reported runway visual range of the day
The landing distance available on the runway
The failure probability of the autoland
cards.explain: The alert height depends on one thing only: the failure probability of the autoland system.

cards.question: Where is the pilot to whom the runway visual range refers assumed to be
options: At the holding point beside the runway
Over the threshold on the glide path
On the centre line of the runway
cards.explain: The definition places the pilot on the runway centre line.

cards.question: The minimum runway visual range required for a CAT III approach depends on which two things
options: The equipment carried and the autoland capability
The decision height and the alert height selected
The runway length and the approach lighting fitted
cards.explain: Installed equipment and autoland capability together fix the minimum RVR.

cards.question: The crew needs to know the capability of their automatic landing system — where do they read it?
options: As an amber light on the ILS deviation alert
As an approach category on the flight annunciator
As a decision height index on the radio altimeter
cards.explain: Capability shows up as the available approach category on the flight mode annunciator.

cards.question: The crew decides to continue the planned approach after a failure — how far down may they go?
options: Its decision height or minimum descent altitude
The alert height of the automatic landing system
The touch down zone marking on the runway
cards.explain: Continue means fly the planned approach to its own minimum.

cards.question: A failure leaves the aircraft able to fly a lesser approach — what does reverting mean here?
options: Changing to a category the reported weather would allow
Changing to a category the runway lighting supports
Changing to a category the remaining equipment allows
cards.explain: Reversion is driven by what the surviving equipment can still do.

cards.question: For what purpose is a go around flown after a system fault
options: To investigate the failure and plan another approach
To allow the ground equipment to be reset by control
To reduce the landing weight before a second attempt
cards.explain: The go around buys time to look at the failure and reconfigure.

cards.question: Besides the type of failure, what else decides the action to be taken
options: The category of runway lighting then in use
The age of the autoflight equipment then installed
The present position of the aircraft on approach
cards.explain: Where the aircraft is on the approach matters as much as what failed.

cards.question: An approach is planned to a decision height of 150 ft with a reported visual range of 400 m — which category applies?
options: CAT I
CAT II
CAT III a
cards.explain: A decision height between 200 ft and 100 ft with at least 300 m visual range is CAT II.

cards.question: The reported runway visual range is 100 m and the decision height is 40 ft — which category covers it?
options: CAT III a
CAT III c
CAT III b
cards.explain: A decision height below 50 ft with a visual range between 200 m and 75 m falls in CAT III b.

cards.question: A failure appears in the redundant part of the autoland system above the alert height — what follows?
options: The failure is ignored and the approach continued
The approach is broken off and a go around flown
The approach reverts to the next higher category
cards.explain: Above the alert height such a failure forces a go around.

cards.question: A CAT III A approach with a decision height below 100 ft is flown with a fail-passive landing system — what is the minimum visual range?
cards.explain: Every CAT III A column in the table shows 200 m.

cards.question: The automatic landing system is fail-passive and the decision height is below 50 ft — is such an approach permitted, and to what visual range?
options: Yes, down to 75 metres
Yes, down to 125 metres
No, it is not authorised at all
cards.explain: In the fail-passive column of the table the row for a decision height below 50 ft reads 'Not authorized'.

cards.question: A CAT III B approach to a decision height below 50 ft with a fail-operational system and a fail-passive roll-out system needs which minimum visual range
cards.explain: Under the fail-operational landing system, the column for a fail-passive roll-out system gives 125 m at a decision height below 50 ft.

cards.question: An approach with no decision height is flown to a runway visual range of 75 m. Which standard must the roll-out system hold
options: Fail-passive
Fail-safe
Fail-operational
cards.explain: In the CAT III RVR table the no decision height row gives 75 m only in the fail-operational roll-out column; the fail-passive roll-out column of that row reads 'Not authorized'.

cards.question: Two aircraft have a fail-operational landing system, one with a roll-out system and one without, both at a decision height below 50 ft — how are the two treated?
options: Both may fly it to the same visual range
Only the one without roll-out may fly the approach
Only the one with roll-out may fly the approach
cards.explain: Without a roll-out system that decision height is not authorised at all.

cards.question: In which band must a failure happen for a reversion to another approach category to be considered
options: Above 1000 ft above the ground
At or below the alert height
Below 1000 ft above the ground
cards.explain: The general rule puts the reversion decision above 1000 ft AGL.

cards.question: A fail-operational autoflight system fails below 1000 ft but above the alert height — what action follows?
options: A reversion to CAT I is flown
A go around is executed
The approach continues to decision height
cards.explain: In that band any failure of a fail-operational system means a go around.

cards.question: After a failure the weather allows a higher minimum and enough autoflight capability remains — what may the crew then do?
options: Descend below the alert height
Continue down to the original minimum
Fly that approach category instead
cards.explain: Both conditions together allow the higher minimum approach to be flown.

cards.question: The objective of CAT II autoflight operation is to hold which level of safety
options: One equivalent to manual flight operation
One set by the aircraft manufacturer alone
One above that of manual flight operation
cards.explain: The aim is equivalence with manual operation, under worse weather.

cards.question: In a fail-safe system the output signal after a failure takes which state
options: The last valid state before failure
A defined and equally safe state
An arbitrary but safe state
cards.explain: Fail-safe gives an arbitrary state that is nevertheless safe.

cards.question: In a fail-passive system the output signal once the system has failed takes which state
options: A well defined failure state
An arbitrary but safe state
A state within acceptable limits
cards.explain: Fail-passive gives a defined, known failure state.

cards.question: The CAT II safety level depends partly on what the crew can see — which outside aid is named?
options: Approach and runway lighting
Runway friction measurement
Ground radar surveillance cover
cards.explain: Outside visual cues from the approach and runway lighting are listed.

cards.question: The aircraft reaches the decision height on a CAT II approach — what is the position regarding a manual landing?
options: It is allowed but is not compulsory
It is compulsory in every single case
It is forbidden in every case
cards.explain: CAT II minima permit a manual landing without requiring one.

cards.question: CAT III autoflight operation holds a safety level equivalent to manual flight under which conditions
options: Conditions no worse than CAT II minima
The worst weather and visibility
Normal weather and visibility conditions
cards.explain: CAT III carries that equivalence into the worst conditions.

cards.question: To what extent is a manual landing possible from a CAT III decision height
options: It is possible but is not compulsory
It is compulsory for the pilot flying
It is normally not possible at all
cards.explain: Unlike the lower categories, CAT III leaves no room for a manual landing from the decision height.

cards.question: An aircraft is to be certified for CAT III operation — which equipment is compulsory?
options: A flight director approach coupler
A head-up ground roll guidance display
An automatic or hybrid landing system
cards.explain: CAT III requires an automatic or hybrid landing system.

cards.question: How does the reliability demanded of CAT III systems compare with that demanded for CAT II?
options: It is very much the same
It is considerably higher
It is somewhat lower still
cards.explain: CAT III calls for considerably higher reliability than CAT II.

cards.question: A designer cuts the number of components in a system — why does availability improve?
options: Fewer components leave fewer ways to fail
Fewer components leave a faster response time
Fewer components leave a lower system weight
cards.explain: Less complexity means fewer ways for the system to fail.

cards.question: What must redundant systems show for CAT III operation
options: Automatic reset after every detected failure
Identical hardware from a single manufacturer
Defined behaviour for any conceivable failure
cards.explain: The behaviour at every conceivable failure must be defined.

cards.question: To behave passively when a fault appears a system needs which provision during normal operation
options: Periodic self testing carried out at every engine start
Manual selection of the standby channel by the crew
Permanent monitoring with suppression of any failure
cards.explain: Continuous monitoring plus suppression is what makes passive behaviour possible.

cards.question: A system that stays operative after a failure is described by which term
options: Failure neutral
Failure suppressed
Failure tolerant
cards.explain: Such a system is called failure tolerant.

cards.question: What does a drop out of the main system cause with passive redundancy
options: An automatic shut down of all parallel systems
A manual selection of the remaining system
An automatic change to the redundant system
cards.explain: The change over happens automatically.

cards.question: In passive redundancy the system held in reserve carries which name
options: The active parallel system
The hot standby system
The monitored main system
cards.explain: The reserve system is called the hot standby.

cards.question: A main channel drops out and a reserve takes over automatically — what can be said of the system function afterwards?
options: The complete functionality is restored
Only the monitored functions are restored
Only half the functionality is restored
cards.explain: The standby restores the full function after the change over.

cards.question: For decision heights below 100 ft the two ILS receivers must feed the pilot stations in which way
options: Both pilot stations from the same receiver
Both receivers into one combined display
Each pilot station from its own receiver
cards.explain: The two stations must be fed from separate receivers.

cards.question: A decision height of 50 ft or greater is planned — what standard must the automatic landing system hold?
options: Fail-operational
Fail-passive
Fail-safe
cards.explain: At 50 ft and above a fail-passive landing system is enough.

cards.question: A decision height below 50 ft is planned — what standard must the automatic go-around system hold?
options: Fail-operational
Fail-safe
Fail-passive
cards.explain: The go-around system is required to be fail-passive there.

cards.question: For a no decision height approach the automatic ground roll control may hold which standards
options: Fail-operational or fail-safe
Fail-passive or fail-safe
Fail-operational or fail-passive
cards.explain: Either standard is accepted for the ground roll function.

cards.question: An approach with no decision height is to be flown — what provision is required for speed control?
options: Automatic throttle control
Head-up speed guidance
Manual throttle control only
cards.explain: Automatic throttle control is on the no decision height equipment list.

cards.question: What is the crew able to judge at a CAT III A decision height
options: Whether touch down will fall in the touch down zone
Whether the autoland has dropped to fail-passive
Whether the roll out can be supervised visually throughout
cards.explain: At CAT III A the crew can still see whether the aircraft will land in the zone.

cards.question: A CAT III B minimum is set so as to secure which crew capability
options: Visual acquisition of the approach light system
Visual supervision of the roll out
Visual confirmation of the touch down point
cards.explain: The CAT III B minimum exists so the roll out can be watched.

cards.question: Automatic guidance of the roll out until taxi speed is reached is demanded for which categories
options: CAT II and CAT III A
CAT III A and CAT III B
CAT III B and CAT III C
cards.explain: Flare and roll out guidance to taxi speed is listed for CAT III B and C.

cards.question: One of several parallel channels drops out and the output signal is unaffected — which redundancy is in use?
options: Active redundancy
Passive redundancy
Monitored redundancy
cards.explain: Only active redundancy keeps the output going with no switch over.

cards.question: An operator wants to certify a CAT II aircraft with no automatic throttle system — what must be shown?
options: That the engines accelerate within the regulated time
That speed can be held by hand without undue workload
That the autopilot can hold speed within ten knots
cards.explain: The way out is an in-flight demonstration of manual speed control.

cards.question: The number of ILS receivers and radio altimeters may have to be raised for which reason
options: To give an alert height indication at both stations
To give fail-operational capability where required
To give a roll out guidance display at both stations
cards.explain: Extra sensors are what makes a fail-operational installation possible.

cards.question: The decision height planned is below 50 ft — what standard must the automatic landing system then meet?
options: Fail-operational
Fail-safe
Fail-passive
cards.explain: Below 50 ft only a fail-operational landing or hybrid system will do.

cards.question: Which wheel provision is required for an approach flown with no decision height
options: An anti-skid braking system
A carbon brake wear indicator
An autobrake disarm warning
cards.explain: An anti-skid braking system is one of the items listed for no decision height.

cards.question: A fail-passive approach system without automatic landing is acceptable at a decision height of 50 ft or greater provided the aeroplane holds which property
options: A high approach speed and a long wheel base
A fail-operational go-around capability fitted
A low approach speed and good manoeuvrability
cards.explain: Those handling properties are what make the manual landing acceptable.

cards.question: Which system is defined as one comprising an automatic and/or a hybrid landing system
options: the flight control system
the landing system
the guidance system
cards.explain: That wording is the definition of the flight control system.

cards.question: Which equipment does the term landing system cover
options: onboard equipment only
onboard and ground equipment
ground equipment only
cards.explain: The definition limits the term landing system to equipment carried on board.

cards.question: Which failure of a control surface can occur on a fail safe flight control system
options: a slow runaway of the control surface
a hard over of the control surface
a complete loss of control surface authority
cards.explain: A hard over of a control surface is named as the most important feature of the fail safe failure case.

cards.question: The autopilot runs a surface hard over while the aircraft is enroute. Within which time must the pilot be able to take over control?
options: 1 second
3 seconds
10 seconds
cards.explain: FAR 25 allows 3 seconds for the takeover enroute.

cards.question: Which kind of redundancy does the parallel operation of two fail safe autopilots show
options: standby redundancy
active redundancy
passive redundancy
cards.explain: Two fail safe autopilots working in parallel are described as active redundancy.

cards.question: Which arrangement inside one and the same autopilot gives fail passive behaviour
options: two autopilots coupled rigidly together
two independent channels working in parallel
three actuators driven by a single channel
cards.explain: Fail passive behaviour can come from two independent channels inside one autopilot.

cards.question: What does the autopilot do when the comparison of its two channels detects a failure
options: it disengages
it reverts to one channel
it limits its authority
cards.explain: A detected failure disengages the autopilot.

cards.question: Which items does the landing system comprise in accordance with JAR-AWO 321
options: all instruments, displays and ground transmitters
all sensors, instruments and power supplies
all sensors, antennas and ground stations
cards.explain: The equipment named in the definition is sensors, instruments and power supplies.

cards.question: What are the differing architectures of the two major transport aircraft manufacturers meant to realize
options: a common standard of autopilot engagement
a lower weight of the autopilot installation
failure modes acceptable for CAT III operation
cards.explain: The architectures exist to produce the fail passive or fail operational modes that CAT III operation accepts.

cards.question: Two fail passive single systems are operated together in dual operation. Which behaviour does the resulting system show?
options: fail operational behaviour
fail safe behaviour
fail passive behaviour
cards.explain: Dual operation of fail passive single systems yields fail operational behaviour.

cards.question: Why is a hard over not suppressed by a fail safe flight control system
options: because it cannot recognize the failure
because its servos have no force limiter
because its actuators have no clutch
cards.explain: Suppression is impossible because the system has no way of recognizing the failure.

cards.question: How is the effect of a failure limited on a fail safe system
options: by comparing the two autopilot channels
by voting between three actuator outputs
by reducing the authority of the servos
cards.explain: Reducing servo authority is the means given for limiting the failure effect.

cards.question: Under which condition is authority limitation allowed at all
options: only if a manual flight control system exists
only if the servos carry a torque limiter
only if a second autopilot is installed
cards.explain: A manual flight control system able to over-power the autopilot is the condition for allowing authority limitation.

cards.question: Which effect does a failure of a fail passive flight control system have on the trim state and the flight path
options: both of them are changed considerably
the trim state changes but the flight path does not
neither of them is changed considerably
cards.explain: A fail passive failure leaves the trim state unchanged and causes no considerable deviation from flight path or attitude.

cards.question: What can no longer be carried out once a fail passive flight control system has failed
options: an ILS approach
an automatic landing
a manual go around
cards.explain: The printed definition says an automatic landing can no longer be performed.

cards.question: The fail passive automatic flight control system fails during an approach. What must happen then?
options: the system continues the approach and landing by itself
the second autopilot takes over control and lands
the pilot has to take over the control of the aircraft
cards.explain: On failure of a fail passive system the pilot has to take over control.

cards.question: How is the independence of two autopilots working in dual operation achieved
options: by one common computer serving both of the channels
by separate supplies, sensors, computers and actuators
by a common power supply feeding two sets of sensors
cards.explain: Independence comes from everything being separate: supplies, sensors, computers, actuators and cable ducts.

cards.question: Which causes make the rigidly coupled actuators of two autopilots work against each other
options: tolerances, pressure differences or poor adjustment
different reference values in the two sensor units
a delay between the two autopilot computers
cards.explain: Force conflicts are attributed to tolerances, pressure differences and poor adjustment.

cards.question: What is done for safety reasons in the two channels of one fail passive autopilot
options: one of the two channels is left unpowered as a spare
different hardware and different programming languages
the same hardware and the same programs in both lanes
cards.explain: The channels differ in hardware and in the programming language of the identical programs.

cards.question: A dual channel autopilot has produced an output in each of its channels. What happens to the two signals before the actuator sees them?
options: they are added together and then released
they are compared for validity and then released
they are sent on separately to two actuators
cards.explain: The outputs are compared for validity, and only then released to the actuator.

cards.question: By which three means is fail passive behaviour reached in a dual channel autopilot
options: parallel processing, mutual monitoring and output comparison
mechanical voting, torque limiting and authority limiting
active redundancy, crosstalk and autopilot synchronisation
cards.explain: Those three together are what makes the dual channel autopilot fail passive.

cards.question: An autopilot that detects its own failure and disengages itself is operated on its own. Which behaviour does the system then show?
options: fail passive behaviour
fail operational behaviour
fail safe behaviour
cards.explain: A single system able to detect and remove its own failure gives fail passive behaviour in single operation.

cards.question: A manufacturer limits the authority of its autopilot servos, but the aircraft has no manual control path strong enough to overrule the autopilot. Why is that not acceptable?
options: because the autopilot could then not recognize its own hard over
because the pilot could then not over-power the autopilot
because the servos would then not reach their full travel range
cards.explain: Authority limitation relies on the pilot being able to apply strong inputs and over-power the autopilot manually.

cards.question: A fail passive system must be able to disengage itself. How does it recognize that it has a failure?
options: by monitoring the hydraulic pressure at the actuator
by comparing the two autopilot computers with each other
by comparing the surface position with the commanded position
cards.explain: Recognition rests on the electrical comparison of actual surface position with commanded actuator position.

cards.question: During dual operation the two autopilot actuators try to deflect one surface in opposite directions. What does the surface do?
options: it runs to its full deflection
it stays in its position
it follows the faster of the two actuators
cards.explain: Opposing actuator commands are voted out, so the surface holds its position.

cards.question: Two fail safe autopilots drive one surface in dual operation. What does the feel system contribute?
options: the neutral reference for the deflection limiter
the torque limit applied at the actuator clutch
the third signal the mid-value voter needs
cards.explain: Mid-value voting needs three inputs, and with two autopilots the feel system provides the missing one.

cards.question: In which respect does a dual channel fail passive autopilot differ from two parallel fail safe autopilots
options: it drives three actuators and needs a mid-value voter
it drives one actuator only and needs no mechanical voting
it drives two actuators and needs a torque limiter
cards.explain: Parallel fail safe autopilots need mechanical voting against force conflicts, while the dual channel autopilot drives a single actuator and does not.

cards.question: Of which two parts does a hybrid landing system consist
options: a fail safe landing system and a mechanical voter
a fail operational landing system and a second autopilot
a fail passive landing system and a guidance system
cards.explain: The main system is a fail passive automatic landing system and it is supported by an independent guidance system.

cards.question: Which systems are usually used as the supporting system of a hybrid landing system
options: yaw damper systems
head up guidance systems
radio altimeter systems
cards.explain: Head up guidance systems are the usual supporting systems.

cards.question: Why does mechanical voting have to be applied in triple operation
options: to prevent force conflicts
to detect a hard over of a surface
to limit the authority of the servos
cards.explain: Voting is applied for the same reason as in dual operation: to prevent force conflicts.

cards.question: Two autopilots run in parallel and each one disengages itself on its own failure. Which kind of redundancy does that architecture show?
options: standby redundancy
passive redundancy
active redundancy
cards.explain: This architecture is described as passive redundancy.

cards.question: The main system of a hybrid landing system fails on the approach. What does the supporting guidance system then allow?
options: automatic continuation of approach and landing
an automatic go around at the alert height
manual continuation of approach and landing
cards.explain: The supporting system lets the crew carry on manually after the main system has failed.

cards.question: Of which units does the hybrid built from fail safe autopilots consist
options: one fail safe autopilot and two flight director systems
three fail safe autopilots and one head up display
two fail safe autopilots and one flight director system
cards.explain: It is built from two fail safe autopilots plus at least one flight director system.

cards.question: Of which units does the hybrid system built around a fail passive autopilot consist
options: one fail passive autopilot and two head up displays
one fail passive autopilot and one flight director system
two fail passive autopilots and one flight director system
cards.explain: This architecture uses a single fail passive autopilot with at least one flight director system.

cards.question: A single autopilot fails below the alert height in a fail operational system. What can the crew still expect of the automatic system?
options: the system disengages and the approach has to be abandoned
approach, flare, landing and roll out are completed automatically
the approach continues but the landing has to be flown manually
cards.explain: Fail operational means the whole sequence down to roll out is still flown automatically.

cards.question: A fail operational system has already suffered one failure. What would a second failure mean now?
options: a hard over may occur, as the system is now fail safe
the landing is still completed, as the system stays fail operational
the pilot must take over, as the system is now fail passive
cards.explain: Once fail passive, a further failure means no automatic landing and the pilot has to take over.

cards.question: In a triple operation system one autopilot output drifts away from the other two. What does the mid- value voter do to the surface?
options: the surface follows the middle actuator and the odd output is lost
the surface follows the odd output until that autopilot is off
the surface takes the average, so the odd output shifts it
cards.explain: Mid-value voting passes only the middle signal, so a single deviating output is suppressed.

cards.question: Two fail passive autopilots work in parallel on the same control train. Why can no force conflict arise there?
options: because a mid-value voter selects the middle of the signals
because only one actuator drives the surface at a time
because a torque limiter is fitted in each actuator clutch
cards.explain: At any instance only one actuator is driving, so nothing can work against it.

cards.question: One of two parallel fail passive autopilots detects its own failure during an automatic landing. What happens next?
options: both of them disengage and the pilot takes over
the faulty one is voted out by the mechanical voter
it disengages itself and the other one keeps control
cards.explain: The failed autopilot takes itself out and the remaining one continues to control the aircraft.

cards.question: Which behaviour does the autopilot system of a hybrid built from two fail safe autopilots show
options: fail safe, augmented by an auto-thrust system
fail passive, augmented by a flight director
fail operational, augmented by a flight director
cards.explain: Two fail safe autopilots make the autopilot system fail passive, and the flight director augments it.

cards.question: The autopilot of a hybrid landing installation fails on short final. How can the landing still be completed?
options: automatically, by the second autopilot taking over
manually, following the supporting guidance system
automatically, after the voter has selected a channel
cards.explain: The hybrid system's reserve is manual flight on the supporting guidance system, not a second automatic system.

cards.question: Why does a hybrid landing system count as fail operational although its automatic landing system is only fail passive
options: the automatic landing system becomes fail operational below the alert height
the two autopilots of the system are voted mechanically
the guidance system allows the landing to be continued manually
cards.explain: The overall capability is kept by the independent guidance system letting the crew finish the landing by hand.

cards.question: Where is the autoland warning displayed
options: on the overhead panel above the pilots
on the engine display of the lower screen
in the glare shield, in the pilot's view
cards.explain: It sits in the glare shield, inside the pilot's field of view.

cards.question: In which colour is the autoland warning displayed
options: red
white
amber
cards.explain: The autoland warning is a red warning.

cards.question: Where are components influencing CAT II and CAT III approach capability specially marked
options: in column 3 of the minimum equipment list
in column 1 of the operations manual part B
in chapter 22 of the aircraft maintenance manual
cards.explain: The MEL marks them in its column 3.

cards.question: The capability logic has checked the serviceability of all required systems. Which supplies does it count as well?
options: the independent pneumatic and electrical power supplies
the independent hydraulic and pneumatic power supplies
the independent hydraulic and electrical power supplies
cards.explain: The number of independent hydraulic and electrical power supplies is counted as well.

cards.question: What does the degree of redundancy determine
options: the failure mode of the system
the decision height of the approach
the alert height of the approach
cards.explain: Redundancy decides whether the system is fail safe, fail passive or fail operational.

cards.question: One fail passive autopilot or flight director is operational and the redundancy is limited. Which capability is reached?
options: CAT 3 SINGLE
CAT 1
CAT 2
cards.explain: With one fail passive autopilot or flight director and limited redundancy only CAT I is available.

cards.question: The autoland warning comes on during an automatic approach. Which reaction is the normal one?
options: the initiation of a go around
the disengagement of one autopilot
a continuation of the approach to CAT I minima
cards.explain: A go around is the normal response to the autoland warning.

cards.question: The autoland warning comes on and the runway is clearly in sight. What is possible besides a go around?
options: a manual landing
an automatic landing
a second automatic approach
cards.explain: With visual conditions permitting, the landing may be completed manually.

cards.question: Above which difference of radio height between two radio altimeters does the autoland warning come on
options: 50 ft
100 ft
10 ft
cards.explain: The warning condition is a radio height difference of more than 10 ft.

cards.question: Required ground equipment fails while the aircraft is still above the alert height and the capability changes. What has to be done?
options: the autopilot has to be disengaged and the approach flown manually
the approach may be continued to CAT I minima
a go around has to be initiated
cards.explain: A capability change above the alert height requires a go around.

cards.question: A single failure occurs below the alert height and degrades the failure mode from fail operational to fail passive. What happens to the displayed capability?
options: it is no longer changed
it is replaced by a red warning
it drops by one category
cards.explain: Below the alert height the capability is frozen even though the failure mode degrades.

cards.question: A single failure below the alert height degrades the failure mode, yet the capability stays as it was. Why is it kept?
options: because the ground equipment can no longer be monitored
because the autopilot can no longer be disengaged
because the autoflight system still performs its duty
cards.explain: The capability stays because the system is still doing its job after the single failure.

cards.question: One fail passive autopilot and one auto-thrust system are operational. Which capability is displayed?
options: CAT 2
CAT 3 DUAL
CAT 3 SINGLE
cards.explain: That combination gives CAT III A, displayed as CAT 3 SINGLE.

cards.question: Two fail passive autopilots and one auto-thrust system are operational. Which capability is displayed and which failure mode does the system have?
options: CAT 3 SINGLE, and the system is fail passive
CAT 2, and the system is fail operational
CAT 3 DUAL, and the system is fail operational
cards.explain: Two fail passive autopilots make the total system fail operational and give CAT 3 DUAL for CAT III B.

cards.question: What does the collective pitch lever control
options: the velocity vector
the main rotor lift
the tail rotor thrust
cards.explain: The collective pitch lever is the lift control.

cards.question: What does the cyclic pitch stick control
options: the velocity vector
the main rotor lift
the tail rotor thrust
cards.explain: The cyclic stick controls the velocity vector.

cards.question: The cyclic stick is moved forward. Which movement of the helicopter results?
options: a nose down movement
a tail down movement
a left sideward movement
cards.explain: Forward cyclic gives a nose down movement.

cards.question: Through which servo do the pedals act
options: the LH servo
the yaw servo
the front servo
cards.explain: Pedal inputs pass through the yaw servo.

cards.question: What is a twist grip throttle
options: a friction lock fitted at the pedal unit
a rotary rpm controller at the collective pitch lever
a rotary trim controller at the cyclic pitch stick
cards.explain: It is the rotary rpm control sitting on the collective pitch lever.

cards.question: On which helicopters is a twist grip throttle found
options: on those powered by a turbine engine
on those powered by a piston engine
on those with a counter clockwise rotor
cards.explain: The twist grip throttle belongs to piston engined helicopters.

cards.question: Which stability does a helicopter have around its longitudinal, lateral and vertical axes
options: positive stability around the longitudinal axis only
no positive stability around any of them
positive stability around the vertical axis only
cards.explain: The helicopter has no positive stability about any of the three axes.

cards.question: Which sensors does a helicopter stabilization system use
options: rate gyros
accelerometers
pressure transducers
cards.explain: Rotation rates about pitch, roll and yaw are sensed by rate gyros.

cards.question: The collective pitch lever is raised. How is the pitch angle of the main rotor blades changed?
options: on half of the blades at once and by the same amount
on all blades at once and by the same amount
on each blade in turn and by a different amount
cards.explain: Collective input acts on every blade simultaneously and equally.

cards.question: How does the cyclic stick produce a variation of the rotor blade pitch angle
options: by changing the pitch of all the blades equally
by changing the thrust produced by the tail rotor
by tilting the main rotor plane around the X or Y axis
cards.explain: The cyclic tilts the rotor plane about the X or Y axis.

cards.question: Only the front servo is driven by a control input. Around which axis is the rotor plane tilted?
options: the lateral axis, Y-Y'
the vertical axis, Z-Z'
the longitudinal axis, X-X'
cards.explain: The front servo tilts the rotor plane about the lateral Y-Y' axis.

cards.question: Which servos tilt the rotor plane around the longitudinal axis
options: the front and LH servos
the front and yaw servos
the LH and RH servos
cards.explain: The LH and RH servos work the longitudinal X-X' axis.

cards.question: What is the up and down movement of the swash plate called
options: collective pitch variation
lateral pitch variation
cyclic pitch variation
cards.explain: That up and down movement is the collective pitch variation.

cards.question: The swash plate is moved up from its initial position. Which quantity at the rotor changes?
options: the length of the blade lever rods
the rotational speed of the main rotor
the angle of attack of the rotor blades
cards.explain: Moving the swash plate up and down alters the blades' angle of attack.

cards.question: What determines the axis about which the swash plate is tilted
options: the position of the two pedal units
the amount of collective pitch applied
the movement direction of the cyclic stick
cards.explain: The tilt axis follows the direction in which the cyclic stick is moved.

cards.question: The swash plate is to be tilted about the lateral axis. Which servo is energized on its own?
options: the yaw servo
the LH servo
the front servo
cards.explain: Only the front servo is energized for a tilt about the lateral axis.

cards.question: A sideward movement is commanded. How are the LH and RH servos driven for it?
options: one after the other, with signals of different magnitude
concurrently, with equal signals in opposite directions
concurrently, with equal signals in the same direction
cards.explain: They get equal signals at the same time, but run opposite to each other.

cards.question: Which movement of the swash plate does a diagonal cyclic stick movement produce
options: a combined tilt about both of the axes
an up and down movement without any tilt
a tilt about the lateral axis only
cards.explain: A diagonal input tilts the swash plate proportionally about both axes at once.

cards.question: The pilot presses one of the pedals. What is changed at the tail rotor?
options: the diameter of the tail rotor disc
the pitch angle of the tail rotor blades
the rotational speed of the tail rotor
cards.explain: The pedals set tail rotor blade pitch.

cards.question: Around which axis does the tail rotor allow the helicopter to be controlled
options: the vertical axis
the lateral axis
the longitudinal axis
cards.explain: Tail rotor thrust gives control about the vertical axis, that is yaw control.

cards.question: What gives an aeroplane the stability a helicopter lacks
options: the rate gyros feeding its stabilization computer
the attenuation signals sent to its control servos
the dihedral and sweep of the wing and the stabilizers
cards.explain: Wing dihedral and sweep together with the stabilizers give the fixed wing aircraft its stability.

cards.question: Why have stabilization systems been developed for helicopters
options: to let the pilot concentrate on navigation and supervision
to allow the main rotor to be driven at a lower speed
to raise the maximum forward speed of the helicopter
cards.explain: They relieve the pilot of the constant control task so he can attend to navigation and supervision.

cards.question: The SCAS has received a rate signal from one of the gyros. What does it drive with its attenuation signal?
options: the trim actuators of the cyclic stick
the servo valves of the control servos
the main servo input levers directly
cards.explain: The attenuation signals go to the servo valves of the control servos.

cards.question: Which stability does the helicopter show once the stabilization system is working
options: neutral stability
positive stability
negative stability
cards.explain: With the stabilization system active the helicopter exhibits neutral stability.

cards.question: What holds the cable system of the main rotor controls in position
options: the control servos
the motion transducers
the trim actuators
cards.explain: The control servos hold that cable system in position.

cards.question: The control servos of a stabilized helicopter are driven by the SCAS computer. What do they move?
options: the swash plate directly
the main servo input levers
the trim control panel switches
cards.explain: The control servos act on the main servo input levers.

cards.question: The pilot returns the cyclic stick to its neutral position. What does the output of the motion transducer do?
options: it becomes zero
it reaches its maximum
it reverses its sign
cards.explain: At neutral the motion transducer output is zero.

cards.question: From which sources is the stored reference value obtained
options: from the rate gyros, via the stability augmentation computer
from the attitude and heading gyros, via the synchronizer
from the motion transducers, via the trim actuator units
cards.explain: It comes from the pitch-roll attitude gyro and the heading gyro through the synchronizer control unit.
