cards.question: To which fixed wing function is the helicopter's stored attitude reference mode comparable
options: to the autothrottle
to control wheel steering
to the yaw damper
cards.explain: Its behaviour is comparable to control wheel steering.

cards.question: What is compared in the flight path control of a helicopter
options: the planned path and altitude with the momentary path parameters
the commanded path with the signals of the three rate gyros
the trim signals with the outputs of the motion transducers
cards.explain: Planned path and altitude are compared against the momentary path parameters.

cards.question: A flight path error has been worked out on a helicopter flying an upper mode. Where is it superimposed on the stabilization signals?
options: in the trim control panel
in the SCAS computer
in the synchronizer control unit
cards.explain: The superposition happens inside the SCAS computer.

cards.question: Through which item does each trim signal reach its trim actuator
options: the synchronizer control unit
the respective motion transducer
the stability augmentation computer
cards.explain: Trim signals pass through the synchronizer control unit on their way to the trim actuator.

cards.question: The cyclic stick is moved to the left-hand side. Which servo stays unenergized and which movement results?
options: the front servo, and the helicopter moves left sideward
the front servo, and the helicopter moves nose down
the LH servo, and the helicopter moves left sideward
cards.explain: A sideward input leaves the front servo unenergized and moves the helicopter sideward to the left.

cards.question: The pedal position is changed in flight. Which quantity at the tail rotor changes as a result of the blade pitch change?
options: the thrust of the tail rotor
the torque of the main rotor
the speed of the tail rotor
cards.explain: Changing tail rotor blade pitch changes the tail rotor thrust.

cards.question: With speed already established the cyclic stick is moved back. Which pair of reactions does that give?
options: a descent like an airplane, with speed being lost
a climb like an airplane, with speed being gained
a climb like an airplane, with speed being lost
cards.explain: With speed on, a rearward cyclic input gives an airplane like climb and the speed falls off.

cards.question: With speed established the left pedal is applied. Which pair of reactions results?
options: a yaw to the left, with a little speed increase
a yaw to the right, with a little speed drop
a yaw to the left, with a little speed drop
cards.explain: Left pedal with speed on yaws the helicopter left and costs a little speed.

cards.question: What follows from the helicopter having no positive stability
options: its rotor speed has to be controlled permanently by the pilot
its attitude has to be controlled permanently by the pilot
its trim actuators have to run permanently in flight
cards.explain: Without inherent stability the pilot has to control the attitude all the time.

cards.question: How does the pilot get feedback of the attitude change at his controls
options: through the rate gyros, driven by the SCAS computer
through the trim actuators, driven by the control panel
through the cable system, driven by the main servos
cards.explain: The main servos feed the movement back to the pilot controls through the cable system.

cards.question: The cyclic stick is returned to neutral after a manoeuvre. What does the SCAS computer do with the attitude reached at that moment?
options: it stores it as the reference value to be maintained
it compares it with the planned flight path of the mission
it passes it to the trim actuators as a trim command
cards.explain: The momentary attitude becomes the new reference the stabilization system holds.

cards.question: A pilot input and the stabilization signals are present at the same time. How does the SCAS computer handle them?
options: it blocks the stabilization signals while the pilot inputs
it overlays the attitude reference and stabilization signals
it passes only the larger of the two signals to the servos
cards.explain: The two are overlaid on each other inside the computer rather than one replacing the other.

questions.question: For which minimum period must a required public address system remain powered after the shutdown or failure of all engines and auxiliary power units
options: At least 5 minutes
At least 3 minutes
At least 10 minutes
questions.explain: The specification sets a time duration of at least 10 minutes.

questions.question: On which technology is the Cabin Intercommunication Data System based
options: A hardwired relay logic
An analogue amplifier chain
A microprocessor
questions.explain: The CIDS is described as a microprocessor based system.

questions.question: How many subsystems make up the Advanced Cabin Entertainment/Service System
options: Five
Seven
Four
questions.explain: Five subsystems are listed for the ACESS.

questions.question: Which subsystem broadcasts flight deck announcements, flight attendant announcements and boarding music to the cabin
options: The Passenger Address System
The Cabin Interphone System
The Passenger Entertainment System
questions.explain: Those announcements and the boarding music are broadcast through the Passenger Address System.

questions.question: An announcement is made on a required public address system. Where in the aeroplane must it be intelligible?
options: At all passenger seats, lavatories and flight crew rest compartments
At all passenger seats, galleys and flight crew seats and work stations
At all passenger seats, lavatories and cabin crew seats and work stations
questions.explain: Intelligibility is demanded at the passenger seats, the lavatories and the cabin crew seats and work stations.

questions.question: Which kind of system is the nice system
options: A modular IP based cabin management system
A centralised IP based flight management system
A modular analogue cabin lighting system
questions.explain: The nice system is a modular, IP based cabin management system.

questions.question: For which aircraft is the nice cabin management system offered
options: Regional commuter aircraft
Long range freighter aircraft
VIP and government aircraft
questions.explain: The system is offered for VIP and government aircraft.

questions.question: To which group does the artificial horizon indicator ADI belong
options: Airframe monitoring
Flight monitoring
Aircraft monitoring
questions.explain: The ADI is listed among the flight monitoring instruments.

questions.question: Of these three flight monitoring instruments, the one that is also provided as a standby device in the modern cockpit is
options: The variometer
The compass
The machmeter
questions.explain: The standby devices are the altimeter, the airspeed indicator, the horizon and the compass; the machmeter and the variometer appear only in the flight monitoring list.

questions.question: A glass cockpit aircraft has no separate round flight instruments. Which statement describes the arrangement of the flight parameters?
options: They are laid out on the PFD in a configuration that replaces the Basic T
They are laid out on the navigation display in Basic T configuration
They are laid out on the PFD and correspond to the Basic T configuration
questions.explain: The PFD keeps the Basic T arrangement rather than abandoning it.

questions.question: How does the temperature behave with increasing height in the troposphere
options: It decreases by 6.5 °C every 100 metres
It increases by 0.65 °C every 100 metres
It decreases by 0.65 °C every 100 metres
questions.explain: The troposphere lapse rate is 0.65 °C per 100 m of climb.

questions.question: How do static pressure, temperature and density behave as altitude increases
options: All three become lower
Only temperature becomes lower
All three become higher
questions.explain: All three listed values fall with increasing altitude.

questions.question: How does the HUD present the PFD data
options: So that the pilot can see it when he looks through the windshield
So that the pilot can see it when he looks down at the centre pedestal
So that the pilot can see it only when the autopilot is engaged
questions.explain: The HUD projects the PFD information into the pilot's forward view.

questions.question: Besides the air data computers, the altimeters and the autopilot in altitude hold mode, which further item is RVSM-sensitive?
options: The transponder antenna and its surroundings
The radio altimeter antennas and their surroundings
The structure and surroundings of the pitot-static sensors
questions.explain: The list of RVSM-sensitive components closes with the structure and surroundings of the pitot-static sensors.

questions.question: A fleet of six aircraft is to be cleared for RVSM. Who must apply for the Airworthiness Approval and for what?
options: The aircraft manufacturer, for each individual aircraft
The aircraft operator, for the whole fleet at once
The aircraft operator, for each individual aircraft
questions.explain: Approval is per aircraft and is applied for by the operator.

questions.question: A navigation computation needs the speed of the aircraft through the surrounding air mass. Which airspeed is this?
options: The true airspeed
The equivalent airspeed
The calibrated airspeed
questions.explain: TAS is the aircraft speed relative to the surrounding air mass.

questions.question: Which correction is applied between CAS and EAS
options: Correction of instrument error
Correction of static source error
Correction of compressibility error
questions.explain: CAS becomes EAS when the compressibility error is corrected.

questions.question: The pressure sensing element of an aneroid barometer is
options: a vertical tube filled with a fluid
a small capsule made of thin metal
a curved tube with an oval cross section
questions.explain: The aneroid barometer senses pressure with a thin metal capsule; the fluid filled vertical tube belongs to the liquid barometer and the oval curved tube to the Bourdon transducer.

questions.question: A Bourdon tube transducer is opened for inspection. Which two parts carry out the pressure conversion?
options: The straight tube and a position sensor
The curved tube and a position sensor
The curved tube and a drive coil
questions.explain: Only the curved oval tube and a position sensor at its tip are required.

questions.question: What is the amount of tube tip movement proportional to
options: The tube temperature
The signal frequency
The applied pressure
questions.explain: Tip travel is proportional to the applied pressure.

questions.question: RVSM airspace lies above FL 290 and is therefore flown on flight levels. The altimeter setting used there is
options: the QNH of the destination airfield
the standard pressure of 1013.2 hPa
the QFE of the departure airfield
questions.explain: RVSM airspace is flight level airspace, and flight levels are flown with the standard pressure of 1013.2 hPa set.

questions.question: The synchro transmitter of a Bourdon tube transducer is found unserviceable while the tube itself is sound. Which step of the pressure measurement is lost?
options: The conversion of the tube tip position into an electrical signal
The supply of static pressure to the curved tube
The deformation of the curved tube by the applied pressure
questions.explain: The synchro transmitter is the position sensor, so with it unserviceable the tube tip still moves but its position is no longer turned into an electrical signal.

questions.question: One transducer gives an output frequency depending on the input pressure, another an output voltage in proportion to the input pressure. These are
options: the micromechanical transducer and the vibrating transducer respectively
the vibrating transducer and the Bourdon tube transducer respectively
the vibrating transducer and the micromechanical transducer respectively
questions.explain: The vibrating transducer produces a frequency; the micromechanical transducer produces a voltage in proportion to the pressure.

questions.question: A pressure sensor consists of a chamber made of silicon, only a few millimetres in size. It is
options: the micromechanical transducer, built as a liquid-based chamber
the micromechanical transducer, built as an aneroid-type chamber
the vibrating transducer, built as an aneroid-type chamber
questions.explain: The micromechanical transducer is the aneroid-type chamber made of silicon whose structure is only a few millimetres in size.

questions.question: During a repair the connection between the left and right hand measuring locations of one static pressure system is left open. What is lost by this?
options: The supply of pitot pressure to the instruments
The heating of the static measuring locations
The compensation for unbalance in pressure measurement
questions.explain: The two locations are joined only to compensate unbalance in pressure measurement, so breaking the joint removes that compensation.

questions.question: The Captain moves the handle of the alternate static source selector valve to its other position. Which static pressure then reaches his instruments?
options: The copilot's static pressure system
The pitot pressure of his own system
His own static pressure system
questions.explain: The valve exists so that the Captain can take his static pressure from the copilot's system instead of his own.

questions.question: Why are static ports placed in areas with low turbulence and ram air distortion
options: Because turbulence and ram air distortion overheat the static port zones
Because turbulence and ram air distortion falsify the static pressure reading
Because turbulence and ram air distortion block the static pressure hoses
questions.explain: A port in a quiet zone senses the true static pressure, while turbulence and ram air distortion at the port falsify that reading.

questions.question: Of the factors the static source error depends on, the two that change with the configuration of the aircraft are
options: The mach number and the angle of attack
The flap position and the nose gear position
The mach number and the position of the flaps
questions.explain: Flaps and nose gear are the two listed items that are set by the aircraft configuration, the other two being flight condition values.

questions.question: In the relation Ptot = q + ps, the quantity ps is delivered to the instrument from
options: The static ports
The pitot probe
The drain hole of the pitot tube
questions.explain: The static pressure ps used in the relation is the pressure measured at the static ports.

questions.question: A pitot tube delivers the pressure present in its cylindrical pipe throughout the flight. What must be supplied in addition before a speed can be obtained?
options: The static pressure from the static ports
A second total pressure from another pitot tube
The total air temperature from a temperature probe
questions.explain: The pitot tube gives total pressure only, and the static pressure from the static ports has to be subtracted from it to get the ram pressure.

questions.question: Both a pitot tube and a Prandtl tube keep water out of the pitot line. Which item does this in the Prandtl tube together with the drain hole?
options: A cover plate
A flapper plate
A baffle
questions.explain: The Prandtl tube works with a flapper plate and a drain hole, the baffle being the item named for the pitot tube.

questions.question: An air data system is to receive the angle of attack and the total pressure from one single sensor. Which type is used?
options: A multi function probe
A pitot tube
A Prandtl tube
questions.explain: Only the multi function probe gives angle of attack as well as total pressure.

questions.question: An aircraft with a modern EFIS carries two pneumatic back up instruments. Which of them has to be connected to the pitot system?
options: Both of them equally
The standby airspeed indicator
The standby altimeter
questions.explain: An airspeed indicator uses pitot pressure as well as static pressure, while an altimeter uses static pressure only.

questions.question: A static line breaks inside an unpressurized cabin during flight. How does the vertical speed indicator behave?
options: It jumps once and then stays at zero
It jumps once and then shows correct data
It slowly drifts into a permanent climb indication
questions.explain: The VSI reacts only to the sudden change and then works normally again.

questions.question: Which behaviour does the vertical speed indicator show after a static system leakage in an unpressurized cabin compared with a pressurized cabin
options: A small jump and then correct data in the unpressurized cabin, and an indication depending on cabin rate in the pressurized cabin
A small jump and then correct data in both cabins
An indication depending on cabin rate in the unpressurized cabin, and a small jump and then correct data in the pressurized cabin
questions.explain: The unpressurized case gives a single small jump and then correct data, while in the pressurized aircraft the indication follows the cabin rate.

questions.question: Why does the airspeed indication fall to zero with a pitot leakage in an unpressurized cabin
options: Static and pitot pressure become nearly the same
The pitot pressure rises with the cabin pressure
The static pressure becomes much greater than the pitot pressure
questions.explain: The airspeed indicator works on the difference between the two pressures, which is now almost nil.

questions.question: Which instruments are disturbed by a leakage in the pitot system alone, compared with a leakage in both the pitot and the static system
options: All three instruments, compared with the airspeed indicator alone
The airspeed indicator and the altimeter, compared with all three instruments
Only the airspeed indicator, compared with all three instruments
questions.explain: A leak in the pitot system alone affects the airspeed indicator only; once the static system leaks as well, the altimeter and the vertical speed indication are disturbed too.

questions.question: How does the airspeed indication behave with a blocked static system during a climb compared with a descent
options: Increasing during the climb and decreasing during the descent
Decreasing during the climb and increasing during the descent
Decreasing during both the climb and the descent
questions.explain: The trapped static pressure stays fixed while the total pressure falls in the climb and rises in the descent, so the indication first decreases and then increases.

questions.question: The pitot inlet of an aircraft is found blocked by ice. Which indication shows that the water drain hole is still open?
options: The airspeed indication stops responding to changes of thrust
The airspeed indication decreases all the way to zero
The airspeed indication increases into the overspeed region
questions.explain: With the drain open the pitot pressure falls to static and the indication drops to zero, which a completely blocked tube does not do.

questions.question: What happens to the pitot pressure and the airspeed indication when the pitot inlet is iced over but the drain is free
options: The pitot pressure falls to static pressure and the airspeed indication decreases to zero
The pitot pressure falls to static pressure and the airspeed indication increases
The pitot pressure remains constant and the airspeed indication decreases to zero
questions.explain: The open drain lets the pitot pressure fall to static pressure, leaving no difference for the indicator to show.

cards.question: For which minimum period must a required public address system remain powered after the shutdown or failure of all engines and auxiliary power units
options: At least 3 minutes
At least 5 minutes
At least 10 minutes
cards.explain: The specification sets a time duration of at least 10 minutes.

cards.question: On which technology is the Cabin Intercommunication Data System based
options: An analogue amplifier chain
A microprocessor
A hardwired relay logic
cards.explain: The CIDS is described as a microprocessor based system.

cards.question: How many subsystems make up the Advanced Cabin Entertainment/Service System
options: Seven
Five
Four
cards.explain: Five subsystems are listed for the ACESS.

cards.question: Which subsystem broadcasts flight deck announcements, flight attendant announcements and boarding music to the cabin
options: The Passenger Address System
The Cabin Interphone System
The Passenger Entertainment System
cards.explain: Those announcements and the boarding music are broadcast through the Passenger Address System.

cards.question: A restraining means is fitted to a megaphone. Which paragraph of the design specification sets the inertia forces it must withstand?
options: CS 25.561, Emergency Landing Conditions
CS 25.1423, Public Address System
CS 25.1421, Megaphones
cards.explain: The megaphone paragraph itself refers the inertia forces out to CS 25.561.

cards.question: An announcement is made on a required public address system. Where in the aeroplane must it be intelligible?
options: At all passenger seats, lavatories and flight crew rest compartments
At all passenger seats, lavatories and cabin crew seats and work stations
At all passenger seats, galleys and flight crew seats and work stations
cards.explain: Intelligibility is demanded at the passenger seats, the lavatories and the cabin crew seats and work stations.

cards.question: Which other system must a required public address system be able to work independently of
options: Any required cabin crew member call system
Any required passenger entertainment system
Any required crew member interphone system
cards.explain: Independence is demanded specifically from any required crew member interphone system.

cards.question: Which emergency exits must have a microphone readily accessible to the seated cabin crew member
options: Required floor-level exits with an adjacent passenger seat
Required floor-level exits with an adjacent cabin crew seat
Required overwing exits with an adjacent cabin crew seat
cards.explain: The requirement is written for required floor-level exits that have an adjacent cabin crew member seat.

cards.question: Which three things does the Cabin Intercommunication Data System do to the cabin systems it serves
options: Controls, tests and monitors them
Controls, records and displays them
Tests, records and announces them
cards.explain: Control, test and monitor are the three functions printed for the CIDS.

cards.question: Which users are the cabin systems of the Cabin Intercommunication Data System dedicated to
options: Cabin attendant and ground service use
Cabin attendant and passenger use
Flight crew and ground crew use
cards.explain: The cabin systems concerned are those dedicated to cabin attendant and passenger use.

cards.question: Where does the audio of the Passenger Address System go
options: To the cabin speakers and the passenger headphones
To the cabin speakers and the attendant handsets
To the passenger headphones and the flight deck speakers
cards.explain: PA audio is fed to the cabin speakers and to the passenger headphones.

cards.question: Video, announcements and recorded audio all have to reach a seat. Which subsystem controls and distributes them to it?
options: The Passenger Services System
The Passenger Entertainment System
The Cabin Interphone System
cards.explain: All three are routed to the seat through the Passenger Entertainment System.

cards.question: Smoke is picked up by a lavatory smoke detector. Which cabin subsystem takes that signal and gives the annunciation?
options: The Cabin Lighting System
The Cabin Interphone System
The Passenger Services System
cards.explain: The interface to the lavatory smoke detector for smoke detection annunciation is a feature of the Passenger Services System.

cards.question: The flight deck needs to speak to the load cargo master. Which subsystem carries that call?
options: The Passenger Address System
The Cabin Configuration System
The Cabin Interphone System
cards.explain: Flight deck to load cargo master is one of the calls made through the Cabin Interphone System.

cards.question: Which lights are controlled by the Cabin Lighting System
options: The ceiling and wash lights
The passenger reading lights
The passenger call lights
cards.explain: The ceiling and wash lights are in the Cabin Lighting System list.

cards.question: Besides the ceiling, wash and night illumination lights, which further lights does the Cabin Lighting System control
options: The crew rest and reading lights
The lavatory call and seat row lights
The lavatory and crew rest lights
cards.explain: The lavatory and crew rest lights complete the Cabin Lighting System list.

cards.question: Which benefit does the Cabin Configuration System give an airline
options: Entertainment audio selectable at every seat
Interior changes with minimal hardware changes
Fault reporting of the whole cabin to the flight deck
cards.explain: The CCS lets the airline change the interior configuration with minimal hardware changes.

cards.question: How is an airplane interior configuration change accomplished through the Cabin Configuration System
options: By reprogramming each passenger service unit
By exchanging the configuration pins of the cabin wiring
By modifying the ACESS configuration database
cards.explain: Configuration changes are made by modifying the ACESS configuration database.

cards.question: A new cabin configuration has to be prepared before it is loaded. Which equipment creates the ACESS configuration database?
options: On-ground personal computer software
On-board central maintenance computer
On-board cabin configuration module
cards.explain: The Airplane Configuration System that creates the database is an on-ground PC software.

cards.question: Which cabin items can be arranged through the ACESS configuration database
options: The seat recline limits and the galley loads
The PA areas and the chime mute zones
The chime tone and the ceiling light brightness
cards.explain: PA areas and chime mute zones are printed in the list of configurable items.

cards.question: Which test of the ACESS Test System runs on-line and continuously
options: The built-in test equipment test
The built-in test
The programming test
cards.explain: The built-in test is the on-line continuous one, while the BITE is off-line.

cards.question: A major fault is found by the ACESS Test System. Besides the Cabin Configuration/Test Module, where is it reported?
options: To the airplane configuration system and the ground station
To the EICAS/EFIS interface units and the maintenance computers
To the passenger service units and the attendant call panels
cards.explain: Major faults go on to the EIUs and the CMCs as well as to the CCTM.

cards.question: The same power source that feeds the public address system also feeds other loads that stay powered when every other source is inoperative. How must those other loads be treated?
options: Those other loads are shed for the whole powering duration
Those other loads are taken into account in the powering duration
Those other loads are transferred to the crew interphone supply
cards.explain: The duration must be achieved while considering the other loads left on the same source.

cards.question: A microphone has been left out of its stowage and unused at a cabin crew station. What must the public address system do in that condition?
options: Become inoperative until that microphone is stowed
Mute the loudspeakers in that cabin zone
Remain fully operative in the cabin
cards.explain: No unused, un-stowed microphone may render the system inoperative, so the system has to remain fully operative.

cards.question: Two required floor-level exits lie close together and each has an adjacent cabin crew member seat. When may one microphone serve both exits?
options: When the two crew member seats face in the same direction
When the two exits are on the same side of the fuselage
When the seated crew members can talk unassisted
cards.explain: One microphone may cover several exits only if their proximity allows unassisted verbal communication between the seated cabin crew members.

cards.question: Two operators want the cabin of the same aeroplane arranged to suit their own service. What does the CIDS design philosophy give them?
options: Flexibility gained by exchanging the cabin wiring looms
Flexibility without complex and time expensive hardware changes
A fixed configuration set once by the airframe manufacturer
cards.explain: The CIDS is designed for high flexibility so that complex and time expensive hardware changes are not needed.

cards.question: Which two items are the special features of the integrated cabin entertainment and service system rather than its subsystems
options: The Passenger Services System and the Passenger Address System
The Cabin Configuration System and the ACESS Test System
The Cabin Lighting System and the Cabin Interphone System
cards.explain: The CCS and the ATS are named as the two special features added to the five subsystems.

cards.question: A reading light and a night illumination light both fail in the same cabin section. Why are two different subsystems involved?
options: Reading lights belong to the lighting system and night illumination to the services system
Reading lights belong to the services system and night illumination to the address system
Reading lights belong to the services system and night illumination to the lighting system
cards.explain: Reading lights sit under the Passenger Services System while night illumination sits under the Cabin Lighting System.

cards.question: Which kind of system is the nice system
options: A modular IP based cabin management system
A centralised IP based flight management system
A modular analogue cabin lighting system
cards.explain: The nice system is a modular, IP based cabin management system.

cards.question: For which aircraft is the nice cabin management system offered
options: Long range freighter aircraft
VIP and government aircraft
Regional commuter aircraft
cards.explain: The system is offered for VIP and government aircraft.

cards.question: Which cabin functions can the crew and the passengers reach through the nice system
options: Illumination, cabin pressure, audio/video and internet access
Window-shades, galley power, audio/video and seat heating
Illumination, window-shades, audio/video and internet access
cards.explain: Illumination, window-shades, audio/video and internet access are the cabin functions printed.

cards.question: Further functions are to be added to an existing nice installation. Which protocol makes the system easy to expand?
options: The spanning tree protocol
The ARINC 429 protocol
The standard TCP/IP protocol
cards.explain: Expandability comes from the use of the standard TCP/IP protocol.

cards.question: To which two subgroups can every instrument of the classical cockpit be assigned
options: Airframe monitoring and aircraft monitoring
Flight monitoring and aircraft monitoring
Flight monitoring and engine monitoring
cards.explain: Classical cockpit instruments divide into flight monitoring instruments and aircraft monitoring instruments.

cards.question: To which group does the artificial horizon indicator ADI belong
options: Airframe monitoring
Aircraft monitoring
Flight monitoring
cards.explain: The ADI is listed among the flight monitoring instruments.

cards.question: A panel layout is described as Basic T. Which four instruments form that T?
options: Airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass
Attitude indicator, altimeter, compass and turn coordinator
Airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator
cards.explain: The four instruments arranged in the T shape are the airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass; turn coordination and vertical speed sit below them.

cards.question: Of these three flight monitoring instruments, the one that is also provided as a standby device in the modern cockpit is
options: The compass
The machmeter
The variometer
cards.explain: The standby devices are the altimeter, the airspeed indicator, the horizon and the compass; the machmeter and the variometer appear only in the flight monitoring list.

cards.question: The group of instruments which the standby set of a modern cockpit duplicates is
options: flight monitoring
engine monitoring
airframe monitoring
cards.explain: Altimeter, airspeed indicator, horizon and compass are all listed as flight monitoring instruments.

cards.question: An exhaust gas temperature indicator is fitted in a classical cockpit. Which group and subdivision does it belong to?
options: Aircraft monitoring, as an engine monitoring device
Flight monitoring, as a pressure monitoring device
Aircraft monitoring, as an airframe monitoring device
cards.explain: Exhaust gas temperature indicators are named as engine monitoring devices under aircraft monitoring.

cards.question: Into which two kinds of devices is aircraft monitoring divided
options: Airframe monitoring devices and standby devices
Airframe monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices
Flight monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices
cards.explain: Aircraft monitoring covers airframe monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices.

cards.question: Why do the aircraft monitoring systems of the modern cockpit carry different names such as EICAS or ECAM
options: Because the name depends on the aircraft type
Because the name depends on the display size
Because the name depends on the flight phase
cards.explain: Aircraft monitoring instruments carry different names depending on the aircraft type.

cards.question: Which task do EICAS and ECAM perform in the modern cockpit
options: They perform aircraft monitoring
They perform maintenance data recording
They perform flight monitoring
cards.explain: EICAS and ECAM are the names given to the aircraft monitoring instruments.

cards.question: Why is the CMS counted as part of aircraft monitoring
options: Because it delivers information to the maintenance personnel
Because it delivers information to the standby instruments
Because it delivers information to the flight crew
cards.explain: The CMS is used for aircraft monitoring because it delivers information to maintenance personnel.

cards.question: The electronic displays of a glass cockpit are lost in flight. Which speed and attitude information remains available from the standby set?
options: Mach number from the standby machmeter and attitude from the standby horizon
Airspeed from the standby airspeed indicator and heading from the standby horizon
Airspeed from the standby airspeed indicator and attitude from the standby horizon
cards.explain: The standby set contains an airspeed indicator and a horizon, but no machmeter.

cards.question: A fuel pressure indication changes during flight. Which value is the instrument responding to?
options: Pressure of air
Earth's magnetism
Pressure of fluids
cards.explain: Fluid pressure is listed separately from air pressure as a value that operates instruments.

cards.question: A pilot reads his magnetic heading and a VOR course deviation from one round instrument. Which indicator is he using?
options: The HSI
The ADI
The variometer
cards.explain: The HSI is the instrument that combines compass and radio navigation information.

cards.question: A glass cockpit aircraft has no separate round flight instruments. Which statement describes the arrangement of the flight parameters?
options: They are laid out on the PFD and correspond to the Basic T configuration
They are laid out on the PFD in a configuration that replaces the Basic T
They are laid out on the navigation display in Basic T configuration
cards.explain: The PFD keeps the Basic T arrangement rather than abandoning it.

cards.question: An aircraft presents its altimeter, airspeed indicator and artificial horizon indicator on cockpit screens. To which system of the modern cockpit are these instruments assigned?
options: EFIS (Electronic Flight Instrument System)
EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System)
CMS (Central Maintenance System)
cards.explain: All three named instruments are listed as flight monitoring instruments, and flight monitoring instruments go to the EFIS.

cards.question: An engineer needs aircraft system information for troubleshooting rather than an indication meant for the crew. Which aircraft monitoring system delivers it?
options: The EFIS (Electronic Flight Instrument System)
The CMS (Central Maintenance System)
The ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitoring)
cards.explain: The CMS is the aircraft monitoring system that delivers information to the maintenance personnel.

cards.question: An instrument is to be fitted in the middle at the top of a Basic T panel and must also display the indication from the flight director system. Which indicator is required?
options: The ADI
The turn coordinator
The HSI
cards.explain: The middle top position of the Basic T carries the attitude indicator, and the ADI is the attitude indicator that also shows the flight director indication.

cards.question: What is the proportion of nitrogen in dry, clean air directly above the surface of the earth
cards.explain: Nitrogen makes up 78% of dry clean air at the surface.

cards.question: What is the proportion of oxygen in dry, clean air directly above the surface of the earth
cards.explain: Oxygen makes up 21% of dry clean air at the surface.

cards.question: What does HUD stand for
options: Heading Up Display
Head Up Display
Head Unit Display
cards.explain: HUD is short for Head Up Display.

cards.question: The transition level is the specified last usable flight level. By what minimum margin must it lie above the 5000 ft MSL level
options: 500 ft
cards.explain: A margin of at least 1000 ft above the 5000 ft MSL level is required.

cards.question: How does the temperature behave with increasing height in the troposphere
options: It increases by 0.65 °C every 100 metres
It decreases by 6.5 °C every 100 metres
It decreases by 0.65 °C every 100 metres
cards.explain: The troposphere lapse rate is 0.65 °C per 100 m of climb.

cards.question: The air data measurement also called atmospheric pressure and the one also called ram pressure are
options: the static pressure and the dynamic pressure respectively
the static pressure and the total pressure respectively
the dynamic pressure and the static pressure respectively
cards.explain: Static pressure is also called atmospheric pressure, and dynamic pressure is also called ram pressure.

cards.question: The two measured pressures alone are not enough for two of the air data indications. Those two indications are
options: barometric altitude and true airspeed
true airspeed and static air temperature
airspeed and vertical speed
cards.explain: Temperature as a corrective value makes true airspeed and static air temperature available.

cards.question: How do static pressure, temperature and density behave as altitude increases
options: All three become lower
Only temperature becomes lower
All three become higher
cards.explain: All three listed values fall with increasing altitude.

cards.question: The true airspeed is to be indicated as well as the pressures already measured. Which value must be applied as a corrective?
options: Density
Humidity
Temperature
cards.explain: Temperature is the corrective value that makes TAS and SAT available.

cards.question: A pneumatic instrument is calibrated in the workshop. Which values form the basis of that calibration?
options: The actual airfield values at the time of installation
The tropopause values of the standard atmosphere
The standard atmosphere values at mean sea level
cards.explain: Calibration is referred to the ISA mean sea level values.

cards.question: Why has the international standard atmosphere been established
options: To predict the weather conditions along a planned route
To set the pressure scale of the altimeter before every flight
To compare flight performance under greatly differing conditions
cards.explain: The ISA exists so performance figures can be compared on a common basis.

cards.question: How does the HUD present the PFD data
options: So that the pilot can see it only when the autopilot is engaged
So that the pilot can see it when he looks down at the centre pedestal
So that the pilot can see it when he looks through the windshield
cards.explain: The HUD projects the PFD information into the pilot's forward view.

cards.question: A crew selects QNH on both altimeters. In which phases of flight is this setting used?
options: During landing and take-off, up to transition altitude and below transition level
During landing and take-off, above transition altitude and above transition level
During cruise, above transition altitude and above transition level
cards.explain: QNH belongs to the low level phases, below the transition altitude or level.

cards.question: A crew flies at a level that lies inside the troposphere over the equator but above it over the poles. Which printed thicknesses account for this?
options: About 16.8 km at the equator and about 11 km at the poles
About 16.8 km at the equator and about 8.5 km at the poles
About 8.5 km at the equator and about 16.8 km at the poles
cards.explain: The troposphere reaches much higher at the equator than at the poles, so the same level can be inside it in one place and above it in the other.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs and its static pressure falls. The indication a mechanical air data instrument derives from that falling pressure is
options: the indicated airspeed
the static air temperature
the barometric altitude
cards.explain: Static pressure falls as altitude increases, and it is the static pressure that a mechanical instrument uses for barometric altitude.

cards.question: An airspeed indicator works on the difference between the total and the static pressure. That difference is which of the two air data measurements required for flight monitoring
options: the static pressure
the barometric altitude
the dynamic pressure
cards.explain: Dynamic pressure is the difference between total and static pressure, so of the two required measurements it is the dynamic pressure the indicator works on.

cards.question: In cruise above the transition altitude all pilots set 1013.2 hPa on the altimeter. Which standard atmosphere value is this setting taken from?
options: The pressure at the transition level
The pressure at mean sea level
The pressure at the tropopause
cards.explain: The standard atmosphere fixes the sea level pressure at 1013,25 hPa, which is the pressure the crew sets for flight levels.

cards.question: How does the air temperature of the standard atmosphere behave with increasing height directly above the tropopause
options: It begins to rise with height
It stops falling and stays constant
It continues to fall at the same rate
cards.explain: Identical temperatures at both levels show the lapse rate has stopped at the tropopause.

cards.question: The air data instruments of an aircraft are electrical indicators fed from a central computing unit. In this fit the mechanical conversion of the pressure into electricity takes place
options: in the pitot and static probes
in the air data calculators
in the indicating instrument itself
cards.explain: Where the instruments are electrical, the mechanical conversion from pressure to electricity happens in the air data calculators and not in the instrument.

cards.question: One screen in the cockpit carries all the air data information and also every Basic T parameter. This screen is
options: the standby horizon
the PFD (Primary Flight Display)
the HUD (Head Up Display)
cards.explain: The PFD is the screen that holds all the air data information, and it shows every one of the Basic T parameters.

cards.question: Two altimeters on the same parked aircraft are read at the airfield, one showing zero and the other showing the airfield elevation. Which settings are selected?
options: QFE on the first and QNH on the second
QFE on the first and QNE on the second
QNH on the first and QFE on the second
cards.explain: With QFE the barometric altimeter reads zero on the airfield, while with QNH it reads the elevation there.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs through the transition altitude after take-off. Which change of altimeter setting is required?
options: From STD (QNE) to QNH
From QFE to QNH
From QNH to STD (QNE)
cards.explain: The transition altitude is the height at which the altimeter is changed from QNH to the standard setting.

cards.question: An aircraft descends through the transition level on the approach. Which change of altimeter setting is required?
options: From QNH to QFF
From STD (QNE) to QNH
From QNH to STD (QNE)
cards.explain: The transition level is the flight level at which the altimeter is changed from the standard setting back to QNH.

cards.question: The low range radio altimeter is unserviceable and the crew needs the height above the airfield. Which setting gives it on the barometric altimeter, and under which condition?
options: QFE, in as far as the aircraft stays below the transition altitude
QNH, in as far as there is no change in air pressure
QFE, in as far as there is no change in air pressure
cards.explain: Height is normally taken from the low range radio altimeter, and the barometric altimeter on QFE gives it only as long as the air pressure does not change.

cards.question: An aircraft in cruise above the transition altitude keeps QNH set instead of the standard pressure. What is no longer ensured
options: the measurement of the height above the ground
the safe vertical separation from other aircraft
the indication of the airfield elevation
cards.explain: The common 1013.2 hPa setting in cruise is what ensures safe vertical separation, so an aircraft left on QNH no longer has it.

cards.question: An aircraft cruises at 4000 ft above mean sea level in an area with a transition altitude of 5000 ft. Which altimeter setting must be used?
options: QNH
QFF
QNE
cards.explain: Standard setting only applies above the transition altitude, so below it the altimeter stays on QNH.

cards.question: An operator prepares its fleet for RVSM operations. What does RVSM do to the separation minima?
options: The halving of vertical safety distances at higher flight altitudes
The doubling of vertical safety distances at higher flight altitudes
The halving of lateral safety distances at higher flight altitudes
cards.explain: Reduced vertical separation minimum halves the vertical spacing used up high.

cards.question: What is RVSM airspace
options: Airspace above FL 285 with 500 ft vertical separation
Airspace above FL 290 with 2000 ft vertical separation
Airspace above FL 290 with 1000 ft vertical separation
cards.explain: RVSM airspace starts above FL 290 and uses 1000 ft spacing.

cards.question: What does the abbreviation IAS stand for
options: Indicated airspeed
Inertial airspeed
Increased airspeed
cards.explain: IAS stands for indicated airspeed.

cards.question: Which airspeed is displayed in aircraft equipped with air data computers and glass cockpits
options: The true airspeed
The equivalent airspeed
The calibrated airspeed
cards.explain: Glass cockpits with an ADC display CAS.

cards.question: For which purpose is the true airspeed needed
options: For design data purposes
For navigation purposes
For engine trim purposes
cards.explain: TAS is the speed required for navigation.

cards.question: What is the function of a Bourdon tube
options: It converts pressure into a proportional temperature signal
It converts pressure into a proportional electrical signal
It converts vibration into a proportional electrical signal
cards.explain: The Bourdon tube arrangement turns pressure into a proportional electrical output.

cards.question: Which cross-sectional shape does the curved tube of a Bourdon transducer have
options: An oval shape
A square shape
A round shape
cards.explain: The tube has an oval cross section in the unpressurised state.

cards.question: Which stroke do diaphragm capsules supply as the measurable value
options: 14 to 15 mm
4 to 5 mm
0.4 to 0.5 mm
cards.explain: The capsule stroke is only 4 to 5 mm.

cards.question: What is the purpose of reducing the vertical separation minimum
options: To reduce the workload of the air data computers
To accommodate more aircraft in the same airspace
To allow aircraft to climb above the tropopause
cards.explain: More usable levels mean more aircraft fit into the same volume of airspace.

cards.question: Why was the separation above FL 285 formerly increased
options: Lack of measurement precision and reduced altimeter sensitivity at high altitude
Lack of autopilot authority and reduced control response at high altitude
Lack of radar coverage and reduced transponder range at high altitude
cards.explain: Altimeters become less precise with height, so a bigger buffer was needed.

cards.question: Besides the air data computers, the altimeters and the autopilot in altitude hold mode, which further item is RVSM-sensitive?
options: The radio altimeter antennas and their surroundings
The transponder antenna and its surroundings
The structure and surroundings of the pitot-static sensors
cards.explain: The list of RVSM-sensitive components closes with the structure and surroundings of the pitot-static sensors.

cards.question: Which transponder requirement applies to an aircraft flying in RVSM airspace?
options: It must transmit altitude and be connected to the radio altimeter
It must transmit heading and be connected to the altitude measurement unit
It must transmit altitude and be connected to the altitude measurement unit
cards.explain: The transponder must report altitude taken from the altitude measurement unit.

cards.question: Which operational advantage is gained by an RVSM approved aircraft
options: It can use the increased number of flight levels to fly above the tropopause
It can use a reduced number of flight levels to save maintenance costs
It can use the increased number of flight levels to save time and fuel
cards.explain: More available levels give better routings, saving time and fuel.

cards.question: A workshop is being prepared for the maintenance of RVSM approved aircraft. Which of the mandatory training subjects concerns the accuracy of the workshop's own measuring instruments?
options: Improved precision of test equipment
The configuration of air data systems
Improved altimeter precision
cards.explain: Improved precision of test equipment is the listed subject that deals with the equipment used to test the aircraft.

cards.question: A fleet of six aircraft is to be cleared for RVSM. Who must apply for the Airworthiness Approval and for what?
options: The aircraft operator, for the whole fleet at once
The aircraft operator, for each individual aircraft
The aircraft manufacturer, for each individual aircraft
cards.explain: Approval is per aircraft and is applied for by the operator.

cards.question: What does the requirement for RVSM Airworthiness Approval mean for each individual aircraft
options: Modification according to required service bulletins and the altitude monitoring programme
Modification according to required service bulletins and a full static system overhaul
Replacement of the air data computers and the altitude monitoring programme
cards.explain: Each aircraft has to be modified in accordance with the required service bulletins and is subject to the altitude monitoring programme.

cards.question: The RVSM training covers surface waviness in the critical area. Which causes of that waviness are named?
options: Rivets, oxygen discharge discs and corrosion pits
Fasteners, oxygen discharge discs and paint drops
Fasteners, static dischargers and paint drops
cards.explain: Those three are the surface waviness causes listed.

cards.question: Which detail of the air data computer must the mandatory RVSM training cover
options: Its cooling airflow
Its part numbers
Its software loading procedure
cards.explain: The training list names the part numbers of the air data computer.

cards.question: Which approval makes the aircraft eligible for the RVSM test flight
options: The RVSM Operational Approval
The MNPS Approval
The RVSM Airworthiness Approval
cards.explain: Airworthiness approval comes first and opens the way to the test flight.

cards.question: The altitude monitoring programme and the test flight have both been completed successfully. Which approval does the operator now receive?
options: The MNPS Approval
The RVSM Airworthiness Approval
The RVSM Operational Approval
cards.explain: Operational approval is the last step and permits use of RVSM airspace.

cards.question: An airspeed indicator with bellows is connected to the pitot and static systems. Which pressure does its indication directly follow?
options: The total pressure as the sum of dynamic and ambient pressure
The static pressure as the difference between ambient and total pressure
The dynamic pressure as the difference between total and static pressure
cards.explain: IAS follows dynamic pressure, which is total pressure minus static pressure.

cards.question: Under which conditions does an airspeed indicator with bellows show the real speed of the aircraft
options: At cruise altitude with standard conditions
At mean sea level with compressibility corrected
At mean sea level with standard conditions
cards.explain: The bellows instrument is only true at mean sea level in standard conditions.

cards.question: An air data computer converts the indicated airspeed into the calibrated airspeed. Which two errors does it remove?
options: The error from the indicator and the error from the static pressure source
The error from the indicator and the error from air compressibility
The error from the pitot source and the error from air density
cards.explain: CAS is IAS corrected for instrument error and static source error.

cards.question: A mechanical standby airspeed indicator with bellows is fed with total and static pressure. Which airspeed does it display?
options: The equivalent airspeed
The calibrated airspeed
The indicated airspeed
cards.explain: A bellows instrument with no computer correction shows IAS.

cards.question: Of the two speeds derived after the calibrated airspeed, the one needed for navigation and the one kept for design data are
options: the true airspeed and the indicated airspeed respectively
the true airspeed and the equivalent airspeed respectively
the equivalent airspeed and the true airspeed respectively
cards.explain: The true airspeed is the one wanted for navigation; the equivalent airspeed is not indicated and serves design data and further calculations.

cards.question: Under which condition is the speed formula valid
options: Only when the medium used is above the tropopause
Only when the medium used is incompressible
Only when the medium used is at standard temperature
cards.explain: The formula assumes an incompressible medium.

cards.question: An aircraft accelerates to a high speed and the total pressure rises more than the speed formula predicts. What produces this additional pressure?
options: Air expands at higher speeds and generates a total pressure decrease
Air compresses at lower speeds and generates a static pressure increase
Air compresses at higher speeds and generates a total pressure increase
cards.explain: Compression of the air at high speed raises the total pressure, which the instrument reads as extra speed.

cards.question: How does the compressibility error change with airspeed and altitude
options: The higher the airspeed and altitude, the smaller the error
The lower the airspeed and the higher the altitude, the larger the error
The higher the airspeed and altitude, the larger the error
cards.explain: The error grows with both airspeed and altitude.

cards.question: What is the equivalent airspeed
options: The true airspeed after the density calculation has been removed
The calibrated airspeed after the compressibility error has been removed
The indicated airspeed after the instrument error has been removed
cards.explain: EAS is what is left when the compressibility error is taken out of CAS.

cards.question: Why is the equivalent airspeed not shown to the crew of a commercial airplane
options: It is only valid below the tropopause in standard conditions
It is only available when the air data computer is in test
It is only important for design data and further calculations
cards.explain: EAS is a design and calculation value, not a cockpit indication.

cards.question: A navigation computation needs the speed of the aircraft through the surrounding air mass. Which airspeed is this?
options: The calibrated airspeed
The equivalent airspeed
The true airspeed
cards.explain: TAS is the aircraft speed relative to the surrounding air mass.

cards.question: The compressibility error for a flight condition is known in knots. What is done with this value to obtain the equivalent airspeed?
options: It is subtracted from the true airspeed
It is added to the calibrated airspeed
It is subtracted from the calibrated airspeed
cards.explain: Compression raises the total pressure, so the calibrated airspeed reads too high and the compressibility error has to be taken off it to leave the equivalent airspeed.

cards.question: In which order are the airspeeds derived from the pressure inputs
options: IAS, CAS, EAS, TAS
CAS, IAS, TAS, EAS
IAS, EAS, CAS, TAS
cards.explain: The summary chain runs IAS to CAS to EAS to TAS.

cards.question: Which step is made between EAS and TAS
options: A static source correction
A density calculation
A compressibility correction
cards.explain: The last step of the chain is the density calculation.

cards.question: Which correction is applied between CAS and EAS
options: Correction of instrument error
Correction of static source error
Correction of compressibility error
cards.explain: CAS becomes EAS when the compressibility error is corrected.

cards.question: The pressure sensing element of an aneroid barometer is
options: a vertical tube filled with a fluid
a small capsule made of thin metal
a curved tube with an oval cross section
cards.explain: The aneroid barometer senses pressure with a thin metal capsule; the fluid filled vertical tube belongs to the liquid barometer and the oval curved tube to the Bourdon transducer.

cards.question: What creates the negative pressure at the top of a liquid barometer tube
options: The fluid flowing out of the tube due to its own weight
The expansion of the glass tube with temperature
The ambient air pressure acting on the container
cards.explain: The weight of the fluid draws it down and leaves a negative pressure above it.

cards.question: A Bourdon tube transducer is opened for inspection. Which two parts carry out the pressure conversion?
options: The straight tube and a position sensor
The curved tube and a drive coil
The curved tube and a position sensor
cards.explain: Only the curved oval tube and a position sensor at its tip are required.

cards.question: A Bourdon tube transducer is fitted with a synchro transmitter. Which quantity does this sensor convert into an electrical signal?
options: The position of the tube tip
The pressure inside the tube
The temperature of the tube wall
cards.explain: The sensor senses tip position, not pressure directly.

cards.question: How is an applied pressure distributed inside a Bourdon tube
options: Equally throughout the whole tube
Only at the sealed tube tip
Only at the oval section of the tube
cards.explain: The pressure acts equally over the whole tube.

cards.question: What is the amount of tube tip movement proportional to
options: The applied pressure
The tube temperature
The signal frequency
cards.explain: Tip travel is proportional to the applied pressure.

cards.question: Of the two capsule error influences, the one that depends on whether the pressure was rising or falling is
options: the hysteresis
the effect of temperature
the elastic aftereffect
cards.explain: Hysteresis is the difference between the rising and the falling pressure curve, while the elastic aftereffect comes from pressure held constant over a long time.

cards.question: A diaphragm capsule delivers only a stroke of 4 to 5 mm with a small force. What must the transfer mechanism do with it?
options: Convert it into a damped rotation of the needle
Convert it into an amplified rotation of the needle
Convert it into an amplified stroke of the capsule
cards.explain: The mechanism amplifies the tiny stroke into needle rotation.

cards.question: Which effect does friction have in the transfer mechanism of an aneroid instrument
options: It falsifies the measured result
It damps the capsule stroke
It raises the capsule hysteresis
cards.explain: Friction in the mechanism corrupts the reading.

cards.question: How is friction in the indicator mechanism kept to a minimum
options: With suitable bearings and clean construction of all moving parts
With heavier levers and increased spring tension on all moving parts
With sealed bearings and grease filling of all moving parts
cards.explain: Good bearings and clean mechanical construction minimise friction.

cards.question: In the altimeter one further measure helps to reduce the effect of friction. Which measure is this?
options: Vibration of the instrument
Damping of the capsule
Balancing of the needle
cards.explain: Vibration keeps the altimeter mechanism from sticking, helping against friction.

cards.question: Play in the gearing between the pinion and the tooth segment would falsify the indication. How is this play taken out?
options: By spring tension on both sides
By increased bearing clearance
By spring tension on one side
cards.explain: A one-sided spring tension takes up the gear backlash.

cards.question: What is meant by the hysteresis of a membrane capsule
options: The curve with increasing pressure differs from the curve with increasing temperature
The curve with increasing pressure differs from the curve with decreasing pressure
The stroke lags behind the pressure when a constant pressure acts for a long time
cards.explain: Hysteresis is the difference between the rising and falling pressure characteristics.

cards.question: What causes the elastic aftereffect of a capsule
options: A temperature change acting on the capsule mounting
A constant pressure acting on the capsule over a longer period of time
A rapidly changing pressure acting on the capsule during a climb
cards.explain: Long-held constant pressure makes the capsule yield slowly.

cards.question: What is the result of the slow yielding of a capsule under constant pressure
options: A change of the residual pressure
A time lag in the stroke
A permanent offset of the needle
cards.explain: The stroke lags in time, which is the elastic aftereffect.

cards.question: Friction in the transfer mechanism, hysteresis, elastic aftereffect and temperature all work against precise operation. Which equipment do these error influences affect?
options: All aneroid type instruments
Only metric scale altimeters
Only digital air data computers
cards.explain: These errors act on all aneroid instruments.

cards.question: RVSM airspace lies above FL 290 and is therefore flown on flight levels. The altimeter setting used there is
options: the QNH of the destination airfield
the standard pressure of 1013.2 hPa
the QFE of the departure airfield
cards.explain: RVSM airspace is flight level airspace, and flight levels are flown with the standard pressure of 1013.2 hPa set.

cards.question: An aircraft has two independent altimeters, an autopilot that can maintain the altitude and a device for indicating when the predetermined height is left. The further item of equipment it needs for flight in RVSM airspace is
options: a radio altimeter with an altitude alerting function
a second independent air data computer
a transponder with altitude transmission
cards.explain: The RVSM equipment list is two independent altimeters, a device indicating departure from the predetermined height, an autopilot able to maintain the selected level and a transponder with altitude transmission connected to the altitude measurement unit; the transponder is the item still missing.

cards.question: An aircraft can no longer hold its selected flight level unless the pilot flies manually. Which requirement for flight in RVSM airspace is no longer met?
options: An autopilot that can maintain the altitude
A device for indicating when leaving the predetermined height
A transponder with altitude transmission
cards.explain: One of the listed items of RVSM equipment is an autopilot able to maintain the altitude, and that is the function lost.

cards.question: A dent is found in the skin close to a static port of an RVSM approved aircraft. Which consequence must be expected?
options: A considerable influence on the radio altimeter indication
A considerable influence on the altitude indication
A considerable influence on the mach number only
cards.explain: Skin damage near the static source disturbs the static pressure and so the altitude reading.

cards.question: An altimeter fails in cruise above FL 290 and the aircraft no longer meets the requirements that apply there. Which action is required?
options: A descent to the transition level
A change of the altimeter setting to QNH
A quick exit of RVSM airspace
cards.explain: Losing RVSM capability means the aircraft must leave RVSM airspace quickly.

cards.question: A standby airspeed indicator with bellows and the airspeed readout of the glass cockpit are read at the same moment and differ. Which airspeeds are the two showing?
options: Calibrated airspeed on the bellows instrument and indicated airspeed on the glass cockpit
Indicated airspeed on the bellows instrument and calibrated airspeed on the glass cockpit
Indicated airspeed on the bellows instrument and true airspeed on the glass cockpit
cards.explain: A bellows instrument shows the indicated airspeed, while the glass cockpit indication is the calibrated airspeed.

cards.question: Navigation needs the real speed of the aircraft measured against the surrounding air, but the cockpit shows only the airspeed indication. Which speed is needed and which value must be applied to obtain it?
options: The true airspeed, obtained by applying temperature as a corrective value
The true airspeed, obtained by applying static pressure as a corrective value
The equivalent airspeed, obtained by applying temperature as a corrective value
cards.explain: Navigation needs the true airspeed, and temperature is the corrective value applied so that the true airspeed can be indicated.

cards.question: Why is the equivalent airspeed lower than the calibrated airspeed at high speed and altitude?
options: Because compression of the air raises the total pressure, so the indication is too high
Because reduced density lowers the total pressure, so the indication is too high
Because compression of the air lowers the static pressure, so the indication is too low
cards.explain: The extra total pressure from compression makes the reading too high, so the correction reduces the speed.

cards.question: Two aircraft fly at the same calibrated airspeed, one at 20,000 ft and one at 40,000 ft. Which one has the larger compressibility error?
options: Both have the same error
The aircraft at 40,000 ft
The aircraft at 20,000 ft
cards.explain: The compressibility error grows with altitude, so at the same calibrated airspeed the higher aircraft has the larger error.

cards.question: The synchro transmitter of a Bourdon tube transducer is found unserviceable while the tube itself is sound. Which step of the pressure measurement is lost?
options: The conversion of the tube tip position into an electrical signal
The deformation of the curved tube by the applied pressure
The supply of static pressure to the curved tube
cards.explain: The synchro transmitter is the position sensor, so with it unserviceable the tube tip still moves but its position is no longer turned into an electrical signal.

cards.question: An altimeter needle must turn 51 times over its full range. Which demand does this place on the instrument?
options: The highest demands on electrical power and signal bandwidth
The highest demands on material and fine mechanical precision
The highest demands on case sealing and static line length
cards.explain: Such fine resolution needs the best material and fine mechanics.

cards.question: Which measures are used to characterize the properties of a capsule for its intended use
options: Special alloys, artificial ageing and particular waveforms
Special coatings, artificial ageing and particular bearing materials
Special alloys, natural ageing and particular residual pressures
cards.explain: The three listed measures are special alloys, artificial ageing and particular waveforms.

cards.question: Which parts make temperature compensation demanding over the range -70 to +50 degrees C
options: The capsule mounting and the flexible tubes in the static system
The capsule mounting and the variable levers in the indicator mechanism
The pinion bearings and the quick release connectors of the instrument
cards.explain: Compensation is hard because of the capsule mounting and the variable steering levers.

cards.question: An altimeter is held at one steady pressure on the test bench for a long time and the indication slowly drifts. Which error influence explains this?
options: The hysteresis of the capsule
The backlash of the pinion gearing
The elastic aftereffect of the capsule
cards.explain: Slow drift under a constant held pressure is the elastic aftereffect, not hysteresis.

cards.question: An altimeter reads slightly differently at the same test pressure depending on whether the pressure was raised or lowered to reach it. Which error influence is shown?
options: Hysteresis of the diaphragm capsule
Elastic aftereffect of the diaphragm capsule
Friction in the transfer mechanism
cards.explain: A difference between the rising and falling approach to the same pressure is hysteresis.

cards.question: Through which parts must the smallest pressure change act to deflect the needle exactly
options: From the capsule via levers, shaft and cogwheel
From the capsule via bellows, resonator and coil
From the diaphragm via strain gauges, bridge and amplifier
cards.explain: The mechanical chain runs capsule, levers, shaft, cogwheel, needle.

cards.question: What is the function of a pressure transducer
options: To convert measured pressures into electrical signals
To convert electrical signals into measured pressures
To convert measured pressures into mechanical needle movement
cards.explain: Transducers turn pressure into electrical signals.

cards.question: In which equipment are pressure transducers used
options: In inertial reference units
In air data computers
In flight control computers
cards.explain: Air data computers are one application of this transducer.

cards.question: Several electronic pressure sensor principles exist. Which one is described as the most commonly used?
options: The force compensated cell
The piezoresistive transducer
The vibrating transducer
cards.explain: The vibrating transducer is the most commonly used type.

cards.question: From which material is the micromechanical pressure transducer chamber made
options: Pyrex material
Metal material
Silicon material
cards.explain: The chamber is made of silicon.

cards.question: What is the size of the micromechanical pressure transducer structure
options: Only a few micrometres
Only a few millimetres
Only a few centimetres
cards.explain: The structure measures only a few millimetres.

cards.question: Pressure transducers are fitted in air data computers because the computer needs the measured pressures
options: as an output frequency of the indicator
as amplified needle rotations
as electrical signals
cards.explain: A transducer turns the measured pressures into electrical signals, which is the form the air data computer works with.

cards.question: Pressure transducers have converted the measured pressures into electrical signals. What happens to these signals next?
options: They are sent to the probe heater and transformed into the required current
They are sent to the computer and transformed into the required outputs
They are sent to the indicator and transformed into the required needle deflection
cards.explain: The signals go to the computer, which makes the required outputs.

cards.question: Which output does a vibrating transducer generate
options: An output frequency which depends on the input pressure
An output voltage which depends on the input pressure
An output frequency which depends on the reference pressure
cards.explain: Its output is a frequency that varies with the measured pressure.

cards.question: Which function does the outer case of a vibrating transducer have
options: It forms the outer wall of the reference pressure chamber
It forms the outer wall of the measured pressure chamber
It forms the inner wall of the reference pressure chamber
cards.explain: The outer case is the outer wall of the reference chamber.

cards.question: What happens when pressure acts on the silicon lid of a piezoresistive transducer
options: The lid is dented and the resistance in its surface changes
The lid is dented and the capacitance in its surface changes
The lid vibrates and the frequency of its surface changes
cards.explain: Denting the lid deforms the surface resistors and changes their resistance.

cards.question: What is the output voltage of a piezoresistive transducer proportional to
options: The input pressure
The supply frequency
The reference pressure
cards.explain: The output voltage rises in proportion to the applied pressure.

cards.question: A force compensated pressure cell is fitted instead of a plain pressure cell. Which two advantages are gained?
options: It is insensitive to pressure changes and has small instrument errors
It is sensitive to pressure changes and has small instrument errors
It is insensitive to pressure changes and needs no separate pressure cells
cards.explain: The force compensated cell is insensitive to pressure changes and keeps instrument errors small.

cards.question: Which pressure sensing type needs no different pressure cells for static and pitot pressure?
options: The force compensated pressure cell
The plain pressure cell type
The vibration pressure transducer
cards.explain: The table gives 'no different pressure cells for static and pitot' for the vibration type; both pressure cell types are listed as needing different cells for static and pitot.

cards.question: An electronic pressure sensor delivers an output frequency that depends on the input pressure. This sensor is
options: the vibrating transducer, the most commonly used type
the piezoresistive transducer, the most commonly used type
the pressure cell transducer, the most commonly used type
cards.explain: The vibrating transducer is named as the most commonly used type and it is the one whose output frequency depends on the input pressure.

cards.question: One transducer gives an output frequency depending on the input pressure, another an output voltage in proportion to the input pressure. These are
options: the vibrating transducer and the micromechanical transducer respectively
the vibrating transducer and the Bourdon tube transducer respectively
the micromechanical transducer and the vibrating transducer respectively
cards.explain: The vibrating transducer produces a frequency; the micromechanical transducer produces a voltage in proportion to the pressure.

cards.question: A vibrating transducer is cut open. Where is the pressure that is being measured found?
options: In the reference chamber outside the vibrating cylinder
In the pressure chamber inside the vibrating cylinder
In the pressure chamber inside the center body
cards.explain: The measured pressure sits in the chamber inside the cylinder.

cards.question: What is done with the signal from the pickup coil
options: It is digitized and used as reference, and fed back to the drive coil
It is amplified and used as output, and fed back to the reference chamber
It is amplified and used as output, and fed back to the drive coil
cards.explain: The pickup signal serves both as the amplified output and as the feedback to the drive coil.

cards.question: Why is the pickup coil signal fed back to the drive coil of a vibrating transducer?
options: To keep the cylinder oscillating at its natural frequency
To keep the reference chamber at a constant vacuum
To keep the output frequency at a constant value
cards.explain: The feedback loop sustains vibration at the natural frequency.

cards.question: A pressure sensor consists of a chamber made of silicon, only a few millimetres in size. It is
options: the micromechanical transducer, built as an aneroid-type chamber
the vibrating transducer, built as an aneroid-type chamber
the micromechanical transducer, built as a liquid-based chamber
cards.explain: The micromechanical transducer is the aneroid-type chamber made of silicon whose structure is only a few millimetres in size.

cards.question: Pressure bends the diaphragm of a piezoresistive transducer and the resistance of the strain gages changes. What does the bridge then deliver, and what is it proportional to?
options: An output voltage, in proportion to the supply voltage
An output voltage, in proportion to the input pressure
An output frequency, in proportion to the input pressure
cards.explain: The four strain gages sit in a wheatstone bridge, and the change in their resistance gives an output voltage in proportion to the input pressure.

cards.question: Pressure is applied to a piezoresistive transducer. How do the two bridge voltages behave?
options: U1 decreases while U2 increases
U1 and U2 both increase
U1 increases while U2 decreases
cards.explain: The two halves of the bridge move in opposite directions when the plate bends.

cards.question: A strain gauge wire is made thicker while its length stays the same. How does its resistance change?
options: It decreases with increasing area
It increases with increasing area
It is independent of the area
cards.explain: A larger cross section lowers the resistance.

cards.question: A strain gauge on the bent side of the diaphragm is stretched. Why does its resistance rise?
options: Because the wire becomes longer and resistance rises with length
Because the material constant of the wire rises with the strain
Because the wire becomes shorter and resistance rises as it shortens
cards.explain: Resistance increases with the length of the wire, so stretching a strain gauge raises its resistance.

cards.question: An airspeed indicator in a simple system is connected to two pressure lines. Which pressures does it use?
options: Static pressure and differential pressure
Pitot pressure and total pressure
Pitot pressure and static pressure
cards.explain: The airspeed indicator is the only one of the three that needs both pitot and static pressure.

cards.question: What is static pressure
options: The actual atmospheric pressure surrounding the aircraft
The build-up of air pressure in a tube facing the airstream
The difference between total pressure and ram pressure
cards.explain: Static pressure is simply the ambient atmospheric pressure around the aircraft.

cards.question: A pneumatic device is calibrated to the international standard atmosphere. Which value of air density at mean sea level applies?
cards.explain: The ISA sea level density is 1,225 kg/m3.
