cards.explain: The air gap is sealed with badger hair.

cards.question: What sets the central position of a diaphragm variometer
options: A permanent magnet
A coiled spring
A hairspring driven by the capillary
cards.explain: A coiled spring sets the central position.

cards.question: Why is a vertical speed indicator connected to the static system only
options: Because it works from changes of static pressure acting on its bellows
Because it works from the delay of the total pressure through a capillary
Because it works from the difference between total pressure and static pressure
cards.explain: The instrument senses air pressure changes with static pressure on both sides of its bellows, so it needs no pitot connection.

cards.question: An aircraft holds a constant altitude so static pressure stays constant. What does the mechanical variometer show?
options: A small descent, because the bellows remain partly compressed
Zero, because the same pressure acts inside and outside the bellows
A small climb, because the capillary keeps the outside pressure higher
cards.explain: With equal pressures either side of the bellows the pointer reads zero.

cards.question: An aircraft with an IVSI enters and leaves a turn with a high bank angle. What should be expected?
options: An inaccurate vertical speed indication, because any vertical acceleration affects the piston
A correct vertical speed indication, because the piston compensates for bank angle
A total loss of indication, because the piston is locked by the acceleration
cards.explain: Any vertical acceleration acts on the piston, so turn entry and exit give a wrong reading.

cards.question: What produces the force that moves the diaphragm and the pointer of a diaphragm variometer
options: The difference between static pressure and total pressure
The difference between static pressure and accumulator pressure
The difference between accumulator pressure and cabin pressure
cards.explain: The driving difference is between static and accumulator pressure.

cards.question: How is pressure balanced out in a diaphragm variometer
options: Via the air gap between the diaphragm and the casing
Via a capillary tube between the diaphragm and the casing
Via a calibrated orifice in the centre of the diaphragm
cards.explain: Balancing takes place through the air gap between diaphragm and casing.

cards.question: A precision variometer is required for a glider. Why is the diaphragm type chosen?
options: Because diaphragm variometers are exact
Because diaphragm variometers need no static source
Because diaphragm variometers have the longest time constant
cards.explain: Their accuracy is the stated reason for their use as precision instruments.

cards.question: Why is the pointer movement of a mechanical variometer delayed when the vertical speed changes
options: Because the change is immediate outside the bellows but delayed inside by capillary action and the larger volume
Because the pointer linkage is deliberately damped by a friction brake
Because the change is immediate inside the bellows but delayed outside by capillary action and the larger volume
cards.explain: The capillary and the larger outer volume delay the outside pressure change.

cards.question: How does the response of a mechanical variometer to a change of vertical speed compare with that of an instantaneous vertical speed indicator
options: Undelayed in the mechanical variometer, and delayed in the IVSI because an acceleration piston is installed
Delayed in the mechanical variometer, and undelayed in the IVSI because an acceleration piston is installed
Delayed in both, because both feed the outside of the bellows through a capillary
cards.explain: The transition from one vertical speed to another is subject to a time delay, so the pointer movement of the mechanical variometer is delayed, while the IVSI eliminates that delay with an acceleration piston.

cards.question: An aircraft begins a descent. How does the IVSI piston give an immediate indication?
options: The negative gravity force moves the piston up and raises the pressure inside the bellows before the outside static pressure changes
The negative gravity force moves the piston down and lowers the pressure inside the bellows before the outside static pressure changes
The negative gravity force closes the capillary so that the outside static pressure changes first
cards.explain: The piston raises bellows pressure ahead of the real static pressure change.

cards.question: A thermometer must read down to minus 150 C. Which filling substance has an application range that reaches this?
options: Toluene
Pentane
Mercury
cards.explain: Only pentane, from -200 C, covers that low a reading; toluene starts at -80 C and mercury at -30 C.

cards.question: A mercury thermometer is offered for work at minus 60 C. Why is it the wrong choice?
options: It allows no remote temperature measurement
Its expansion coefficient is temperature-dependent
Its application range only starts at minus 30 C
cards.explain: Mercury is only listed from minus 30 C upwards, so minus 60 C is outside its range.

cards.question: A filling is wanted that reads up to 1000 C without a poison hazard. Which substance fits, and what must be accepted with it?
options: Galinstan, with heavy wetting of the thermometer tube
Galinstan, with a health risk from inflammable vapour
Mercury, with heavy wetting of the thermometer tube
cards.explain: Galinstan is the non-poisonous alloy listed up to 1000 C, and its drawback is heavy wetting of the tube.

cards.question: The airspeed value that the temperature display is used to determine is
options: IAS
TAS
EAS
cards.explain: The temperature display is used among other things for determining the TAS.

cards.question: The hazard that the temperature display helps the crew detect is
options: Possible ice formation
Possible engine surge
Possible pitot blockage
cards.explain: Air temperature is the indication used to judge whether ice can form.

cards.question: What is static air temperature (SAT)
options: The ambient temperature plus the rise from air compression
The free airstream temperature with a built-in deflection error
The actual temperature of the ambient air
cards.explain: SAT is the true ambient air temperature, with no ram rise in it.

cards.question: What is total air temperature (TAT)
options: The ambient temperature minus the temperature generated by air compression
The ambient temperature with no allowance for air compression
The ambient temperature plus the temperature generated by air compression
cards.explain: TAT is ambient temperature plus the heating caused by compression of the air.

cards.question: The temperature value that is determined directly by the measuring probe is
options: RR
SAT
TAT
cards.explain: Only TAT comes straight off the probe; SAT and the ram rise are worked out from it.

cards.question: What does a TAT measuring probe contain as its sensing elements
options: One temperature dependent PTC resistor
Two or three temperature dependent PTC resistors
Two or three temperature dependent capillary tubes
cards.explain: The probe carries two or three temperature dependent PTC resistors.

cards.question: The engine related use of the temperature display is
options: Calculating engine performance and determining engine limits
Calculating engine oil quantity and determining oil limits
Calculating engine vibration and determining balance limits
cards.explain: Air temperature feeds engine performance calculation and the engine limits.

cards.question: What does an electronic OAT display need in order to show a reading
options: An OAT thermometer read directly in the cockpit
An analogue OAT scale attached to the display
An external OAT sensor
cards.explain: The electronic display has no sensing element of its own, so an external OAT sensor is required.

cards.question: The simple OAT indicating system is used on
options: small propeller aeroplanes and helicopters
supersonic transport aeroplanes
large commercial jet aeroplanes
cards.explain: The simple system is restricted to small propeller driven aeroplanes and helicopters.

cards.question: A fast jet aeroplane cannot use the simple OAT indicating system. What is the reason?
options: It cannot be protected against ice
It needs a bleed air supply that jets cannot provide
It is only accurate up to an airspeed of 250 kts
cards.explain: Its accuracy runs out at 250 kts, which is why it is limited to slow aircraft.

cards.question: In a modern temperature indicating system, the display and the calculation
options: are performed separately, the calculation being done in the computer
are performed separately, the calculation being done in the measuring probe
are performed together in the instrument, as in conventional analogue construction
cards.explain: Modern instruments display digitally and do the calculation separately, in the computer, unlike the conventional analogue indicator that carries its switching inside the instrument.

cards.question: Why is the TAT always higher than the SAT during flight
options: Ram air is present at the measuring probe and raises its temperature
The probe is flush with a skin that is warmed by the sun
The probe heater adds heat to the measurement in flight
cards.explain: Ram air at the probe produces the ram rise that lifts TAT above SAT.

cards.question: What causes the built-in error that makes RAT differ from TAT
options: The air is deflected as it flows around the aircraft fuselage
The air is warmed by the probe anti-icing element
The air is brought completely to rest inside the probe neck
cards.explain: The free airstream over the probe is deflected around the fuselage, which is the built-in RAT error.

cards.question: The form of temperature supplied by a probe mounted flush with the aircraft skin is
options: RAT
TAT
SAT
cards.explain: A flush probe gives ram air temperature; the TAT probe is the one held off the skin.

cards.question: A temperature probe is carried on a spacing foot clear of the fuselage skin. What is this arrangement for?
options: To let bleed air be blown back over the skin
To determine the total air temperature out in the airstream
To keep the probe clear of the skin heating system
cards.explain: Holding the probe out in the airstream, like a pitot tube, is what lets it sense TAT.

cards.question: Where does the switching sit in an analogue temperature indicator of conventional construction
options: Directly in the instrument, except for the measuring resistor
In the air data computer, together with the measuring resistor
Directly in the probe, except for the measuring resistor
cards.explain: Only the measuring resistor sits outside; the rest of the switching is in the instrument.

cards.question: Besides the display instrument and the flight recorder, which user is supplied with the outside air temperature?
options: The stall warning computer, to set the shaker threshold
The ADC or FMC, to calculate values that cannot be measured directly
The cabin pressure controller, to set the cabin rate of climb
cards.explain: The ADC and FMC use it to work out values that cannot be measured directly.

cards.question: What produces the temperature rise seen at the measuring probe in flight
options: Friction in the probe heating element
Radiation from the warm aircraft skin
Compression of the air
cards.explain: The rise is the ram rise, caused by the air being compressed at the probe.

cards.question: How does the TAT probe heating behave in flight and on the ground
options: In flight it has no effect on the measurement, and on the ground it is switched on automatically
In flight it has no effect on the measurement, and on the ground it is often switched off automatically
In flight it raises the measurement, and on the ground it is often switched off automatically
cards.explain: Airflow in flight carries the heat away, and on the ground the heating is normally cut automatically.

cards.question: What is an aspirated TAT probe supplied with
options: Conditioned cabin air
Pitot pressure air
Bleed air
cards.explain: An aspirated probe uses bleed air to draw outside air through it.

cards.question: The measuring wire of a TAT probe is broken. Which indication results, and why?
options: The plus 50 C upper stop, because the resistance falls to zero
The minus 70 C lower stop, because the resistance is infinitely high
The plus 50 C upper stop, because the resistance is infinitely high
cards.explain: An open circuit looks like infinite resistance, which drives the pointer to the upper stop.

cards.question: The measuring wire of a TAT probe is short circuited. Which indication results, and why?
options: The plus 50 C upper stop, because the resistance is 0 ohm
The minus 70 C lower stop, because the resistance is 0 ohm
The minus 70 C lower stop, because the resistance is infinitely high
cards.explain: A short gives zero resistance, which drives the pointer to the lower stop.

cards.question: How does the resistance of the TAT probe sensing elements change as the sensed temperature rises
options: It stays constant
It increases
It decreases
cards.explain: The sensing elements are PTC resistors, and with a PTC a rise in temperature gives a rise in resistance.

cards.question: In flight, how do the three measured air temperature values compare with one another?
options: TAT is the highest, RAT is lower than TAT but higher than SAT
RAT is the highest, TAT is lower than RAT but higher than SAT
SAT is the highest, RAT is lower than SAT but higher than TAT
cards.explain: Full ram rise gives the highest value at the TAT probe, RAT loses part of it, and SAT has none.

cards.question: A flush skin probe supplies temperature in the RAT form. Why can that reading not be used as the ambient air temperature?
options: RAT is taken downstream of the probe heater, so it reads higher than the ambient SAT
RAT still contains part of the ram rise, so it reads higher than the ambient SAT
RAT is deflected around the fuselage, so it reads lower than the ambient SAT
cards.explain: RAT sits between TAT and SAT, so it is still above ambient and the SAT has to be calculated.

cards.question: Why does a fast aeroplane need an air data computer for ambient air temperature while a light propeller aeroplane manages with a simple thermometer?
options: At high speed the ambient air temperature falls below the range of a direct reading thermometer
At high speed the ram rise is large, so the ambient SAT must be calculated from the measured value
At high speed the probe heating is permanently on, so the measured value must be corrected
cards.explain: The simple temperature indicating system is accurate only up to an airspeed of 250 kts, and in fast aeroplanes the SAT must be calculated by an air data computer.

cards.question: An aeroplane accelerates to a higher mach number while the static air temperature stays the same. What happens to the gap between TAT and SAT?
options: It shrinks, because the ram rise falls away at a higher mach number
It stays the same, because the ram rise depends only on the static air temperature
It grows, because the ram rise depends on the mach number
cards.explain: The gap between TAT and SAT is the ram rise, and that grows with mach number.

cards.question: In cruise the crew needs the static air temperature. How is that value produced?
options: It is calculated from the TAT and the mach number in the air data computer
It is read directly from the ram air temperature indicator
It is read directly from a second, unheated static temperature probe
cards.explain: SAT cannot be sensed directly, so the ADC derives it from the measured TAT and the mach number.

cards.question: The air in a TAT probe is slowed at the resistor heads to the point where a ram effect occurs. Which temperature value does the probe then supply, and how is the ambient value obtained from it
options: TAT, and the SAT is calculated from it in the air data computer
SAT, and the TAT is calculated from it in the air data computer
RAT, and the SAT is calculated from it in the air data computer
cards.explain: The slowed air gives the probe the total air temperature, and the static air temperature cannot be determined directly but is calculated in the air data computer.

cards.question: An aeroplane stands in strong sunshine and its skin is hot. Which probe design keeps these conditions out of the temperature reading, and how?
options: A standard TAT probe, because its heating element masks the effect of the sun
A flush skin probe, because the skin and the probe then settle at the same temperature
An aspirated TAT probe, because compressed air blown backwards carries outside air along
cards.explain: The aspirated probe keeps outside air moving through it, so sun and skin temperature on the ground can be ignored.

cards.question: The heating of a TAT probe has failed and the aircraft is in icing conditions. What is the consequence and the indication?
options: Icing of the probe, with the upper stop indicated
Loss of the signal, with the lower stop indicated
Icing of the probe, with ice temperature indicated
cards.explain: Without heating the probe ices up and then reads the temperature of the ice on it.

cards.question: The abbreviation CADC stands for
options: Central Air Data Computer
Corrected Air Data Computer
Combined Air Data Computer
cards.explain: CADC stands for Central Air Data Computer, also called ADC in short.

cards.question: The analogue air data computer is built from three modules, which are
options: an altitude module, an airspeed module and a Mach module
an altitude module, a vertical speed module and a temperature module
a pitot module, a static module and a temperature module
cards.explain: The analogue air data computer has an altitude module, an airspeed module and a Mach module.

cards.question: The indicated airspeed depends directly on
options: the total pressure, the sum of static and dynamic pressure
the static pressure, the difference between total and dynamic pressure
the dynamic pressure, the difference between total and static pressure
cards.explain: IAS is a direct function of dynamic pressure, which is total minus static pressure.

cards.question: MASI is the abbreviation for
options: manual airspeed indicator
Mach/altitude signal indicator
Mach/airspeed indicator
cards.explain: The instrument combines the Mach and airspeed indications in one display.

cards.question: When the air data computer has compensated the compressibility error, the result is called
options: calibrated airspeed
equivalent airspeed
true airspeed
cards.explain: Compensating compressibility turns CAS into EAS.

cards.question: The flag fitted to a vertical speed indicator driven by an air data computer is
options: the STDBY flag
the ALT flag
the OFF flag
cards.explain: The vertical speed indicator with analogue input carries an OFF flag.

cards.question: An engineer asks why aircraft manufacturers introduced the central air data computer. What is the reason?
options: It made the standby air data instruments unnecessary
It sorted out the muddle of individual pressure instruments
It removed the need for pitot and static ports on the fuselage
cards.explain: Conventional air data conversion meant installing many separate aneroid and differential pressure instruments; the CADC replaced that muddle.

cards.question: Among the main uses of the central air data computer is the correction of
options: pitot blockage errors and drain errors
compass deviation and compass variation
static source errors and instrument errors
cards.explain: Correcting static source error and instrument error is listed as a main task of the CADC.

cards.question: The pitot and static supply of the standby air data instruments
options: is an additional system of its own
is shared with the number one air data computer
is taken from the air data computer in use
cards.explain: The standby air data instruments have their own pitot and static system in addition to those of the computers.

cards.question: One of the main uses of the central air data computer is
options: to pass the barometric setting out to the static ports
to determine values which are not directly measurable
to measure the deviation of the magnetic compass
cards.explain: Deriving values that cannot be measured directly is listed as one of the CADC main tasks.

cards.question: A technician traces the vertical speed output of an analogue air data computer. Which module produces it?
options: The Mach module
The airspeed module
The altitude module
cards.explain: The altitude module converts static pressure into both the altitude and the vertical speed signal.

cards.question: The airspeed module of an analogue air data computer calculates the dynamic pressure from
options: the static pressure and the temperature
the total pressure and the Mach number
the static pressure and the total pressure
cards.explain: Dynamic pressure is derived in the airspeed module from static and total pressure, giving CAS.

cards.question: Which features of the aircraft itself does the static source error depend on
options: the position of the temperature probe and the shape of the wing
the length of the static lines and the size of the drain holes
the location of the static ports and the shape of the fuselage
cards.explain: Static port location and fuselage shape are the further factors given for the static source error.

cards.question: With pin programming, an air data computer receives its aircraft characteristic data as
options: a reference voltage set by the altitude module
a coded word on the output data bus
a ground signal on a specific rack connector pin
cards.explain: Pin programming grounds a particular rack connector pin to tell the computer which aircraft type it is in.

cards.question: Why does an air data computer have to be supplied with aircraft characteristic data
options: Because the computer has to correct the compressibility error of the airspeed
Because the same computer can be used in different aircraft types
Because the computer has to be matched to the indicators connected to it
cards.explain: One computer can be fitted to different aircraft types, so it must be told the characteristics of the aircraft it is installed in.

cards.question: The purpose of supplying angle of attack, flap position and gear position to some air data computers is
options: To make the static source error correction more accurate
To make the instrument error correction more accurate
To make the compressibility error correction more accurate
cards.explain: These extra inputs are used to sharpen the static source error correction.

cards.question: In the synchrotel of a servo corrected altimeter, the altitude transmitted by the air data computer is compared with
options: the altitude set on the baro scale
the altitude recorded by the pressure capsule
the altitude held by the drum pointer motor
cards.explain: The synchrotel compares the ADC altitude against the capsule altitude.

cards.question: If the altitude from the air data computer and the altitude from the capsule do not coincide
options: the baro window is driven back to the standard setting
the STDBY flag comes into view at once
an error voltage builds up in the coil of the synchrotel
cards.explain: A difference between the two altitudes produces an error voltage in the synchrotel coil.

cards.question: The error voltage in a servo corrected altimeter has fallen to about zero. What does this tell the engineer?
options: The indication agrees with the altitude from the air data computer
The correction has been switched to standby
The pressure capsule has been disconnected from the drum pointer
cards.explain: Zero error voltage is the state in which indication and transmitted altitude agree.

cards.question: With the switch in STBY, a servo corrected altimeter
options: works purely mechanically and shows the STDBY flag
works purely mechanically and shows the ALT flag
works purely electrically and shows the STDBY flag
cards.explain: Deactivating the correction leaves a purely mechanical instrument with the STDBY flag in view.

cards.question: A servo corrected altimeter contains an internal vibrator. What is it there for?
options: To damp the pointer during rapid climbs
To warn the crew that the correction has dropped out
To reduce friction
cards.explain: The vibrator is fitted to reduce friction inside the mechanism.

cards.question: In a servo corrected altimeter the barometric correction made with the BARO button is
options: a combination of capsule movement and servo drive
purely mechanical
purely electrical, through the air data computer
cards.explain: The baro setting acts mechanically on the instrument, not through the computer.

cards.question: In a servo corrected altimeter the movement of the pressure capsule reaches the pointer and drum
options: via the amplifier and the motor
via the rotor of the synchrotel
via differential gearing
cards.explain: The capsule acts on the pointer and drum through differential gearing.

cards.question: The supply voltage to a servo corrected altimeter is lost. Why does the correction stop?
options: Because the ALT flag has to be valid before the correction can continue
Because voltage present is one of the requirements for continuous operation of the correction
Because the error voltage has to be about zero before the correction can continue
cards.explain: Voltage present is listed as one of the requirements for the correction to keep running, so losing the supply stops it.

cards.question: The altitude transmitted to an electrical altimeter by the air data computer is based on
options: the standard of 1013 mbar
the pressure set on the baro knob
the elevation of the departure aerodrome
cards.explain: The computer sends altitude referenced to the standard setting; the baro correction is applied afterwards in the indicator.

cards.question: An aircraft makes only small changes of height. What happens to the coarse synchro value in the electrical altimeter?
options: It is blocked by the HIGH LEVEL detector
It is blocked by the OFF flag monitor
It is blocked by the LIMITER
cards.explain: For small height changes the fine value alone is used and the HIGH LEVEL detector blocks the coarse value.

cards.question: An aircraft makes a large change of altitude. What happens in the electrical altimeter?
options: The coarse synchro value predominates and the fine value is suppressed by the HIGH LEVEL detector
The fine synchro value predominates and the coarse value is suppressed by the LIMITER
The coarse synchro value predominates and the fine value is suppressed by the LIMITER
cards.explain: Large changes let the coarse value take over, with the LIMITER suppressing the fine value.

cards.question: Why is the indicated airspeed treated as a very important parameter for safe flight?
options: It gives the real speed of the aircraft at every altitude
Lift, drag and control effectiveness all follow the dynamic pressure
It is already corrected for instrument and static source error
cards.explain: IAS matters because the aerodynamic effects and control effectiveness follow dynamic pressure.

cards.question: A glass cockpit aircraft displays calibrated airspeed. What has been corrected to obtain it?
options: The error from the indicator and the error from the compressibility of the air
The error from the pitot source and the error from the air density
The error from the indicator and the error from the static pressure source
cards.explain: CAS is IAS corrected for instrument error and static source error.

cards.question: CAS is often also taken to mean computed airspeed because
options: the correction is done by an air data computer
the value is computed inside the indicator
the value is computed from the Mach number
cards.explain: The computer performs the correction, which is why the second reading of the abbreviation is used.

cards.question: The transmission of the speed value from the air data computer to the indicator
options: is made as a digital data word in every case
is technically the same as for an altimeter
is technically the same as for a vertical speed indicator
cards.explain: The speed value is sent to its indicator in technically the same way as the altitude value is sent to an altimeter.

cards.question: The Mach number is transmitted from the air data computer to the indicator
options: as a discrete that is valid for all parameters
as a pneumatic signal from the pitot connection
in technically the same way as the CAS value
cards.explain: Mach uses the same transmission technique as the calibrated airspeed value.

cards.question: A technician is asked where the compressibility error comes from. What is the correct explanation?
options: Air compresses at higher speeds and so increases the total pressure
Air density falls with altitude and so the dynamic pressure drops
Air compresses at higher altitudes and so the static pressure falls
cards.explain: The speed formula assumes an incompressible medium, and the compression of the air at speed raises the total pressure.

cards.question: True airspeed and equivalent airspeed are identical
options: at the speed of sound
at mean sea level
at the tropopause
cards.explain: Only at mean sea level does the real density equal the standard density used for EAS.

cards.question: A student asks why navigation needs the true airspeed rather than the indicated airspeed. What is the correct reply?
options: Navigation needs the real speed of the aircraft, measured against the ground
Navigation needs the real speed of the aircraft, measured against the surrounding air
Navigation needs the speed the structure can stand, measured as dynamic pressure
cards.explain: Navigation needs the real speed of the aircraft, and that is the true airspeed, measured against the surrounding air.

cards.question: The OFF flag of a vertical speed indicator with analogue input monitors
options: the indicator and the air data computer signal
the indicator only
the static source error correction
cards.explain: The flag covers both the indicator itself and the signal arriving from the computer.

cards.question: An aircraft is fitted with two air data computers. How are their pressure sources arranged?
options: Both computers are fed from one common pitot and static system
Each computer has its own separated pitot and static system
Both computers are fed from the standby pitot and static system
cards.explain: Each of the two computers is given a separate pitot and static system of its own.

cards.question: The temperature supply to an analogue air data computer is lost. Which outputs can no longer be produced?
options: Vertical speed and total air temperature
Calibrated airspeed and altitude
True airspeed and static air temperature
cards.explain: TAS and SAT are the outputs that depend on the temperature being supplied to the Mach module.

cards.question: The Mach module of an analogue air data computer fails. Why is the static source error correction affected as well?
options: The correction depends on the static pressure, which is routed through that module
The correction depends primarily on the Mach number, which comes from that module
The correction depends primarily on the calibrated airspeed, which comes from that module
cards.explain: Static source error depends first of all on Mach number, and that value is supplied by the Mach module.

cards.question: The static pressure reaching an analogue air data computer is in error. What is the effect of this on the Mach indication
options: The Mach number is wrong as well, because the Mach module works from the temperature input
The Mach number stays correct, because the Mach module has a pressure input of its own
The Mach number is wrong as well, because the Mach module works from the other two modules
cards.explain: The Mach module takes its information from the altitude and airspeed modules, both of which use the static pressure, so an error in that pressure carries into the Mach number.

cards.question: A servo corrected altimeter reads several thousand feet away from the altitude sent by the air data computer. Why does the correction not bring it into agreement?
options: Correction only works above the altitude set on the baro scale
Correction is inhibited while the internal vibrator is running
Correction is only possible within a few hundred feet
cards.explain: Continuous correction requires the error voltage to be about zero, which limits it to a few hundred feet.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs at a constant indicated airspeed. Why does the IAS no longer give the real speed of the aircraft?
options: The indicator is calibrated to the standard air pressure and the real pressure is not taken into account
The dynamic pressure is no longer the difference between total and static pressure
The indicator is calibrated to the standard air density and the real density is not taken into account
cards.explain: Calibration to standard density means IAS is only the real speed at mean sea level under standard conditions.

cards.question: An air data computer stops working altogether. What is seen on the Mach/airspeed indicator?
options: A red flag for the Mach value only, because CAS is taken from a capsule
No flag at all, because the indicator holds the last values received
A red flag for each value, because the valid discretes are no longer transmitted
cards.explain: Loss of the valid discrete for a value raises the red flag for that value.

cards.question: A red flag shows against one parameter on a Mach/airspeed indicator while the other parameter reads normally. What should the engineer conclude?
options: The fault must lie in the air data computer itself
The fault may lie in the air data computer or in the indicator
The fault must lie in the pitot and static system
cards.explain: The indicator raises the same flag for its own internal faults, so the flag alone does not isolate the computer.

cards.question: How does the air data computer obtain true airspeed from equivalent airspeed?
options: It adds the static source error correction to the equivalent airspeed
It replaces the standard pressure used before with the real pressure
It replaces the standard density used before with the real density
cards.explain: The step from EAS to TAS is the substitution of real air density for standard density.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs while holding a constant equivalent airspeed. What happens to the true airspeed?
options: It stays the same, because the two values are identical at every altitude
It decreases, because the true airspeed falls with increasing altitude
It increases, because the true airspeed rises with increasing altitude
cards.explain: For a given EAS the TAS increases with increasing altitude, and is identical to the EAS only at mean sea level.

cards.question: The analogue output data of a hybrid air data computer is provided in the format
options: ARINC 565
ARINC 629
ARINC 429
cards.explain: ARINC 565 is the analogue format, ARINC 429 the digital one.

cards.question: The pressure transducers of a digital air data computer are used to
options: hold the input pressures at a reference value
convert the input pressures into electrical signals
convert the input pressures into a mechanical movement
cards.explain: The transducer turns pitot and static pressure into an electrical quantity.

cards.question: The data format used by a digital air data computer is usually
options: ARINC 429
ARINC 565
ARINC 573
cards.explain: ARINC 429 is given as the usual format for the digital computer output.

cards.question: A hybrid air data computer is described as hybrid because
options: it uses both pressure capsules and pressure transducers
it provides output data in analogue form as well as digitally
it can be supplied with either AC or DC power
cards.explain: The mixture of analogue and digital outputs is what makes the computer hybrid.

cards.question: An analogue air data computer is unserviceable and a DADC is offered as a replacement. What applies?
options: The DADC may be installed in place of the analogue computer
The DADC may only be installed if both computers are changed together
The DADC may not be installed in place of an analogue computer
cards.explain: The replacement is allowed in that direction only, because the DADC also provides analogue outputs.

cards.question: Compared with an analogue computer, the internal arrangement of a hybrid air data computer
options: keeps the three modules but adds a digital output stage
has an additional module for true airspeed
has no division into altitude, airspeed and Mach modes
cards.explain: The hybrid computer drops the modular split used in the analogue computer.

cards.question: Two types of pressure transducer used in digital air data computers are
options: the aneroid capsule and the vibrating cylinder
the resistive bridge and the differential bellows
the resistive bridge and the vibrating cylinder
cards.explain: The two types are the resistive bridge transducer and the vibrating cylinder.

cards.question: A technician asks how the digital computer of a DADC produces its many outputs. What is correct?
options: It calculates them one after the other and refreshes the data in a predetermined cycle
It calculates a value only when an indicator asks for it
It calculates them all at the same instant and refreshes them continuously
cards.explain: Outputs are computed in sequence and refreshed on a fixed cycle.

cards.question: The computed values of a digital air data computer reach the instruments and other users
options: over several digital data busses
over one single analogue data bus
over separate synchro lines for each value
cards.explain: Distribution is by several digital data busses.

cards.question: A digital air data computer normally learns which aircraft type it is fitted to from
options: a pin programming
the temperature probe
the angle of attack sensor
cards.explain: Aircraft type information comes from pin programming; the other inputs serve the correction itself.

cards.question: An inertial reference unit mixes its own accelerometer signal with the air data computer signal before sending vertical speed. Why?
options: the air data signal corrects the accelerometer for position error
the accelerometer signal alone cannot be converted to a digital output
the quick accelerometer and slow air data signals give a smooth indication
cards.explain: Mixing the fast accelerometer signal with the slow air data signal produces a smooth vertical speed indication.

cards.question: The disadvantage of a vertical speed signal taken from an air data computer is that
options: it shows the vertical speed with a delay
it shows the vertical speed without any delay
it shows the vertical speed only above a set altitude
cards.explain: The air data derived signal lags, which is why the inertial signal is preferred.

cards.question: The inertial reference unit is unable to calculate vertical speed. What appears on the indicator?
options: A yellow ALT flag
A red AS flag
A yellow IVS flag
cards.explain: Loss of the inertial vertical speed calculation is annunciated by the yellow IVS flag.

cards.question: The second back up fitted to some vertical speed indicators is
options: the offside standby altimeter
the onside inertial reference unit
the offside air data computer
cards.explain: Beyond the onside air data computer, some indicators can also use the offside air data computer.

cards.question: A digital air data computer has lost its angle of attack, flap and gear position inputs. Which of its functions is degraded?
options: The conversion of the input pressures into electrical signals
The transmission of the computed values on the output busses
The data corrections, such as the static source error correction
cards.explain: Those inputs are used for the data corrections, so only the correction accuracy suffers.

cards.question: Which inputs does a digital air data computer take from the aircraft sensing elements, and in which form do its computed values leave it
options: Pitot pressure, static pressure and temperature in, digital data on several data busses out
Pitot pressure, static pressure and dynamic pressure in, digital data on several data busses out
Pitot pressure, static pressure and temperature in, analogue signals on separate wires out
cards.explain: The computer is fed with pitot pressure, static pressure and temperature, and sends its computed values out digitally on several data busses; dynamic pressure is not sensed but worked out from the two pressures.

cards.question: The barometric setting is changed on an altimeter with digital input. Which way does that signal travel?
options: In analogue form from the indicator to the DADC
In analogue form from the DADC to the indicator
In digital form from the indicator to the DADC
cards.explain: The baro value runs back the other way, from the indicator to the computer, and in analogue form.

cards.question: The air data computers have failed, yet the digital vertical speed indicator still gives a usable indication. Why?
options: It normally works from the static pressure rate measured in the indicator itself
It normally works from the inertial vertical speed signal of the inertial reference unit
It normally works from the vertical speed output of the air data computer
cards.explain: The normal source is the IRU, so the indication survives the loss of the air data computers.

cards.question: In flight the inertial vertical speed signal from the inertial reference unit is lost. What happens at the vertical speed indicator?
options: The indicator freezes at the last valid vertical speed
The indicator blanks until another source is selected by hand
The vertical speed from the air data computer is used automatically
cards.explain: The changeover to air data vertical speed is automatic, so the indication continues.

cards.question: A pilot's air data selector is moved out of its normal position. Which indications change over?
options: That pilot's vertical speed indicator goes to the other digital air data computer
That pilot's airspeed indicator and altimeter go to the other digital air data computer
That pilot's standby instruments go to the other digital air data computer
cards.explain: The air data selector transfers the air data indicators, airspeed and altitude, to the other air data computer; the vertical speed indicator is fed from an inertial source.

cards.question: The installation of a glass cockpit in an aircraft
options: replaces the pitot probes and static ports
replaces the digital air data computers
replaces the individual indicators
cards.explain: The glass cockpit takes the place of the separate indicators, not of the computers or the sensing system.

cards.question: The primary flight display is a display which shows
options: most of the air data
the engine parameters
the true airspeed only
cards.explain: The PFD is where most of the air data is presented.

cards.question: EFIS means
options: Electronic Flight Instrument Switching
Electronic Flight Display System
Electrical Flight Director System
cards.explain: EFIS stands for Electronic Flight Display System.

cards.question: In a system built around air data inertial reference units, the air data modules
options: convert the total air temperature instead of air data computers
convert the pitot and static pressure instead of air data computers
amplify the air data computer output for the indicators
cards.explain: The pressure conversion that an air data computer used to do is done by the air data modules.

cards.question: ADIRU is short for
options: air data inertial reference unit
airspeed and altitude data reference unit
air data integrated reference unit
cards.explain: ADIRU is the name of the combined air data and inertial reference box.

cards.question: ADM means
options: Altitude Data Module
Air Data Module
Air Data Monitor
cards.explain: ADM stands for Air Data Module.

cards.question: An aircraft has a glass cockpit. Where does the crew read airspeed, altitude and vertical speed?
options: On the display management computer
On the primary flight display
On the navigation display
cards.explain: The PFD carries most of the air data, including airspeed, altitude and vertical speed.

cards.question: Which equipment must an aircraft have before a glass cockpit can be installed in place of its indicators
options: Analogue air data computers
An air data module at every port
Digital air data computers
cards.explain: A glass cockpit replacing the indicators is possible in aircraft fitted with digital air data computers.

cards.question: On many aircraft the baro select knob can be pulled or pushed. What does this do?
options: It changes the altitude display to metric
It sets the field elevation as the altitude reference
It sets standard baro correction immediately
cards.explain: Pulling or pushing the knob is a shortcut to the standard setting.

cards.question: An air data module is opened up for inspection. What sort of pressure transducer is found inside?
options: the same type as are used in the digital air data computer
a simpler analogue type than those used in the digital air data computer
aneroid capsules of a type not used in the digital air data computer
cards.explain: The transducer itself is unchanged; only its location and the form of its output have moved.

cards.question: Why can the air data computer be integrated with the inertial reference unit
options: the computer consists of the digital parts only and so requires little space
the inertial reference unit no longer needs its own accelerometers
the air data is now computed by the display management computers
cards.explain: Once the pressure sensing has moved out to the modules, the computer is small enough to share a box with the IRU.

cards.question: Air data modules are located near the static port or pitot probe and there they
options: convert the air pressure into a proportional analogue voltage
convert the air pressure directly into a digital data word
amplify the air pressure for transmission along the tubes
cards.explain: Conversion to a digital data word happens at the module, right by the sensing point.

cards.question: In the latest generation of air data module, the static port or pitot probe is united with the module so that
options: there is only a short flexible hose between them
there is no tube between them
there is no electrical connector between them
cards.explain: Uniting the sensing point with the module removes the pneumatic tube altogether.

cards.question: An aircraft fitted with air data modules is lighter and cheaper to maintain than one with long pneumatic runs. Why?
options: the data is sent to the computers via a digital data bus
the modules need no electrical power supply
the pressure transducers are simpler than those in a digital air data computer
cards.explain: Wiring a data bus replaces long runs of pneumatic tubing, which is where the weight and maintenance saving comes from.

cards.question: The altitude shown on the primary flight displays disagrees with the standby instrument. Which settings should be compared?
options: The baro correction on the EFIS control panel and the BARO setting on the standby instrument
The baro correction on the EFIS control panel and the air data source selection
The BARO setting on the standby instrument and the selected altitude on the mode control panel
cards.explain: The baro correction for the primary flight displays is selected at the EFIS control panel, while the standby instrument has its own BARO rotary knob, so the two references are set separately and a disagreement points to the two settings being different.

cards.question: A student looks for the Mach number on the navigation display and cannot find it. Why not?
options: Mach number is only shown when the autopilot is engaged
Mach number is only shown above the Mach changeover altitude
True airspeed is the only air data indication on that display
cards.explain: The ND carries TAS alone; the rest of the air data, Mach included, is on the primary flight display.

cards.question: An aircraft has air data modules fitted at its probes and ports. What does its air data computing section no longer need?
options: A digital output to the display management computers
A connection to the inertial reference unit
An analogue pressure sensing section of its own
cards.explain: With the modules doing the pressure conversion the computer keeps only digital parts, which is what makes it small enough to combine with the IRU.

cards.question: An air data module at a pitot probe has converted the pressure it senses. Which path does the resulting signal then follow?
options: To the standby instruments, and from there on to an air data inertial reference unit
To the display management computers, and from there on to an air data inertial reference unit
To an air data inertial reference unit, and from there on to the user systems
cards.explain: The module feeds the ADIRU, which is the computer that produces the air data outputs for the displays and other systems.

cards.question: An aircraft uses air data modules at its probes and ports. Which equipment must still be supplied by pneumatic tubes?
options: The primary flight displays
The standby instruments
The air data inertial reference units
cards.explain: Everything else is fed by data bus; the standby instruments keep their pneumatic supply.

cards.question: An air data inertial reference unit is removed for repair. What is the consequence for the air data module associated with it?
options: The module loses its power supply
The module continues to work on its own internal battery
The module is powered instead by the display management computer
cards.explain: Because the module takes its power from the related ADIRU, removing that unit leaves the module unpowered.

cards.question: The three tasks united in one box by a GNADIRU are those of the
options: digital air data computer, air data module and GPS receiver
inertial reference unit, display management computer and GPS receiver
digital air data computer, inertial reference unit and GPS receiver
cards.explain: The GNADIRU is an ADIRU with a GPS receiver added.

cards.question: The main signal generators of the inertial reference section are
options: the ring laser gyro and the acceleration sensors
the ring laser gyro and the pressure transducers
the acceleration sensors and the GPS antenna
cards.explain: Gyro and accelerometers together generate the inertial signals.

cards.question: The data supplied by the air data components of a GNADIRU comprises
options: attitude, heading, vertical acceleration and body rates
airspeed, Mach, angle of attack, temperature and barometric altitude
present position, satellite status and receiver clock error
cards.explain: These are the air data outputs; attitude and position come from the other two sections.

cards.question: The data supplied by the inertial reference component of a GNADIRU comprises
options: attitude, flight path vector, speed above ground and position
total pressure and static pressure converted at the probes
present position and other parameters from the satellites
cards.explain: These are the inertial outputs of the unit.

cards.question: The advantage of the ring laser gyro over an older mechanical gyroscope is that
options: it has no moving parts at all
it needs no electrical power supply
it needs no alignment before flight
cards.explain: The absence of moving parts is what makes it robust and light.

cards.question: The GPS receiver inside a GNADIRU calculates present position and transmits it
options: to the air data modules on data buses
to the flight manager system on data buses
to the standby instruments on discrete lines
cards.explain: The GPS output is passed on digitally to the flight manager system.

cards.question: How do the first laser gyros differ from the latest ones
options: The first had moving parts, the latest are based on glass fibre technology
The first were based on glass fibre technology, the latest are equipped with prisms
The first were equipped with prisms, the latest are based on glass fibre technology
cards.explain: The first laser gyros used prisms and the latest ones use glass fibre technology.

cards.question: How does the air data section of a GNADIRU work
options: It operates like an analogue air data computer
It operates like a digital air data computer
It operates like an air data module
cards.explain: The air data components of the GNADIRU operate like a DADC, a digital air data computer.

cards.question: The digital air data computer triggers the overspeed warning discrete
options: as soon as the aircraft climbs above the VMO to MMO changeover altitude
as soon as the indicated airspeed exceeds VMO or MMO by a set margin
as soon as the indicated airspeed is as big as VMO or MMO
cards.explain: The discrete is produced on reaching the limit, with no extra margin.

cards.question: The form taken by the overspeed warning in the cockpit is
options: a red flag appearing in the airspeed indicator
a red light or message with an aural warning sound
an amber caution message with no aural sound
cards.explain: Overspeed is a warning level alert: red visual plus an aural sound.

cards.question: The value the ISIS indicator displays as standard rather than as an option is
options: The Mach number
The metric altitude
The barometric correction in inches of mercury
cards.explain: Mach number is in the standard ISIS display, while metric altitude and the barometric correction in inches of mercury are the optional displays.

cards.question: A GNADIRU is fitted but the aircraft has no air data computer as a separate box. How does the unit obtain its pressures?
options: From air data modules placed as near as possible to the pitot and static sensors
From pneumatic tubes run from the probes to the unit in the avionics bay
From the inertial reference section, which derives them from acceleration
cards.explain: The air data section works like a digital air data computer but is fed digitally by modules mounted close to the probes and ports.

cards.question: The antenna connection to the GPS part of a GNADIRU is broken. Which function of the box is lost, and which data stops reaching the flight management system?
options: The inertial reference function, and the present position it calculates
The GPS receiver function, and the barometric altitude it calculates
The GPS receiver function, and the present position it calculates
cards.explain: The GPS receiver needs the antenna to receive the satellite signals, so without it the present position it calculates and sends to the flight management system is lost.

cards.question: The high speed limit marking on a jet aircraft airspeed display moves as the aircraft climbs. What accounts for this?
options: The indicator processor moves the marking by a fixed amount for each altitude band
The digital air data computer sends an overspeed limit that varies with altitude
The marking is driven by the selected airspeed from the autopilot mode control panel
cards.explain: The limit itself is computed in the air data computer and changes with altitude, and the indicator simply displays the value it is sent.

cards.question: A digital air data computer fails completely. What is lost in addition to its air data indications?
options: Nothing, because the warning system calculates the overspeed limit itself
Only the maximum allowable airspeed pointer, because the warning comes from the indicator
The overspeed warning, because the limit and the warning discrete come from that computer
cards.explain: Both the limit and the discrete that triggers the warning originate in the air data computer.

cards.question: An integrated standby instrument system fails completely. Which standby indications are lost?
options: Standby altitude, standby airspeed and standby vertical speed
Standby altitude, standby attitude and standby heading
Standby altitude, standby attitude and standby airspeed
cards.explain: One unit does the work of the three separate standby instruments, so all three indications go together.

cards.question: Altitude, airspeed and attitude all disappear from an ISIS indicator although its pressure sensors and gyrometers are serviceable. Which module is suspect?
options: The pressure module
The inertial module
The computation module
cards.explain: All three parameters are worked out, and the picture generated, in the computation module, so a single fault there takes out everything at once.

cards.question: The static line to an ISIS indicator becomes blocked. Which indications are affected?
options: Attitude is affected, while altitude and airspeed continue from the computation module
Altitude and airspeed are affected, while attitude continues from the inertial module
All indications are lost, because every parameter is derived from the pressure module
cards.explain: Attitude comes from the gyrometers and accelerometers of the inertial module, so it is independent of the pressure supply.

cards.question: A technician has to set a QNH on an ISIS indicator. Which control is used, and in what unit is the reference shown as standard?
options: The LS pushbutton switch, with the reference pressure shown in hectopascals
The BARO rotary knob, with the reference pressure shown in hectopascals
The BARO rotary knob, with the reference pressure shown in inches of mercury
cards.explain: The rotary knob sets the pressure and the standard display of the reference is in hectopascals, inches of mercury being an option.

cards.question: The magnetic heading indication on an ISIS indicator is missing while its attitude, altitude and airspeed are normal. Which input is suspect?
options: The digital input from the ILS or multi mode receiver
The digital input from the inertial reference
The discrete input from the attitude and heading selector switch
cards.explain: Heading is the only thing that digital input provides, and the parameters the unit computes for itself are unaffected.

cards.question: The LS function cannot be engaged on an ISIS indicator although the pushbutton switch is serviceable. Which input should be checked?
options: The digital output to the central maintenance system
The digital input from the ILS or multi mode receiver
The digital input from the inertial reference
cards.explain: The LS display depends on the digital input from the ILS or multi mode receiver.

cards.question: All digital inputs to the ISIS indicator are lost. Which indications can the unit still produce?
options: Attitude, altitude and airspeed, from its own inertial and pressure modules
Only altitude, because the pressure module is the only module left working
None, because every displayed parameter arrives as a digital input
cards.explain: The ISIS contains its own pressure module, inertial module and computation module, so the attitude, altitude and airspeed it works out for itself do not depend on the digital inputs.

cards.question: Air data modules digitise the pressures everywhere else on the aircraft, yet the ISIS indicator still has pneumatic connectors. Why?
options: Because the ISIS pressure module needs a reference for its gyrometers
Because the standby instruments still have to be supplied by tubes
Because the air data modules cannot work with total pressure
cards.explain: The ISIS indicator receives pitot pressure and static pressure, because only the standby instruments still have to be supplied by tubes.

cards.question: The angle that an angle of attack sensing system determines is
options: the angle between the air stream and the wing chord
the angle between the air stream and the vertical axis of the aircraft
the angle between the wing chord and the horizontal
cards.explain: Angle of attack is measured between the oncoming air stream and the wing chord.

cards.question: The lift generated by a wing depends mainly on
options: the airspeed, the air temperature and the angle of attack
the wing geometry, the altitude and the angle of attack
the wing geometry, the airspeed and the angle of attack
cards.explain: Those three are the main factors given for lift.

cards.question: Alpha max is the angle of attack at which
options: the slats and flaps must be extended to keep the lift constant
the airflow cannot follow the upper surface and separation occurs
the greatest airspeed is obtained for a given wing geometry
cards.explain: Alpha max marks the onset of airflow separation.

cards.question: The angle between the air stream and the wing chord is
options: The angle of incidence
The dihedral angle
The angle of attack
cards.explain: The angle between the air stream and the wing chord is called the angle of attack.

cards.question: The condition present at the beginning of the loss of airflow is
options: Minimum manoeuvre speed
Initial buffet
Stall speed
cards.explain: The beginning of the loss of airflow is the initial buffet, also called low speed buffet.

cards.question: The name given to the digital stall warning system is
options: Stall warning controller system
Stall warning management computer system
Stall warning monitor card system
cards.explain: The extended digital system is called the stall warning management computer system.

cards.question: The three parts that make up the SWMCS are
options: Stall warning management computer, master monitor card and stick shaker
Master monitor card, angle of attack sensor and stick shaker
Stall warning management computer, flap position transmitter and stick shaker
cards.explain: Those three items make up the SWMCS.

cards.question: The relationship between angle of attack and the lift acting on the wings is that
options: the greater the angle of attack, the smaller the lift
the greater the angle of attack, the greater the lift
the lift is independent of the angle of attack
cards.explain: Lift rises with angle of attack, up to the individual maximum for the profile.

cards.question: If the individual maximum angle of attack of a wing profile is exceeded
options: the airflow over the surface breaks down
the lift continues to increase steadily
the angle between the air stream and the wing chord becomes zero
cards.explain: Beyond that value the flow separates from the surface.

cards.question: A lift transducer determines the angle of attack by
options: sensing the angle of the air stream with a vane on the side of the fuselage
sensing changes in direction and intensity of the stagnation point below the forward wing surface
comparing the pressures at two rows of holes in a tube lying crosswise to the air stream
cards.explain: The lift transducer works off the movement of the stagnation point; the other two describe the vane and the airstream tube.

cards.question: An angle of attack sensor is a tube lying crosswise to the air stream, pierced by two rows of holes. How does it sense the angle?
options: by sensing the movement of the stagnation point between the rows
by measuring the total pressure at the forward row
by comparing the pressures at the two rows
cards.explain: The tube senses the angle as a pressure difference between its two rows of holes.

cards.question: The wind vane type of angle of attack sensor is made force-free by
options: a spring, so that it returns to the neutral position on the ground
counterweights, so that it is articulated and free to take any position
a damper, so that it is held still while the aircraft is on the ground
cards.explain: Counterweights balance the vane so nothing but the airflow moves it.

cards.question: An aeroplane must hold its lift while the airspeed is reduced. What are the two ways of doing it?
options: increase the angle of attack or change the wing geometry by extending slats and flaps
decrease the angle of attack or change the wing geometry by retracting slats and flaps
increase the angle of attack or retract the slats and flaps
cards.explain: Either a larger angle of attack or more wing camber and area makes up for the lost airspeed.

cards.question: An angle of attack indication shows the pilot
options: the margin remaining up to alpha max
the maximum angle of attack permitted for the wing
the actual angle of attack measured by the alpha vane
cards.explain: The indication is of the actual measured angle.

cards.question: A pilot pulls the stick back past the critical angle and the aircraft loses lift. What is the cause?
options: An increase of air density over the wing
Loss of airflow over the upper surface of the wing
Loss of airflow under the lower surface of the wing
cards.explain: Lift is lost because the airflow over the upper wing surface breaks down.

cards.question: An aeroplane gives no noticeable initial buffet as its speed decays towards the point of lift loss. What must be installed?
options: An angle of attack indicator
A stall warning system
An altitude alert system
cards.explain: A stall warning system must be installed when the approaching stall speed is not immediately noticeable through initial buffet.

cards.question: A stall warning system is fitted to an aeroplane. What does it do
options: It reduces the angle of attack automatically at the stall
It alerts the crew to the hazardous situation of a stall
It prevents the control column from being pulled back at the stall
cards.explain: The system alerts; it does not act on the controls.

cards.question: Where are errors in the SWMCS reported
options: To the CMC and the FCUs
To EICAS and the CMC
To EICAS and the GPWC
cards.explain: Fault reporting goes to EICAS and to the central maintenance computer.

cards.question: A technician wants to check the SWMCS with the CMC. When can this be done?
options: On the ground only
On the ground and in the air
In the air only
cards.explain: The CMC check is available in both phases.

cards.question: The speed that the SWMCS calculates as the stick shaker speed is
options: VBFLO, displayed as minimum operating speed
VBFLO, displayed as minimum manoeuvre speed
VMO, displayed as maximum operating speed
cards.explain: VBFLO is the stick shaker speed and is shown as the minimum operating speed.

cards.question: The users of the pitch limit calculated by the SWMCS are
options: EICAS and the FCUs
The CMC and the IRS
EICAS and the GPWC
cards.explain: The pitch limit is calculated for EICAS and the ground proximity warning computer.

cards.question: The maximum angle of attack used by the SWMC
options: is a variable value
is a fixed value set at build
is selected by the crew before each flight
cards.explain: The maximum angle of attack is a variable value rather than a fixed one.

cards.question: Where does the SWMC get the flap position it needs to calculate the maximum angle of attack
options: From the FCUs
From the ADC
From the IRS
cards.explain: Flap position for the maximum angle of attack calculation comes from the flap control units.

cards.question: The unit that corrects the calculated pitch limit signal is
options: The IRS
The GPWC
The ADC
cards.explain: Pitch limit correction is an IRS function.

cards.question: Why is the stall warning management computer system switched off below 40 kts
options: Because the aircraft is then on the ground
Because the flap position is then not available from the FCUs
Because the stick shaker motors are then unpowered
cards.explain: Below that speed the aircraft is on the ground, which is why the system is switched off.

cards.question: An aeroplane slows down in level flight with the slats and flaps left retracted. What happens to the angle of attack indication?
options: It increases, and approaches alpha max as the speed falls
It stays constant, because the lift in level flight does not change
It decreases, because less lift is being produced at the lower speed
cards.explain: With the wing geometry unchanged, holding the lift at a lower airspeed demands a larger angle of attack, which moves the indication toward alpha max.

cards.question: A crew extends the slats and flaps while holding the same airspeed. Why does this help keep the angle of attack away from alpha max?
options: The alpha vane is biased by the slat position, so it reads a lower angle
The wing geometry is changed, so the lift is produced at a smaller angle of attack
The airspeed sensed by the wing is increased, so less lift has to be generated
cards.explain: Changing the wing geometry is the alternative to increasing the angle of attack for the same lift.

cards.question: In flight the maximum possible angle of attack for the flap position in use is exceeded. What happens?
options: The flaps extend automatically
A motor shakes the control column
An amber lamp illuminates and a chime sounds
cards.explain: Exceeding the flap dependent maximum angle drives the stick shaker motor.

cards.question: An aeroplane is on stand with the APU supplying the busses and ground power also connected. What is the state of the wind vane heating?
options: It does not start
It starts only when external power is selected
It starts as soon as the APU generator comes on line
cards.explain: Heating needs engine generator power, so with APU or external power it stays off.

cards.question: A technician holds the module switch at TEST and sees the warning lamp go off. What does this prove?
options: The heating has been deactivated
The shaker motor is unserviceable
Voltage and heating power are present
cards.explain: The lamp going off in TEST is the indication that voltage and heating power are there.

cards.question: What does the HTR OFF position do to the system
options: It simulates FLIGHT status with the heating still energised
It simulates FLIGHT status with the heating deactivated
It isolates the system from the AC and the DC supply
cards.explain: HTR OFF simulates FLIGHT status for normal operation but removes the heating.

cards.question: With the module in HTR OFF, how are the response values for flap position in the Operation Manual checked?
options: By moving the flap lever through each detent until the shaker motor vibrates
By turning the wind vane until the shaker motor vibrates
By applying 20 V DC to the shaker test button on the back of the module
cards.explain: The wind vane is turned and the shaker motor must vibrate at the published response values.

cards.question: The motor does not shake in TEST or HTR OFF mode. How can the shaker motor be checked directly?
options: By pressing the shaker test button on the front panel and applying 28 V DC
By pressing the shaker test button on the back of the module and applying 20 V DC
By pressing the TEST switch and applying 115 V AC
cards.explain: The direct shaker check uses the button on the back of the module with 20 V DC applied.

cards.question: An aeroplane is taxiing at 30 kts with the pitch attitude unchanged. What is the state of the SWMCS?
options: Switched off
Active and able to drive the shaker
Active but with the shaker inhibited
cards.explain: At less than 40 kts the system is off, which is the normal ground case.

cards.question: The maximum angle of attack is exceeded in flight. What is the response of the digital system?
options: Only one stick shaker motor responds
The stick shaker is inhibited until the pitch limit is passed
Both stick shaker motors respond
cards.explain: The digital system shakes both columns when the maximum angle of attack is exceeded.

cards.question: The ADC fails and its M and CAS signals are lost. Which SWMC calculation loses its correction?
options: The correction of the calculated pitch limit
The correction of the maximum angle of attack
The calculation of flap position
cards.explain: M and CAS from the ADC correct the maximum angle of attack; the pitch limit is corrected by the IRS instead.

cards.question: An aeroplane is on its take-off roll at 50 kts with the pitch attitude unchanged. Is the stall warning management computer system active?
options: Yes, it is active from the start of the take-off roll until touchdown
Yes, it is active above 40 kts whatever the pitch angle of the aircraft
No, it is active only above 140 kts or above 5 deg of pitch angle
cards.explain: The system becomes active above 140 kts or above 5 deg of pitch angle and is switched off below 40 kts; at 50 kts with the pitch unchanged neither activation condition is met, so it is not yet active.

cards.question: Which air data quantities does the selected ADC pass to the stall warning management computer?
options: Flap position, speedbrake lever position and Mach
AOA, pitch angle, pitch rate and normal acceleration
AOA, TAS, CAS, Mach and VMO/MMO
cards.explain: The selected air data computer supplies those air data values; the pitch and acceleration terms come from the IRS.

cards.question: In flight the pitch angle becomes greater than the calculated pitch limit. What does this mean?
options: The minimum operating speed has been recalculated
There is the danger of a stall condition
The aircraft has exceeded the maximum operating speed
cards.explain: Passing the calculated pitch limit is the warning of a stall danger.

cards.question: On the airspeed tape, where does the minimum operating speed lie in relation to the minimum manoeuvre speed?
options: Above it
At the same point, as the two marks coincide
Below it
cards.explain: The tape shows the minimum operating speed lower down than the minimum manoeuvre speed.

questions.question: Where is the altitude alert system usually integrated
options: In the autoflight or central warning system
In the ATC transponder system
In the air data computer system
questions.explain: It normally sits inside the autoflight or central warning system, though a dedicated computer also exists.

questions.question: The indications given shortly before the desired height is reached are
options: A red lamp and a continuous horn
An amber lamp and a short sound
A white box and a steady chime
questions.explain: The approach information is an amber lamp with a short sound.

questions.question: The altitude alert lamp is flashing and a short continuous sound is heard. Which mode is active?
options: The deviation mode
The approach mode
The capture mode
questions.explain: A flashing lamp distinguishes deviation from approach, where the lamp is steady.

questions.question: The conditions for the reset mode of the digital altitude alert system are
options: Deviation greater than 900 ft and approach greater than 900 ft
Deviation greater than 900 ft and approach less than 300 ft
Deviation greater than 300 ft and approach less than 900 ft
questions.explain: Reset applies for a deviation beyond 900 ft and for an approach closer than 300 ft.

questions.question: The crew changes ALT SEL on the control panel during the cruise. What is the effect on the altitude alert system?
options: The system gives an approach warning
The system goes into deviation mode
The system is inoperative
questions.explain: Changing the selected altitude makes the system inoperative rather than producing a warning.

questions.question: The secondary function of the clock is
options: To give a display of date and year
To supply a time reference to the flight management computers
To give a display of elapsed time or chronograph time
questions.explain: Elapsed and chronograph time are the secondary function.

questions.question: A trainee reads HUMS in a helicopter wiring diagram and asks what kind of system it is. What is the answer?
options: It is one of the names used for the monitoring system
It is one of the names used for the voice recorder system
It is one of the names used for the maintenance system
questions.explain: HUMS is listed as one of the manufacturers' names for the monitoring system.

questions.question: Engineering wants an engine left on the wing as long as it is sound, yet changed at the home base before it causes trouble. Which installed system makes that possible?
options: The flight data recording system, which records for the investigators
The monitoring system, which records data from various systems
The on board maintenance system, which stores reported faults
questions.explain: Only the monitoring system records condition data that lets a part be used to its limit and still be changed at base.

questions.question: At which point does the flight data recorder start recording automatically
options: when an engine is started, or at the latest when the aircraft is in the air
when the parking brake is released, or at the latest when an engine is started
when the aircraft is in the air, or at the latest when the gear is retracted
questions.explain: Engine start is the trigger, and being airborne is the latest point at which recording must have begun.

questions.question: From where does the acquisition unit receive its date and leg information
options: the flight management computer
the data management unit
the on board maintenance computer
questions.explain: Date and flight leg come to the acquisition unit from the flight management computer.

questions.question: A recorder is set to begin taking data the moment the aircraft starts to taxi under its own power. Which requirement does that miss?
options: It must record from engine start until the brake is set
It must record only once the aircraft has left the ground
It must record from before the aircraft moves independently
questions.explain: The requirement reaches back to before the aircraft moves on its own, so recording cannot start at taxi.

questions.question: A line station is able to fix the recorder where the aircraft stands but wants to dispatch under the eight flight allowance. Is that allowed?
options: No, that allowance needs repair on the spot to be impossible
Yes, that allowance holds whenever the recorder is defective
Yes, that allowance holds for 72 hours from the failure
questions.explain: The first condition is that repair or replacement cannot be done where the aircraft is.

questions.question: The beacon battery is due for replacement. What has to be done to the recorder first?
options: The recorder memory must be downloaded before the beacon is opened
The recorder must be removed so the beacon can be taken off its panel
Nothing, the beacon can be serviced without disassembly of the recorder
questions.explain: The beacon is serviceable in place, with no need to take the recorder apart.

questions.question: Why do some aviation authorities require a quick access recorder at all, when the flight data recorder holds the same data?
options: Because the copy of flight data then holds more parameters
Because the copy of flight data then survives a crash better
Because the copy of flight data then stays easily accessible
questions.explain: Easy access to the copy is the stated reason for the requirement.

questions.question: On aircraft of which weight is a single unit holding both the flight recorder and the cockpit voice recorder permitted
options: above 5700 kg
above 27,000 kg
below 5700 kg
questions.explain: The combined unit is allowed below the 5700 kg mark.

questions.question: The combined recorder has been running for eleven hours. What has become of its earliest hour of flight data?
options: It has been kept, because recording stops once the memory is full
It has been transferred into the voice section of the memory
It has been overwritten, because the oldest recording goes first
questions.explain: Once the holding time is full the oldest data is overwritten.

questions.question: Why is the helicopter recorder put in the aft compartments or the tailboom rather than further forward?
options: Because those areas are less damaged in case of a crash
Because those areas are easier to reach for a battery change
Because those areas are further from the electrical interference
questions.explain: Crash damage is lower there, which is why the recorder is placed aft.
