questions.question: A recorder is lying on the sea bed after a ditching and nobody has touched it. What has set its beacon transmitting?
options: The loss of aircraft electrical supply to the recorder
The impact sensed by the inertia sensor of the recorder
Its battery coming in contact with water
questions.explain: Water reaching the battery starts the transmission automatically.

questions.question: Which three areas does the aircraft integrated data system monitor and analyse continuously
options: engine data, voice data and flight data
engine data, aircraft data and APU data
engine data, aircraft data and gearbox data
questions.explain: The three listed are engine, aircraft and APU data.

questions.question: What does APM stand for in the aircraft condition monitoring system
options: auxiliary power monitoring
aircraft parameter monitoring
aircraft performance monitoring
questions.explain: APM is aircraft performance monitoring.

questions.question: Which unit manages the monitoring and analysis tasks in the ACMS
options: the data management unit
the centralised data acquisition module
the flight data interface unit
questions.explain: The DMU manages those tasks.

questions.question: When is the recorded data of the wireless quick access recorder compressed, encrypted and transmitted
options: while the aircraft is being powered down
while the aircraft is on the ground
while the aircraft is in the cruise
questions.explain: The transfer takes place with the aircraft on the ground.

questions.question: The monitoring system is to be modified by loading from disks. Which of its interfaces is used?
options: MCDU
ADL
ACARS
questions.explain: Modification by disk goes through the airborne data loader.

questions.question: A quick access recorder is coming to the end of its writing time. What must be done?
options: The recording medium must be changed before the 50 hours have elapsed
The recording medium must be downloaded before the 25 hours have elapsed
The recording medium must be erased before the 50 hours have elapsed
questions.explain: There is no erase button, so the recording medium has to be replaced inside the 50 hours.

questions.question: Gross weight is recorded and set against the recorded flight envelope. What is that comparison looking for?
options: Possible excess of the safe life limit of a component
Possible overstress to components and structural limits
Possible loss of vital fluid from a pressurised system
questions.explain: The comparison is made to find overstress of components and structural limits.

questions.question: On which three bases do the gyroscopes used in aviation today work
options: a mechanical basis, a pneumatic basis and a magnetic basis
an optical basis, a thermal basis and an oscillation basis
a mechanical basis, an optical basis and an oscillation basis
questions.explain: The three families named are mechanical, optical and oscillation gyroscopes.

questions.question: For which three flight instruments are the properties of a gyroscope used
options: the directional gyro, the altimeter and the turn-and-bank indicator
the artificial horizon, the airspeed indicator and the vertical speed indicator
the artificial horizon, the directional gyro and the turn-and-bank indicator
questions.explain: Those three instruments are the ones named as built on gyroscopic properties.

questions.question: A fully gimballed vertical gyro stands at the equator and an observer watches it for a full day. Through how much does it appear to topple?
options: 360° in 24 hours
180° in 24 hours
360° in 12 hours
questions.explain: At the equator the gyroscope appears to topple 360° in 24 hours.

questions.question: An exterior force has been applied to the axis of a running gyro and is held there. When does the gyro stop precessing?
options: when its sense of rotation corresponds to the rotational direction acting upon it
when the inertia of its rotating mass has fully absorbed the applied force
when its axis has turned through a right angle from the direction it started in
questions.explain: The gyro precesses until its sense of rotation corresponds to the rotational direction acting upon it.

questions.question: A gyroscope frame is constrained by means of springs. What is the freedom of that whole gyro system?
options: 1 degree of freedom
1 1/2 degrees of freedom
2 1/2 degrees of freedom
questions.explain: A spring constrained frame counts as a half degree, so the gyro system has 1 1/2 degrees of freedom.

questions.question: An aircraft rolls and pitches into a completely new attitude. What has happened to the axis of its space stable gyro?
options: it has followed the aircraft into the new attitude
it has precessed through a right angle to the new attitude
it still points to the same direction
questions.explain: When the aircraft changes attitude the gyro axis still points in the same direction.

questions.question: A free gyroscope is left standing at the equator. Which of the two apparent errors is at its greatest there?
options: transport wander
apparent topple
apparent drift
questions.explain: Apparent topple is greatest at the equator.

questions.question: A fully gimballed directional gyro is over the North Pole and an observer turning with the earth watches it for a day. Through how much does it appear to rotate?
options: 360° in 24 hours
360° in 12 hours
180° in 24 hours
questions.explain: At the pole the gyroscope appears to rotate 360° in 24 hours.

questions.question: An optical gyroscope is being explained to a trainee. According to which optical principle does it work?
options: the Doppler effect
the Sagnac effect
the swirl effect
questions.explain: Optical gyroscopes work according to the optical principle known as the Sagnac effect.

questions.question: Two gyros stand at the North Pole, one with its axis upright and one with its axis lying along the ground. Which apparent error is at its maximum there?
options: topple, for the gyro whose axis stands vertical to it
drift, for the gyro whose axis is parallel to the surface
neither, both of those errors fall to zero at the pole
questions.explain: Drift is greatest at the poles and belongs to the gyro with its axis parallel to the surface, while topple is zero there.

questions.question: A gyroscope is found with its two frames lined up with each other. What can still be done with it?
options: it can be used once its frames are re-sprung
nothing, an instrument in that state is unusable
it can be used for drift but not for topple
questions.explain: Gimbal lock, where the two frames are aligned, makes the gyroscope unusable.

questions.question: An erection system is fitted to a directional gyro. In which direction does it hold that gyro's axis?
options: horizontal
vertical
along the aircraft centre line
questions.explain: The erection keeps the axis horizontal for the directional gyro and vertical for the vertical gyro.

questions.question: Coherent light has been made to interfere inside the optical circuit of a gyro. What can then be measured?
options: the direction of the earth's gravity vector
the temperature of the resonance cavity
the speed of rotation, that is the arc velocity
questions.explain: Because coherent light can interfere, speed of rotation, that is arc velocity, can be measured with the structure of the optical circuit.

questions.question: By which three means can laser rays be produced
options: by gas, solid state or semi-conductor lasers
by gas, liquid or semi-conductor lasers
by solid state, liquid or crystal lasers
questions.explain: Laser rays can be produced by gas, solid state or semi-conductor lasers.

questions.question: The fibre optic gyro reference system is expected to give general aviation an inexpensive and precise position and navigation system when it is combined with
options: an air data computer
GPS
a ring laser gyro
questions.explain: Together with GPS the fibre optic gyro reference system is intended to offer that system for general aviation.

cards.question: The two warning conditions of the altitude alert system are
options: Deviation warning and reset warning
Approach warning and capture warning
Approach warning and deviation warning
cards.explain: The analogue system distinguishes an approach and a deviation warning.

cards.question: The altitude difference that activates the approach mode is
options: 900 ft
300 ft
cards.explain: The approach mode is triggered at an altitude difference of 900 ft.

cards.question: The modes of the digital altitude alert system are
options: Approach, deviation, capture and warning
Approach, deviation, alert and reset
Approach, deviation, capture and reset
cards.explain: Four modes are listed: approach, deviation, capture and reset.

cards.question: In the digital altitude alert system a deviation warning is given when
options: the aircraft deviates 1000 ft from the selected altitude
the aircraft deviates 900 ft from the selected altitude
the aircraft deviates 300 ft from the selected altitude
cards.explain: The deviation mode works on a deviation of 300 ft from the selected altitude.

cards.question: Where is the altitude alert system usually integrated
options: In the air data computer system
In the autoflight or central warning system
In the ATC transponder system
cards.explain: It normally sits inside the autoflight or central warning system, though a dedicated computer also exists.

cards.question: The indications given shortly before the desired height is reached are
options: A white box and a steady chime
An amber lamp and a short sound
A red lamp and a continuous horn
cards.explain: The approach information is an amber lamp with a short sound.

cards.question: The indications given in the approach mode are
options: A repeated chime and a continuously illuminated lamp
A short continuous sound and a flashing lamp
A short continuous sound and a continuously illuminated lamp
cards.explain: In approach mode the lamp is steady, not flashing.

cards.question: An aircraft is climbing towards its preset altitude in the approach mode. When does the altitude alert end?
options: When the preset altitude is reached exactly
When the preset altitude is 900 ft away
When the preset altitude is 300 ft away
cards.explain: The approach alert stops 300 ft short of the preset altitude.

cards.question: The altitude alert lamp is flashing and a short continuous sound is heard. Which mode is active?
options: The approach mode
The deviation mode
The capture mode
cards.explain: A flashing lamp distinguishes deviation from approach, where the lamp is steady.

cards.question: The landing gear is selected down. What is the state of the altitude alert system?
options: Inoperative
In the approach mode
In the deviation mode
cards.explain: A gear down condition is one of the INOP conditions of the altitude alert system.

cards.question: The altitude is not in the alert range. Which mode is the digital altitude alert system in?
options: Approach
Capture
Reset
cards.explain: Capture is the mode for the altitude not being in the alert range.

cards.question: Where is the altitude alert computer located
options: In the master monitor card
In the air data computer
In the crew alerting card
cards.explain: The function lives on the crew alerting card.

cards.question: The signals the altitude alert system receives from the AP/FD mode control panel are
options: Glideslope capture, parking brake status and selected ADC
Selected altitude, baro corrected altitude and FCC communication
Selected altitude, glideslope capture and FCC communication
cards.explain: Those three signals are the mode control panel inputs.

cards.question: The information the altitude alert system takes from the parking brake system is
options: That the parking brake is set
That the parking brake accumulator is charged
That the parking brake is not set
cards.explain: The input is the parking brake not set condition.

cards.question: The digital altitude alert system enters the approach mode. What does the crew see on the PFD?
options: A flashing amber lamp beside the selected altitude
A white box around the current altitude
A white box around the selected altitude
cards.explain: Approach mode draws a white box around the selected altitude.

cards.question: The conditions for the reset mode of the digital altitude alert system are
options: Deviation greater than 300 ft and approach less than 900 ft
Deviation greater than 900 ft and approach greater than 900 ft
Deviation greater than 900 ft and approach less than 300 ft
cards.explain: Reset applies for a deviation beyond 900 ft and for an approach closer than 300 ft.

cards.question: A ground radar paints an aircraft. What can air traffic control establish from the radar alone?
options: The direction and the distance of an aircraft
The altitude and the distance of an aircraft
The direction and the altitude of an aircraft
cards.explain: Radar alone gives direction and distance, not altitude.

cards.question: Why is an ATC transponder installed in the aircraft
options: Because for normal civil air surveillance the altitude cannot be found out directly
Because the ground station cannot determine the direction of the aircraft
Because radar cannot find out the distance of the aircraft directly
cards.explain: The transponder exists because altitude is the quantity surveillance radar cannot get directly.

cards.question: The sources from which the ATC transponder receives altitude information are
options: An encoding altimeter or a radio altimeter
An encoding altimeter or an air data computer
An air data computer or the altitude alert computer
cards.explain: Either an encoding altimeter or an air data computer supplies the transponder.

cards.question: After a deviation warning the aircraft goes on drifting away from the original altitude. At what point does the alert end?
options: When the aircraft reaches the altitude selected on the control panel
When the aircraft is more than 900 ft from the original altitude
When the aircraft is more than 300 ft from the original altitude
cards.explain: The deviation alert ends either on regaining the altitude or on passing 900 ft away from it.

cards.question: Why is the altitude alert system deactivated by flap or landing gear extension on approach
options: Because the altitude will then be constantly changing
Because the ATC transponder takes over the altitude reporting
Because the flap and gear signals interfere with the alert computer
cards.explain: A continuously changing altitude on approach would otherwise give constant alerts.

cards.question: The crew changes ALT SEL on the control panel during the cruise. What is the effect on the altitude alert system?
options: The system gives an approach warning
The system goes into deviation mode
The system is inoperative
cards.explain: Changing the selected altitude makes the system inoperative rather than producing a warning.

cards.question: An aircraft is 1200 ft above its selected altitude. What indication does the altitude alert system give?
options: Approach warning
No warning
Deviation warning
cards.explain: Beyond 900 ft either side of the selected altitude the profile shows no warning.

cards.question: An aircraft is climbing towards its selected altitude and passes 700 ft below it. Which warning is given?
options: No warning
Deviation warning
Approach warning
cards.explain: Closing on the selected altitude inside the 300 to 900 ft band gives the approach warning.

cards.question: An aircraft established at the selected altitude drifts down until it is 500 ft below it. Which warning is given?
options: No warning
Approach warning
Deviation warning
cards.explain: Leaving the selected altitude into the 300 to 900 ft band gives the deviation warning.

cards.question: A technician checks when the altitude alert is inhibited. Which two conditions do that?
options: The aircraft being in landing configuration, or the parking brake being set
The aircraft being in landing configuration, or knob rotation being detected
Knob rotation being detected, or the chime having already sounded
cards.explain: Either the landing configuration or a detected knob rotation inhibits the alert.

cards.question: The altitude readout box on the PFD changes from white to yellow. Which mode has the system entered?
options: Capture mode
Deviation mode
Approach mode
cards.explain: A white to yellow change of the altitude readout box marks the deviation mode.

cards.question: An altitude deviation occurs in the cruise. What does the crew get on EICAS and aurally?
options: An advisory message ALTITUDE ALERT with no aural indication
The warning message ALTITUDE ALERT with Master Warning and a bell
The caution message ALTITUDE ALERT with Master Caution and the owl tone
cards.explain: It is a caution level alert with Master Caution and an owl tone.

cards.question: Which configuration inputs does the crew alerting card use to inhibit the altitude alert?
options: Landing gear down and locked, and the parking brake set
Flaps in range, and speedbrakes stowed
Flaps in range, and landing gear down and locked
cards.explain: The crew alerting card takes flaps in range and landing gear down and locked; the parking brake comes in as a not set condition.

cards.question: A ground station transmits an interrogation to an aircraft. What does the aircraft equipment do?
options: The ATC transponder answers with a reply that contains the altitude
The ATC transponder answers with a reply that contains the distance
The encoding altimeter answers with a reply that contains the altitude
cards.explain: The transponder replies to the interrogation, and the reply carries the altitude.

cards.question: The primary function of the clock is
options: To display the elapsed time and the chronograph time
To give a time reference to other systems and display UTC
To supply the altitude alert system with a time reference
cards.explain: Time reference to other systems plus the UTC display is the stated primary function.

cards.question: The secondary function of the clock is
options: To supply a time reference to the flight management computers
To give a display of date and year
To give a display of elapsed time or chronograph time
cards.explain: Elapsed and chronograph time are the secondary function.

cards.question: Which information does the on board maintenance system store so that repairs can be sped up
options: faults reported by the computers of various aircraft systems
parameters taken from the sensors of the flight controls
voices and sounds picked up in the cockpit during flight
cards.explain: The on board maintenance system stores the faults that the system computers report to it.

cards.question: In most aircraft that carry an on board maintenance system, in which ATA chapter is that system filed
options: ATA chapter 31
ATA chapter 23
ATA chapter 45
cards.explain: Chapter 45 is the usual filing for the on board maintenance system, chapter 31 only in some aircraft.

cards.question: An operator asks whether the voice recorder and the flight data recorder may be left out of an aircraft to save weight. What is the position?
options: Only the voice recorder is mandatory, the data recorder is optional
Both systems are mandatory and must be fitted
Both systems are optional and may be left out
cards.explain: Both the cockpit voice recorder and the flight data recording system are mandatory, so neither may be left out.

cards.question: Which ATA chapter holds both the flight data recording system and the monitoring system
options: chapter 23
chapter 31
chapter 45
cards.explain: Both the flight data recording system and the monitoring system are filed in chapter 31.

cards.question: What does the engineering department use a monitoring system to find out
options: which aircraft systems reported a fault during the last flight
which parts are in a critical condition and risk a malfunction
what the crew said to each other before an accident happened
cards.explain: The monitoring system exists to show engineering which parts are close to failing.

cards.question: A trainee reads HUMS in a helicopter wiring diagram and asks what kind of system it is. What is the answer?
options: It is one of the names used for the voice recorder system
It is one of the names used for the monitoring system
It is one of the names used for the maintenance system
cards.explain: HUMS is listed as one of the manufacturers' names for the monitoring system.

cards.question: What can the flight recorder system and the monitoring system have in common when both are fitted to one aircraft type
options: They share some components
They share one cockpit area microphone
They share one crash protected memory
cards.explain: In some aircraft types the flight recorder system and the monitoring system share some components.

cards.question: Engineering wants an engine left on the wing as long as it is sound, yet changed at the home base before it causes trouble. Which installed system makes that possible?
options: The on board maintenance system, which stores reported faults
The monitoring system, which records data from various systems
The flight data recording system, which records for the investigators
cards.explain: Only the monitoring system records condition data that lets a part be used to its limit and still be changed at base.

cards.question: A part is drifting towards a critical condition while the aircraft is still away from base. How can engineering learn of it before the aircraft lands?
options: The flight data recorder plays its data back to them over the voice radio
The monitoring data can be sent to them in flight over a data transmission system
The monitoring data is held in the recorder until the aircraft reaches the home base
cards.explain: Monitoring data is not only stored, it can also be transmitted to engineering during the flight.

cards.question: Two of the four systems are fed from both sensors and system computers. Which pair is that?
options: The flight data recording system and the monitoring system
The cockpit voice recorder and the monitoring system
The on board maintenance system and the voice recorder
cards.explain: Only the flight data recording system and the monitoring system take both sensors and system computers as sources.

cards.question: At which point does the flight data recorder start recording automatically
options: when an engine is started, or at the latest when the aircraft is in the air
when the aircraft is in the air, or at the latest when the gear is retracted
when the parking brake is released, or at the latest when an engine is started
cards.explain: Engine start is the trigger, and being airborne is the latest point at which recording must have begun.

cards.question: The engines have just been switched off on the ground. How much longer does the flight data recording run?
options: 5 minutes later
25 minutes later
10 minutes later
cards.explain: The run-on time after engine shutdown is 5 minutes.

cards.question: What does the acquisition unit of a digital flight data recorder system receive
options: various data from aircraft systems and parameters from some sensors
the switching signals that come from the logic and the panel
the recorded data played back from the crash protected memory
cards.explain: Its inputs are the aircraft system data together with sensor parameters.

cards.question: With which standard does the digital flight data recorder comply
options: ARINC 573
ARINC 429
ARINC 717
cards.explain: The standard named for the DFDR is ARINC 717.

cards.question: In what does the digital flight data recorder store all aircraft information
options: removable PCMCIA memory cards
CMOS bulk erasable EEPROM devices
polyester magnetic tape cassettes
cards.explain: The storage medium of the DFDR is CMOS bulk erasable EEPROM.

cards.question: With which unit does the solid state flight recorder have a direct interface
options: the centralised data acquisition module
the flight warning computer
the flight management computer
cards.explain: Its direct interface is with the CDAM.

cards.question: In which form is the transmission data sent from the acquisition module to the recorder
options: pulse code modulation
frequency shift keying
pulse width modulation
cards.explain: The data reaches the recorder as pulse code modulation.

cards.question: What does the transmitter fitted to the flight data recorder make possible
options: Marking the beginning of each radio call
Sending the recorded parameters to the ground
Locating it under water
cards.explain: The stated purpose of the transmitter is underwater location of the recorder.

cards.question: What governs the installation of a flight data recorder in a large aeroplane
options: the relevant construction regulations such as CS-25 or FAR-25
the recording leaflet issued as JAA Leaflet No.19
the operating requirement Part - CAT CAT.GEN.MPA.195
cards.explain: Installation falls under the construction regulations, CS-25 or FAR-25 for large aeroplanes.

cards.question: With the approval of the responsible authority, greater acceptance regarding recording parameters is given to flight recorder systems installed
options: before 01.04.98
before 01.01.87
cards.explain: The relaxation covers recorder systems installed before 01.04.98.

cards.question: Which recorder is digital recording technology quickly putting in place of the conventional tape recorder
options: the digital airborne recorder
the solid state flight data recorder
the quick access recorder
cards.explain: It is the SSFDR that is replacing the tape recorder.

cards.question: From where does the acquisition unit receive its date and leg information
options: the flight management computer
the data management unit
the on board maintenance computer
cards.explain: Date and flight leg come to the acquisition unit from the flight management computer.

cards.question: Why does the acquisition unit carry a different name on some aircraft types?
options: Because the unit is then filed in another ATA chapter
Because the unit is then supplied by another manufacturer
Because the unit might have additional functions there
cards.explain: Extra functions on some types are the reason given for the different name.

cards.question: Which parameters does the accelerometer provide to the recording system
options: angular rate about all three axis
linear acceleration along all three axis
pitch and roll attitude about two axis
cards.explain: The accelerometer delivers linear acceleration in three axes.

cards.question: What follows from the digital flight data recorder being a solid state device
options: It needs no built-in test equipment
It has no moving parts
It needs no electrical power
cards.explain: Solid state construction means there are no moving parts in the recorder.

cards.question: Which unit collects the data that the digital flight data recorder holds for the last 25 hours
options: the CVR
the FDIU
the DMU
cards.explain: It is the FDIU whose collected data fills the 25 hours of recorder storage.

cards.question: What maintenance does the underwater locator beacon call for in service?
options: Replacement of its memory at set times
Replacement of its battery at set times
A functional transmission test at every flight
cards.explain: The scheduled task on the beacon is battery replacement.

cards.question: How many parameters in total can be saved by the recording system
cards.explain: A total of 1891 parameters can be saved.

cards.question: How long can each word sent to the solid state flight data recorder be
options: 8 bits long
16 bits long
12 bits long
cards.explain: Word length under ARINC 717 is 12 bits.

cards.question: An aeroplane with a take-off weight under 5700 kg is being certified. How much recording capacity does its flight data recorder need?
options: 10 hours
5 hours
25 hours
cards.explain: Below the 5700 kg take-off weight the capacity required drops to 10 hours.

cards.question: An engineer must decide how much data capacity a recorder needs for an aircraft of a given weight, seat count and certification date. Which rule governs that?
options: The recording approval given in JAA Leaflet No.19
Part - CAT CAT.GEN.MPA.195, or FAR 121.343
The construction regulation CS-25, or FAR-25
cards.explain: Capacity against weight, seats and certification date is set by the operating requirement, not the construction regulation.

cards.question: An aeroplane weighs more than 27,000 kg and was certified before 01.01.87. Which further parameters must its recorder take?
options: Each voice radio transmission, pitch attitude and roll attitude
Thrust of each engine, air temperature and angle of attack
Pitch trim, radio altitude and landing gear position
cards.explain: Those three are the extra parameters listed for the heavier aircraft certified before that date.

cards.question: An aeroplane weighs more than 27,000 kg and was certified after 01.01.87. Which parameter group is then added on top of the rest?
options: Pitch attitude, roll attitude and the start of each radio transmission
Primary flight control position, pitch trim, radio altitude and gear position
Thrust of each engine, air temperature and auto flight control mode
cards.explain: That heavier post-87 group adds the flight control positions, pitch trim, radio altitude and gear position.

cards.question: A recorder is set to begin taking data the moment the aircraft starts to taxi under its own power. Which requirement does that miss?
options: It must record only once the aircraft has left the ground
It must record from before the aircraft moves independently
It must record from engine start until the brake is set
cards.explain: The requirement reaches back to before the aircraft moves on its own, so recording cannot start at taxi.

cards.question: Why did the rising FAA parameter demands push manufacturers away from the tape recorder?
options: Tape recorders could not be protected against thermal stresses
Tape recorders were no longer accepted for aircraft above 5700 kg
Recording that many parameters would demand too much from a tape recorder
cards.explain: Recording the number of parameters the FAA came to demand would ask too much of a tape recorder, which is what accelerated the change to solid state.

cards.question: A recorder has failed and cannot be repaired or replaced where the aircraft stands. How many subsequent flights may the aircraft make?
options: No more than twelve subsequent flights
No more than four subsequent flights
No more than eight subsequent flights
cards.explain: The dispatch relief is limited to eight subsequent flights.

cards.question: A recorder failed 70 hours ago and the aircraft has flown three sectors since. What is the time limit that still has to be watched?
options: No more than 90 hours may be exceeded following the failure
No more than 72 hours may be exceeded following the failure
No more than 25 hours may be exceeded following the failure
cards.explain: The elapsed time condition on dispatch is 72 hours after the failure.

cards.question: An aircraft is to be dispatched with a defective air data recorder. What condition is placed on the cockpit voice recorder?
options: It must be operative, provided it is combined with the flight recorder
It must be operative, provided it is not combined with the flight recorder
It may be inoperative, provided the repair is done within eight flights
cards.explain: The voice recorder has to be serviceable, and that condition applies where it is a separate unit.

cards.question: A line station is able to fix the recorder where the aircraft stands but wants to dispatch under the eight flight allowance. Is that allowed?
options: Yes, that allowance holds whenever the recorder is defective
No, that allowance needs repair on the spot to be impossible
Yes, that allowance holds for 72 hours from the failure
cards.explain: The first condition is that repair or replacement cannot be done where the aircraft is.

cards.question: A helicopter is on the ground with its rotor turning at 60%. What does the recording logic do?
options: It provides the recorder with power, because rotor speed is above 50%
It provides power only once the panel switch has been used
It withholds power, because the rotor is turning on the ground
cards.explain: On helicopters the logic powers the recorder once rotor speed passes 50%.

cards.question: The aircraft is parked with its engines off and a technician needs the recorder running for a check. How can that be achieved?
options: Through the panel, whose switch overrides the logic
Through the accelerometer, which triggers the recorder on movement
Through the acquisition unit, which commands the recorder directly
cards.explain: The panel switch overrides the logic so the recorder can be powered on the ground.

cards.question: How is it confirmed that the recorder has actually written the data correctly?
options: The recorder sends the recorded data back to the acquisition unit
The panel compares the logic signal against the recorder status
The acquisition unit compares its own data against the aircraft systems
cards.explain: Correct recording is monitored by returning the recorded data to the acquisition unit.

cards.question: An operator wants more than 25 hours of flight parameters held in the recorder. What makes that possible?
options: Using the right combination of capacity and data rate
Using a second recorder in parallel with the first
Using a shorter word than twelve bits
cards.explain: Storage beyond 25 hours comes from matching recorder capacity with data rate.

cards.question: The beacon battery is due for replacement. What has to be done to the recorder first?
options: The recorder must be removed so the beacon can be taken off its panel
Nothing, the beacon can be serviced without disassembly of the recorder
The recorder memory must be downloaded before the beacon is opened
cards.explain: The beacon is serviceable in place, with no need to take the recorder apart.

cards.question: A frame is made up of four sub frames. How long does one frame take to record?
options: 1 second
16 seconds
4 seconds
cards.explain: Four sub frames of one second each give a frame time of four seconds.

cards.question: The identification data is spread out rather than held complete in one frame. How is it laid down?
options: Distributed over several frames, usually in a specified word of a sub frame
Written once at the start of recording, in the first frame only
Repeated in every sub frame, always in the first word of the frame
cards.explain: The super frame spreads that data across several frames in a set word position.

cards.question: Why is one parameter written several times within a frame while another appears only once?
options: Because it is more important or changes more quickly
Because it is carried in a discrete rather than a word
Because it is a mandatory parameter required by law
cards.explain: Repetition within a frame follows the importance of the parameter and how fast it changes.

cards.question: Why do some aviation authorities require a quick access recorder at all, when the flight data recorder holds the same data?
options: Because the copy of flight data then survives a crash better
Because the copy of flight data then holds more parameters
Because the copy of flight data then stays easily accessible
cards.explain: Easy access to the copy is the stated reason for the requirement.

cards.question: What is the single unit called that combines the new generation voice and flight data recording of small aircraft
options: the cockpit voice flight data recorder
the combined flight data interface recorder
the cockpit voice data acquisition recorder
cards.explain: The combined unit is the CVFDR.

cards.question: When does the cockpit voice flight data recorder start recording
options: when the rotor rpm exceeds 50%
when the control panel test switch is pressed
when electrical power is applied
cards.explain: Application of electrical power is what starts the unit recording.

cards.question: A Class II data recorder is fitted to a civil commercial aircraft. Where is it mainly located?
options: the tail section
the forward cargo hold
the cockpit floor area
cards.explain: The usual position for a Class II recorder is the tail section.

cards.question: Where on a helicopter is the flight data recorder usually found
options: the nose compartment or the cockpit roof
one of the aft compartments or the tailboom
one of the engine bays or the main gearbox deck
cards.explain: Those are the two areas named for the helicopter installation.

cards.question: At which frequency does the underwater locator beacon send out its audio signal
options: 40 MHz
40 Hz
40 kHz
cards.explain: The beacon signal is at 40 kHz.

cards.question: By which other name is the inertia sensor of the helicopter recording installation known
options: the area microphone
the immersion sensor
the accelerometer
cards.explain: The inertia sensor of the helicopter recording installation is the accelerometer.

cards.question: When does the flight data recording within the combined unit start
options: When the area microphone picks up sound
When the electrical power is applied
When the rotor rpm exceeds 50%
cards.explain: Flight data recording is tied to rotor speed above 50%.

cards.question: What does the control panel switch of the combined voice and flight data recorder allow to be done
options: a memory download on ground
a battery change on ground
a BITE test on ground
cards.explain: The panel test switch runs a BITE test on the ground.

cards.question: Besides combining all data to a recordable format, what else does the flight data acquisition unit do
options: It monitors the recording
It erases the oldest data
It allocates the flight leg
cards.explain: Besides formatting the data the unit monitors the recording.

cards.question: Which condition stops both the voice recording and the flight data recording of the combined unit
options: the voice erase button being pressed
the rotor rpm falling below 50%
the electrical power being disconnected
cards.explain: Disconnecting the electrical power stops the unit recording; falling below 50% rotor rpm stops only the flight data part.

cards.question: On aircraft of which weight is a single unit holding both the flight recorder and the cockpit voice recorder permitted
options: above 27,000 kg
below 5700 kg
above 5700 kg
cards.explain: The combined unit is allowed below the 5700 kg mark.

cards.question: On what do the possible installation positions for a flight data recorder depend
options: the classification of the recorder
the number of parameters recorded
the capacity of the recorder memory
cards.explain: Where the recorder may go follows from its classification.

cards.question: What makes the helicopter recorder easy to pick out at a crash site?
options: It is painted matt black with white stripes
It is painted bright yellow or orange
It is painted bright red with a flashing lamp
cards.explain: Bright yellow or orange paint is what makes it easy to find.

cards.question: Which equipment picks up the signal from the locator beacon
options: a shipboard radio receiver
an underwater microphone
a cockpit area microphone
cards.explain: An underwater microphone is what receives the beacon.

cards.question: For what minimum period does the beacon transmission continue once it has started
options: 30 days
90 days
25 days
cards.explain: The minimum transmission period is 90 days.

cards.question: The combined recorder has been running for eleven hours. What has become of its earliest hour of flight data?
options: It has been kept, because recording stops once the memory is full
It has been overwritten, because the oldest recording goes first
It has been transferred into the voice section of the memory
cards.explain: Once the holding time is full the oldest data is overwritten.

cards.question: The rotor has run down below 50% but the electrical power is still on. Which recording is still running?
options: Neither recording, because the rotor has fallen below fifty per cent
The flight data recording, while the voice recording has stopped
The voice recording, while the flight data recording has stopped
cards.explain: Flight data stops with rotor speed below 50%, the voice recording runs until power is removed.

cards.question: Why is the helicopter recorder put in the aft compartments or the tailboom rather than further forward?
options: Because those areas are easier to reach for a battery change
Because those areas are further from the electrical interference
Because those areas are less damaged in case of a crash
cards.explain: Crash damage is lower there, which is why the recorder is placed aft.

cards.question: A recorder is lying on the sea bed after a ditching and nobody has touched it. What has set its beacon transmitting?
options: The loss of aircraft electrical supply to the recorder
Its battery coming in contact with water
The impact sensed by the inertia sensor of the recorder
cards.explain: Water reaching the battery starts the transmission automatically.

cards.question: Which three areas does the aircraft integrated data system monitor and analyse continuously
options: engine data, aircraft data and gearbox data
engine data, aircraft data and APU data
engine data, voice data and flight data
cards.explain: The three listed are engine, aircraft and APU data.

cards.question: What does APM stand for in the aircraft condition monitoring system
options: aircraft parameter monitoring
auxiliary power monitoring
aircraft performance monitoring
cards.explain: APM is aircraft performance monitoring.

cards.question: Which data does the quick access recorder record
options: the same data as the digital flight data recorder
only the data that the data management unit programmes
a shortened selection of the flight data recorder data
cards.explain: Its records are identical to those of the DFDR.

cards.question: About how long does a quick access recorder write before its recording time is used up?
options: 10 hours
25 hours
50 hours
cards.explain: The writing time of the quick access recorder is about 50 hours.

cards.question: Besides recording and storing digital flight data, what is the wireless quick access recorder there to do
options: transmit digital flight data without wires
erase digital flight data after transfer
format digital flight data for the recorder
cards.explain: Recording, storing and wireless transmission are the three stated purposes.

cards.question: A technician has to take the recorded data off a wireless quick access recorder. On which medium is it held?
options: a polyester magnetic tape cassette
a standard PCMCIA removable PC Card
a bulk erasable EEPROM device
cards.explain: It records on a standard PCMCIA removable PC Card.

cards.question: In the flight avionics of which aircraft are health and usage monitoring systems a common component
options: a modern large aeroplane
a modern business jet
a modern helicopter
cards.explain: Health and usage monitoring systems are a common component in the flight avionics of modern helicopters.

cards.question: Exact data about the manoeuvres flown has been recorded. Which additional usage parameter is that?
options: gross weight
flight envelope
flight endurance
cards.explain: Flight envelope is the parameter carrying the manoeuvres flown.

cards.question: Which unit manages the monitoring and analysis tasks in the ACMS
options: the centralised data acquisition module
the flight data interface unit
the data management unit
cards.explain: The DMU manages those tasks.

cards.question: Which further task does the data management unit take on with its smart airborne recorder or wireless quick access recorder
options: checking the mandatory parameters for integrity
recording pre-programmed parameters
erasing the oldest recorded parameters
cards.explain: Through those recorders the DMU records parameters that have been pre-programmed.

cards.question: What else can be done with the data of all the systems connected to the data management unit?
options: It can be retrieved for trouble-shooting
It can be erased before the next flight
It can be written to the crash protected memory
cards.explain: That connected data is available for trouble-shooting.

cards.question: Two aircraft carry the same monitoring system but one calls it ADAS and the other ACMS. How does that come about?
options: The system name is given by the manufacturer
The system name is given by the ATA chapter it is filed in
The system name is given by the certifying authority
cards.explain: It is the manufacturer who names the system.

cards.question: From where does the digital airborne recorder get the free programmed data it writes
options: the data management unit
the flight warning computer
the flight data interface unit
cards.explain: Its free programmed data is supplied by the DMU.

cards.question: Where does the digital flight data handled by the wireless quick access recorder generally come from
options: the flight data interface and management unit
the flight warning computer
the centralised data acquisition module
cards.explain: The FDIMU is the normal source of its data.

cards.question: When is the recorded data of the wireless quick access recorder compressed, encrypted and transmitted
options: while the aircraft is on the ground
while the aircraft is in the cruise
while the aircraft is being powered down
cards.explain: The transfer takes place with the aircraft on the ground.

cards.question: Over which link is the recorded flight information sent securely from the aircraft on the ground
options: a commercial wireless cellular data link
a satellite voice communication link
a wired ground support equipment link
cards.explain: A commercial cellular data link carries the transfer.

cards.question: What makes up the user interface of the wireless quick access recorder
options: a control display unit and a station printer
a front panel keypad and an alphanumeric display
a front panel test connector and a fail indicator lamp
cards.explain: The user works through a keypad and an alphanumeric display on the front panel.

cards.question: On what do the parameters monitored by a health and usage monitoring system depend
options: the certification date of the helicopter and its weight
the flight time flown since the last scheduled inspection
the helicopter configuration, such as engines, gearboxes and rotors
cards.explain: The configuration of the helicopter decides what gets monitored.

cards.question: What do speed probes enable maintenance to identify on rotating components
options: A component overpressure
A component overheat
A component overspeed
cards.explain: The speed probes exist to catch an overspeed of a rotating component.

cards.question: What can a monitored exceedance of temperature limits or a tendency to run hot be
options: the sign of a loss of vital system fluid
the beginning of a major component or system failure
the result of an overspeed of a rotating component
cards.explain: Rising temperature is treated as the start of a major component or system failure.

cards.question: Why is vibration measured on bearings in particular?
options: Because they carry no temperature or pressure sensor of their own
Because they turn faster than the components around them
Because they are not inspected at preflight or are out of reach to inspect
cards.explain: Bearings get the attention because a preflight inspection cannot see or reach them.

cards.question: What does a rising vibration reading on a monitored component indicate about that component
options: It is beginning to wear out and may cause severe damage
It is beginning to overspeed and may cause an overstress
It is beginning to run hot and may cause a fluid loss
cards.explain: Vibration growth indicates wear that could go on to damage the system badly.

cards.question: How does the data used by usage monitoring compare with that used by health monitoring
options: the same set with some extensions
a separate set taken from other sensors
a reduced set limited to the rotor system
cards.explain: Usage monitoring works from the health monitoring data, extended a little.

cards.question: Which part of the operation do the parameters recorded for usage monitoring serve
options: the logistic and maintenance part
the flight planning and dispatch part
the accident investigation part
cards.explain: Those parameters are there for logistics and maintenance.

cards.question: Flight endurance recorded by usage monitoring gives an exact helicopter run time instead of a time
options: rounded down to the last full hour
rounded up to the next 5 minutes
rounded up to the next 15 minutes
cards.explain: The gain is an exact run time instead of rounding up to the next 5 minutes.

cards.question: Data has to reach the evaluation computer on the ground while the aircraft is still flying. Which interface carries it?
options: ADL
MPRT
ACARS
cards.explain: The ground computer is fed through ACARS.

cards.question: The ground computer is to be supplied with print reports through the station terminals. Which interface produces them?
options: ADL
ACARS
MPRT
cards.explain: The multi-printer interface is what delivers the print reports.

cards.question: The monitoring system is to be modified by loading from disks. Which of its interfaces is used?
options: ACARS
MCDU
ADL
cards.explain: Modification by disk goes through the airborne data loader.

cards.question: A quick access recorder is coming to the end of its writing time. What must be done?
options: The recording medium must be erased before the 50 hours have elapsed
The recording medium must be changed before the 50 hours have elapsed
The recording medium must be downloaded before the 25 hours have elapsed
cards.explain: There is no erase button, so the recording medium has to be replaced inside the 50 hours.

cards.question: The digital airborne recorder runs at a faster recording speed than the quick access recorder. What follows from that?
options: Its maximum writing time is longer
Its maximum writing time is shorter
Its stored data is harder to access
cards.explain: A faster recording speed fills the same medium sooner, so the writing time is shorter.

cards.question: A unit of this type is fitted with no radios at all. What is it then identified as?
options: A digital airborne quick access recorder
A PC Card quick access recorder
A wireless quick access recorder
cards.explain: Without radios the unit is the PQAR, the PC Card quick access recorder.

cards.question: A main gearbox has no cockpit instrument or warning of its own. Why does that make its speed probe reading so valuable?
options: Because a vibration there could otherwise be felt through the controls
Because an overheat there could otherwise be read on the oil gauge
Because an overspeed there could otherwise go unidentified by the crew
cards.explain: Components the crew cannot watch are exactly the ones whose overspeed the probe would otherwise miss.

cards.question: A monitored circuit shows a steady tendency towards low pressure. What does the monitoring read into that?
options: An upcoming failure or a loss of vital system fluid
An overstress of a component or abnormal wear
A bearing beginning to wear out in the gearbox
cards.explain: A drifting pressure points to a coming failure or to fluid being lost.

cards.question: Acceleration readings come back higher than normal after a sortie. What does the monitoring system take that to mean?
options: A component has run hot or a system failure is beginning
A component has been overstressed or abnormal wear is occurring
A component has overspeeded or a bearing has failed
cards.explain: High acceleration is read as overstress or abnormal wear.

cards.question: Metal particles are detected in a gearbox oil system. What does the monitoring system conclude from that?
options: A gear is overspeeding and could shed teeth if not slowed
A bearing is wearing abnormally and could fail if not checked
A bearing is running hot and could seize if not cooled
cards.explain: Metal in the oil points to abnormal bearing wear that may end in failure.

cards.question: A component is limited by the safe life principle and its limit is approaching. How can usage monitoring help?
options: The time can be extended when no fatigue or damage has been recorded
The time can be extended when no overspeed has been reported by the crew
The limit can be removed once the component has been vibration checked
cards.explain: Recorded absence of fatigue or damage is what allows the safe life time to be extended.

cards.question: Gross weight is recorded and set against the recorded flight envelope. What is that comparison looking for?
options: Possible overstress to components and structural limits
Possible loss of vital fluid from a pressurised system
Possible excess of the safe life limit of a component
cards.explain: The comparison is made to find overstress of components and structural limits.

cards.question: On which three bases do the gyroscopes used in aviation today work
options: an optical basis, a thermal basis and an oscillation basis
a mechanical basis, an optical basis and an oscillation basis
a mechanical basis, a pneumatic basis and a magnetic basis
cards.explain: The three families named are mechanical, optical and oscillation gyroscopes.

cards.question: For which three flight instruments are the properties of a gyroscope used
options: the directional gyro, the altimeter and the turn-and-bank indicator
the artificial horizon, the airspeed indicator and the vertical speed indicator
the artificial horizon, the directional gyro and the turn-and-bank indicator
cards.explain: Those three instruments are the ones named as built on gyroscopic properties.

cards.question: Around how many axes can any body move in free space
options: three
two
four
cards.explain: Any body can move around three axes in free space.

cards.question: A gyro has one degree of freedom. What movement is open to it?
options: movement around any axis in free space
movement around an axis perpendicular to its own
movement around its own axis only
cards.explain: With one degree of freedom the gyroscope can only move around its own axis.

cards.question: What do the letters ERP stand for
options: Earth Rotation Precession
Equator Rate Precession
Earth Rate Precession
cards.explain: ERP is Earth Rate Precession.

cards.question: What is the horizontal component of apparent wander called
options: apparent drift
apparent topple
transport wander
cards.explain: The horizontal component of apparent wander is apparent drift.

cards.question: What does a running gyroscope tend to do
options: maintain the direction of its axis in space
align its axis with the earth's magnetic field
hold its axis square to the aircraft structure
cards.explain: The gyroscope makes every effort to maintain the direction of its axis in space.

cards.question: The inertia of a gyroscope against the forces acting on it increases with
options: rotational speed, bearing friction and frame weight
rotational speed, mass and distance from the rotational axis
mass, ambient temperature and distance from the rotational axis
cards.explain: Inertia in relation to forces acting on the gyro increases with rotational speed, mass and distance from the rotational axis.

cards.question: Which two actions is a gyroscope free to accept without opposing them
options: a force at right angles to the axis and a parallel shift of the gyro axis
a force along the direction of the axis and a tilting of the gyro axis
a force along the direction of the axis and a parallel shift of the gyro axis
cards.explain: The gyroscope resists neither a force acting along its axis nor a parallel shift of that axis.

cards.question: At what angle to an exterior force trying to change the direction of its axis does a gyroscope precess
cards.explain: The gyroscope precesses at a 90 degree angle to the force acting on it.

cards.question: On what does the direction in which a gyroscope precesses depend
options: the size of the exterior force
the rotation of the gyroscope
the mass of the gyroscope
cards.explain: The direction of precession depends on the rotation of the gyroscope itself.

cards.question: A gyro running at medium speed is pulled out of its mounting anyway. What is the damage to be expected?
options: the bearings and the frame can be destroyed
the electrical drive winding can be burnt out
the gimbal springs can be stretched beyond repair
cards.explain: A gyro removed at medium speed will flounder and the bearings and frame can be destroyed.

cards.question: What is said of a body whose movement around one axis is limited
options: it has a low degree of freedom
it has a half degree of freedom
it has a total degree of freedom
cards.explain: Limiting the movement around one axis gives a low degree of freedom.

cards.question: What does a body that can move around all of its axes have
options: a high (total) degree of freedom
a low degree of freedom
a half degree of freedom
cards.explain: Movement around all axes gives a high, that is total, degree of freedom.

cards.question: How is a gyroscope with two degrees of freedom mounted
options: in a frame which can itself rotate around an axis parallel to the gyro axis
in two frames which can rotate around axes perpendicular to each other
in a frame which can itself rotate around an axis perpendicular to the gyro axis
cards.explain: Two degrees of freedom come from one frame that can rotate about an axis perpendicular to the gyro axis.

cards.question: A gyroscope with three degrees of freedom is gimballed in cardan frames. How many cardan frames does it have?
options: three
one
two
cards.explain: Three degrees of freedom are obtained from two frames, the inner and the outer cardan frame.

cards.question: A gyroscope can be set to any position at all in free space. What is such a gyroscope called?
options: a spring restrained gyroscope
a fully gimballed gyroscope
a rate gyroscope
cards.explain: A gyroscope which can assume any position in free space is a fully gimballed gyroscope.

cards.question: By what means is a gyroscope frame constrained so that it finds a position of rest
options: by liquid level switches
by torque motors
by springs
cards.explain: The frame is constrained by means of springs so that it has a rest position to return to.

cards.question: Which degree of freedom does American literature leave out
options: the one around the spin axis
the one around the outer cardan frame
the one around the inner cardan frame
cards.explain: American literature does not count the degree of freedom around the spin axis.

cards.question: At what angle to each other are the frames of a fully gimballed gyro system set
cards.explain: The three frames of the fully gimballed mounting stand at 90° to each other.

cards.question: Which two instruments are based on the space stability of the gyroscope
options: the artificial horizon and the vertical speed indicator
the directional gyro and the turn-and-bank indicator
the directional gyro and the artificial horizon
cards.explain: Directional gyro and artificial horizon are the two space stability devices named.

cards.question: What causes the apparent wander of the axis of a free gyroscope that is called ERP
options: the east-west movement of the aircraft carrying the gyroscope
the friction of the bearings acting on the frames of the gyroscope
the rotation of the earth acting on the space stability of the gyroscope
cards.explain: ERP is apparent wander caused by the rotation of the earth acting on the gyro's space stability.

cards.question: Into which two components is the three dimensional wander divided in relation to the earth's surface
options: a horizontal and a vertical component
a longitudinal and a lateral component
a real and an apparent component
cards.explain: Relative to the earth's surface the wander splits into horizontal and vertical components.

cards.question: To what does apparent drift amount per hour
options: 15 deg cosine of latitude
15 deg sine of latitude
15 deg tangent of latitude
cards.explain: Apparent drift amounts per hour to 15° Sinus of latitude.

cards.question: To what does apparent topple amount per hour
options: 15 deg cosine of latitude
15 deg sine of latitude
15 deg tangent of latitude
cards.explain: Apparent topple amounts per hour to 15° cosinus of latitude.

cards.question: Which aircraft movement causes the apparent wander called transport wander
options: east-west movement
vertical movement
north-south movement
cards.explain: Transport wander is caused by the east-west movement of the aircraft.

cards.question: A fully gimballed vertical gyro stands at the equator and an observer watches it for a full day. Through how much does it appear to topple?
options: 360° in 24 hours
180° in 24 hours
360° in 12 hours
cards.explain: At the equator the gyroscope appears to topple 360° in 24 hours.

cards.question: What happens to the apparent topple of a vertical gyro at higher latitudes
options: it becomes larger and is greatest at the poles
it becomes smaller and is zero at the poles
it stays the same at every latitude
cards.explain: Apparent topple becomes smaller at higher latitudes and is zero at the poles.

cards.question: Which way does the axis of a gyro point when apparent topple is being considered
options: along the aircraft's direction of flight
vertical related to the earth's surface
parallel to the earth's surface
cards.explain: Apparent topple is described for a fully gimballed vertical gyro whose axis is vertical to the earth's surface.

cards.question: An exterior force has been applied to the axis of a running gyro and is held there. When does the gyro stop precessing?
options: when its sense of rotation corresponds to the rotational direction acting upon it
when its axis has turned through a right angle from the direction it started in
when the inertia of its rotating mass has fully absorbed the applied force
cards.explain: The gyro precesses until its sense of rotation corresponds to the rotational direction acting upon it.

cards.question: A gyroscope was switched off approximately three minutes ago and a technician wants to take it out now. What is the position?
options: it may be removed, because only a stationary rotor can be damaged
it may in no case be removed, because the gyro will tend to flounder
it may be removed, because the rotor has already come to rest
cards.explain: Approximately three minutes after switching off the gyro is running at medium speed, and at medium speed it may in no case be removed.

cards.question: A gyroscope frame is constrained by means of springs. What is the freedom of that whole gyro system?
options: 2 1/2 degrees of freedom
1 degree of freedom
1 1/2 degrees of freedom
cards.explain: A spring constrained frame counts as a half degree, so the gyro system has 1 1/2 degrees of freedom.

cards.question: Why does a spring constrained frame count as only half a degree?
options: because it can move about only half of the axes that a free frame can
because it has a position of rest to which it constantly tries to return
because it is driven through only half of its travel before it is stopped
cards.explain: The spring gives the frame a position of rest, so it no longer has its full freedom of movement.

cards.question: An aircraft rolls and pitches into a completely new attitude. What has happened to the axis of its space stable gyro?
options: it still points to the same direction
it has precessed through a right angle to the new attitude
it has followed the aircraft into the new attitude
cards.explain: When the aircraft changes attitude the gyro axis still points in the same direction.

cards.question: The tail of a propeller aircraft is lifted during the take-off run and the pilot does not react. What does the nose do?
options: it turns to the right
it turns to the left
it rises further
cards.explain: Lifting the tail applies a force to the propeller axis which is transferred clockwise into the plane of precession, so the nose turns left.

cards.question: The landing gear is being retracted while the wheels are still spinning. Why does that matter?
options: the spinning wheels drag the gyro instruments out of their rest position
the spinning wheels lose their space stability once they leave the airflow
the spinning wheels carry precession forces like any other rotating component
cards.explain: Wheels turning during gear retraction are listed among the rotating components that carry precession forces.

cards.question: A free gyroscope is left standing at the equator. Which of the two apparent errors is at its greatest there?
options: apparent topple
apparent drift
transport wander
cards.explain: Apparent topple is greatest at the equator.

cards.question: A free gyro is no longer standing at one place but is being carried along. Why do the plain earth rate figures no longer cover all of its apparent error?
options: because those figures hold only on the ground, where the bearings are unloaded
because those figures hold only with no aircraft movement, so transport wander is added
because those figures hold only for a gyro with a half degree of freedom
cards.explain: The earth rate statements are only true if the gyroscope remains at the same place; once the aircraft moves, transport wander comes on top.

cards.question: A gyro axis is seen to move although nothing mechanical is wrong with it. Under which heading does that movement fall?
options: gimbal error, the indication error that builds up during a turn
real wander, the precession motion set up by friction in the bearings
apparent wander, the apparent motion relative to the rotating earth
cards.explain: Apparent wander is apparent movement caused by maintaining a position in space, relative to the rotating earth or by transport.

cards.question: Why does a gyro that holds its direction appear to topple to someone standing beside it at the equator?
options: because the bearings of the gyro drag its axis round with the earth
because gravity pulls the heavy end of the gyro axis downwards
because the earth is spinning below the space stable gyroscope
cards.explain: The gyro keeps its direction in space while the earth spins below it, so the observer sees it topple.

cards.question: What kind of influences cause real drift and real topple
options: atmospheric influences
magnetic influences
constructional influences
cards.explain: Real drift and real topple come from constructional influences.

cards.question: By which other name is the gimbal error of the directional gyro known
options: the cardan error
the gimbal lock
the transport error
cards.explain: Gimbal error of the directional gyro is known as the cardan error.

cards.question: An erection system needs something to judge the earth's surface by. What does it use as a reference signal?
options: the magnetic field of the earth
the static pressure of the atmosphere
the gravity of the earth
cards.explain: The erection system uses the gravity of the earth as its reference signal.

cards.question: Which two types of optical gyroscope are there
options: the ring laser gyro and the fibre optic gyro
the fibre optic gyro and the quartz oscillating gyroscope
the ring laser gyro and the hemispherical resonator gyro
cards.explain: The two optical types are the ring laser gyro and the fibre optic gyro.

cards.question: Which parts does the ring laser gyroscope have
options: a double laser exciter, prisms, a fibre coil and a photodetector
a double laser exciter, mirrors, prisms and light sensors
a single laser exciter, mirrors, lenses and light sensors
cards.explain: The RLG has a double laser exciter, mirrors, prisms and light sensors.

cards.question: What is interference
options: the overlapping of oscillations and waves
the cancelling of oscillations by waves
the splitting of oscillations into waves
cards.explain: Interference is the overlapping of oscillations and waves.

cards.question: A fully gimballed directional gyro is over the North Pole and an observer turning with the earth watches it for a day. Through how much does it appear to rotate?
options: 360° in 24 hours
360° in 12 hours
180° in 24 hours
cards.explain: At the pole the gyroscope appears to rotate 360° in 24 hours.

cards.question: What happens to the apparent drift of a directional gyro at lower latitudes
options: it stays the same at every latitude
it becomes larger and is greatest at the equator
it becomes smaller and is zero at the equator
cards.explain: Apparent drift becomes smaller at lower latitudes and is zero at the equator.

cards.question: How does the axis of the directional gyro lie when apparent drift is being considered
options: at 45° to the earth's surface
vertical to the earth's surface
parallel to the earth's surface
cards.explain: Apparent drift is described for a fully gimballed directional gyro whose axis lies parallel to the earth's surface.

cards.question: Which two faults cause real drift and real topple
options: defective gyro and frame bearings, and the rotation of the earth
unbalance of the gyro and frame, and the east-west transport of the aircraft
defective gyro and frame bearings, and unbalance of the gyro and frame
cards.explain: The two causes named are defective gyro and frame bearings, and unbalance of the gyro and frame.

cards.question: A directional gyro is suffering from its gimbal error. During which manoeuvre does that mainly happen?
options: a turn
a sideslip
a climb
cards.explain: Gimbal error of the directional gyro mainly occurs during a turn.

cards.question: What does the gimbal effect in the directional gyro result in
options: a loss of rotor speed
a direction indication error
a jammed outer frame
cards.explain: Gimbal error of the directional gyro results in a direction indication error.

cards.question: What is the state of the two frames when gimbal lock has occurred
options: they are aligned
they are held apart by their springs
they are at 90° to each other
cards.explain: In gimbal lock, the extreme case of frame error, the two frames are aligned.

cards.question: What must be eliminated before a gyro can be used for aircraft instruments
options: the total effect of topple
the whole of the spin axis friction
the half degree of freedom of the frame
cards.explain: The total effect of topple must be eliminated with an erection system.

cards.question: What does the erection system control the gyro axis to keep
options: a constant direction to the earth's surface
a constant angle to the aircraft centre line
a constant speed of rotation about its own axis
cards.explain: The erection system controls the gyro axis so that it keeps a constant direction to the earth's surface.

cards.question: By which two means is the erection reference signal detected
options: by a moving mass like a pendulum or by liquid level switches
by liquid level switches or by a pressure capsule
by a moving mass like a pendulum or by a magnetic flux valve
cards.explain: The reference is detected either by a moving mass such as a pendulum or by liquid level switches.

cards.question: By which two means is the erection force applied to the gyro
options: by electrical torque motors or by air jets on the rotor
by mechanic force of gravity or by electrical torque motors
by mechanic force of gravity or by restraining springs
cards.explain: Depending on the gyro type the erection is done by mechanic force of gravity or by electrical torque motors.

cards.question: What occurs between two coherent beams of light running opposite ways on the same course if the apparatus is rotated
options: a phase displacement
a change of colour
a loss of coherence
cards.explain: Rotating the apparatus produces a phase displacement between the two counter-running beams.

cards.question: An optical gyroscope is being explained to a trainee. According to which optical principle does it work?
options: the Doppler effect
the swirl effect
the Sagnac effect
cards.explain: Optical gyroscopes work according to the optical principle known as the Sagnac effect.

cards.question: On which principle does the ring laser gyroscope work
options: a single laser beam in a ring cavity is compared with a fixed reference
two counterpropagating laser beams in a ring cavity are added to each other
two counterpropagating laser beams in a ring cavity are compared with each other
cards.explain: The RLG compares two counterpropagating laser beams in a ring cavity with each other.

cards.question: Under which condition is light coherent
options: when it has been gathered by reflection from several light packets
when it has been filtered to one single wave length
when it has been split by reflection from one single light packet
cards.explain: Light is coherent if it has been split by reflexion from one single light packet.

cards.question: Two gyros stand at the North Pole, one with its axis upright and one with its axis lying along the ground. Which apparent error is at its maximum there?
options: drift, for the gyro whose axis is parallel to the surface
neither, both of those errors fall to zero at the pole
topple, for the gyro whose axis stands vertical to it
cards.explain: Drift is greatest at the poles and belongs to the gyro with its axis parallel to the surface, while topple is zero there.

cards.question: An artificial horizon gyro whose axis points to the centre of the earth at the north pole is carried down to the equator. How does its axis finish up to an observer on the earth?
options: horizontal
turned through a right angle in the horizontal plane
still vertical
cards.explain: The axis appears to topple during the journey until it is horizontal at the equator.

cards.question: A gyro has worn frame bearings and is also carried east-west across the earth. How do the two error sources add up?
options: the bearing error is cancelled by the earth rotation and transport errors
the bearing error takes the place of the earth rotation and transport errors
the bearing error sits on top of the earth rotation and transport errors
cards.explain: Real errors from construction are error values over and above those due to the earth's rotation and transport.

cards.question: A gyroscope is found with its two frames lined up with each other. What can still be done with it?
options: it can be used once its frames are re-sprung
it can be used for drift but not for topple
nothing, an instrument in that state is unusable
cards.explain: Gimbal lock, where the two frames are aligned, makes the gyroscope unusable.

cards.question: An erection system is fitted to a directional gyro. In which direction does it hold that gyro's axis?
options: horizontal
vertical
along the aircraft centre line
cards.explain: The erection keeps the axis horizontal for the directional gyro and vertical for the vertical gyro.

cards.question: What decides whether a given gyro is erected mechanically or by torque motors?
options: the latitude the aircraft is operating at
the type of gyro
the number of frames the gyro is gimballed in
cards.explain: The erection is done by mechanic force of gravity or by electrical torque motors depending on the gyro type.

cards.question: An erection system is set to work against the total topple of a gyro. Which two errors make up that total?
options: real topple and real drift
apparent topple and real topple
apparent topple and apparent drift
cards.explain: Total topple is the sum of apparent topple and real topple.

cards.question: A designer is choosing how big to make the beam cavity of an optical gyro. Why is a larger one wanted?
options: the laser needs less power to keep the beams going
the interference pattern can be measured more easily
the two beams stay in phase over a wider speed range
cards.explain: In general, the larger the beam cavity is, the easier the interference pattern can be measured.

cards.question: At extremely small angular velocities the beams of light still interfere. What is the difficulty then?
options: the interference is difficult to measure
the interference pattern no longer forms at all
the two beams stop running in opposite directions
cards.explain: Beams interfere at extremely small angular velocities, but in such a case they are difficult to measure.

cards.question: An optical gyro is built with mirrors rather than with fibre optics. What does that choice bring with it?
options: easy measurement and a very large orbit
difficult measurement but a size constrained unit
easy measurement but a size constrained unit
cards.explain: Optical gyroscopes with mirrors are easy to measure but are constrained by the size of the unit.

cards.question: The gyroscope block is turned clockwise. What happens to the beam that runs in the direction of that rotation?
options: it stops returning to its starting point at all
it travels slightly further before returning to its starting point
it travels slightly less far before returning to its starting point
cards.explain: The beam moving in the direction of rotation travels slightly further than the one running the other way.

cards.question: One of the two beams has been forced onto the longer course by the rotation. What has become of its frequency?
options: it is unchanged
it is slightly lower
it is slightly higher
cards.explain: The beam on the longer course has the now longer resonator and so a slightly lower frequency.

cards.question: The two wave trains are keeping exactly the same frequencies. What are the bright and dark strips doing?
options: they wander over the photodiodes
they double in number
they remain stationary
cards.explain: As long as the wave trains keep the same frequencies the strips remain stationary.

cards.question: The frequencies of the two wave trains begin to differ. What does the counter then receive?
options: alternating light-dark impulses as the strips wander over the photodiodes
a steady light level as the strips settle over the photodiodes
a single bright pulse as the strips cancel at the photodiodes
cards.explain: When the frequencies differ the strips wander over the photodiodes, which are alternately in light and dark, and those impulses are metered.

cards.question: The photodiodes have told the electronics which way the interference strips are wandering. What is that used for?
options: the rotational direction, carried as a preceding symbol in the pulse count
the rotational speed, carried as a count of the pulses per unit of time
the path length, carried as a correction to the setting of the mirrors
cards.explain: The direction of wander indicates the rotational direction and is taken into account with a preceding symbol when the pulses are added up.

cards.question: Coherent light has been made to interfere inside the optical circuit of a gyro. What can then be measured?
options: the direction of the earth's gravity vector
the speed of rotation, that is the arc velocity
the temperature of the resonance cavity
cards.explain: Because coherent light can interfere, speed of rotation, that is arc velocity, can be measured with the structure of the optical circuit.

cards.question: To which specification does the fibre optic gyro conform entirely
options: ARINC 561
ARINC 704
ARINC 705
cards.explain: The fibre optic gyro conforms entirely to the requirements of the ARINC 705 specification.

cards.question: Which medium do the gas laser gyroscopes that have prevailed in practice use
options: helium/neon
neon/krypton
helium/argon
cards.explain: The gas laser gyroscopes that prevailed use helium/neon as a medium.

cards.question: What determines the frequency of the laser light
options: the length of the cavity between cathode and anode
the current drawn by the laser exciter
the number of mirrors in the light path
