cards.explain: The voice announcement is the synthetic voice output, while the acoustic one is the aural alert.

cards.question: Which computer decides what is to appear on the centralized monitoring displays
options: The flight warning computer
The system data acquisition concentrator
The display management computer
cards.explain: The flight warning computer determines the content of the ECAM displays.

cards.question: To which two sets of computers does a system data acquisition concentrator forward its data
options: The flight warning computers and the other concentrator
The display management computers and the control panels
The flight warning computers and the display management computers
cards.explain: The concentrator feeds both the flight warning computers and the display management computers.

cards.question: Which computer puts the engine parameters and the system page parameters onto the displays?
options: The flight warning computer
The system data acquisition concentrator
The display management computer
cards.explain: Overlaying the engine and system page parameters is the display management computer's job.

cards.question: Which three kinds of warning are generated by the modularized avionics warning electronics assembly
options: Optical, tactile and synoptic warnings
Optical, aural and visual warnings
Optical, aural and tactile warnings
cards.explain: It produces optical, aural and tactile warnings.

cards.question: Through which item of equipment are the warnings of the avionics warning electronics assembly generated
options: Through the control panel
Through the display select panel
Through the interface unit
cards.explain: The warnings are generated by way of the EFIS/EICAS interface unit.

cards.question: Which three items are controlled by the avionics warning electronics assembly itself?
options: The master warning light, the aural warn speaker and the stick shaker
The master caution light, the aural warn speaker and the stick shaker
The master warning light, the aural warn speaker and the display units
cards.explain: Those three are the items it drives directly.

cards.question: An aircraft without a glass cockpit is being compared with one that has it. What does flight monitoring use on the older aircraft?
options: two central displays and the indicators of a central warning panel
two displays for each pilot and some other navigation indicators
the basic T instruments and some other navigation indicators
cards.explain: Without displays the job is done by the basic T instruments plus other navigation indicators.

cards.question: On which display is the crew told that a value somewhere in the aircraft has gone out of limit
options: On the navigation display of each pilot
On one of the two engine and system data displays
On the primary flight display of each pilot
cards.explain: One of the two engine and system displays additionally carries the alerts for out of limit conditions.

cards.question: An aircraft is fitted with only the minimum number of display computers, so what does it lack compared with a large aircraft?
options: The computer that is there for redundancy
The computer that handles the analogue inputs
The computer that drives the centre displays
cards.explain: The minimum fit is two computers, so the third one carried for redundancy on large aircraft is missing.

cards.question: Which part inside a second generation display unit makes a picture out of the data it is sent
options: Its integrated symbol generator
Its integrated control panel
Its integrated display computer
cards.explain: These units are sent data rather than video, so the symbol generator built into them draws the picture.

cards.question: Which Boeing display does the same job as the Airbus system display
options: The engine and warning display
The auxiliary EICAS display
The upper EICAS display
cards.explain: The auxiliary EICAS does the job that the system display does on the other manufacturer's fit.

cards.question: Which path is taken by the signal that produces an amber caution
options: From the sensors and computers through the data concentrator to the warning computer
From the sensors and computers direct to the warning computer
From the sensors and computers through the display computer to the warning computer
cards.explain: An amber caution reaches the flight warning computer by way of the system data acquisition concentrator.

cards.question: Both system data acquisition concentrators are lost, so which colour of warning can still be generated?
options: Neither colour
The red warnings
The amber cautions
cards.explain: Red warnings reach the warning computer without passing through the concentrator, so they survive its loss.

cards.question: The engine and warning screen stays blank but the aural alerts are still heard, so which computer is suspected?
options: The display management computer
The flight warning computer
The data acquisition concentrator
cards.explain: The warnings are still being generated, so the fault lies in the computer that feeds the display unit.

cards.question: The stick shaker does not operate although the conditions for it are met, so which unit is first suspected?
options: The EICAS display select panel
The avionics warning electronics assembly
The EFIS and EICAS interface unit
cards.explain: The stick shaker is one of the items the warning electronics assembly controls directly.

cards.question: The master warning light comes on but no message reaches the screens, so which item is suspected?
options: The EICAS display select panel
The avionics warning electronics assembly
The EFIS and EICAS interface unit
cards.explain: The light is driven directly and works, so the path through the interface unit to the screens is at fault.

cards.question: What appears on the display in place of a parameter whose input signal is not available
options: A flag
An amber box
A dash
cards.explain: The indication disappears and a flag is shown instead.

cards.question: What does a cathode ray tube display unit do first when it detects an internal overheat
options: It switches the display off
It switches the raster colours off
It switches the strokes off
cards.explain: The first step is to switch off the raster colours.

cards.question: What is left on the screen after the first step of the overheat reaction
options: Only strokes, with the warnings removed
Only strokes, with all information still given
Only the raster, with all information still given
cards.explain: Only the strokes remain but none of the information is lost.

cards.question: Why does switching the raster colours off help a display unit that is running hot?
options: Less light is needed from the backlight
Less current is drawn by the cooling fan
Less heat is produced then
cards.explain: Dropping the raster colours makes the tube produce less heat.

cards.question: What does the display unit do as the second step of its overheat reaction
options: It switches the display to the cross side computer
It switches the raster colours off
It switches the display off
cards.explain: The second step is to switch the display off altogether.

cards.question: Which two conditions can cause an overheat of a display unit?
options: An internal failure or a problem in the cooling system
An internal failure or a problem in the power supply
A high cabin temperature or a problem in the cooling system
cards.explain: The two causes given are an internal failure and problems in the cooling system.

cards.question: What happens to the white in the picture when one electron beam of a cathode ray tube fails
options: There is no white in the picture
The white is replaced by amber in the picture
The white turns to grey in the picture
cards.explain: With one beam gone the picture contains no white at all.

cards.question: What becomes of the information that is normally presented in the colour of a failed electron beam
options: It will not be shown
It is shown in white instead
It is shown as a flag instead
cards.explain: Information carried by the missing colour simply disappears from the screen.

cards.question: What does the display do when the red electron beam fails
options: It turns monochrome
It loses only the white
It switches itself off
cards.explain: A failed red beam makes the whole display go monochrome.

cards.question: Which electron beam has failed when the crew sees the whole display in one colour
options: The red beam
The green beam
The blue beam
cards.explain: Only the failure of the red beam makes the display go monochrome.

cards.question: Which part of the display is affected when one input signal to a display unit is lost
options: Only the warning labels of the display
Only the indication of the related parameter
The whole of the display unit
cards.explain: Only the indication belonging to the missing signal goes away.

cards.question: On which panels does a helicopter crew find the engine alerts and the navigation picture
options: The alert on the centre panel and the picture on the outboard panels
The alert on the outboard panels and the picture on the centre panel
Both of them on the centre instrument panel
cards.explain: Engine and warning indications sit in the centre while the flight and navigation displays sit in front of the crew.

cards.question: Where does the information of a primary flight display appear when that display goes blank in flight
options: On the navigation display
On the opposite primary flight display
On the centre engine display
cards.explain: The information of a failed primary flight display is switched automatically onto the navigation display.

cards.question: A pilot's primary flight display goes dark, so what must he do before the information comes back?
options: Nothing, because the transfer happens on its own
Select the cross side computer on his control panel
Nothing, because the failed screen restarts on its own
cards.explain: The takeover by another screen is automatic, so no crew action is needed to get the information back.

cards.question: A display unit that switched itself off because of overheat has cooled down again, so what happens next?
options: The picture comes back without any crew action
The picture comes back without the raster colours
The picture stays off until the crew resets it
cards.explain: Once it is back within the limits the unit activates its display again on its own.

cards.question: Which failure fits a screen that has lost its colours but still shows every item of information
options: A total loss of the display unit
The second step of the overheat reaction
The first step of the overheat reaction
cards.explain: Losing the raster colours while keeping all the information is the first overheat step.

cards.question: What comes next when a screen has already dropped its raster colours and the cause has not been cleared
options: The screen switches to the cross side computer
The screen switches itself off
The screen drops its strokes as well
cards.explain: The two step reaction goes on to its second step, in which the display is switched off.

cards.question: A pilot reports that the green symbols have gone and nothing on the screen looks white any more, so what has happened?
options: The raster colours have been switched off
An input signal to the display has been lost
One electron beam of the tube has failed
cards.explain: Loss of one beam removes both the white and everything drawn in that beam's colour.

cards.question: Why is the display turned monochrome rather than left with its remaining colours when the red beam fails
options: Because the warning labels are red and must not be allowed to disappear
Because the warning labels are red and must not be allowed to flicker
Because the remaining colours would produce too much heat
cards.explain: Warnings are drawn in red, so losing that beam would hide them unless the whole picture is made monochrome.

cards.question: Why is a failure of the red beam treated differently from the failure of another beam?
options: Because it carries more of the picture than the others
Because it produces more heat than the others
Because the information it carries must never be lost
cards.explain: The red beam draws the warning labels, which may not be allowed to disappear.

cards.question: Two screens have lost a beam and only one of them went monochrome, so what separates the two cases?
options: The monochrome one lost the beam that draws the green symbols
The monochrome one lost the beam that draws the warnings
The monochrome one lost two beams instead of one
cards.explain: Only the loss of the beam that draws the red warning labels turns the whole picture monochrome.

cards.question: What is wrong when a single scale on the primary flight display is replaced by a flag
options: The input signal for that parameter is not available
One electron beam of the display tube has failed
The display unit has started its overheat reaction
cards.explain: A flag in place of one parameter is the sign that the input signal for it is missing.

cards.question: Several indications are gone and flags stand in their place, so what does this tell the engineer?
options: The display unit has begun to overheat
The display unit has an electron beam failure
The signals for those parameters are missing
cards.explain: Flags are the signature of missing input signals, not of a fault inside the display unit.

cards.question: One screen has lost some of its symbols and another shows flags in their place, so are the causes the same?
options: No, the flags come from a failed beam and the lost symbols from missing signals
Yes, both of them come from a failure inside the display unit
No, the flags come from missing signals and the lost symbols from a failed beam
cards.explain: A flag marks a missing input, while symbols that vanish without a flag point to a beam failure in the tube.

cards.question: Which display units normally show the ND contents
options: The inboard display units
The outboard display units
The lower display unit
cards.explain: The two inboard display units normally carry the navigation display contents.

cards.question: Which movement of the pilot is avoided by the use of a head up display
options: Turning his head from the cockpit window to the overhead panel
Lowering his head from the cockpit window to the displays below
Lowering his head from the cockpit window to the control pedestal
cards.explain: The pilot no longer has to lower his head to the conventional displays below the window.

cards.question: Under which condition is the head up display meant to give guidance information on the ground and at take-off and landing
options: When the landing gear is extended
When the autopilot is engaged
When visibility is reduced
cards.explain: That guidance is provided for the case of reduced visibility.

cards.question: Which automatic procedure is the head up display used to monitor?
options: The auto approach
The auto land flare
The auto thrust reduction
cards.explain: One stated purpose is to monitor the auto approach.

cards.question: How does the head up display help the pilot at an airfield that has no instrument landing system
options: It gives the pilot information for the visual approach
It gives the pilot the localizer deviation
It gives the pilot the glide slope deviation
cards.explain: Where no instrument landing system exists the head up display supports the visual approach.

cards.question: Visibility is poor on the approach, so why can the pilot keep his eyes on the outside world?
options: The information is presented on a screen at head height
The information is read out to him by a synthetic voice
The information is presented on a screen below the window
cards.explain: Because the screen sits at head height he can read the guidance without looking down into the cockpit.

cards.question: Why does the picture seen on the head up display change as the aircraft goes from take-off to cruise?
options: Because the display depends on the selected control panel
Because the display depends on the flight configuration
Because the display depends on the available input signals
cards.explain: The pilot is given different displays according to the flight configuration.

cards.question: Which segment of the head up display image is used while the automatic system flies the aircraft down to the runway
options: The ground roll information segment
The approach trajectory deviation segment
The system messages segment
cards.explain: Monitoring an automatic approach calls for the segment that shows how far the aircraft is off the trajectory.

cards.question: Why can a parameter be absent from a display at one point in the flight and present at another
options: Because the control panel is reset between the flight phases
Because much data is only shown in the flight phase it belongs to
Because the display units are tested one after the other in flight
cards.explain: The flexibility of the screen lets much data be displayed only during the respective flight phase.

cards.question: A mechanic finds a glass cockpit aircraft with no separate DME or marker indicator fitted, so what does that tell him?
options: Those two systems are not installed
Those indications are handled by the EFIS
Those indications are only on the standby panel
cards.explain: The DME indicator and the marker lights are both among the instruments the EFIS replaces.

cards.question: Which display is affected by four of the five basic EFIS control panel functions
options: The lower display unit
The ND
The PFD
cards.explain: Mode, range, TCAS and additional information selections all act on the ND, leaving only baro correction for the PFD.

cards.question: A pilot selects TCAS on the EFIS control panel, so where does the traffic picture appear?
options: On the PFD
On the ND
On the standby instrument
cards.explain: Selection of the TCAS indication is a basic function and the indication appears on the ND.

cards.question: A mechanic moves to a new aircraft type and finds an unfamiliar switch on its EFIS control panel, so how should he treat it?
options: As a type specific additional function
As a basic function common to every type
As a function that acts on the standby instruments
cards.explain: Beyond the common basic functions, many types carry some type specific additional functions.

cards.question: An outboard display unit goes blank in flight, so what happens to the PFD picture?
options: It can be switched to the inboard display unit
It is moved to the standby attitude instrument
It is lost until the display unit is replaced
cards.explain: On failure of the outboard display the PFD can be switched automatically or manually to the inboard DU.

cards.question: In which two ways can the PFD reach the inboard display unit after an outboard display failure
options: Automatically or manually
Manually from either seat
Automatically after a delay
cards.explain: The switching to the inboard DU can be done automatically or manually.

cards.question: A pilot wants his navigation picture on the lower display unit, so how does he get it there?
options: He selects it on the source select module
It appears there automatically
He switches it there manually
cards.explain: The captain's or F/O's ND can be switched onto the lower display unit manually.

cards.question: Both outboard display units fail, so what does the crew lose on the inboard screens?
options: The normal warning indications
The normal navigation pictures
The normal engine indications
cards.explain: The inboard units normally show the ND, so taking the PFDs onto them costs the crew those navigation pictures.

cards.question: On which display unit is the PFD normally shown
options: The outboard one
The inboard pair
The lower one
cards.explain: The PFD is normally presented on the outboard display unit.

cards.question: From which viewpoint does the navigation display present the aircraft situation
options: From behind
From above
From the side
cards.explain: The ND shows the situation of the aircraft seen from above.

cards.question: Which conventional instrument is fully replaced by the navigation display
options: The HSI
The ADI
The RMI
cards.explain: The ND fully replaces the horizontal situation indicator.

cards.question: During which part of the flight does the ND ILS mode indicate its parameters
options: During the ILS approach
During the initial climb out
During the taxi out
cards.explain: The ILS mode indicates ILS parameters during the ILS approach.

cards.question: A pilot selects the ILS mode on his ND, so which two deviations does he then see?
options: Localizer and track
Glideslope and vertical speed
Localizer and glideslope
cards.explain: The ILS mode of the ND indicates localizer and glideslope deviation.

cards.question: Which three items are added in the navigation sector mode of the ND
options: The waypoint, the range selection and the route indication
The range selection, the localizer scale and the waypoint
The waypoint, the glideslope scale and the route indication
cards.explain: The nav sector mode additionally displays waypoint, range selection and route indication.

cards.question: A pilot's PFD appears on the inboard screen in flight, so what has most likely happened?
options: The normal display unit has failed
The control panel has been reset
The baro correction has been changed
cards.explain: The PFD is switched to the inboard display unit on failure of its normal one.

cards.question: What is the small aircraft symbol on the navigation display there for
options: To show the attitude of the aircraft
To show the aircraft type being flown
To act as a reference for the picture
cards.explain: The small aircraft symbol is used as a reference and is normally in the centre of the screen.

cards.question: Which navigation point does the basic waypoint data on the ND refer to
options: The destination one
The next one
The last one passed
cards.explain: The waypoint data gives information about the next navigation point.

cards.question: A trainee asks what ground speed on the navigation display means, so what is the answer?
options: The speed limit on the ground
The speed through the air
The speed above the ground
cards.explain: Ground speed is the speed above the ground.

cards.question: Which ND parameter comes from somewhere other than the navigation systems
options: The wind velocity
The heading
The ground speed
cards.explain: Apart from the heading, all information on the ND is based on data from the navigation systems.

cards.question: Where on the navigation display is the small aircraft symbol normally shown?
options: At the edge of the selected range
At the top of the compass rose
In the centre of the screen
cards.explain: The small aircraft symbol is normally displayed in the centre of the screen, while the top of the compass rose is where the actual heading is read.

cards.question: Which aircraft system supplies the parameters shown in the ND ILS mode
options: The air data computer system
The flight management computer system
The instrument landing system
cards.explain: The ILS mode indicates parameters coming from the instrument landing system.

cards.question: A route indication is missing from a navigation display in the sector mode, so which system should be suspected?
options: The instrument landing system
The ground proximity warning system
The flight management system
cards.explain: The route indication in that mode is supplied by the flight management system.

cards.question: Which system supplies the AFCS information shown on the PFD
options: The navigation system
The air data system
The autoflight system
cards.explain: The AFCS information on the PFD comes from the autoflight system.

cards.question: The pressure setting on a PFD will not change, so which control should be suspected first?
options: The baro correction on the EFIS control panel
The mode selection on the EFIS control panel
The range selection on the EFIS control panel
cards.explain: The pressure setting on the PFD is the baro correction, which is set from the EFIS control panel.

cards.question: Which two deviations are shown together on the PFD in the ILS mode
options: The localizer and the glide slope
The glide slope and the radio height
The localizer and the vertical speed
cards.explain: The ILS mode displays the localizer and the glide slope alongside the ILS source and the marker.

cards.question: A mechanic is asked why there is no separate ILS indicator in an EFIS cockpit, so what should he say?
options: The ILS is only monitored from the standby instrument
The PFD takes that job in the ILS mode
The ILS picture is only available on the ground
cards.explain: The PFD itself is used as the display for the instrument landing system.

cards.question: Why does the wind indication stay on the navigation display whatever mode is selected
options: Because the control panel cannot reach that part of the screen
Because it is one of the basic items always present
Because it is only drawn by the air data computer
cards.explain: Wind direction and velocity is one of the basic pieces of information present no matter what is selected.

cards.question: A pilot changes the ND mode and loses an indication he wanted, so what does that tell him about it?
options: It is not one of the basic always present items
It is only shown while the autopilot is engaged
It is only driven by the flight management system
cards.explain: Only the listed basic pieces of information are present no matter what is selected on the control panel.

cards.question: The navigation systems feeding an ND are lost but the heading is still drawn, so what does that say about the heading?
options: It is the one item that is not navigation data
It is navigation data like every one of the others
It is drawn by the flight management computer
cards.explain: Apart from the heading, all information on the ND is based on data from the navigation systems.

cards.question: Why can the localizer deviation be read on the PFD and on the ND at the same time
options: Because the ND copies the whole PFD picture in that mode
Because the ILS feeds only the navigation display units
Because both displays can present ILS parameters
cards.explain: The PFD has an ILS mode and the ND has an ILS mode, and both show the localizer indication.

cards.question: Why does selecting the navigation sector mode change what the pilot can read on the display
options: Because that mode removes the compass rose from the picture
Because that mode moves the picture onto the lower display unit
Because that mode adds flight management data
cards.explain: The nav sector mode adds the waypoint, range selection and route indication, all from the FMS.

cards.question: A pilot swaps from the ILS mode to the navigation sector mode, so what replaces the ILS parameters on his display?
options: Inertial reference information
Flight management information
Radio altimeter information
cards.explain: The ILS mode shows ILS parameters while the nav sector mode adds information from the flight management system.

cards.question: How do the pushbuttons appear while everything is operating normally
options: Amber
White
Dark
cards.explain: All pushbuttons are dark during normal operation.

cards.question: Which colour is used when an immediate action is necessary
options: Red
Amber
White
cards.explain: Red is the colour used when an immediate action is necessary.

cards.question: Which colour indicates the normal operation of a backup system
options: Green
Blue
White
cards.explain: Green indicates the normal operation of a backup system.

cards.question: Which colour indicates the normal operation of a temporarily used system
options: Green
Amber
Blue
cards.explain: Blue indicates the normal operation of a temporarily used system.

cards.question: Where is the centralised caution panel installed
options: On the centre pedestal
At the pilots' eye level
On the overhead panel
cards.explain: The centralised caution panel is installed at the pilots' eye level.

cards.question: Where is the local warning light of a system covered by the centralised caution panel fitted
options: On the glareshield
On the centralised caution panel
On the overhead panel
cards.explain: The local warning light sits on the overhead panel while the centralised panel sits in view.

cards.question: What two forms of information do central warning displays give the flight crew
options: Text and aural information
Graphic and tactile information
Text and graphic information
cards.explain: The displays provide text and graphic information.

cards.question: What kind of system is ECAM
options: A flight management system
A central warning system
An autoflight system
cards.explain: ECAM is a central warning system.

cards.question: Which two displays make up ECAM in the cockpit
options: The primary flight display and the system display
The engine/warning display and the navigation display
The engine/warning display and the system display
cards.explain: ECAM is present as the E/WD and the SD.

cards.question: Apart from calling up pages and messages, which display property is set from the ECAM control panel
options: The contrast ratio
The brightness
The refresh rate
cards.explain: The control panel is used to control the brightness of the ECAM display units.

cards.question: What is simulated when the TO CONFIG pushbutton is used
options: The take-off power configuration
The approach configuration
The emergency electrical configuration
cards.explain: The TO CONFIG pushbutton simulates the T/O power configuration.

cards.question: Which two kinds of page does the SD of an ECAM installation show
options: The engine and warning pages
The system and status pages
The memo and alert pages
cards.explain: The SD shows the system and the status pages.

cards.question: How many system pages are provided in total
options: Five
Eight
Twelve
cards.explain: One of twelve system pages can be shown.

cards.question: What happens to the related system when an illuminated pushbutton is pressed
options: Its switching state is changed
Its warning is only acknowledged
Its light test is only started
cards.explain: Pressing the illuminated pushbutton changes the state of the switch behind it.

cards.question: A pushbutton on the overhead panel has just lit up, so what does that tell the crew?
options: The pushbutton lamp is being tested by the crew
A local warning or an abnormal switching state exists
The system has returned to its normal switching state
cards.explain: A pushbutton lights only for a local warning or for an abnormal switching state.

cards.question: Why are the pushbutton lights given a colour code
options: To make abnormal conditions easy to identify
To show which bus supplies each panel
To group the pushbuttons by aircraft system
cards.explain: The colour code exists to help in the easy identification of abnormal conditions.

cards.question: Besides an abnormal pushbutton position, which condition is shown by a white light
options: A maintenance operation
A backup system running
A failure needing awareness
cards.explain: White covers a pushbutton in an abnormal position or a maintenance operation.

cards.question: Which shortcoming of the master caution and master warning lights led to a centralised panel
options: They cannot be cancelled once they are on
They do not stay on long enough to be seen
They do not say which system is affected
cards.explain: The master lights give no information about which system is affected or which local light is on.

cards.question: What does the centralised caution panel tell the crew about a fault
options: How many flight hours remain before rectification
Which circuit breaker has tripped
Which particular system it is in
cards.explain: The panel indicates a fault in a particular system.

cards.question: How is the master caution light cancelled
options: By pressing the local warning light
By switching off the affected system
By pressing its light cover
cards.explain: The master caution light is cancelled by pressing its light cover.

cards.question: Why does the crew cancel the master caution light rather than leave it on?
options: So that another fault can be indicated
So that the local warning light goes out
So that the centralised panel can be tested
cards.explain: Cancelling the light frees it so that a further fault can be indicated.

cards.question: What does the information on a central warning display describe
options: The flight phase being computed
The present failure condition
The maintenance action already carried out
cards.explain: The displays describe the present failure condition.

cards.question: An engineer compares the central warning systems of two different aircraft types, so what will he mostly find?
options: Different functions under the same name
The same function under different names
The same name and the same hardware
cards.explain: Central warning systems in different types generally share the function but not the name.

cards.question: Under what condition is the symbol ADV displayed
options: When a status page becomes available
When ECAM is working as a mono display
When a caution message is cancelled
cards.explain: ADV appears when ECAM is working as a mono display, that is with only one display.

cards.question: One of the two ECAM displays has failed, so which symbol appears in the lower part of the engine/warning display?
options: STS
RCL
ADV
cards.explain: With only one ECAM display left, ECAM works as a mono display and ADV is shown.

cards.question: Which two pages are combined in the cruise page
options: The air and hydraulic pages
The engine and air pages
The engine and fuel pages
cards.explain: The cruise page consists of the engine and air pages.

cards.question: A memo message has to be read, so which display and which part of it does the crew use?
options: The lower part of the system display
The upper part of the engine/warning display
The lower part of the engine/warning display
cards.explain: Memo messages are in the lower part of the E/WD.

cards.question: Which three things can be done to warnings and messages from the ECAM control panel
options: Record, print or transmit them
Cancel, delete or call them up again
Dim, enlarge or colour them
cards.explain: The panel cancels, deletes or calls up again the warnings and messages.

cards.question: In which position must the slats and flaps be for the take-off configuration check to pass
options: In the T/O range
In the fully extended position
In the fully retracted position
cards.explain: The check requires the slats and flaps to be in the T/O range.

cards.question: What condition of the speed brakes is required by the take-off configuration check
options: They must be extended
They must be retracted
They must be armed
cards.explain: The check requires the speed brakes to be retracted.

cards.question: What condition of the wheel brakes is required by the take-off configuration check
options: They must be released
They must not be overheated
They must be parked
cards.explain: The check requires the wheel brakes not to be OVHT.

cards.question: The take-off configuration check is run with a cabin door still open, so what will the crew find?
options: The check will be bypassed automatically
The normal message will not appear
The master caution will be inhibited
cards.explain: Door closed is one of the items checked, so an open door prevents the normal result.

cards.question: A continuous aural alert is sounding and the crew wants it silenced, so which ECAM control panel pushbutton is used?
options: CLR
RCL
EMER CANC
cards.explain: The EMER CANC pushbutton cancels the aural warnings.

cards.question: What happens when the ALL pushbutton is pressed and held
options: The status page is called up again after five seconds
The system pages are frozen on the display
The system pages are called up at one second intervals
cards.explain: Pressing and holding ALL calls up the system pages at one second intervals.

cards.question: What happens when the ALL pushbutton is pressed only briefly
options: The displayed system page is deleted
The system page moves forward by one page
The system pages cycle continuously
cards.explain: A brief press moves the system page forward by one page.

cards.question: When does the light in the CLR pushbutton come on
options: When the recall function has just been used
When warning, caution or status messages appear
When the system pages are being cycled by the crew
cards.explain: The CLR light comes on when warning, caution or status messages appear on the ECAM display.

cards.question: Which message is removed each time the CLR pushbutton is pushed
options: Every warning at once
The warning at the top
The oldest warning in the list
cards.explain: Each push of CLR deletes the warning at the top.

cards.question: What reappears on the display after the last clearance has been made with CLR
options: The memo messages
The status page
The caution messages
cards.explain: After the last clearance the memo messages reappear.

cards.question: How long after the status pushbutton is used do the normal messages return when no status messages are present
options: After 10 seconds
After 5 seconds
After 2 seconds
cards.explain: With no status messages present the normal messages are displayed again after 5 seconds.

cards.question: The brightness of the engine/warning and system displays has to be changed, so which panel is used?
options: The ECAM control panel
The EICAS display select panel
The centralised caution panel
cards.explain: Brightness is controlled from the ECAM control panel.

cards.question: How many system pages can be shown on the system display at any one time
options: Four
One
Two
cards.explain: Only one of the twelve system pages can be displayed at any one time.

cards.question: Which two air temperatures are shown among the permanent data on a system page
options: TAT and EGT
SAT and ITT
TAT and SAT
cards.explain: The permanent data includes TAT and SAT.

cards.question: Which item is shown as an alternative to the G-load among the permanent data
options: The static air temperature
The selected altitude
The gross weight
cards.explain: The permanent data ends with G-load or selected altitude.

cards.question: A pilot needs the total air temperature while a system page is up, so where is it shown?
options: On the upper part of the page
On the lower part of the page
On the engine/warning display
cards.explain: TAT is one of the permanent data items on the lower part of the system page.

cards.question: A system is working normally but its pushbutton has been left out of its normal switching position, so what will the crew see on that pushbutton?
options: It will stay dark because no fault exists
It will be lit even though no fault exists
It will flash until the fault is cleared
cards.explain: A pushbutton lights for an abnormal switching state as well as for a local warning, so it is lit with no fault present.

cards.question: A pushbutton carries an amber FAULT legend, so how urgent is the crew action?
options: Action is not needed at all
Action is needed at once
Action is needed but not at once
cards.explain: Amber is used when action is required but not necessarily at once.

cards.question: A pushbutton is lit in a colour that reports normal operation, so which two colours could it be?
options: Green or blue
Red or amber
Amber or white
cards.explain: Green and blue are the two colours for normal operation, green for a backup system and blue for a temporarily used system.

cards.question: A system has been selected off and no fault exists, so which colour will its pushbutton show?
options: Amber
Green
White
cards.explain: A pushbutton left in an abnormal position is coded white, and no failure is being reported.

cards.question: Which two colours on a pushbutton both report a failure of some kind
options: White and green
Red and amber
Green and blue
cards.explain: Red and amber are the two colours for a failure, red needing immediate action and amber only awareness.

cards.question: A fault occurs in a system whose local light is on the overhead panel out of the pilot's sight, so how does the crew learn which system it is?
options: The overhead local light is repeated on the glareshield
The master caution light names the affected system
The centralised caution panel names the affected system
cards.explain: The master light says only that something is wrong, so the panel at eye level is what identifies the system.

cards.question: A pilot sees STS in the lower part of the engine/warning display but no status page is being shown, so where will that status page appear once it is called up?
options: On the system display
On the engine/warning display
On the centralised caution panel
cards.explain: STS says a status page is available and the status page is displayed on the SD.

cards.question: A page made up of the engine and air pages is on the system display, so where is the aircraft in its flight?
options: In the take-off run
In the cruise
In the approach
cards.explain: The cruise page, which consists of the engine and air pages, is the one shown in cruise flight.

cards.question: A crew member has cleared several caution messages with CLR and then wants to read them again, so what must be done?
options: Press RCL to recall them
Press CLR again to restore them
Press STS to bring up the status page
cards.explain: CLR deletes the messages one by one and RCL is the pushbutton that recalls them.

cards.question: The status pushbutton has been pressed and after a short time the normal display returns on its own, so what does that tell the crew?
options: The status page has been cleared by CLR
The ECAM is working as a mono display
No status messages are present
cards.explain: The normal messages come back by themselves only when there are no status messages to show.

cards.question: A level 3 alert has triggered an aural warning and the master warning lights, and the crew uses EMER CANC, so what is left showing on the ECAM?
options: Nothing at all is left on the display
Only the system page is cancelled
The message on the display stays
cards.explain: EMER CANC removes the aural warnings, the master warning lights and the caution messages, so a warning message itself is not in that list.

cards.question: STS is showing on the engine/warning display and the crew presses the status pushbutton, so what appears?
options: The normal messages, since no status messages exist
The status page with its messages
The cruise page with its engine data
cards.explain: STS means a status page is available, so pressing the pushbutton brings that page up rather than returning the normal messages.

cards.question: A pilot wants to see a second system page while one is already up, so what happens to the page already displayed?
options: It is replaced, because only one can be shown at a time
It stays, because two pages can be shown side by side
It stays, because the second page opens on the E/WD
cards.explain: Only one of the twelve system pages can be displayed at any one time.

cards.question: A pilot reading a system page wants the gross weight, so where on that page does he look?
options: On the right side, among the inoperative systems
On the upper part, among the engine parameters
On the lower part, among the permanent data
cards.explain: GW is among the permanent data on the lower part of the system page.

cards.question: Which aircraft condition is associated with a level 3 alert
options: A configuration to monitor
An abnormal configuration
An emergency configuration
cards.explain: Level 3 is the warning raised for an emergency configuration.

cards.question: Which aircraft condition is associated with a level 2 alert
options: An emergency configuration
A configuration to monitor
An abnormal configuration
cards.explain: Level 2 is the caution raised for an abnormal configuration.

cards.question: What priority do level 3 warnings carry
options: The highest priority
A medium priority
The lowest priority
cards.explain: Level 3 warnings are the warnings with the highest priority.

cards.question: How quickly must the crew react to a level 3 warning
options: Without any delay
Before the next flight phase
Before the next scheduled check
cards.explain: A level 3 warning is a real emergency and the crew must react immediately.

cards.question: What influence does a level 2 caution have on the flight
options: An influence only during the approach
No direct influence
A direct and immediate influence
cards.explain: Level 2 cautions have no direct influence on the flight.

cards.question: What is required of the crew when a level 2 caution appears
options: Greater attention
An immediate reaction
No reaction at all
cards.explain: A level 2 caution calls for greater attention.

cards.question: On which display do level 1 cautions appear
options: The centralised caution panel
The engine/warning display
The system display
cards.explain: Level 1 cautions appear on the E/WD.

cards.question: Which indications are absent for a level 1 caution
options: Memo messages and status messages
Aural alarms and warning lights
Text messages and system pages
cards.explain: There are no aural alarms or warning lights for a level 1 caution.

cards.question: Which flight phase does the flight warning system select by default when it has no data
options: The preflight phase
The approach phase
The cruise phase
cards.explain: With the data unavailable the FWS defaults to the cruise phase.

cards.question: Which parameters are permanently displayed on the upper EICAS
options: The status information
The secondary engine parameters
The primary engine parameters
cards.explain: The upper EICAS permanently displays the primary engine parameters.

cards.question: How many EFIS/EICAS interface units are fitted
options: Four
Three
Two
cards.explain: There are three EFIS/EICAS interface units.

cards.question: Which two parameters are the primary engine parameters on the EICAS display
options: N2 rotor speed and fuel flow in kilogrammes
N1 rotor speed and exhaust gas temperature
Oil pressure and oil temperature in degrees
cards.explain: The primary engine parameters are the N1 rotor speed and the exhaust gas temperature.

cards.question: Which colour is used for a Level A warning message in the alert message field
options: Red
White
Amber
cards.explain: Level A warning messages are shown in red.

cards.question: How many manual snapshots can be stored for each system
options: Up to 5
Up to 10
Up to 3
cards.explain: Storage is available for up to 5 manual snapshots per system.

cards.question: A snapshot has just been taken because a parameter went outside its preset value, so where is it kept?
options: In the manual event non-volatile memory
In the auto event non-volatile memory
In the real time data storage buffer
cards.explain: Auto snapshots go to the auto event non-volatile memory.

cards.question: Which alert level is classified as a warning rather than a caution
options: Level 2
Level 3
Level 1
cards.explain: Level 3 carries the title warnings while levels 2 and 1 are cautions.

cards.question: In what manner does the master warning light behave for a level 3 warning
options: It flashes
It stays dark
It stays steady
cards.explain: The master warning light flashes for a level 3 warning.

cards.question: Besides the level 3 warning itself, which page may be shown if one is available
options: A system page, if one is available
A cruise page, if one is available
A status page, if one is available
cards.explain: If available, a system page may also appear on the SD.

cards.question: How many chimes are sounded for a level 2 caution
options: None
Three
One
cards.explain: A level 2 caution is given with a single chime.

cards.question: What kind of system does a level 1 caution draw attention to
options: A serviceable system temporarily switched off
A defective system needed for the flight to continue
A defective system not required for the flight to continue
cards.explain: Level 1 cautions point at a defective system which is not required for the flight to continue.

cards.question: A caution message has appeared on the engine/warning display with no sound and no light, so which level has been reached?
options: Level 3
Level 1
Level 2
cards.explain: Level 1 is the only level with no aural alarm and no warning light.

cards.question: From which system does the flight warning system take its compressed or not compressed signal
options: The air data system
The brake control system
The landing gear system
cards.explain: The gear compressed or not compressed information comes from the L/G system.

cards.question: Which number is given to the default flight phase of the flight warning system
cards.explain: The default is the cruise phase, numbered 8.

cards.question: Which four items can be shown on the lower EICAS
options: Primary engine parameters, synoptics, memo messages and maintenance pages
Secondary engine parameters, system pages, status information and alert messages
Secondary engine parameters, synoptics, status information and maintenance pages
cards.explain: The lower EICAS can show secondary engine parameters, synoptics, status information and maintenance pages.

cards.question: Which panel brings synoptics and status information onto the lower screen
options: The ECAM control panel
The EICAS display select panel
The centralised caution panel
cards.explain: Synoptics and status information are selected with the EICAS display select panel (EDSP).

cards.question: Through which unit are the maintenance pages called up on the lower EICAS
options: The EDSP
The EIU
The CMC
cards.explain: The maintenance pages are called up via the CMC.

cards.question: Which data appears on the lower EICAS immediately after power-up
options: The primary engine data
The status information
The secondary engine data
cards.explain: After power-up the lower EICAS shows the secondary engine data.

cards.question: Which data bus supplies the EICAS display units
options: An ARINC 629 data bus
An ARINC 573 data bus
An ARINC 429 data bus
cards.explain: The display units are supplied via an ARINC 429 data bus.

cards.question: A message shows in the alert message field in amber and indented, so which level is it?
options: Level B caution
Level D memo
Level C advisory
cards.explain: Only the Level C advisory messages are both amber and indented.

cards.question: Why is information that is not required removed from the EICAS display
options: To reduce the heat produced by the screens
To save electrical power in the display units
To maintain a quiet, dark flight deck
cards.explain: Removing unneeded information is what keeps the flight deck quiet and dark.

cards.question: What makes an automatic snapshot occur for a system
options: Parameters that exceed preset values
Selection of the real time display mode
A request made by the maintenance crew
cards.explain: An auto snapshot is taken when parameters go beyond their preset values.

cards.question: What causes a manual snapshot of the real time format to be taken
options: An action by the flight or maintenance crew
A parameter that goes out of its limits
A report sent to the printer or to ACARS
cards.explain: A manual snapshot follows an action by the flight or maintenance crew.

cards.question: An engine fire breaks out in flight, so what must the crew do about it?
options: Note it and continue, as the flight is not affected
React before the next flight phase begins
React immediately, as it is a real emergency
cards.explain: Engine fire is a level 3 warning and a level 3 warning is a real emergency needing an immediate reaction.

cards.question: A level 3 warning and a level 1 caution are annunciated at the same moment, so which one is handled first?
options: The caution, which has the highest priority
The warning, which has the highest priority
Either one, since the two carry the same priority
cards.explain: Level 3 warnings are the warnings with the highest priority.

cards.question: An instructor asks what separates a warning from a caution in practice, so what is the difference in the reaction required?
options: A warning needs an immediate reaction, a caution does not
A caution needs an immediate reaction, a warning does not
Each one needs the same immediate reaction from the crew
cards.explain: The level 3 warning is a real emergency needing an immediate reaction, while the level 2 caution has no direct influence on the flight.

cards.question: A single chime sounds and the master caution light comes on, so what does the crew know about the failure?
options: It is a real emergency needing an immediate reaction
It has no direct influence on the flight
It gives no aural alarm and no warning light
cards.explain: A single chime with the master caution light is a level 2, and level 2 failures have no direct influence on the flight.

cards.question: A failure needs greater attention but no immediate reaction, so which aural alert will the crew hear?
options: A single chime
No sound at all
A continuous alarm
cards.explain: Greater attention without an immediate reaction is a level 2, and a level 2 is given with a single chime.

cards.question: A system that the flight does not need has become defective, so what will the crew hear?
options: A continuous alarm from the master warning
Nothing, as there is no aural alarm
A single chime from the master caution
cards.explain: A defective system not required to continue the flight is a level 1 caution, and level 1 has no aural alarm.

cards.question: A recorder fault and a stall warning occur in the same flight, so how do the two alerts differ in what the crew gets?
options: Each one gives an aural alarm but only one gives a light
One gives a single chime while the other gives no sound
One gives no sound or light while the other gives both
cards.explain: A recorder fault is a level 1 with no aural alarm or warning light, while a stall warning is a level 3 with an aural alarm and a flashing master warning light.

cards.question: Which indication may be given at all three alert levels if one is available
options: A light coming on at the eye level
A system page on the system display
A chime sounding from the loudspeaker
cards.explain: Each of the three levels carries the note that a system page may also appear on the SD if available.

cards.question: A technician wants to bring the maintenance pages up on the lower EICAS, so why will the display select panel not do it?
options: Because that panel only works after the aircraft is powered up
Because that panel only selects synoptics and status information
Because that panel only selects the primary engine parameters
cards.explain: The EDSP selects synoptics and status information while the maintenance pages come via the CMC.

cards.question: An aircraft has just been powered up and no selection has been made, so what is seen on the two EICAS display units?
options: Primary engine data above and secondary engine data below
Primary engine data above and the status information below
Secondary engine data above and primary engine data below
cards.explain: After power-up the upper unit shows the primary and the lower unit the secondary engine data.

cards.question: All three interface units have failed, so what will the EICAS display units show?
options: Nothing, because all the data to the screens passes through them
Primary engine data only, taken direct from the engines
Maintenance pages only, taken direct from the CMC
cards.explain: The display units are fed by one of the three EIUs, and all the important systems supply their data to those units.

cards.question: A pilot needs the secondary engine parameters while a synoptic is up on the lower EICAS, so what must happen on that display?
options: The synoptic and the parameters appear together
The upper display must be used to show them
The synoptic must be deselected to show them
cards.explain: The lower EICAS carries the secondary parameters, synoptics, status and maintenance pages in turn, while the upper one is permanently the primary parameters.

cards.question: A synoptic is wanted on the lower EICAS straight after power-up, so what must be done?
options: It must be called up through the maintenance computer
It must be selected on the display select panel
It is already there after power-up
cards.explain: After power-up the lower unit shows the secondary engine data, so a synoptic has to be selected on the EDSP.

cards.question: The upper EICAS display unit is showing data that cannot be deselected, so what is on it?
options: The secondary engine parameters
The synoptics of the systems
The primary engine parameters
cards.explain: The upper EICAS permanently displays the primary engine parameters, the selectable items being on the lower unit.

cards.question: Every indication that is not needed has been removed from the main EICAS display, so which two groups are still shown?
options: The primary engine parameters and the fuel system data
The cabin altitude and the duct pressure readouts
The landing gear status and the flap indications
cards.explain: Those two groups are the ones stated to show at all times.

cards.question: A caution and an advisory both show in amber in the alert message field, so how is the advisory told apart?
options: It is flashing
It is underlined
It is indented
cards.explain: The advisory is the amber message that is indented.

cards.question: An engine exceedance occurs while the aeroplane stands with its parking brake set, so what becomes of the event?
options: It is lost, since the brake has to be released first
It is lost, since two engines have to be running
It is stored, since that storage is not inhibited
cards.explain: Engine exceedance page storage is not inhibited, so the running and brake conditions do not apply to it.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the GPWS
options: To warn the flight crew when the aircraft comes too close to the ground
To warn the flight crew of another aircraft on a conflicting track
To warn the flight crew of a windshear encountered on approach
cards.explain: The system warns the crew when the aircraft mistakenly comes too close to the ground.

cards.question: By which two means is the basic GPWS warning given to the pilot
options: A master caution and a single chime
An aural alert and annunciator lights
A flashing display and a stick shaker
cards.explain: The warning is an aural alert plus annunciator lights in front of the pilot.

cards.question: On which display does the enhanced ground proximity warning system show the surrounding terrain
options: On the navigation display
On the primary flight display
On the engine indication display
cards.explain: The terrain picture is presented on the navigation display.

cards.question: Which three parts are the main parts of a ground proximity warning system
options: One warning computer, a radio altimeter and a speaker
One warning computer, indications and inhibit switches
Two warning computers, indications and a control panel
cards.explain: The computer, the indications and the inhibit switches are the main parts.

cards.question: A basic GPWS is checked, so at which radio altitude does its operative range begin?
options: 50 ft
30 ft
10 ft
cards.explain: The operative range of the basic GPWS begins at 30 ft radio altitude.

cards.question: An aircraft is fitted with the enhanced system, so which two functions does it have on top of the basic modes?
options: Terrain awareness alerting and display, and terrain clearance floor
Radio altitude callouts, and the modulation of alerting envelopes
Windshear alerting for take-off, and excessive bank angle alerting
cards.explain: Those two are the additional functions listed for the enhanced system.

cards.question: The enhanced computer needs the height above the ground for its warning calculation, so which unit supplies it?
options: The instrument landing system
The digital air data computer
The downward looking radio altimeter
cards.explain: The downward looking radio altimeter is the primary sensor for the warning calculation.

cards.question: A ground proximity alert sounds in the flight deck, so what kind of voice is heard?
options: A synthetic voice
A rising tone sequence
A recorded crew voice
cards.explain: The aural alert uses a synthetic voice.

cards.question: One class of aircraft only rarely carries a ground proximity warning system, so which class is it?
options: Four-engined aeroplanes
Twin-engined aeroplanes
Helicopters
cards.explain: The system is rarely installed in helicopters.

cards.question: Where else are GPWS alert messages presented in some aircraft
options: On the engine indication display
On the navigation displays
On the primary flight displays
cards.explain: Some aircraft add alert messages on the primary flight displays.

cards.question: In which aeroplanes is the ground proximity warning system installed
options: In the very small ones only
In all of them without any exception
In all of them except the very small ones
cards.explain: Every aeroplane except the very small ones carries the system.

cards.question: Which signal can the terrain functions of the enhanced system do without
options: The glide slope deviation
The radio altitude
The barometric altitude
cards.explain: The enhanced terrain functions do not depend on the radio altitude.

cards.question: A crew is told their fit is the advanced version, so what does it do that the basic one does not?
options: It shows the terrain around the aircraft
It lights annunciators in front of the pilot
It sounds its alerts with a synthetic voice
cards.explain: The terrain picture is what the advanced system adds.

cards.question: From which sources does the GPWC receive its inputs
options: From the autopilot and the flight control computers
From the flight data recorder and the engine computers
From an air data computer and various navigation systems
cards.explain: Its inputs come from an air data computer and from the navigation systems.

cards.question: Only some aeroplanes carry one of the three main parts of the system, so which part is it?
options: The inhibit switches
The warning computer
The indications
cards.explain: The inhibit switches are the part fitted to some aeroplanes only.

cards.question: Which kind of accident is the enhanced system intended to prevent
options: Controlled flight into terrain
Loss of control in flight
Runway incursion on landing
cards.explain: Its stated purpose is to help prevent CFIT accidents.

cards.question: With what does the enhanced system compare the aircraft position
options: With an internal database
With the weather radar picture
With the radio altitude signal
cards.explain: The aircraft position is compared with an internal database.

cards.question: Which two sources can supply the aircraft position used in that comparison
options: The FMS or the GPS
The ILS or the VOR
The ADC or the IRS
cards.explain: The position comes from the FMS or the GPS.

cards.question: Windshear alerting is fitted to an aircraft, so which mode number does it carry?
options: Mode 6
Mode 7
Mode 5
cards.explain: Windshear alerting is mode 7.

cards.question: What does the enhanced system do with the variety of aircraft parameters it accepts
options: It applies alerting algorithms to them
It transmits them to the ground station
It records them for later readout
cards.explain: The parameters are taken in and alerting algorithms are applied to them.

cards.question: Which two products were introduced in the late 1980s
options: MARK II for analogue aircraft and MARK III for digital aircraft
MARK V for digital aircraft and MARK VII for analogue aircraft
MARK VI for digital aircraft and MARK I for analogue aircraft
cards.explain: The two late 1980s products were MARK V for digital and MARK VII for analogue aircraft.

cards.question: Which two introductions improve the terrain awareness and the warning times of the enhanced system
options: The terrain display and the terrain data base look ahead protection
The altitude callouts and the alert for an excessive bank angle
The terrain clearance floor and the modulation of the envelopes
cards.explain: Terrain display and terrain data base look ahead protection are the named improvements.

cards.question: Why can the warning time be short when the aircraft flies towards steep terrain
options: The primary sensor is a downward looking radio altimeter
The aural message volume is reduced to one half below 300 feet
The alerting boundaries are computed from the barometric height
cards.explain: The warning is calculated from a downward looking sensor, which sees steep terrain late.

cards.question: Rising ground is approached at 2600 ft radio altitude, so why does the basic GPWS stay quiet?
options: Its aural alerts are suppressed with the landing gear up
Its boundaries are computed from the barometric altitude
Its automatic operation begins at a lower height
cards.explain: The aircraft is still above the radio altitude at which the basic system begins to operate automatically.

cards.question: The radio altimeter has failed in flight, so what can still warn the crew about high ground ahead?
options: The below glide slope alert of mode 5
The enhanced system terrain functions
The basic ground proximity modes
cards.explain: The enhanced terrain functions work independently of the radio altitude, while the basic modes need it.

cards.question: The crew sees the surrounding high ground pictured on the navigation display at 3000 ft, so which system provides it?
options: The weather radar system
The enhanced system
The basic warning system
cards.explain: The enhanced system shows the terrain around the aircraft on the navigation display and gives a warning when the aircraft gets too near the terrain, and those functions are independent of the radio altitude.

cards.question: The limits of one of the alerting envelopes are exceeded, so what does the enhanced system give the flight crew?
options: Aural alert messages with visual annunciations and displays
An automatic pull-up commanded through the autopilot
A master warning that has to be reset by the crew
cards.explain: Exceeding an envelope limit produces aural messages together with visual annunciations and displays.

cards.question: A stable non-precision approach is flown in low visibility with the gear down and the landing flaps out, so why does the early system stay silent?
options: It is inhibited below 500 feet
It expects the aeroplane to land
It has lost its radio altitude input
cards.explain: In the landing configuration the early system expects a landing and issues no warning.

cards.question: A system is required to see steep rising ground that the downward looking sensor would find too late, so which protection is needed?
options: The modulation of the alerting envelopes
The terrain data base look ahead protection
The terrain clearance floor protection
cards.explain: Look ahead protection works from the database instead of the downward looking sensor.

cards.question: The aircraft is recognised as landing at one of the troublesome airports held in the database, so what does the system do?
options: It switches off all of its aural warnings
It changes over to the terrain display only
It adjusts the warning modes for that airport
cards.explain: At such an airport the warning modes are adjusted, and only under specific conditions.

cards.question: A terrain clearance floor function is found on an aircraft, so which generation of the system is installed?
options: The MARK I system
The enhanced system
The MARK V system
cards.explain: The terrain clearance floor belongs to the enhanced system only.

cards.question: Which unit is the control unit of the EGPWS
options: The display management computer
The air data computer
The enhanced computer
cards.explain: The EGPWC is the control unit of the system.

cards.question: Which condition does mode 1 alert on
options: An excessive descent rate
An excessive terrain closure rate
An altitude loss after take-off
cards.explain: Mode 1 is the excessive descent rate mode.

cards.question: Which aural message is generated when the aircraft penetrates the outer alert boundary of mode 1
options: SINK RATE
DON'T SINK
PULL UP
cards.explain: The outer boundary gives the SINK RATE message.

cards.question: Which condition does mode 2 alert on
options: An excessive terrain closure rate
An unsafe clearance from the terrain
An excessive descent rate
cards.explain: Mode 2 covers an excessive rate of closure with the terrain.

cards.question: For how long after take-off is the mode 2B configuration valid
options: For the first 90 seconds
For the first 30 seconds
For the first 60 seconds
cards.explain: Mode 2B applies for the first 60 seconds after take-off.

cards.question: Which condition does mode 3 alert on
options: An unsafe clearance from terrain
An excessive rate of descent
An altitude loss after take-off
cards.explain: Mode 3 is the altitude loss after take-off mode.

cards.question: A DON'T SINK message is heard in the flight deck, so which mode has generated it?
options: Mode 3
Mode 1
Mode 4
cards.explain: Mode 3 gives the DON'T SINK message.

cards.question: Which condition does mode 4 alert on
options: An unsafe clearance from the terrain
An excessive rate of descent
An altitude loss after the take-off
cards.explain: Mode 4 covers unsafe terrain clearance.

cards.question: How many submodes does mode 4 have
options: Four
Two
Three
cards.explain: Mode 4 has three submodes.

cards.question: Which condition does mode 5 alert on
options: A deviation below the glide slope beam
An unsafe clearance from the terrain
An excessive rate of descent near ground
cards.explain: Mode 5 covers a deviation below the glide slope.

cards.question: How many levels of mode 5 operation does the computer provide
options: Two
Three
One
cards.explain: There are two levels of mode 5 operation.

cards.question: Which additional protection does mode 6 provide
options: A comparison of the aircraft position with a terrain database
A selectable menu of radio altitude callouts during the approach
An alert for an excessive rate of closure with the terrain
cards.explain: Mode 6 offers selectable radio altitude callouts on the landing approach.

cards.question: Which part of the system's operation is independent of the other functions
options: The warning function
The terrain awareness display function
The built-in test equipment function
cards.explain: The warning function is the one stated to be independent of the others.

cards.question: The descent continues after the first mode 1 message and the inner alert boundary is penetrated, so what is heard then?
options: TERRAIN TERRAIN
TOO LOW TERRAIN
PULL UP
cards.explain: The inner boundary gives the PULL UP message.

cards.question: Which three inputs define the two alert boundaries of mode 1
options: Barometric vertical speed, inertial vertical speed and radio altitude
Barometric altitude, glide slope deviation and gear position
Radio altitude, computed airspeed and the position of the flaps
cards.explain: Those three inputs define the two mode 1 boundaries.

cards.question: What does the computer produce besides the aural message in both mode 1 cases
options: A command to the autopilot to level the aircraft
A terrain picture on the navigation display
A discrete output to drive the visual annunciations
cards.explain: A discrete output drives the visual annunciations in both cases.

cards.question: In which flight conditions can the aircraft be when a mode 2 alert is generated
options: In the landing configuration only
In descent, level flight or climb
In descent or level flight only
cards.explain: Mode 2 alerts are possible in descent, in level flight and in the climb.

cards.question: A mode 2 alert boundary is being computed, so which two signals are combined?
options: Vertical speed and radio altitude
Airspeed and the position of the flaps
Barometric altitude and glide slope deviation
cards.explain: Vertical speed and radio altitude are the two signals used.

cards.question: When is the mode 2A alert generated
options: With the flaps set to the landing position on an approach
In any configuration other than the one defined for 2B
Within the first sixty seconds following the take-off
cards.explain: Mode 2A covers every configuration that is not a mode 2B configuration.

cards.question: Which aural message comes first when the aircraft penetrates the mode 2A alerting boundaries
options: TERRAIN TERRAIN
SINK RATE
PULL UP
cards.explain: The first mode 2A message is TERRAIN TERRAIN.

cards.question: The aircraft goes on penetrating the mode 2A boundaries after the first message, so which message is repeated until it leaves the envelope?
options: DON'T SINK
TERRAIN TERRAIN
PULL UP
cards.explain: PULL UP is repeated until the aircraft exits the warning envelope.

cards.question: What makes the upper alert boundary of mode 2A vary
options: The rate of closure with the terrain
The position of the landing flaps
The speed of the aircraft
cards.explain: The upper boundary of this mode varies with aircraft speed.

cards.question: Within how many dots of the localizer or glide slope centreline does the mode 2B configuration apply during an ILS approach
options: Within plus or minus 3 dots
Within plus or minus 2 dots
Within plus or minus 1 dot
cards.explain: The tolerance is plus or minus 2 dots.

cards.question: Which messages are suppressed when both gear and flaps are in the landing position in mode 2B
options: The TERRAIN messages
The PULL UP messages
The TOO LOW GEAR messages
cards.explain: In that configuration the PULL UP messages are suppressed.

cards.question: In which two flight phases does mode 3 provide its alerts
options: During the final approach and the landing roll
During the cruise and during a precision approach
Immediately after take-off and during a missed approach
cards.explain: The two phases are immediately after take-off and during a missed approach.

cards.question: Until when do the mode 3 visual annunciators remain active
options: Until the landing gear has been retracted
Until the warning envelope has been left
Until a positive rate of climb is established
cards.explain: They stay active until a positive rate of climb exists.

cards.question: Which configuration must exist after take-off before the computer initiates a mode 3 alert
options: The gear down and the flaps at landing
The gear up and the flaps not at landing
The gear up and the flaps set to landing
cards.explain: The alert needs the gear up and the flaps away from the landing position.

cards.question: By reference to what does mode 4 detect an insufficient terrain clearance
options: The glide slope and the localizer
The phase of flight and the speed
The vertical speed and the bank angle
cards.explain: Detection is made with reference to the phase of flight and the speed.

cards.question: When is mode 4A active
options: During take-off with the gear and the flaps still retracted
During an ILS approach with the flaps in landing position
During cruise and approach with the landing gear not at landing
cards.explain: Mode 4A covers cruise and approach with the gear not in the landing configuration.

cards.question: At which speed does a mode 4A penetration with the landing gear up give the TOO LOW GEAR message
options: At 250 knots and above
At 190 knots or below
At 159 knots or below
cards.explain: The speed for that message is 190 knots or below.

cards.question: The airspeed builds up during the cruise, so what happens to the mode 4A upper boundary?
options: It decreases linearly
It stays constant
It increases linearly
cards.explain: The boundary increases linearly with airspeed.

cards.question: In which configuration does mode 4B give the TOO LOW FLAPS message
options: With the gear down and the flaps not at landing
With the gear and the flaps both still fully retracted
With the gear up below one hundred and fifty nine knots
cards.explain: That message belongs to the gear down, flaps not at landing case.

cards.question: On what is mode 4C based
options: A fixed boundary of five hundred feet during the approach
A deviation of the flight path below the glide slope beam
A minimum terrain clearance floor that increases during take-off
cards.explain: Mode 4C uses a minimum terrain clearance floor that rises during take-off.

cards.question: Mode 5 alerts are not given on every kind of approach, so on which one are they given?
options: A front course ILS approach
A non-precision radio approach
A back course ILS approach
cards.explain: Mode 5 works on a front course ILS approach.

cards.question: How loud is the soft alert GLIDE SLOPE message
options: The same as the other alert message volume levels
About one half of the other alert volume levels
About twice the other alert message volume levels
cards.explain: The soft alert is at approximately one half, minus 6dB, of the other levels.

cards.question: A hard alert activation occurs on an approach, so below which radio altitude is the aircraft?
options: 500 feet
245 feet
300 feet
cards.explain: The hard alert belongs to radio altitudes below 300 feet.

cards.question: How far below the glide slope must the aircraft be for the hard alert activation
options: More than 3 dots
More than 1.3 dots
More than 2 dots
cards.explain: The hard alert needs more than 2 dots below the glide slope.

cards.question: The terrain awareness display function has been lost, so what happens to the ground proximity warning functions?
options: They fall back to the excessive descent rate mode
They are lost together with the display function
They go on working while the necessary inputs are there
cards.explain: The warning functions keep working as long as their inputs remain available.

cards.question: An installation carries only the modes that are basic system requirements, so which basic GPWS alerting mode is missing?
options: Mode 6
Mode 5
Mode 4
cards.explain: There are six basic modes, of which only modes 1 to 5 are basic system requirements, so mode 6 is the one an installation limited to the requirements leaves out.

cards.question: A warning lamp stays dark although the aural message is heard, so which computer function is suspect?
options: The terrain awareness display
The input signal processing
The alert output processing
cards.explain: The warning lamp drivers belong to the alert output processing.

cards.question: A replacement enhanced computer is being fitted, so what has to be set so that it works with the right modes?
options: The inhibit switches, before the first flight
The maintenance pages, after the installation
The program pins, before it is installed
cards.explain: The modes are selected by program pins before the computer is installed.

cards.question: The crew reduces the descent rate as soon as the first mode 1 message is heard, so which boundary has not been penetrated?
options: The upper alert boundary
The inner alert boundary
The outer alert boundary
cards.explain: The first message comes from the outer boundary, so the inner one has still not been crossed.

cards.question: Both the landing gear and the flaps are in the landing position when the mode 2B envelope is penetrated, so which message is repeated?
options: PULL UP
TERRAIN TERRAIN
TERRAIN
cards.explain: With gear and flaps at landing the repeated message is TERRAIN.

cards.question: The mode 2B envelope is penetrated with the landing gear down but the flaps still up, so which message is heard first?
options: TERRAIN TERRAIN
TOO LOW TERRAIN
PULL UP
cards.explain: With either gear or flaps not at landing the initial message is TERRAIN TERRAIN.

cards.question: The flaps are at the landing position and the aircraft is within two dots of the localizer on an ILS approach, so which submode boundary applies?
