options: Mode 2A
Mode 2B
Mode 4B
cards.explain: That configuration is one of those listed for mode 2B.

cards.question: A go-around is flown with the gear up and the flaps away from landing when a larger altitude loss than permitted is detected, so which alert is initiated?
options: The mode 4 alert
The mode 3 alert
The mode 1 alert
cards.explain: That is exactly the condition for the mode 3 alert.

cards.question: A computer has to decide how much height may be lost before a mode 3 alert is given, so what does it do?
options: It reads the loss from the terrain database
It calculates the amount of permitted loss
It compares the loss with a fixed boundary
cards.explain: The computer itself calculates the permitted loss before alerting.

cards.question: Which mode uses altitude above sea level information in its computation
options: Mode 3
Mode 1
Mode 2
cards.explain: Mode 3 is the mode whose computation is stated to take altitude above sea level information, while mode 1 works from vertical speed and radio altitude and mode 2 from vertical speed and radio altitude.

cards.question: The mode 4A boundary is penetrated at 250 knots with the landing gear still retracted, so which message does the computer generate?
options: TOO LOW GEAR
TOO LOW TERRAIN
TOO LOW FLAPS
cards.explain: With the gear still up the boundary is penetrated at 190 knots or below as TOO LOW GEAR, while the boundary that rises with airspeed to 1000 feet at 250 knots gives TOO LOW TERRAIN.

cards.question: Just after take-off with gear and flaps up the radio altitude falls below the long term filter value, so which message is generated?
options: TOO LOW GEAR
TOO LOW TERRAIN
DON'T SINK
cards.explain: That decrease below the filter value gives TOO LOW TERRAIN.

cards.question: An approach is flown at 140 knots with the gear down and the flaps still up, so which submode watches the terrain clearance?
options: Mode 4C
Mode 4B
Mode 4A
cards.explain: Mode 4B is the submode that applies once the landing gear is lowered.

cards.question: The aircraft drifts 1.5 dots below the beam centre at 800 feet radio altitude, so which activation occurs?
options: The soft alert activation
No alert activation at all
The hard alert activation
cards.explain: The aircraft is beyond 1.3 dots below the beam centre, so the soft alert comes; the hard alert needs below 300 feet radio altitude and more than 2 dots.

cards.question: A glide slope deviation message is heard noticeably quieter than the other warnings, so what does that tell the crew?
options: It is the hard alert activation
It is a failure of the loudspeaker
It is the soft alert activation
cards.explain: Only the soft alert is given at about half the normal volume.

questions.question: One of the approaching call-outs is given with its own altitude selection instead of the normal trigger height, so which call-out is that?
options: plus hundred
approaching minimums
approaching decision height
questions.explain: Of the three approaching call-outs, plus hundred is the one with its own altitude selection, set for decision height + 100 feet, instead of the normal 80 feet above the decision height.

questions.question: On a low go-around at 60 feet radio altitude the pilot rolls to 20 degrees, so what does Mode 6 do?
options: It gives the aural BANK ANGLE, BANK ANGLE
It gives no roll call-out at that height
It gives the aural MINIMUMS, MINIMUMS
questions.explain: 60 feet lies between 30 and 130 feet and 20 degrees is larger than 10 degrees, so the call-out is given.

questions.question: A windshear warning is triggered on take-off, so how do its indications differ from those of the pre-alert?
options: An ARINC 429 output is added
An aural indication is added
A visual indication is added
questions.explain: The warning adds the aural to the visual and ARINC 429 indications the caution already gives.

questions.question: On final approach at 900 feet AGL the head wind increases quickly and a severe up draft is met, so what does Mode 7 do?
options: It stays quiet, because the gear is not yet down
It alerts only after the aeroplane is below 500 feet
It alerts, because the height is inside the active band
questions.explain: 900 feet lies inside the 10 to 1500 feet AGL detection band, so Mode 7 gives its alert.

questions.question: The aeroplane is near a listed airport but the glide slope deviation and runway heading fail to match, so what does the GPWC conclude?
options: No modulation condition exists
The terrain database must be in error
A modulation condition exists anyway
questions.explain: Position alone is not enough; the extra parameters must also confirm the condition.

questions.question: Both GPS and FMS position data are lost in the cruise, so which EGPWS function can no longer work?
options: The barometric altitude correction in the ADC
The radio altimeter height measurement function
The look-ahead comparison with the terrain database
questions.explain: Without latitude and longitude there is no position to compare with the terrain database.

questions.question: An aural is heard and exactly seven seconds later the same words come again, so which envelope is still penetrated?
options: The clearance floor envelope
The caution envelope
The warning envelope
questions.explain: A seven second repeat is the caution level; the warning level repeats continuously.

questions.question: On which three quantities are the terrain clearance floor alerts based
options: Aircraft heading, runway length and barometric altitude data
Ground speed, flight path angle and nearest terrain elevation
Aircraft location, nearest runway centre point and radio altitude
questions.explain: Location, nearest runway centre point and radio altitude are the three inputs.

questions.question: The terrain display relays have been energised by the alert discretes, so what do the navigational displays then carry?
options: The weather radar picture as before
The terrain test pattern in cyan
The conflicting ground in yellow or red
questions.explain: Once the relays are energised the conflicting ground is painted solid yellow or solid red.

questions.question: The yellow LED is lit on the front panel while the green one stays on, so where should the engineer look first?
options: At the power supply to the computer
At the equipment feeding the computer
Inside the computer itself
questions.explain: Yellow marks an external fault while green still says the computer is good, so the trouble is outside it.

questions.question: What can be identified from the engine vibration indication
options: An oil filter blockage
A rotor imbalance
A fuel control fault
questions.explain: The vibration indication reveals a rotor imbalance.

questions.question: What do the engine vibration sensors deliver to the computer
options: Pneumatic pressure signals
Electrical signals
Hydraulic pressure signals
questions.explain: The sensors send electrical signals to the computer.

questions.question: How is the permanent magnet carried inside an electromagnetic vibration sensor
options: It is held in the centre by a fixed coil, with two springs around it
It is held on a base plate by an inertia mass, with a coil around it
It is held in the centre by two springs, with a fixed coil around it
questions.explain: Two springs hold the magnet centrally and the coil is the fixed part around it.

questions.question: What does the marking REL AM on a vibration indicator tell the technician
options: That the scale carries no units and only follows a trend
That the scale shows the speed difference of the rotors
That the scale is graduated in mils of displacement
questions.explain: REL AM means an unitless scale meant only for trend following.

questions.question: In which two formats is the vibration value put on an EICAS display
options: In an analog and a colour coded format
In an analog and a digital format
In a digital and a bar graph format
questions.explain: The display gives the value both in analog and in digital form.

questions.question: The vibration sensor near the N1 rotor shaft of an engine has failed, so which part of the engine has lost its pick-up?
options: The turbine area
The accessory gearbox area
The compressor area
questions.explain: The sensor near the N1 rotor shaft is the one in the compressor area, so that area is the one left unmonitored.

questions.question: How can one sensor signal be turned into separate N1 and N2 vibration indications
options: By comparing its frequency with the two rotor speed signals
By switching the filter between the forward and the aft pick-up
By comparing its amplitude with the two stored limit values
questions.explain: The frequency of the vibration signal is compared with the two rotor speed signals to sort it into N1 and N2.

questions.question: Which three components make up the main rotor rpm monitoring system
options: A magnetic pick up, an rpm indicator and a triple tachometer
A magnetic pick up, an rpm warning unit and a master caution light
A magnetic pick up, an rpm indicator and an rpm warning unit
questions.explain: These three are the components of the system.

questions.question: A technician must find the rotor rpm magnetic pick up, so where is it installed?
options: Within the main gear box
Within the tail rotor gearbox
Within the rotor mast
questions.explain: It sits inside the main gear box.

questions.question: A pilot reads the rotor rpm on the triple tachometer, so which part of the dial shows it?
options: The small pointer R on the inner scale
The large pointer N1 on the outer scale
The digital window at the foot of the dial
questions.explain: Rotor rpm is the small R pointer on the inner scale.

questions.question: A tail rotor gearbox develops a malfunction, so how will the crew learn of it?
options: By a caution light only
By its own analog instrument
By a pointer leaving the green arc
questions.explain: Gearboxes other than the main transmission are only covered by caution lights.

questions.question: A helicopter without EFIS was started without the bending load indicator being calibrated, so what is now in doubt?
options: The supply to the strain gauge bridge
The aural warning of the rotor rpm
The accuracy of the mast moment indication
questions.explain: Without the pre-start calibration the indicated mast moment can no longer be trusted.

questions.question: On which aeroplanes is the ultrasonic fuel measuring principle used
options: On larger ones only
On smaller ones only
On all of them
questions.explain: The ultrasonic method is restricted to larger aeroplanes.

questions.question: How are the fuel quantity probes installed in a tank
options: Vertically, from the top down to about half depth
Vertically, from the bottom right up to the top
Horizontally, lying along the floor of the tank
questions.explain: They stand vertically and run the full depth of the tank.

questions.question: Two probes in the same tank are both completely covered by fuel yet give different values, so what explains it?
options: Their plates differ in spacing because they differ in fuel cover
Their plates differ in area because they differ in length
Their plates differ in area because they differ in fuel cover
questions.explain: Probes in one tank are of different lengths, so their plate areas differ even when both are fully covered.

questions.question: Which property of air and fuel does the capacitance method of quantity measurement make use of
options: Their differing dielectric constants
Their differing boiling points
Their differing electrical resistances
questions.explain: The capacitance method uses the differing dielectric constants of air and fuel.

questions.question: Why is the amount of fuel carried indicated in units of weight
options: The energy available from the fuel depends on volume
The energy available from the fuel depends on weight
The tank capacity is certified in terms of weight
questions.explain: The energy present in the form of fuel is dependent on weight, so weight is indicated.

questions.question: What makes a direct weight indication of the fuel necessary on a large commercial aircraft
options: Fuel density is constant so the weight can be read straight from the volume
Fuel is always loaded by volume and the tank gauges are marked in litres only
Fuel can be half the take-off weight and the approved weights need it
questions.explain: Fuel can be up to one half of take-off weight, so direct weight indication is needed for the approved take-off and landing weights.

questions.question: The fuel level in a tank alters, so what does the multi-tubular surface condenser in it do?
options: It changes its resistance
It changes its capacity
It changes its excitation frequency
questions.explain: The condenser changes its capacity depending on the level of fuel in the tank.

questions.question: The amplifier of a capacitive fuel gauge puts out a voltage, so what does that voltage drive?
options: A motor that turns the potentiometer
A heater that trims the reference condenser
A solenoid that trips the warning flag
questions.explain: The amplifier output voltage drives a motor which turns the potentiometer.

questions.question: When does the cadensicon sensor take its measurements of K and D
options: As the engines are started
As the tank runs nearly empty
As fuel enters the tank
questions.explain: The cadensicon measures K and D separately as fuel enters the tank.

questions.question: Water has collected between the plates of a capacitance probe, so how does the probe capacitance compare with the same probe covered in fuel?
options: Slightly lower
The same
Much higher
questions.explain: Water is given a far larger dielectric constant than fuel, and the capacitance rises with the dielectric constant of whatever fills the probe.

questions.question: A float sinks further in one fuel sample than in another of the same temperature, so what does that tell the computer?
options: That the two samples differ in dielectric constant
That the two samples differ in volume
That the two samples differ in density
questions.explain: The float of predetermined weight submerges in accordance with the density, so a deeper float means a different density.

questions.question: Refuelling has to stop before a tank overflows, so what is built into the fuel quantity computer system for this?
options: A totaliser that sums all of the master systems
A trimming condenser at the cockpit indicator
A preselection of the wanted load with a shutoff
questions.explain: The system integrates a preselection of the desired volume together with a shutoff on reaching it or shortly before overflowing.

questions.question: In a liquid level metering system that works by timing an echo, which kind of signal do the tank units transmit
options: An ultrasonic signal
A radio frequency signal
A light signal
questions.explain: The tank units transmit an ultrasonic signal.

questions.question: A tank of an ultrasonic system is opened for inspection, so how many tank units will be found in it?
options: Exactly two units
Numerous units
A single unit
questions.explain: Each tank contains numerous tank units.

questions.question: Unlike an ultrasonic tank unit, which property of the fuel does the capacitance of a tank unit respond to
options: Its dielectric constant
Its temperature in flight
Its density in the tank
questions.explain: Capacitive measurement works from the differing dielectric constants, while the ultrasonic unit works from a reflected signal.

questions.question: An ultrasonic system has to display a fuel weight, so which two measurements must the processor unit bring together?
options: The fuel height and the fuel density
The fuel density and the velocity of sound
The fuel height and the fuel temperature
questions.explain: Height comes from the tank units and density from the densitometer, and the FQPU calculates the fuel weight from them.

questions.question: A densitometer in one tank of an ultrasonic system has failed, so which calculation is lost first?
options: The water level in that tank
The fuel weight for that tank
The fuel height in that tank
questions.explain: Height still comes from the tank unit, but without the density from the densitometer the processor unit cannot work out that tank's fuel weight.

questions.question: A tank unit reads correctly on the tester but the cockpit indication is still wrong, so which further tester function would be used on the wiring?
options: Measuring the tank unit currents
Measuring contact resistances
Simulating the probe capacities
questions.explain: Besides measuring and simulating capacities the tester measures contact resistances, which is what a wiring check needs.

cards.question: What makes the EGPWS give Mode 6 alerts and call-outs
options: The aircraft climbing above predefined altitudes
The aircraft descending below predefined altitudes
The aircraft exceeding a predefined airspeed
cards.explain: Mode 6 is triggered by the aircraft descending below predefined altitudes such as DH and minimums.

cards.question: Which indications do Mode 6 alerts and call-outs give to the crew
options: Visual warnings and aural messages only
Visual warnings and ARINC 429 outputs only
Aural messages and ARINC 429 outputs only
cards.explain: Mode 6 produces aural messages and ARINC 429 outputs but no visual indication.

cards.question: Which flight phases does the Mode 7 windshear alerting cover
options: Take-off and final approach
Cruise and initial descent
Taxi and initial climb
cards.explain: Mode 7 alerts during take-off and final approach.

cards.question: Between which heights above ground is the windshear detection active
options: 50 and 2500 feet AGL
10 and 1500 feet AGL
200 and 1000 feet AGL
cards.explain: Detection is active between 10 and 1500 feet AGL.

cards.question: Airports that need envelope modulation are kept in the GPWC memory, so how are they identified there?
options: By their runway heading alone
By their ICAO four-letter code
By their latitude and longitude
cards.explain: Those airports are held in memory identified by latitude and longitude.

cards.question: What does the terrain awareness alerting function use to predict a conflict ahead
options: The aircraft position and altitude with an internal database
The radio altimeter signal with the nearest runway length
The weather radar returns with the aircraft ground speed
cards.explain: Geographic position and altitude are compared with the internal terrain database.

cards.question: Terrain awareness is working normally, so which two systems supply its aeroplane data?
options: The FMS and the WXR
The ADIRS and the GPS
The ADC and the ILS
cards.explain: Aeroplane data comes from the ADIRS and the GPS.

cards.question: Which alerting envelopes does the terrain alerting function compute
options: A caution-level envelope and a warning-level envelope
A take-off envelope and a final approach envelope
A look-up envelope and a lateral offset envelope
cards.explain: Two envelopes are computed, one for caution level and one for warning level.

cards.question: Where does the minimums call-out take its decision height from
options: The setting on the EFIS control panels
The runway elevation in the terrain database
A fixed preset inside the radio altimeter
cards.explain: The minimums call-out uses the decision height set on the EFIS control panels.

cards.question: An approaching minimums call-out is selected, so how far above the decision height does it normally come on?
options: 130 feet
100 feet
80 feet
cards.explain: The approaching minimums call-out normally comes on 80 feet above the decision height.

cards.question: One of the approaching call-outs is given with its own altitude selection instead of the normal trigger height, so which call-out is that?
options: plus hundred
approaching minimums
approaching decision height
cards.explain: Of the three approaching call-outs, plus hundred is the one with its own altitude selection, set for decision height + 100 feet, instead of the normal 80 feet above the decision height.

cards.question: The windshear pre-alert comes up on take-off, so which indications does it give?
options: ARINC 429 outputs and a stick shaker actuation
Visual indications and ARINC 429 outputs
Visual indications and a flashing master warning light
cards.explain: The windshear caution, or pre-alert, provides visual and ARINC 429 output indications.

cards.question: What does the measured windshear value represent
options: The vector sum of inertial and air mass accelerations
The rate of change of barometric altitude
The difference between ground speed and airspeed
cards.explain: The value is the vector sum of inertial versus air mass accelerations along and across the flight path.

cards.question: Which further aeroplane parameters does the GPWC check near an airport listed for envelope modulation
options: Ground speed, roll attitude and calculated flight path angle
Vertical speed, true heading and terrain elevation data
Radio altitude, magnetic track and glide slope deviation
cards.explain: Radio altitude, magnetic track and glide slope deviation are all among those inputs.

cards.question: Which navigational signals can the envelope modulation feature use
options: Localizer and glide slope beam deviation signals
Updated VOR and DME range and bearing signals
GPS or updated flight management system signals
cards.explain: The feature uses GPS or updated FMS navigational signals.

cards.question: Which sources does terrain awareness use for latitude and longitude
options: GPS or FMS
GPS or WXR
ADIRS or ADC
cards.explain: Latitude and longitude come from GPS or FMS.

cards.question: Which of the terrain awareness input quantities is worked out by the EGPWC itself
options: Ground track
Flight path angle
Barometric altitude
cards.explain: Only the flight path angle is noted as calculated by the EGPWC; the others are received.

cards.question: What does the EGPWC compare with its terrain database to find a threat
options: The aeroplane position and track
The aeroplane speed and flap setting
The aeroplane pitch and roll
cards.explain: Position and track are compared with the database.

cards.question: How does the terrain display show terrain height relative to the aeroplane
options: By solid contour lines
By numeric height labels
By different coloured dots
cards.explain: Terrain height relative to the aeroplane is shown by different coloured dots.

cards.question: The caution level aural has just been heard and the envelope is still penetrated, so when does it come again?
options: Every three seconds
Every seven seconds
Without any pause
cards.explain: The caution message repeats every seven seconds while the envelope is penetrated.

cards.question: The aeroplane stays inside the terrain warning envelope, so how is PULL UP given?
options: Twice and then once per 20% height loss
Continuously
Every seven seconds
cards.explain: PULL UP repeats continuously for as long as the warning envelope is penetrated.

cards.question: What are the alert discretes of the look-ahead function provided for
options: To reset the radio altimeter output
To energise the terrain display relays
To inhibit the weather radar transmitter
cards.explain: The discretes energise the terrain display relays.

cards.question: By which three dimensions are the terrain alerting envelopes sized
options: A ground speed, a flight path angle and a roll attitude
A runway distance, a radio altitude and a ground track angle
A look-ahead distance, an altitude offset and a lateral distance
cards.explain: The three sizing dimensions are look-ahead distance, altitude offset and lateral distance.

cards.question: At 2500 feet the operator rejects the aural TWENTY FIVE HUNDRED, so which other aural can be selected instead?
options: The aural MINIMUMS MINIMUMS
The aural RADIO ALTITUDE
The aural TOO LOW TERRAIN
cards.explain: At 2500 feet the alternative to TWENTY FIVE HUNDRED is the aural RADIO ALTITUDE.

cards.question: The aeroplane is at 300 feet radio altitude and the roll is increased steadily, so at which angles does the call-out occur?
options: 10, 20 and 30 degrees
15, 30 and 45 degrees
35, 40 and 45 degrees
cards.explain: Above 130 feet the bank angle call-out comes at 35, 40 and 45 degrees.

cards.question: On a low go-around at 60 feet radio altitude the pilot rolls to 20 degrees, so what does Mode 6 do?
options: It gives the aural BANK ANGLE, BANK ANGLE
It gives no roll call-out at that height
It gives the aural MINIMUMS, MINIMUMS
cards.explain: 60 feet lies between 30 and 130 feet and 20 degrees is larger than 10 degrees, so the call-out is given.

cards.question: A windshear warning is triggered on take-off, so how do its indications differ from those of the pre-alert?
options: A visual indication is added
An ARINC 429 output is added
An aural indication is added
cards.explain: The warning adds the aural to the visual and ARINC 429 indications the caution already gives.

cards.question: On final approach at 900 feet AGL the head wind increases quickly and a severe up draft is met, so what does Mode 7 do?
options: It stays quiet, because the gear is not yet down
It alerts only after the aeroplane is below 500 feet
It alerts, because the height is inside the active band
cards.explain: 900 feet lies inside the 10 to 1500 feet AGL detection band, so Mode 7 gives its alert.

cards.question: The aeroplane is near a listed airport but the glide slope deviation and runway heading fail to match, so what does the GPWC conclude?
options: A modulation condition exists anyway
The terrain database must be in error
No modulation condition exists
cards.explain: Position alone is not enough; the extra parameters must also confirm the condition.

cards.question: At some locations the top radio altitude limit of the mode 2 alert area is lowered, so what does that allow?
options: To let the aeroplane descend faster without any alerts
To let the aeroplane approach without lowering the gear
To let the aeroplane fly closer to the terrain without alerts
cards.explain: Lowering the mode 2 area lets the aeroplane fly closer to the terrain without alerts.

cards.question: An approach needs mode 5 annunciations higher than normal and with the gear still up, so which change makes that possible?
options: The descent rate limit is increased and the alert area raised
The alert area is increased and the gear down requirement removed
The alert area is lowered and a gear down requirement added
cards.explain: Mode 5 modulation increases the alert area limits and removes the gear down requirement.

cards.question: Both GPS and FMS position data are lost in the cruise, so which EGPWS function can no longer work?
options: The look-ahead comparison with the terrain database
The barometric altitude correction in the ADC
The radio altimeter height measurement function
cards.explain: Without latitude and longitude there is no position to compare with the terrain database.

cards.question: An aural is heard and exactly seven seconds later the same words come again, so which envelope is still penetrated?
options: The clearance floor envelope
The caution envelope
The warning envelope
cards.explain: A seven second repeat is the caution level; the warning level repeats continuously.

cards.question: How does the look-ahead distance change as the aeroplane accelerates, and for what reason
options: It increases, to keep the alerting time about equal
It decreases, to keep the envelope narrow
It stays fixed, because altitude alone sets it
cards.explain: The distance grows with ground speed so that alerting times stay roughly the same.

cards.question: Which colour paints ground that violates the terrain caution envelope
options: 50 per cent magenta
100 per cent red
100 per cent yellow
cards.explain: Caution envelope violations are painted solid yellow.

cards.question: Which colour paints ground that violates the terrain warning envelope
options: 100 per cent yellow
50 per cent green
100 per cent red
cards.explain: Warning envelope violations are painted solid red.

cards.question: What does the TCF alert function build around the intended runway
options: An increasing terrain clearance envelope
A fixed glide slope deviation envelope
A circular windshear detection envelope
cards.explain: TCF builds a terrain clearance envelope that grows with distance from the runway.

cards.question: Which two sources feed the navigational displays through the select relays
options: The ADIRS and the flight management system
The EGPWC and the WXR transceiver
The GPWC and the radio altimeter
cards.explain: The two sources are the EGPWC and the weather radar transceiver.

cards.question: Under which condition is terrain kept off the display
options: When it lies more than 2000 ft above the runway
When it lies more than 2000 ft below reference altitude
When it lies more than 1000 ft above reference altitude
cards.explain: Terrain more than 2000 ft below reference altitude is not painted.

cards.question: On which three quantities are the terrain clearance floor alerts based
options: Aircraft heading, runway length and barometric altitude data
Aircraft location, nearest runway centre point and radio altitude
Ground speed, flight path angle and nearest terrain elevation
cards.explain: Location, nearest runway centre point and radio altitude are the three inputs.

cards.question: When is the terrain clearance floor active during take-off
options: When mode 4 protection is not available
When the flaps have been retracted
When the landing gear is still down
cards.explain: In the take-off mode TCF covers the gap where mode 4 protection is missing.

cards.question: The aeroplane moves further away from the airport, so how does the height of the clearance envelope change?
options: It increases as the distance increases
It stays the same at every distance
It decreases as the distance increases
cards.explain: The envelope gets higher the further the aeroplane is from the airport.

cards.question: Which aeroplane data does the EGPWC compare with the clearance envelope data
options: Latitude, longitude and barometric altitude
Latitude, longitude and radio altitude
Heading, ground speed and radio altitude
cards.explain: Latitude, longitude and radio altitude are compared with the envelope data.

cards.question: On which data bus standard is the terrain and weather display data carried
options: ARINC 429
ARINC 453
ARINC 629
cards.explain: The display data runs on ARINC 453 buses.

cards.question: Which equipment receives the data from the terrain weather select relays
options: The display electronics units
The flight warning computers
The air data computers
cards.explain: The relays feed the display electronics units, which drive the NDs.

cards.question: What happens when the TERR switch is selected a second time
options: The relay deenergises and the weather radar is connected
The relay deenergises and a test pattern is shown
The relay stays energised and the terrain stays shown
cards.explain: A second selection deenergises the relay and reconnects the weather radar.

cards.question: The aeroplane is in level flight and an area ahead is painted high density red, so where does that ground lie?
options: More than 2000 ft below the aeroplane
Between 1000 and 2000 ft above it
More than 2000 ft above the aeroplane
cards.explain: In level flight the reference altitude is the aircraft altitude, so high density red is more than 2000 ft above it.

cards.question: A QFE approach is flown into a field with an extreme surface temperature, so why does the EGPWS need no special procedure?
options: The radio altimeter replaces the air data input
Corrected barometric altitude is used instead
Its computed altitude copes with both conditions
cards.explain: The geometric altitude function covers temperature extremes and QFE operation together.

cards.question: Why does the terrain awareness function still work properly when the altimeter subscale has been set wrongly
options: The air data computer recomputes the corrected value
The radio altimeter replaces every altitude input
Its computed altitude is not susceptible to that error
cards.explain: Geometric altitude is immune to an incorrect altimeter setting, so terrain awareness is unaffected.

cards.question: The aeroplane flies through a strong inversion layer, so why can the corrected barometric altitude mislead the EGPWS?
options: It freezes at the last valid value
It can be in error against the true height
It is replaced by uncorrected altitude
cards.explain: Under non-standard conditions such as inversions the corrected barometric altitude differs from the true altitude.

cards.question: The landing gear is lowered in the descent, so how does the lower edge of the medium density yellow band change?
options: From 500 ft below to 250 ft below the reference altitude
From 1000 ft below to 500 ft below the reference altitude
From 250 ft below to 500 ft below the reference altitude
cards.explain: With the gear up the band reaches 500 ft below, with the gear down only 250 ft below.

cards.question: The landing gear is up and ground lies 400 ft below the reference altitude, so in which band is it painted?
options: Medium density yellow
Light density green
Medium density green
cards.explain: With the gear up the medium density yellow band runs down to 500 ft below, so 400 ft below falls in it.

cards.question: TERR is selected on an EFIS control panel, so what does the select relay do?
options: It energises and connects the hazard bus to the display units
It deenergises and connects weather data to the display units
It energises and connects terrain data to the display units
cards.explain: Selecting TERR energises the relay and connects terrain data to the display units.

cards.question: What do the transfer relays do while the weather radar is on and the caution criteria become fulfilled
options: They connect both buses to the display units at once
They drop the terrain bus and switch to the weather bus
They drop the weather bus and switch to the terrain bus
cards.explain: With the criteria fulfilled the relays swap the weather bus out for the terrain bus.

cards.question: A predictive windshear alert arrives while the terrain picture is up, so which picture is then shown?
options: The weather one, with the shear data on it
The terrain test pattern
The terrain one, with the shear data on it
cards.explain: A shear alert overrides the terrain picture and reverts to the weather display.

cards.question: The terrain display relays have been energised by the alert discretes, so what do the navigational displays then carry?
options: The terrain test pattern in cyan
The conflicting ground in yellow or red
The weather radar picture as before
cards.explain: Once the relays are energised the conflicting ground is painted solid yellow or solid red.

cards.question: A siren is followed by the same word three times during the climb-out at 300 feet, so which mode has alerted?
options: Mode 2
Mode 7
Mode 5
cards.explain: Only the mode 7 warning begins with a siren and repeats its word three times.

cards.question: The short level 1 test aural sequence begins with glideslope INOP, so what does that tell the engineer?
options: The test was started below 2000 feet
The glide slope lamp itself has failed
No valid glide slope input is present
cards.explain: The INOP annunciation in the sequence means the glide slope input is missing.

cards.question: A level one test is run from the front panel of the computer, so why is the GPW module used instead for an operational test?
options: The front panel test only checks the power supply
The flight deck annunciations cannot be seen there
The front panel test gives out no aural messages at all
cards.explain: From the computer front panel the flight deck annunciations are out of sight.

cards.question: An engineer looks at the front of the ground proximity warning computer, so how many status LEDs are fitted there?
options: Two LEDs
Five LEDs
Three LEDs
cards.explain: Three status LEDs are fitted on the front panel.

cards.question: When do the status LEDs on the front panel of the GPWC turn on
options: When the aeroplane has left the ground
When a self-test has been started from the cockpit
When there is power to the computer
cards.explain: The three status LEDs come on whenever the computer has power, not for any particular event.

cards.question: Which colour marks the external fault indication on the computer front panel
options: Green
Red
Yellow
cards.explain: The external fault LED is yellow.

cards.question: The green LED on the computer front panel is on, so what does that say?
options: The computer is serviceable
The computer has failed
An external fault is present
cards.explain: Green is the computer OK indication.

cards.question: Which colour marks a failure of the computer itself
options: Red
Yellow
Green
cards.explain: The computer fail LED is red.

cards.question: Level 2 reports No Faults but the engineer must still see what went wrong on earlier flights, so which level is needed?
options: Level 6
Level 4
Level 3
cards.explain: Current faults are level 2; the history of earlier legs is level 4.

cards.question: The yellow LED is lit on the front panel while the green one stays on, so where should the engineer look first?
options: Inside the computer itself
At the equipment feeding the computer
At the power supply to the computer
cards.explain: Yellow marks an external fault while green still says the computer is good, so the trouble is outside it.

cards.question: What can be identified from the engine vibration indication
options: A rotor imbalance
An oil filter blockage
A fuel control fault
cards.explain: The vibration indication reveals a rotor imbalance.

cards.question: An engine vibration reading is seen in the cockpit, so how is its level expressed?
options: Usually in percent
Usually in units
Usually in millimetres
cards.explain: The cockpit indication is normally given in units.

cards.question: Which kind of transducer is used as an engine vibration sensor
options: A tachometer generator
An accelerometer
A strain gauge bridge
cards.explain: The vibration sensors on an engine are accelerometers.

cards.question: A technician counts the vibration sensors fitted to one engine, so how many does he normally find?
options: Four
Two
One
cards.explain: Two sensors per engine is the usual fit.

cards.question: Which two types of accelerometer are used as engine vibration sensors
options: The electromagnetic type and the variable reluctance type
The piezoelectric-crystal type and the strain gauge type
The electromagnetic type and the piezoelectric-crystal type
cards.explain: Only these two accelerometer types are used on engines.

cards.question: What makes a piezoelectric crystal generate a voltage
options: A current passed through the crystal
A force applied to the crystal
A magnet moved across the crystal
cards.explain: Applying force to the crystal is what produces the voltage.

cards.question: A test switch is fitted to an analogue vibration display, so how much of it can be checked?
options: The filter setting only
The sensor wiring only
The entire indicator
cards.explain: The test switch checks the whole indicator.

cards.question: A glass cockpit display shows the engine vibration, so how many vibration indications are given per engine?
options: Four
Two
One
cards.explain: Two indications are given for each engine.

cards.question: An EICAS display shows the engine vibration, so how many values are given for each engine?
options: One
Two
Four
cards.explain: Only one value per engine is shown on this display.

cards.question: Why does a rotor imbalance matter to the engineer
options: It always means a bearing has already failed
It can be the first sign of engine damage
It shows the engine is running overspeed
cards.explain: An imbalance can be the earliest sign that the engine is being damaged.

cards.question: What do the engine vibration sensors deliver to the computer
options: Electrical signals
Hydraulic pressure signals
Pneumatic pressure signals
cards.explain: The sensors send electrical signals to the computer.

cards.question: What does the computer do with the data it receives from the sensors
options: It turns it straight into a cockpit warning indication
It passes it unchanged to the flight data recorder
It filters it for indication and trend monitoring
cards.explain: The computer collects and filters the data for both indication and trend monitoring.

cards.question: Vibration sensors are not fitted to the engines alone on a helicopter, so which other parts carry them on many types?
options: Rotors and gearboxes
Flight control actuators
Fuel pumps and filters
cards.explain: On many helicopters the rotors and gearboxes also carry vibration sensors.

cards.question: Which quantity of the rotor system is sensed by an engine vibration pick-up
options: The radial acceleration of the rotor system
The axial displacement of the rotor system
The rotational speed of the rotor system
cards.explain: The accelerometer senses acceleration in the radial direction.

cards.question: One of the two vibration sensors of an engine sits in the compressor area, so where is the other one?
options: In the turbine area
In the accessory gearbox area
In the combustion chamber area
cards.explain: The second of the two sensors is in the turbine area.

cards.question: How is the permanent magnet carried inside an electromagnetic vibration sensor
options: It is held in the centre by two springs, with a fixed coil around it
It is held on a base plate by an inertia mass, with a coil around it
It is held in the centre by a fixed coil, with two springs around it
cards.explain: Two springs hold the magnet centrally and the coil is the fixed part around it.

cards.question: The housing of an electromagnetic vibration sensor shakes with the engine, so what does the magnet inside do?
options: It turns with the rotor system
It stays almost still because of its inertia
It moves up and down with the housing
cards.explain: Inertia keeps the magnet nearly stationary while the housing and coil move.

cards.question: What produces the AC output voltage of an electromagnetic vibration sensor
options: The difference in motion between the coil and the magnetic field
The pressure of an inertia mass on the base plate
The force of the two springs acting on the permanent magnet
cards.explain: Relative motion between coil and field induces the voltage, as in a generator.

cards.question: What is the job of the attuned filter inside an analogue vibration indicator
options: It amplifies the undesired frequencies
It screens out the undesired frequencies
It rectifies the critical frequencies
cards.explain: The attuned filter removes the frequencies that are not wanted.

cards.question: What does the marking REL AM on a vibration indicator tell the technician
options: That the scale carries no units and only follows a trend
That the scale shows the speed difference of the rotors
That the scale is graduated in mils of displacement
cards.explain: REL AM means an unitless scale meant only for trend following.

cards.question: Which two rotor systems are covered by the two vibration indications of one engine
options: The N2 rotor system and the accessory drive system
The N1 rotor system and the fan rotor system
The N1 rotor system and the N2 rotor system
cards.explain: One indication is for N1 and the other for N2.

cards.question: From how many sensor signals does the monitoring unit make the two vibration indications
options: From one single sensor signal on its own
From one sensor signal for each indication
From the two sensor signals added together
cards.explain: Both indications come from a single sensor signal.

cards.question: An engine vibration value is shown on the glass cockpit display, so which of the two engine vibration sensors normally feeds it?
options: The forward one
The aft one
Whichever reads higher
cards.explain: The forward sensor is the one normally used.

cards.question: The forward vibration sensor of an engine fails, so what does the monitoring unit do?
options: It freezes the last indicated value
It removes the N2 indication only
It switches over to the aft one
cards.explain: On failure of the forward sensor the unit changes over to the aft sensor.

cards.question: In which two formats is the vibration value put on an EICAS display
options: In a digital and a bar graph format
In an analog and a colour coded format
In an analog and a digital format
cards.explain: The display gives the value both in analog and in digital form.

cards.question: A technician studies the vibration display, so what is put on it beside the value itself?
options: The stored limit values for the engine
The rotor speeds used for the comparison
The sensor and filter functions in use
cards.explain: The sensor and filter functions being used are shown with the value.

cards.question: The vibration sensor near the N1 rotor shaft of an engine has failed, so which part of the engine has lost its pick-up?
options: The accessory gearbox area
The compressor area
The turbine area
cards.explain: The sensor near the N1 rotor shaft is the one in the compressor area, so that area is the one left unmonitored.

cards.question: A vibration signal reaches the monitoring unit with a high voltage but a low frequency, so what has it been told?
options: A small acceleration at a fast vibration
A large acceleration at a slow vibration
A large rotor speed at a slow acceleration
cards.explain: Voltage carries the acceleration level and frequency carries the vibration frequency, so high voltage with low frequency is a big acceleration vibrating slowly.

cards.question: A technician wants the indication of a low frequency vibration on an older system, so which switch does he use?
options: The one that picks the engine
The one that picks the sensor
The one that picks the filter
cards.explain: Frequency band is set by the filter switch, not by the sensor switch.

cards.question: An older vibration system must show the oscillations of the add-on components, so which filter position is used?
options: The low frequency one
The broad band one
The high frequency one
cards.explain: Add-on components give the low oscillations, so the low frequency filter is selected.

cards.question: An analogue vibration indicator is driven by a moving coil, so what must be done to the alternating sensor signal before it can drive that movement?
options: It must be attenuated
It must be rectified
It must be digitised
cards.explain: A moving coil instrument needs a unidirectional current, so the alternating signal is rectified before display.

cards.question: Why does an analogue vibration indicator need a filter selection at all
options: Because motor and add-on vibrations fall in different frequency ranges
Because the sensor output is an alternating current, not a direct one
Because the scale carries no units of measurement, only a trend
cards.explain: High oscillations come from the motor and low ones from the add-on components, so the filter has to be set to the range being looked at.

cards.question: The pointer of a vibration indicator sits below the zero mark, so what has happened?
options: The filter has been switched off
A system error has occurred
The vibration has fallen to nothing
cards.explain: A pointer below zero on the OFF / Error mark means a system error, not a zero vibration.

cards.question: Why does the vibration monitoring system need the tachometer signals as well as the accelerometer signals
options: Because the charge amplifiers must be supplied with power
Because the tracking filter must follow the rotor speed
Because the indicator scale must be set to the right range
cards.explain: The filter has to track the rotor speed, and it is the tachometer signals that tell it that speed.

cards.question: How can one sensor signal be turned into separate N1 and N2 vibration indications
options: By comparing its frequency with the two rotor speed signals
By switching the filter between the forward and the aft pick-up
By comparing its amplitude with the two stored limit values
cards.explain: The frequency of the vibration signal is compared with the two rotor speed signals to sort it into N1 and N2.

cards.question: A rotor speed signal is not available to the monitoring unit, so which indication mode is used?
options: BB
FAN
LPT
cards.explain: Without a rotor speed signal the filters cannot track, so the unfiltered broad band mode is used.

cards.question: Which actions may a pilot take after a vibration indication begins to pulse
options: Checking the oil pressure, closing the bleeds or re-lighting the engine
Selecting the aft pick-up, resetting the filter or changing the mode
Scanning other engine indications, reducing power or shutting down
cards.explain: The pilot has to look for the reason, by scanning other engine indications, reducing power or shutting the engine down.

cards.question: Which three components make up the main rotor rpm monitoring system
options: A magnetic pick up, an rpm indicator and a triple tachometer
A magnetic pick up, an rpm indicator and an rpm warning unit
A magnetic pick up, an rpm warning unit and a master caution light
cards.explain: These three are the components of the system.

cards.question: A technician must find the rotor rpm magnetic pick up, so where is it installed?
options: Within the tail rotor gearbox
Within the rotor mast
Within the main gear box
cards.explain: It sits inside the main gear box.

cards.question: Which three components make up the mast moment monitoring system
options: A strain gauge bridge, a magnetic pick up and indicators
A strain gauge bridge, a sensor transmitting unit and indicators
A sensor transmitting unit, an rpm warning unit and indicators
cards.explain: These three are the components listed for the system.

cards.question: A strain gauge bridge is fitted for the bending moment monitoring, so where does it sit?
options: In the rotor mast
In the rotor head
In the main transmission
cards.explain: The bridge is installed in the rotor mast.

cards.question: Which kind of sensor measures the main rotor speed
options: A piezoelectric type
A magnetic type
A capacitive type
cards.explain: The rotor speed pickup is a magnetic sensor.

cards.question: What is the voltage peak from the rotor speed pickup proportional to
options: The frequency of the interrupter
The temperature of the main gear box
The movement of the interrupter
cards.explain: The peak is in proportion to the interrupter frequency.

cards.question: A pilot reads the rotor rpm on the triple tachometer, so which part of the dial shows it?
options: The small pointer R on the inner scale
The large pointer N1 on the outer scale
The digital window at the foot of the dial
cards.explain: Rotor rpm is the small R pointer on the inner scale.

cards.question: The rotor rpm is shown permanently in two places in the cockpit, so which two are they?
options: The triple tachometer and the caution and advisory display
The rpm warning unit and the central engine display unit
The triple tachometer and the central engine display unit
cards.explain: Both the triple tachometer and the central engine display unit carry the rotor rpm.

cards.question: Through which unit do the speed pickup signals pass on their way to the indicators
options: The RPM warning unit
The sensor transmitting unit
The central engine display unit
cards.explain: The signals go through the rotor RPM warning unit.

cards.question: The rotor rpm falls below the operating range, so what is given to the crew?
options: A removal of the rpm indication
A visual warning only
A visual and an audio warning
cards.explain: Going outside the range either way sets off both visual and audio warning.

cards.question: Where are the sampled transmission data indicated constantly
options: On the analog instruments or on the Caution and Advisory Display
On the triple tachometer or on the rpm warning unit
On the analog instruments or on the mast moment indicator
cards.explain: Either the analog indicators or the CAD carry them constantly.

cards.question: Which two transmission parameters have their own instruments showing them constantly
options: The oil temperature and the oil pressure
The oil temperature and the chip detection
The oil pressure and the vibration level
cards.explain: Transmission oil temperature and pressure are the two indicated constantly.

cards.question: A sampled transmission value goes outside its operational range, so what happens?
options: The indication is frozen at the limit value
The parameter is taken off the display
A warning appears on the respective warning unit
cards.explain: Out-of-range data produce a warning on the respective warning unit.

cards.question: What does the mast moment monitoring system measure
options: The bending moment between the rotor mast and the main transmission
The twisting moment between the engine and the main transmission
The vibration between the rotor mast and the rotor head
cards.explain: It is the bending moment between mast and main transmission.

cards.question: Through which unit does the measured mast moment reach the indicators
options: The sensor transmitting unit
The caution and advisory display
The rpm warning unit
cards.explain: The signal passes through the sensor transmitting unit.

cards.question: The maximum mast moment is exceeded in flight, so what comes with the warning light?
options: An automatic power reduction
An entry in the fault memory
An aural indication
cards.explain: An aural indication accompanies the visual one.

cards.question: How is an exceeded mast moment shown on an electronic mast moment indicator
options: By a red marking
By a warning light
By a flashing scale
cards.explain: On the electronic indicator it is a red marking; the warning light belongs to the analog one.

cards.question: A helicopter is not fitted with an EFIS, so what must be done to the mast moment indicator before each engine start?
options: It must be zeroed by the pilot
It must be calibrated
It must be tested against its warning light
cards.explain: Without an EFIS the indicator has to be calibrated before each engine start.

cards.question: A helicopter does carry an EFIS, so how is that mast moment indicator check carried out?
options: It is done by the pilot before each engine start
It is done automatically by the system
It is done by maintenance at the daily check
cards.explain: With an EFIS fitted the check is done automatically.

cards.question: A tail rotor gearbox develops a malfunction, so how will the crew learn of it?
options: By a caution light only
By its own analog instrument
By a pointer leaving the green arc
cards.explain: Gearboxes other than the main transmission are only covered by caution lights.

cards.question: A helicopter without EFIS was started without the bending load indicator being calibrated, so what is now in doubt?
options: The supply to the strain gauge bridge
The accuracy of the mast moment indication
The aural warning of the rotor rpm
cards.explain: Without the pre-start calibration the indicated mast moment can no longer be trusted.

cards.question: Which two methods are basically used to measure the fuel quantity
options: A capacitor system and an ultrasonic system
A capacitor system and a float switch system
An ultrasonic system and a flow meter system
cards.explain: Capacitors and the ultrasonic principle are the two methods given.

cards.question: What decides the number of fuel quantity probes in a tank
options: The size and shape of the aircraft
The size and shape of that tank
The number of pumps in that tank
cards.explain: Tank size and shape set how many probes are needed.

cards.question: Which electrical component is a fuel quantity probe
options: A resistor
An inductor
A capacitor
cards.explain: Each probe is a capacitor.

cards.question: What is the material dependent factor that affects a probe's capacitance called
options: The dielectric constant
The specific gravity
The capacitive reactance
cards.explain: It is named the dielectric constant.

cards.question: A large aeroplane carries an extra fuel quantity indication outside the cockpit, so who needs it?
options: The loadmaster in the hold
The flight crew on the walk round
The fuelling personnel
cards.explain: The indication at the fuelling station is there for the fuelling personnel.

cards.question: On which aeroplanes is the ultrasonic fuel measuring principle used
options: On all of them
On larger ones only
On smaller ones only
cards.explain: The ultrasonic method is restricted to larger aeroplanes.

cards.question: How are the fuel quantity probes installed in a tank
options: Vertically, from the bottom right up to the top
Horizontally, lying along the floor of the tank
Vertically, from the top down to about half depth
cards.explain: They stand vertically and run the full depth of the tank.

cards.question: A technician lays out the probes taken from one tank, so what does he notice about them?
options: They are of different length
They are of different diameter
They are all of the same length
cards.explain: Because the tank depth varies the probes come in different lengths.

cards.question: The amount of fuel in a tank changes, so what changes at the probe?
options: Its capacity
Its resistance
Its inductance
cards.explain: The probe's capacity follows the amount of fuel.

cards.question: How are the two tubes of a fuel quantity probe arranged
options: Coaxially and electrically isolated from each other
Side by side and electrically bonded to each other
Coaxially and electrically bonded to each other
cards.explain: They sit one inside the other and are isolated, which is what makes them a capacitor.

cards.question: What is meant by the capacitance of a fuel quantity probe
options: Its opposition to the flow of current
Its capability to store electrical energy
Its ability to generate a voltage
cards.explain: Capacitance is the ability to store electrical energy.

cards.question: On which two features of the plates does the capacitance of a probe depend
options: Their area and the thickness of them
Their area and the distance between them
Their length and the thickness of them
cards.explain: Plate area A and plate separation d are the two given.

cards.question: The fuel level rises past the middle of a probe, so what has happened between its two tubes?
options: The gap between the tubes has become smaller
All of the air has been replaced by fuel
Part of the air has been replaced by fuel
cards.explain: The gap is filled to the same level as the tank, so a half covered probe has fuel in part of it and air in the rest.

cards.question: Two probes in the same tank are both completely covered by fuel yet give different values, so what explains it?
options: Their plates differ in spacing because they differ in fuel cover
Their plates differ in area because they differ in fuel cover
Their plates differ in area because they differ in length
cards.explain: Probes in one tank are of different lengths, so their plate areas differ even when both are fully covered.

cards.question: Why does a capacitive probe give a different reading as the tank fills
options: Because the area of its tubes changes
Because the spacing between its tubes changes
Because the material between its tubes changes
cards.explain: Filling the tank swaps air for fuel between the tubes, and that material change alters the capacitance.

cards.question: Which property of air and fuel does the capacitance method of quantity measurement make use of
options: Their differing boiling points
Their differing dielectric constants
Their differing electrical resistances
cards.explain: The capacitance method uses the differing dielectric constants of air and fuel.

cards.question: A bridge transformer has a centre tap and two secondary windings, so what phase relationship do the windings have to the tap?
options: Opposite
Identical
Ninety degrees apart
cards.explain: The two secondary windings are in opposite phase to the centre tap.

cards.question: How is the immersion depth measured in the fuel quantity computer system
options: By a float and an LVDT at the tank units and the compensator
By travel time of a pulse at the tank units and the compensator
By capacity changes at the tank units and the compensator
cards.explain: Immersion depth is measured by capacity changes using the tank units and the compensator.

cards.question: Which two quantities does the cadensicon sensor measure separately for the computer
options: The density and the dielectric constant
The temperature and the specific gravity
The volume and the dielectric constant
cards.explain: The cadensicon measures density and dielectric constant separately.

cards.question: Which four items make up the fuel quantity indicating system that compensates fuel scatter
options: Tank units, a totaliser, a repeater and a compensator
Tank units, a computer, a densitometer and a water detector
Tank units, a computer, a cadensicon and a compensator
cards.explain: The system has tank units, a fuel quantity indicating computer, a cadensicon sensor and a compensator.

cards.question: A technician looks for the compensator inside a fuel tank, so where in the tank is it installed?
options: Near the highest point
At about mid height
Near the lowest point
cards.explain: The compensators are installed near to the lowest point of the tanks.

cards.question: Why is the amount of fuel carried indicated in units of weight
options: The tank capacity is certified in terms of weight
The energy available from the fuel depends on volume
The energy available from the fuel depends on weight
cards.explain: The energy present in the form of fuel is dependent on weight, so weight is indicated.

cards.question: What makes a direct weight indication of the fuel necessary on a large commercial aircraft
options: Fuel density is constant so the weight can be read straight from the volume
Fuel can be half the take-off weight and the approved weights need it
Fuel is always loaded by volume and the tank gauges are marked in litres only
cards.explain: Fuel can be up to one half of take-off weight, so direct weight indication is needed for the approved take-off and landing weights.

cards.question: The same number of litres of fuel is loaded on a very cold day and on a very hot day, so what differs between the two loads?
options: The weight on board
The dielectric constant of the fuel
The capacity of the empty tank
cards.explain: Volume and specific gravity change with temperature, so the same number of litres can differ by several tonnes.

cards.question: The fuel level in a tank alters, so what does the multi-tubular surface condenser in it do?
options: It changes its excitation frequency
It changes its capacity
It changes its resistance
cards.explain: The condenser changes its capacity depending on the level of fuel in the tank.

cards.question: What is the total capacity of the tank condenser made up of
options: The empty tank capacity minus the change from fuel displacing air
The change from fuel displacing air on its own
The empty tank capacity plus the change from fuel displacing air
cards.explain: Total capacity is the empty tank capacity plus the capacity change due to the displacement of air between the plates.

cards.question: What happens to the capacitance of a tank sensor as the tank fills with fuel
options: It stays constant
It increases
It decreases
cards.explain: Fuel has a dielectric strength more than twice that of air, so sensor capacitance rises with fuel content.

cards.question: A tank sensor has changed its capacitance as the tank filled, so where is that change used?
options: In a chopper circuit that gives a pulse train output
In a resolver circuit that gives a shaft angle output
In a bridge circuit that gives an amplified signal
cards.explain: The change in capacitance is used in a bridge circuit to provide an amplified signal.

cards.question: What does the amplified signal from the capacitance bridge act on
options: The shutoff valve in the refuelling gallery line
The pointer or the digital display
The excitation winding of the tank unit sensor
cards.explain: The amplified signal rotates the pointer or actuates the digital display in the indicator.

cards.question: What condition exists when the tank unit capacitance and the reference condenser capacitance are equal
options: Maximum current runs through the instrument
A current runs that drives the pointer to full
No current runs through the instrument
cards.explain: With equal capacitances the two currents compensate each other and nothing flows through the instrument.

cards.question: What is true of the two points across which the instrument is connected when the bridge is balanced
options: They are at the supply potential
They are at opposite electrical potential
They are at the same electrical potential
cards.explain: At balance the two points have the same electrical potential, so no current flows.

cards.question: What does the position of the potentiometer arm represent once the bridge has been rebalanced
options: The ratio of the two capacitance values
The sum of the two capacitance readings
The supply voltage applied to the bridge
cards.explain: The potentiometer arm position indicates the ratio of the two capacitance values.

cards.question: How is the capacitive bridge of a fuel quantity indicator rebalanced in service
options: Automatically, by amplifying the difference signal
Manually, by the crew turning a trimming knob
Automatically, by switching in reference condensers
cards.explain: Fuel quantity capacitive bridges are balanced automatically by amplifying the difference signal.

cards.question: The amplifier of a capacitive fuel gauge puts out a voltage, so what does that voltage drive?
options: A heater that trims the reference condenser
A solenoid that trips the warning flag
A motor that turns the potentiometer
cards.explain: The amplifier output voltage drives a motor which turns the potentiometer.

cards.question: Fuel is being burned off in flight and the gauge is following it down, so what brings the rebalancing motor to rest at each new reading?
options: The potentiometer reaching its end stop
The difference signal falling to zero
The amplifier output reaching its limit
cards.explain: The motor stops when the difference signal is zero.

cards.question: Why does the relationship between dielectric constant and density have to be corrected
options: It varies with the altitude the aircraft is flown at
It varies with the age of the tank units in the tank
It varies with the fuel consistency of each country
cards.explain: The ratio of K to D varies in accordance with fuel consistency in individual countries.

cards.question: How is the dielectric constant obtained inside a cadensicon sensor
options: From the travel time of an ultrasonic pulse
From the capacity change of a condenser
From the depth of immersion of a float
cards.explain: K is calculated from the capacity change of a condenser.

cards.question: How is the density obtained inside a cadensicon sensor
options: By a thermistor bridge sensing the fuel temperature
By a condenser whose capacity changes with the fuel
By a cardanically suspended float of fixed weight
cards.explain: D is found mechanically by a cardanically suspended float of predetermined weight.

cards.question: The cadensicon float has sunk to a certain depth in the fuel, so how is that depth turned into a signal for the computer?
options: By an LVDT
By a strain gauge
By a synchro resolver
cards.explain: The depth of immersion is measured by an LVDT and sent to the computer.

cards.question: How is density found in systems that damp a mass instead of floating one
options: From the force needed to hold the damped mass still
From the time the damped mass takes to come to rest
From the ratio of oscillations added to those removed
cards.explain: In those systems the ratio of oscillations added to oscillations removed determines density.

cards.question: What does the fuel quantity indicating computer work out from the probes it monitors
options: The density of fuel in the related tank
The volume of fuel in the related tank
The mass of fuel in the related tank
cards.explain: The computer uses signal conditioning on the probe signals to calculate the volume of fuel in the related tank.

cards.question: When does the cadensicon sensor take its measurements of K and D
options: As the engines are started
As the tank runs nearly empty
As fuel enters the tank
cards.explain: The cadensicon measures K and D separately as fuel enters the tank.

cards.question: In what form does the cadensicon deliver its two outputs to the computer
options: One electrical and one pneumatic
Both as electrical signals
Both as mechanical movements
cards.explain: Outputs K and D are both electrical signals.

cards.question: A cadensicon sensor measures two properties of the fuel, so which one of them is sensed mechanically?
options: The dielectric constant
The density
The temperature
cards.explain: K is measured electrically only while D is measured mechanically by a float.

cards.question: What is the fuel scatter effect
options: The K to D relationship is not constant between fuel samples
The K to D relationship alters as the fuel temperature changes
The capacitance of a probe drifts as the probe gets older
cards.explain: Fuel scatter is the phenomenon that the relationship of K to D between different fuel samples is not constant.

cards.question: The fuel in a tank warms up over a long flight, so what happens to the relationship between K and D?
options: It is pulled back onto the average law
It is not influenced by temperature
It changes in step with the fuel density
cards.explain: A change in temperature will not influence this relationship.

cards.question: Water has collected between the plates of a capacitance probe, so how does the probe capacitance compare with the same probe covered in fuel?
options: Slightly lower
The same
Much higher
cards.explain: Water is given a far larger dielectric constant than fuel, and the capacitance rises with the dielectric constant of whatever fills the probe.

cards.question: Water has collected in the bottom of a tank, so how would the quantity indication be affected?
options: It would read below the fuel actually present
It would stay at the correct reading
It would read above the fuel actually present
cards.explain: The capacitance follows the dielectric constant of what fills the probe, and water's is far above that of fuel, so the gauge reads more fuel than is there.

cards.question: Why is the capacity of a tank condenser compared with its capacity when the tank is empty
options: The difference corresponds to the quantity of fuel present
The difference corresponds to the temperature of the fuel
The difference corresponds to the dielectric constant of the fuel
cards.explain: The capacity above the empty tank value is the part caused by fuel, and that difference corresponds to the fuel quantity.

cards.question: What is gained by leaving the tank unit as the only variable in the bridge
options: A lower supply current to the bridge
A faster response of the indication
Greater precision of the indication
cards.explain: Having only the tank unit variable increases indicator precision.

cards.question: The aircraft is being refuelled and the level in a tank is rising, so what is happening at the master indicator?
options: Tank unit current falls and the indication moves downscale
Compensator current rises and the indication holds steady
Tank unit current rises and the indication moves upscale
cards.explain: A rising level raises the tank unit capacitance and current, and the quantity indicator moves upscale.

cards.question: Why does the indicator run downscale when the fuel quantity test switch is operated
options: The compensator current that normally drives it to full is missing
The supply to the rebalancing motor is reversed
The tank unit current that normally drives it to full is missing
cards.explain: Operating the test switch removes the tank unit current that normally moves the indicator towards FULL, so it runs downscale.

cards.question: The rebalancing motor of a capacitive gauge has just run to a stop, so what is true of the two bridge currents at that moment?
options: They are both at zero
They are equal
They are in opposite phase
cards.explain: The motor runs until the two currents are equal, and that is where it stops.

cards.question: The master indicator already shows the figure it has worked out, so how do the repeater and the fuel summation unit come to show the same?
options: The synchronising voltage is sent to them from the totaliser
The computed value is sent to them over the compensator line
The tank unit current is sent to them over the coaxial cable
cards.explain: The value shown on the master indicator is transmitted in a further circuit via the compensator line to the repeater and the fuel summation unit.

cards.question: How does the built-in test of the computerised system differ from the test started by the flight deck switch
options: One runs automatically and tests the displays, the other codes faults
One runs automatically and codes faults, the other tests the displays
One tests the displays, the other codes faults found on the ground only
cards.explain: The built-in test runs automatically and shows any fault as an error code, while the FQ test switch starts a display test of all indicators.

cards.question: A computerised fuel quantity indicator is showing an error code instead of a quantity, so which of the computer circuits produced it?
options: The one sending the signal out to the tank units
The one feeding the repeater and the summation unit
The one running the automatic system check
cards.explain: The error code comes from the separate circuit that runs the automatic system check by built-in test.

cards.question: A float sinks further in one fuel sample than in another of the same temperature, so what does that tell the computer?
options: That the two samples differ in dielectric constant
That the two samples differ in volume
That the two samples differ in density
cards.explain: The float of predetermined weight submerges in accordance with the density, so a deeper float means a different density.

cards.question: Refuelling has to stop before a tank overflows, so what is built into the fuel quantity computer system for this?
options: A totaliser that sums all of the master systems
A preselection of the wanted load with a shutoff
A trimming condenser at the cockpit indicator
cards.explain: The system integrates a preselection of the desired volume together with a shutoff on reaching it or shortly before overflowing.

cards.question: Why does the aircraft attitude matter to the preselection and shutoff function
options: The dielectric constant of the fuel depends on aircraft position
The point at which a tank overflows depends on aircraft position
The density measured by the float depends on aircraft position
cards.explain: Shutoff occurs on reaching the preselected value or shortly before overflowing, which depends on aircraft position.

cards.question: What does the computer derive from the cadensicon and compensator data it monitors
options: The density of the fuel in the tanks
The temperature of the fuel in the tanks
The volume of the fuel in the tanks
cards.explain: Cadensicon and compensator data are used to calculate the density of the fuel in the tanks.

cards.question: The probes alone can only tell the computer how much space the fuel fills, so what else must it have before a figure in kilograms can be shown?
options: The density of the fuel
The temperature of the fuel
The usable capacity of the tank
cards.explain: The computer needs both the volume and the fuel density before it can calculate the fuel mass.

cards.question: The outer tanks still hold fuel from the previous flight when fresh fuel is loaded, so how does the computer handle the mixture?
options: It applies the values of the fresh fuel to both quantities
It ignores the old fuel until that tank has been emptied
It calculates a mean value from the old and the new fuel
cards.explain: The computer can calculate a mean value from the remaining fuel and the replenished fuel.

cards.question: Why can fuel taken on at two different airports upset the quantity indication unless the computer allows for it
options: The two loads can have different K to D values
The two loads can have different fuel temperatures
The two loads can have different tank unit capacitances
cards.explain: Fuel consistency differs between countries, so the remaining and replenished fuel can have different K to D values that the computer has to average.

cards.question: In a liquid level metering system that works by timing an echo, which kind of signal do the tank units transmit
options: An ultrasonic signal
A radio frequency signal
A light signal
cards.explain: The tank units transmit an ultrasonic signal.

cards.question: A tank of an ultrasonic system is opened for inspection, so how many tank units will be found in it?
options: A single unit
Numerous units
Exactly two units
cards.explain: Each tank contains numerous tank units.

cards.question: A technician surveys an ultrasonic fuel tank installation, so how many densitometers will each tank have?
options: Two
One for every tank unit
One
cards.explain: Each fuel tank has one densitometer.

cards.question: Where are the water detectors fitted
options: At the low point in each fuel tank
In the refuelling gallery pipework
At the highest point of each fuel tank
cards.explain: Water detectors are at the low point in each fuel tank.

cards.question: On which kind of quantity measuring system is the GF-2 fuel tester used
options: Ultrasonic measuring systems
Float operated gauging systems
Capacitance measuring systems
cards.explain: The tester is used for capacitance measuring systems for fuel and oil.

cards.question: Where is the signal sent out by an ultrasonic tank unit reflected
options: At the surface of the liquid
At the bottom of the tank sump
At the wall of the stillwell tube
cards.explain: The signal is reflected at the surface of the liquid.

cards.question: What picks up the echo in an ultrasonic quantity metering system
options: A separate receiver at the tank top
The tank unit that sent the signal
The compensator near the tank bottom
cards.explain: The same tank unit that transmits also receives the echo.

cards.question: A computer has received the echo from an ultrasonic tank unit, so what does it use to find the liquid level?
options: The frequency shift of the returned echo
The running time of the signal
The strength of the returned echo
cards.explain: The computer calculates the liquid level from the running time of the signal.

cards.question: What does the fuel quantity processor unit measure in order to find the fuel height
options: The travel time of the pulse
The frequency of the returned pulse
The strength of the returned pulse
cards.explain: The processor unit measures the travel time of the pulse and uses it to find the fuel height.

cards.question: What does the sonic pulse travel through on its way to the fuel surface
options: The fuel in the stillwell
The wall of the tank unit
The air space above the fuel
cards.explain: The pulse goes through the fuel in the stillwell to the fuel surface and back to the receiver.

cards.question: Some tank units also carry calibration targets, so what does the processor unit get from the pulses that come back off them?
options: The depth of water in the tank sump
The density of the fuel in the tank
The velocity of sound in the fuel
